text: Enterprise AI, Agents & Applied ML A practical book for moving from enterprise AI delivery and backend platform foundations into agent protocols, applied machine learning, deep learning, LLM fine‑tuning, and alignment. It is organized as a sequence of small-to-large examples: first the mental model, then the implementation pattern, then the production tradeoffs. 6 parts · 54 chapters + companion labs · delivery, platform, agents, ML, deep learning, and reference material Reading guide and concept map Delivery / Lead path Backend & platform path Agent systems path ML foundations path Deep learning & LLM path Appendices Book-wide concept map The concept map explains how the parts fit together, which chapters provide the primary explanation for each major concept, and where later chapters revisit the same idea as an implementation, enterprise, or reference view. How to read this book The book has six parts. They are presented in the order an enterprise team usually encounters them — delivery first, then platform, then agents, then the ML/DL fundamentals that power them. If you are a new learner, you almost certainly want to read the parts in a different order. Pick the path that matches your role: New to ML or just learning the field Part IV — ML Foundations (PyTorch, regression, classification, trees) Part V — Deep Learning & LLMs in order: FFN → CNN → RNN → Transformers → fine‑tuning → alignment Part III — Agent Protocols once you understand what an LLM is Part II and Part I when you start shipping Backend / platform engineer learning AI Part II chapters 1–6 (FastAPI, Pydantic contracts, concurrency, background work) — already familiar territory Part II chapters 7–16 for the auth + identity + multi‑tenancy stack Part III end‑to‑end (MCP → A2A → LangChain) Spot‑read Transformers (Part V Ch. 11), fine‑tuning (Ch. 12), and alignment (Ch. 13) Part I when you take your first AI project to production Lead / Principal AI engineer or architect Part I end‑to‑end (delivery lifecycle) Part II Ch. 7–16 for the auth/identity story you'll review Part III for protocol‑level vocabulary in design reviews Transformers, fine‑tuning, alignment as conceptual reference Appendix A for a 60‑minute narrative covering all of the above Preparing for a Lead DS / Lead AI interview Appendix A — Lead DS interview talk track (start here) Drill the delivery lifecycle and auth deep‑dive Be able to whiteboard attention and explain the difference between SFT/PEFT/DPO and ORPO/GRPO/KTO Reading the book front‑to‑back is also valid — it tells the story from the business side inward. Just be aware that Part III assumes Part II Ch. 1–3, and Part V assumes Part IV. part-i · delivery-leadership Part I — Enterprise AI Delivery Lifecycle From a business pain point to a shipped pilot: intake, response, kickoff, HLD/LLD, architecture review, provisioning, and scale. From business pain to AI lead The intake package AI lead response document Pilot kickoff meeting Seven days after kickoff Architecture reference design HLD and service selection After HLD: next steps Architecture review HLD → LLD & sprint plan Provisioning, services, scale part-ii · platform-engineering Part II — Backend, Platform & Security FastAPI fundamentals, Pydantic data contracts, concurrency & user isolation, background work, the full auth stack (OIDC/OAuth2/PKCE/JWT), workload identity, multi‑tenancy, external integrations, GitHub governance, and modern auth additions (Passkeys/WebAuthn, DPoP, mTLS). FastAPI & Uvicorn basics HTTP methods FastAPI request mapping Pydantic data models Concurrency & user isolation Background tasks & retries SSO / OAuth2 / OIDC primer OIDC + OAuth2 + PKCE in FastAPI Registering new users Authentication deep dive Modern auth additions (Passkeys, DPoP, mTLS) End‑user vs workload identity Tenant isolation, IAM & AD groups GCP workload identity External service integration GitHub governance & CI part-iii · agents-mcp-a2a Part III — Agent Protocols & Integration MCP from first principles through the enterprise pattern and its 2025-to-2026 protocol evolution, A2A 1.0 for multi-agent collaboration, plus a JS/TS primer and the LangChain → LangGraph → Flowise journey. MCP fundamentals MCP discovery, remote & auth MCP enterprise pattern MCP protocol evolution: 2025 foundations to the 2026 stateless core A2A protocol 1.0 JavaScript & TypeScript primer LangChain → LangGraph → Flowise part-iv · classical-ml Part IV — ML Foundations The geometric view of ML, linear regression and classification in PyTorch, and the tree/ensemble family (Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost). PyTorch foundations ML as geometry Linear regression Linear classification Trees, bagging & boosting part-v · neural-nets-llms Part V — Deep Learning & LLMs From the single neuron to feed‑forward nets, CNNs, sequence models, and into Transformers, LLM fine‑tuning, and modern alignment methods such as ORPO, GRPO, and KTO. FFN concepts FFN training & debugging FFN single-chapter reference CNN — convolution CNN — architecture CNN — PyTorch implementation CNN — dropout & train/eval Forecasting & sequence data Autoregressive linear model Companion lab: animated RNN walkthrough Recurrent neural networks Transformers & attention LLM fine‑tuning Modern LLM alignment: ORPO, GRPO, KTO part-vi · reference Part VI — Appendices Lead Data Science interview talk track and the LaTeX print edition of the classification chapter. description: This page is the book-level map. It explains the main spine of the book, where each concept is introduced, and where the same idea is revisited from an implementation, architecture, enterprise, or reference angle. Rep...
text: This page is the book-level map. It explains the main spine of the book, where each concept is introduced, and where the same idea is revisited from an implementation, architecture, enterprise, or reference angle. Repetition is intentional when it helps a reader move from first intuition to production practice. How to use this map For each major concept, start with the primary chapter, then follow the related chapters when you want a second angle: a beginner introduction, an applied implementation, an enterprise design pattern, or a reference edition. Book Spine Part Primary purpose How to read it Part I Enterprise AI delivery lifecycle: intake, kickoff, HLD, architecture review, LLD, sprint planning, provisioning, and scale. Read as a process story. Repeated roles, artifacts, and gates are intentional lifecycle continuity. Part II Backend runtime, HTTP/FastAPI mechanics, Pydantic data contracts, authentication, identity, tenancy, workload identity, external integrations, and governance. Read in four blocks: runtime basics, Pydantic data boundaries, auth identity, then tenancy/IAM/GCP implementation. Part III Agent protocol integration: MCP fundamentals, remote/auth/enterprise patterns, 2025-to-2026 evolution, A2A 1.0, JS/TS, and LangChain/LangGraph/Flowise. Read the MCP chapters together, then A2A as the separate agent-to-agent delegation protocol. Part IV Classical ML foundations: PyTorch, geometry, regression, classification, trees, bagging, boosting, and XGBoost. Read before Part V. Regression and classification share the same training workflow but differ in target, output, and loss. Part V Deep learning and LLM track: FFNs, CNNs, forecasting, RNNs, Transformers, fine-tuning, and alignment. Read by cluster: FFN, CNN, sequence models, then LLMs. Part VI Supporting references: interview talk track and print-oriented classification source. Use as review material or a printable companion. Concept Map Concept cluster Primary chapter Related chapters and why they revisit it Enterprise delivery artifacts, roles, gates, and decision flow Part I Ch. 5 for the post-kickoff document pack; Ch. 10 for sprint conversion. Ch. 1-4 introduce the same people and artifacts from intake and kickoff. Ch. 6-11 reuse them during architecture, review, implementation, and provisioning. HTTP and FastAPI request handling Part II Ch. 3 Ch. 1 introduces FastAPI/Uvicorn and briefly names methods. Ch. 2 owns HTTP verb semantics. Ch. 3 owns the exact mapping from raw HTTP to FastAPI function arguments. Pydantic data modeling, dataclass bridge, validation, serialization, settings, aliases, and LLM output contracts Part II Ch. 4 Ch. 3 introduces Pydantic through a FastAPI request body. Ch. 4 gives the full explanation from Python classes/dataclasses through production API, settings, queue, and LLM validation patterns. OAuth2, OIDC, PKCE, bearer tokens, JWTs, opaque tokens, and API keys Part II Ch. 10 Ch. 7 is the beginner primer, Ch. 8 is the FastAPI implementation, Ch. 9 is user bootstrap, and Ch. 11 adds modern sender-constrained and passwordless patterns. MCP auth chapters reference this theory instead of redefining it. End-user identity, tenant isolation, IAM, AD/Workspace groups, and workload identity Part II Ch. 12 Ch. 13 applies the same three-lane model to AD groups and bootstrap policy. Ch. 14 implements it on GCP. Part I Ch. 6-7 mention it only at architecture-decision level. MCP mental model, resources, prompts, tools, discovery, remote servers, and auth Part III Ch. 2 Ch. 1 is the first-principles local database example. Ch. 3 applies MCP to an enterprise Salesforce pattern. Ch. 4 preserves the 2025 foundation and maps it to the current stateless core. A2A 1.0 in Ch. 5 is deliberately separate: inter-agent delegation, not host-to-tool integration. Classical ML workflow: features, target, model, loss, optimizer, fit/predict/score Part IV Ch. 2 Ch. 3 instantiates the workflow for numeric regression. Ch. 4 instantiates it for classification with logits, sigmoid/softmax, and accuracy. Ch. 5 branches to trees and ensembles for tabular baselines. Feed-forward neural networks, neurons, activations, backprop, batching, and debugging Part V Ch. 1 and Ch. 2 Ch. 3 is the optional single-chapter reference edition. It repeats the same concepts in one article for print/reference use. CNN convolution, feature maps, pooling, implementation, dropout, and train/eval behavior Part V Ch. 4 through Ch. 6 Ch. 7 expands the short dropout and train/eval section from Ch. 6 into a full conceptual and coding deep dive. Sequence forecasting, autoregressive windows, leakage, recursion, RNNs, and Transformers Part V Ch. 8 Ch. 9 implements the autoregressive linear baseline. Ch. 10 replaces a fixed window with recurrent state, builds from vanilla RNN into GRU/LSTM gates, then uses encoder-decoder translation to show tokens, embeddings, padding, teacher forcing, and autoregressive decoding. Ch. 11 builds from that translation model into cross-attention, self-attention, causal masking, and GPT generation. LLM adaptation, SFT, PEFT, LoRA/QLoRA, DPO/RLHF, ORPO, KTO, GRPO, RLAIF Part V Ch. 12 for adaptation; Ch. 13 for alignment comparison. Ch. 12 introduces SFT/PEFT and first-generation preference methods. Ch. 13 deliberately repeats the DPO/RLHF baseline only to compare newer alignment methods in one decision framework. Cross-Referenced Concept Clusters Related pages How to read them Part II Ch. 12 and Ch. 13: tenant identity, IAM, group gating. Ch. 12 owns the three-lane model. Ch. 13 is the applied policy/bootstrap chapter. Part III Ch. 1, Ch. 2, Ch. 3, and Ch. 4: MCP resources/prompts/tools, discovery, remote servers, auth, and enterprise patterns. Ch. 2 owns the full technical model. Ch. 1 remains the beginner example, Ch. 3 the enterprise pattern, and Ch. 4 the 2025-to-2026 protocol evolution. Part V Ch. 1, Ch. 2, and Ch. 3: FFN concepts, training, batching, backprop, and debugging. Ch. 1-2 are the teaching path. Ch. 3 is an optional single-article reference edition. Part V Ch. 6 and Ch. 7: dropout and train/eval behavior in CNN code. Ch. 6 introduces the implementation requirement. Ch. 7 is the detailed behavior chapter. Part V Ch. 12 and Ch. 13: DPO, RLHF, preference data, and alignment objectives. Ch. 12 introduces adaptation and earlier alignment methods. Ch. 13 owns the modern comparison across ORPO, KTO, GRPO, RLAIF, and PPO-style RLHF. Part IV Ch. 3 and Ch. 4: training loops, loss, optimizer, and evaluation. The shared workflow is intentional. Ch. 3 is regression; Ch. 4 is classification and changes target type, activation, loss, and metric. Page-by-Page Map Part I - Enterprise AI Delivery Lifecycle ChapterRole in the book 1. text: This part walks the entire lifecycle of an enterprise AI initiative — from a business unit raising a pain point, through the lead AI engineer's intake and response, kickoff, the seven days that follow, the High‑Level Design and its review, the LLD & sprint plan, and the provisioning realities of running on a real cloud platform. Who this part is for Lead / Principal AI engineers, AI program managers, architects who need a reproducible playbook for getting from “we have a pain point” to “the pilot is in production.” Prerequisites None for the lifecycle narrative itself. Chapters 6–7 (architecture, HLD/service selection) refer to FastAPI, OIDC, multi‑tenancy, and GCP — the relevant deep dives live in Part II. You can read this part end‑to‑end first and dip into Part II as needed. Lifecycle ownership map Chapters 1–4 establish the same roles, pain point, scope, and sponsor vocabulary from intake through kickoff. Chapter 5 is the canonical post-kickoff operating map. Chapters 6–11 then reuse those artifacts during architecture, service selection, review, LLD, sprint planning, and provisioning. The repetition is deliberate continuity: the same enterprise artifacts mature as the project moves from idea to build. Chapters in order From business pain point to AI lead — roles, BUs, the typical flow. The intake package — what should arrive on the lead AI engineer's desk on day 1. AI lead response document — exec summary, scope, metrics, controls, risks, asks. Pilot kickoff meeting — why, who, agenda, the 3 non‑negotiable decisions. Seven days after kickoff — day‑by‑day playbook + document pack. Architecture reference design — React, FastAPI, OIDC, multi‑tenancy. HLD & service selection — concrete GCP service choices, alternatives, enterprise delays. After HLD: next steps — what changes, what you produce, up‑managing. Architecture review — agenda, prep, capturing approval conditions. HLD → LLD & sprint plan — epics, vertical slice, story slicing, team shape. Provisioning, services, scale — tickets, latency, 1000s of users.

description: This is a practical, beginner-friendly guide to how an AI use case typically originates and travels through a large enterprise (e.g., a major bank or a national airline) until it lands with a Lead AI Engineer. It also...
text: This is a practical, beginner-friendly guide to how an AI use case typically originates and travels through a large enterprise (e.g., a major bank or a national airline) until it lands with a Lead AI Engineer. It also explains common roles: EA, Ops, EM, GM, and Business Units (BUs). Big picture Roles glossary What a BU is The end-to-end flow Concrete example What arrives to the AI lead What the AI lead does on day 1 1) Big picture In large enterprises, AI work rarely begins with “let’s build an LLM.” It begins with: a business pain → a formal initiative → governance and triage → delivery ownership. Key idea: The “AI lead” is usually brought in once the problem needs cross-system design (identity, data access, retrieval, model, audit), not when someone has a vague idea. 2) Roles glossary (who is who) Titles vary by company; these are typical meanings in Australia-based enterprises. Role What they do Why they matter to the AI project EA (Executive Assistant) Supports an executive: calendars, meetings, packs, minutes, action items, briefings. Often the “workflow owner” for meeting artifacts and “what was decided.” EAs are often power users who can define the top recurring questions and what “proof” looks like (citations, links, timestamps). They validate whether the tool saves real time. Ops (Operations) “Run the business day-to-day.” In airlines, this can include operations control/disruption recovery. In banks, business ops, service ops, incident/change, compliance operations, etc. Ops stakeholders define urgency, failure tolerance, and what a “wrong answer” costs. They will demand reliability, speed, and auditability. SME (Subject Matter Expert) Domain expert in policy/process/operations. Knows the right sources and interpretations. Provides ground truth for evaluation sets, validation of answers, and “what’s allowed” guidance. Business Owner Accountable for business outcomes: scope, priorities, success metrics, adoption. Often the person who “accepts” the product for business use. Without a business owner, pilots often become demos with no adoption. This person drives change management. Sponsor Senior executive champion who removes blockers and provides authority (and often budget). Helps secure access approvals, resolves conflicts, and unlocks resources. EM (Engineering Manager) Manages engineering team delivery: staffing, planning, quality, execution, career support. Partner to the AI lead: ensures team capacity, delivery cadence, and operational readiness. GM (General Manager) Senior leader for a function or business line (e.g., GM Digital, GM Operations, GM Data/AI). Owns strategy, budget, and high-level outcomes. Often the decision-maker who approves the initiative and sets constraints (risk appetite, pilot group, timelines). Security / IAM Defines identity, access control, least privilege, secrets handling, network requirements. AI projects fail without secure-by-design access to data sources and proper audit controls. Privacy / Legal / Risk Ensures compliance obligations are met (PII, retention, audit, customer data restrictions). Defines what data the model can see and under what controls; reviews release readiness. Data Owner Accountable for a dataset/document corpus (approves access, usage, retention). Approves what documents you can ingest and how you classify/store them. Lead AI Engineer Designs and delivers production AI systems end-to-end: data → retrieval → model → evaluation → ops. Converts vague ideas into an executable plan with guardrails, metrics, and reliable delivery. 3) What is a BU (Business Unit) and why does it matter? A Business Unit (BU) is a major organisational division that owns a slice of the business: its goals, processes, teams, data, and budgets. Examples (varies by company): Airline BU examples: Network Ops, Customer Experience, Digital, Loyalty, Revenue Management Bank BU examples: Retail Banking, Business Banking, Wealth, Risk, Technology, Operations Why BUs matter for your tool: BUs often have different data owners and different risk appetite. They may require different access boundaries (who can see what documents). Funding and sponsorship often comes from a specific BU. Practical: Many initiatives start in one BU (pilot), then expand cross-BU if proven safe and valuable. 4) The typical flow: pain point → AI lead This is the “enterprise conveyor belt” a use case rides before it becomes a real build. Pain felt in BU → Quantified by EA/Ops/SME → BU manager/GM sponsorship → Brief written → AI/Architecture intake gate → Security/Privacy triage → Routed to AI delivery team → Lead AI Engineer owns plan Step 1 — Pain point appears inside a BU It shows up as a workflow problem, not “AI”: Time loss: execs/EAs searching meeting notes/packs/emails Decision friction: hard to reconstruct “who said what and when” Operational risk: staff can’t find latest approved guidance during incidents Customer impact: frontline teams can’t find policy answers quickly The BU feels it because it directly impacts throughput and outcomes. Step 2 — Someone makes it real (EA/Ops/Compliance) This is the trigger point. Typical voices: EA: “We spend 5–10 hours/week per exec chasing meeting artifacts and compiling answers.” Ops: “During disruptions/incidents, information retrieval is the bottleneck.” Risk/Compliance: “We spend days reconstructing evidence and decision trails.” Why EAs matter: they live inside the executive workflow and define what “useful output” looks like. Why Ops matters: they define urgency and what “wrong answer” costs. Step 3 — The BU converts pain into an initiative The BU manager or GM (often with a sponsor) decides: “this is worth pursuing.” It becomes: a roadmap item (internal product) a transformation initiative (knowledge management / AI uplift) a risk/governance program (auditability) an ops improvement effort (incident response) A short brief is drafted: problem, users, constraints, desired outcome, rough ROI. Step 4 — AI intake / architecture / governance triage Enterprises run gate checks before they invest: Is it actually AI, or should we fix search/metadata/source systems first? Do we have data access rights and clear data ownership? What is the sensitivity classification (PII, strategy, HR)? What’s the failure risk (wrong answers) and what controls are required? Can success be measured? Common outcome: “Pilot only” with a tightly approved corpus and strict access controls. Step 5 — Work is routed to delivery (AI lead gets it) Now it lands as an actionable request, usually with constraints like: “We need citations and audit logs.” “Access must be restricted by user / business unit / group membership.” “We must meet security/privacy controls.” The AI lead gets it because it spans identity, ingestion, retrieval, model behavior, evaluation, and operations. 5) Concrete example (meeting-note Q&A) Problem: Exec asks “What did Chandima mention about no meeting on 1 Dec?” Current state: EA manually searches packs/minutes/emails and compiles a reply. Desired state: tool returns: short answer citation: exact snippet from the 1 Dec meeting note + link safe behavior: if not found, say so and suggest next best query EA success signal: “I can copy/paste this to the exec and it has evidence.” Ops success signal: “It’s fast, reliable, and never guesses when evidence is missing.” 6) What arrives on the AI lead’s desk (typical package) Brief: the business problem, users, constraints Sponsor: a GM or senior leader backing it Business owner: accountable for adoption and success metrics Data owners: who approves the corpus (meeting notes/packs) Security/privacy constraints: what must be enforced At this stage, the AI lead is expected to turn this into: scope, architecture, pilot plan, eval plan, and operating model. 7) What the Lead AI Engineer does on day 1 Day 1 outputs (what “lead-level” looks like) Problem reframing: “Cited Q&A over approved meeting corpus, scoped by identity.” MVP slice: one BU/corpus + top 1–2 question types Access model: who can see what (group gating + document corpus allowlist) Success metrics: citation correctness, groundedness, time saved Evaluation plan: a “golden set” of questions + release gates Delivery plan: team lanes + dependencies + timeline Key lead move: co-design with EAs and Ops early. They define workflow reality and failure tolerance. Companion artifacts The working pack for this stage should include (1) a stakeholder map for EA, Operations, Security, Privacy, the Data Owner, and the GM, including each role's concerns and common objections, and (2) a sample intake brief plus AI lead response document for the meeting-notes Q&A pilot.

text: This HTML tutorial is designed for future Lead AI Engineers in large enterprises (banks/airlines). It describes the typical “package” you receive when a business use case is ready to become a real AI delivery. The goal is to help you quickly assess readiness, risks, and your day-1 actions. Why this package exists What you should receive Who the people are Red flags & missing pieces What you do on day 1 Copy/paste intake template 1) Why an “intake package” exists In an enterprise, “AI requests” are filtered through governance (security/privacy/risk/architecture) so delivery teams don’t start with a vague idea. When the request reaches you, it should already have: a defined business problem an owner accountable for outcomes approved or approvable data sources constraints (privacy/security/audit) made explicit Lead-level expectation: you convert the package into scope, architecture, evaluation gates, operating model, and a pilot plan — not “build a demo.” 2) What you should receive (the “minimum viable intake”) If you don’t receive these, ask for them immediately. You can still proceed in discovery mode, but you should treat it as “not ready for build.” Business brief problem statement (“what hurts”) users + workflow (who does what today) example questions/tasks success metrics (time saved, accuracy, adoption) Ownership Sponsor (senior leader who backs it) Business owner (accountable for outcomes + adoption) named representatives: EA + Ops + SME Data scope which sources (Drive/SharePoint/Confluence/email/transcripts) who the data owner is for each source what is in-scope vs out-of-scope data sensitivity classification (PII/confidential/etc.) Constraints & controls access control expectations (“who can see what”) audit/logging requirements privacy requirements (PII handling, retention) risk tolerance: “what happens if it’s wrong?” Delivery expectations pilot cohort size and timeline support model (who owns it after launch) non-functional requirements: latency, uptime Approvals / gates security/IAM contact for approvals privacy/legal/risk contact if needed architecture review process (if required) 3) Who the people are (and what you should expect from them) Role What they provide in the intake What you should ask them Sponsor (often GM-level) Authority, budget influence, unblock access issues, approve pilot scope “What’s the business outcome, and how will we measure success?” Business owner Accountability for adoption, priorities, and acceptance criteria “Which workflows are must-have for pilot? What is the rollout plan?” EA (Executive Assistant) Real workflow + top recurring exec questions + acceptable answer format “What does ‘proof’ look like? Link/snippet/timestamp? What’s the top 20 questions?” Ops (Operations) Urgency constraints + failure tolerance + what “wrong answer” costs “When it’s wrong, what’s the impact? When it’s missing, how should it behave?” SME (Subject Matter Expert) Ground truth interpretations + what docs matter + evaluation support “What sources are authoritative? What are common ambiguous cases?” Data owner Approval for access, usage, retention, classification rules “What is allowed to be ingested? Any exclusions? How should retention work?” Security/IAM Access model constraints, least privilege guidance, secrets/network expectations “What’s the approved pattern for identity, service accounts, and audit logging?” Privacy/Legal/Risk PII/regulated-data constraints, release conditions, policy compliance “What data can leave the boundary? What redaction/logging rules apply?” EM (Engineering Manager) Resourcing, delivery cadence, quality bar, operational ownership “What’s the team capacity and what must we trade off to hit pilot?” Quick reminder: “EA” and “Ops” are not merely “stakeholders.” They often define the workflow reality and the acceptable output format. If you skip them, you risk building something that demos well but doesn’t get used. 4) Red flags (signals the intake is not ready) No business owner: nobody accountable for adoption → high risk of “demo only.” No data owner identified: access will stall later. Unbounded scope: “search all documents in the company” on day 1 → push back to a pilot corpus. No success metric: you can’t prove impact → define baseline and targets. No risk statement: “wrong answers are fine” is rarely true in enterprise. No access model: unclear whether users have different document permissions. Hard stop pattern: If they want “free-form Q&A over everything” without citations, auditing, or access control, you should reframe to a safe pilot first. 5) What you do on day 1 (as Lead AI Engineer) Your day-1 goal Turn the intake package into a delivery-ready plan with measurable outcomes and safety controls. Day-1 outputs (typical) Problem reframing into a single sentence that implies controls (e.g., “cited answers over approved corpus”). MVP definition: one BU, one corpus, 1–2 question patterns. Evaluation plan: a golden set of 30–50 questions + citation correctness rubric. Risk register: cross-user leakage, hallucinations, sensitive data exposure, adoption failure. Architecture sketch: ingestion → canonical store → retrieval → LLM → citations → audit log. Team plan: lanes (ingestion, backend/security, retrieval/LLM/eval) + owners + sprint goals. Lead-level move: schedule a co-design session with EAs and Ops within week 1. Ask them for the top recurring questions and define “acceptable evidence.” 6) Copy/paste template: “What I expect to receive” You can copy/paste this into an email/Confluence page and use it as your standard intake checklist. 6.1 Intake summary Problem statement: … BU / business area: … Users: … Top 5 user questions/tasks: … 6.2 Ownership Sponsor: … Business owner: … EA representative: … Ops representative: … SME: … 6.3 Data scope Sources: … Data owners: … Classification: … Out of scope: … 6.4 Constraints & controls Access control model: … Audit/logging requirements: … Privacy requirements (PII): … Failure tolerance: … 6.5 Success criteria Business metrics: … Quality metrics: … Operational metrics: … 6.6 Delivery expectations Pilot cohort: … Timeline: … Support model: … Approvals needed: … Rule of thumb: If you can’t fill these fields, you’re still in discovery, not delivery. Want a realistic example filled out (meeting notes Q&A for execs)? Tell me whether the documents are in Drive, SharePoint, Confluence, email, or transcripts and I’ll generate a completed intake package.

description: This document is the typical Lead AI Engineer output after receiving a business intake brief. It turns “we want an LLM tool for docs” into a delivery-ready plan: scope, safety, evaluation, architecture, and a pilot ro...
text: This document is the typical Lead AI Engineer output after receiving a business intake brief. It turns “we want an LLM tool for docs” into a delivery-ready plan: scope, safety, evaluation, architecture, and a pilot roadmap. The example context is an Executive Document Q&A assistant (meeting notes/packs) that returns cited answers. Initiative Executive Document Intelligence (Meeting Notes/Packs) — Pilot Owner Lead AI Engineer (delivery) + Business Owner (outcome/adoption) Target Users Execs + EAs (Executive Assistants); optionally Ops leadership Core Promise Fast, grounded answers with citations over an approved corpus, with strict access control. Summary Target workflow Pilot scope Success metrics Safety & controls Architecture Evaluation plan Operations Team plan & timeline Risks & mitigations Dependencies / asks 1) Executive summary We will deliver a pilot assistant that answers natural-language questions over approved meeting notes/packs and returns grounded answers with citations (source link + excerpt; timestamp if transcript exists). The pilot is intentionally narrow: one controlled corpus, one exec cohort, and a small set of question patterns. This ensures we can meet enterprise requirements: access control, auditability, safe failure behavior, and measurable impact. Pilot objective: reduce EA time spent searching/compiling answers, while keeping answers provably grounded and access-controlled. 2) Target workflow (validated with EA + Ops) Why EA and Ops are first-class stakeholders EA (Executive Assistant): owns the exec workflow (meeting packs, minutes, action logs). Defines “usable output” and proof format. Ops (Operations): cares about speed, reliability, and failure tolerance. Defines “what goes wrong if the answer is wrong.” Primary user story (pilot) “As an executive (or EA supporting an exec), I ask: What did Chandima mention about no meeting on 1 Dec? and receive a short answer plus citations to the exact source text.” Response contract Answer: 2–6 sentences Citations: document title + link + quoted excerpt (and timestamp if applicable) Safe failure: if evidence isn’t found, respond “not found” and suggest next-best queries EA acceptance test: “I can copy/paste the answer into a briefing email and it includes proof.” Ops acceptance test: “It doesn’t guess when evidence is missing; it fails safely.” 3) Pilot scope (smallest safe slice) In scope One exec cohort (e.g., 5–10 execs + their EAs) One approved corpus (e.g., one recurring meeting series) Question patterns: “Who said what, when” (speaker + date + topic) “What was agreed / actioned” (initially via cited retrieval; structured extraction later) Audited Q&A with citations Out of scope (pilot) Searching all enterprise docs across all BUs Write-back actions (auto-email, auto-ticketing) Customer PII-heavy corpora (unless explicitly approved for a later phase) Scope guardrail: “All docs in the company” is a phase-2 ambition, not a phase-1 pilot. 4) Success metrics (business + quality + operations) Business impact EA time saved per exec per week (baseline + post-pilot measurement) Time-to-answer for top recurring questions (before/after) User adoption: weekly active users in pilot group Quality Citation correctness: cited doc/chunk actually supports the answer Groundedness: answer statements are supported by retrieved context Refusal correctness: says “not found” when evidence is insufficient Operational Latency P50/P95 (target defined with business; typical: a few seconds) Error rate and dependency health (retrieval, model, ingestion freshness) Cost per question (LLM tokens + retrieval cost) 5) Safety & controls (enterprise non-negotiables) Access control (who can see what) Users authenticate via SSO (e.g., Google Workspace) Group gate: only users in an approved org group can access the tool Corpus gate: retrieval is limited to document sets approved by data owners Per-request audit log: who asked, what sources were used, and when Model safety behavior Require citations for all factual claims Refuse if insufficient evidence Minimize context sent to the LLM (only retrieved snippets) Principle: “If you can’t cite it, you can’t say it.” 6) Architecture (high level) Ingestion path Fetch approved documents/transcripts Extract canonical text + metadata (meeting date, title, participants/speaker if available, source link) Store canonical text + metadata as system-of-record Build retrieval index that supports semantic search + strict filters (date/speaker/corpus) Query path User asks a question Verify identity and authorization (group + corpus) Retrieve relevant chunks (with strict filters) Generate answer using retrieved context only Return answer + citations; write audit log User → (SSO) → API → retrieve (filtered) → LLM (context only) → answer + citations → audit log 7) Evaluation plan (how we avoid “demo success”) Golden set (week 1) Collect 30–50 real questions from EAs/Ops For each question, identify expected source doc(s) Define scoring rubric: citation correctness groundedness refusal correctness Release gates Minimum citation correctness on sampled set No cross-user/cross-corpus leakage in tests Acceptable latency/cost for pilot cohort Why this matters: enterprises ship what they can measure and defend. “Looks good in a demo” is not a release criterion. 8) Operations & support model Observability Metrics: latency, error rate, token usage, retrieval hit rate Logs: request audit trail, citation trace, dependency errors Alerting: dependency outages, cost anomalies, ingestion failures Runbook essentials How to diagnose “wrong answer” reports (check citations + retrieved chunks) How to handle “not found” (ingestion freshness, metadata coverage) How to disable a corpus quickly if misconfigured 9) Team plan & timeline (example for a 5-person team) Work lanes Lane Owner Key deliverables Ingestion & metadata 2 engineers connectors, extraction, incremental sync, canonical schema Backend & security 2 engineers SSO validation, group/corpus gating, audit logs, API endpoints Retrieval/LLM & eval 1 engineer + AI lead chunking, filters, prompting, citation formatting, eval harness Milestone sketch Week 1: stakeholder workshop (EA/Ops), golden set, schema, first ingestion slice Week 2: retrieval + citations prototype, baseline eval Week 3–4: harden access control, improve retrieval/prompting, expand golden set Week 5–6: pilot rollout, monitoring, feedback loop, measured outcomes 10) Risks & mitigations Risk Why it matters Mitigation Cross-user / cross-corpus leakage Severe privacy breach Strict gating + tests + audit logs; limit pilot corpus Hallucinated answers Loss of trust; governance risk Citations required; refuse if insufficient evidence; eval gates Sensitive data exposure to model provider Compliance & privacy exposure Send minimal retrieved context; redaction rules; approved corpora only Low adoption “Demo trap” Co-design with EA; output format matches briefings; weekly feedback loop Source documents are messy Retrieval fails without metadata Define canonical schema; enrich metadata; iterate on chunking 11) Dependencies / asks (what I need to proceed) Named pilot cohort + business owner confirmation Document source list + data owner sign-off for pilot corpus Security/IAM contacts to confirm approved patterns EA and Ops representatives for weekly co-design and acceptance testing Agreement on pilot success metrics and how we will measure them Next step: schedule a 60–90 minute workshop with the EA rep + Ops rep + Business owner to finalize: (1) top questions, (2) “proof format,” (3) corpus boundaries, and (4) baseline measurement plan. Optional appendices you can add for real enterprise rollout: A) Data classification & retention rules, B) release checklist, C) incident response plan, D) cost/FinOps policy.

7) Outputs you produce after the meeting (within 24–48 hours)
8) Common failure modes (and how to avoid them)
description: This tutorial explains the kickoff meeting that happens right after the AI Lead submits the “AI Lead Response Doc”. The example is your Executive Document Q&A tool (meeting notes/packs → cited answers). The purpose of...
text: This tutorial explains the kickoff meeting that happens right after the AI Lead submits the “AI Lead Response Doc”. The example is your Executive Document Q&A tool (meeting notes/packs → cited answers). The purpose of this kickoff is to turn the plan into committed decisions so delivery can start safely. Why this meeting exists Inputs to bring Who must attend Agenda (60–90 mins) The 3 decisions you must get Questions to ask (by role) Outputs you produce after Common failure modes 1) Why this kickoff meeting exists In enterprise delivery, pilots fail when you start building before the organisation commits to: who is in the pilot, what data is approved, and how success will be measured. Kickoff objective: leave the meeting with hard decisions so engineering does not stall on approvals later. In plain English The business wants a tool. You (AI lead) want to build it safely. Security/privacy/data owners want control. This meeting aligns everyone and locks the minimum safe pilot. 2) Inputs you bring (so the meeting is productive) Document 1 AI Lead Response Doc Scope, safety, architecture sketch, evaluation plan, asks. Document 2 Business Intake Brief Problem statement, users, desired outcomes, constraints. Pre-work Candidate pilot corpus list Example: “Exec Forum minutes folder + packs folder (last 6 months)”. Pre-work Draft success metrics Time saved baseline plan + citation correctness measurement plan. AI lead tip: Put the “decisions required” at the top of the invite so people understand it is not a status meeting. 3) Who must attend (and why) Role Why they must be there What decision they influence Business Owner Accountable for outcome + adoption. Pilot cohort, success metrics, rollout approach. Sponsor / GM Authority + unblocker (budget, access, priority). Go/no-go, escalation path, cross-team alignment. EA representative Defines exec workflow and what “usable output” looks like. Output format, top questions, acceptance criteria. Ops representative Defines reliability needs and failure tolerance. Safe failure behavior, latency expectations, incident concerns. Data Owner(s) Approves corpus access and exclusions. What documents are allowed in pilot and how they’re classified. Security / IAM Confirms approved patterns (identity, access control, secrets, logging). Access model constraints, audit requirements, network controls. Privacy / Risk Ensures the pilot meets obligations for sensitive data. Redaction/retention rules, allowed processing boundary. EM (Engineering Manager) Confirms team capacity and delivery plan. Resourcing, sprint cadence, definition of done. Lead AI Engineer Chair of the meeting. Converts decisions into build plan. Defines evaluation gates, architecture pack, and delivery approach. Common mistake: leaving out the data owner or EA rep. Result: you build something nobody can approve or nobody finds usable. 4) Agenda (60–90 minutes) Context recap (5 mins) — problem, pilot intent, why citations and access control are mandatory. Workflow + output contract (15 mins) — EA validates “what good looks like”. Pilot scope decisions (20 mins) — cohort, corpus, exclusions, timeline. Security/privacy gates (15 mins) — confirm constraints and approval path. Success metrics + evaluation gates (15 mins) — define baseline and go-live criteria. Next steps & owners (10 mins) — assign people to each dependency. Chairing tip: Treat this as a decision-making meeting, not brainstorming. If discussion loops, park it and force a decision on the minimum safe pilot. 5) The 3 decisions you must get (non-negotiable) Decision 1 — Pilot cohort Exactly who gets access (names or an org group) Who is the pilot champion (often an EA manager) Decision 2 — Pilot corpus (approved document sets) Exact doc locations/sources Explicit exclusions (HR/legal/customer PII-heavy docs) Named data owner approval path Decision 3 — Success metrics and go-live gate 2–3 measurable metrics (time saved, citation correctness, adoption) Definition of “ready to launch pilot” (minimum eval thresholds) If you get only these three decisions, you can start delivery. Everything else can iterate, but these prevent rework and approval deadlocks. 6) Questions to ask (by role) Questions for the Business Owner “What is the one outcome we must prove in 6 weeks?” “Which user cohort will actually use this weekly?” “Who owns change management and onboarding?” Questions for the Sponsor / GM “If access approvals stall, who can unblock within 48 hours?” “What is the acceptable pilot timeline and what tradeoffs are allowed?” Questions for the EA representative “What are the top 20 recurring questions execs ask?” “What counts as proof: snippet + link, or snippet + timestamp, or both?” “If the tool says ‘not found’, what should it suggest next?” Questions for Ops “What happens if the answer is wrong?” “What latency is acceptable in urgent moments?” “What must the tool do when evidence is insufficient?” Questions for Data Owners “Which folders/sites are approved, and which are explicitly excluded?” “Are there retention rules or classification tags we must enforce?” Questions for Security/IAM + Privacy/Risk “What is the approved pattern for identity, service accounts, and audit logging?” “What data can be sent to the LLM and what must be redacted/blocked?” “What is the minimum go-live checklist for a pilot?” 7) Outputs you produce after the meeting (within 24–48 hours) Output A — Decision record (1 page) Pilot cohort (names/group) Pilot corpus + exclusions Success metrics + go-live gate Owners for approvals and dependencies Output B — Architecture review pack (HLD) System diagram + trust boundaries Identity/access model Data flow (what is stored, what is sent to the LLM) Audit + logging plan Risks + mitigations Output C — Sprint-ready backlog Epics by lane (ingestion, backend/security, retrieval/LLM/eval) Owners + milestones (vertical slice early) AI lead tip: If you don’t write a decision record, the organisation will “remember” the meeting differently. 8) Common failure modes (and how to avoid them) Failure: “We’ll decide the corpus later.” → Fix: no corpus, no pilot. Decide now. Failure: “It should search everything.” → Fix: pilot needs boundaries; scale comes later. Failure: “We want it to be smart, no need for citations.” → Fix: enterprise trust requires citations. Failure: No EA/ops voice in the room → Fix: co-design is mandatory. Failure: No owner for approvals → Fix: assign a person per dependency. What kills pilots fastest: unclear data ownership + unclear access control + unclear success metrics. Reusable artifacts Complete this stage with a filled-out Kickoff Meeting Agenda Email and Decision Record. Use the concrete scenario “Chandima mentioned no meeting on 1 Dec” so assumptions, corpus boundaries, and expected citations are testable rather than abstract.

part: Part I - Enterprise AI Delivery Lifecycle

description: This tutorial is a step-by-step guide for what an AI Lead Engineer does immediately after the pilot kickoff meeting. It is aligned to our example project: Executive Document Q&A (meeting notes/packs → cited answers) w...
text: This tutorial is a step-by-step guide for what an AI Lead Engineer does immediately after the pilot kickoff meeting. It is aligned to our example project: Executive Document Q&A (meeting notes/packs → cited answers) with strict access control. The focus is not “build a demo” — it’s “ship a safe, measurable pilot.” Project Executive Document Q&A (Cited RAG Assistant) Enterprise reality Governance + access + evaluation gates must exist before users see it AI Lead outcome Convert kickoff decisions into approvals + backlog + evaluation + operating model Team shape (example) 5 engineers (data + software) + stakeholders (EA/Ops/Security/Data Owners) North Star (what we’re building) 7-day plan Document pack (templates) Who writes what Release gates AI lead checklist 0) North Star: what we’re actually building A pilot tool that answers questions like: “What did Chandima mention about no meeting on 1 Dec?” and returns: Short answer (2–6 sentences) Citations (doc title + link + excerpt; timestamp if transcript exists) Safe failure (“not found” when evidence is insufficient) Audit trail (who asked, what evidence was used) Lead-level framing: “If you can’t cite it, you can’t say it.” Pilot constraint: we only answer over an approved, bounded corpus. “All company docs” is a later phase. 1) The 7 days after kickoff (what I do, day by day) Day 0–1: Freeze decisions + unblock access Goal Make the pilot buildable by eliminating ambiguity and starting approval workflows. Publish the Decision Record (pilot cohort, corpus, exclusions, success metrics, named owners). Create the Approvals Tracker (data owner approvals, IAM/service identity requests, privacy/risk checks). Confirm the pilot cohort mechanism: names vs org group (recommended: group). Why this is first: approvals take longer than engineering. Start them immediately or delivery stalls in week 2. Day 2–3: Produce reviewable design + sprint-ready execution plan Goal Get “approval to build” and start engineering with a clear vertical slice milestone. Write the Architecture Review Pack (HLD) with trust boundaries, access model, data flows, risks. Write 3–5 ADRs documenting key decisions (citations-only, tenant isolation, corpus gating, etc.). Convert the plan into epics + stories and define the vertical slice milestone. Vertical slice definition: ingest a small approved sample → retrieve with filters → answer with citations → audit log → eval run. Day 3–4: Co-design with EA + Ops and build the “Golden Set” Goal Lock real workflow and create evaluation gates. Run a co-design session with EA + Ops to define what “usable output” looks like. Collect 30–50 real questions and record expected source documents. Define the scoring rubric (citation correctness, groundedness, refusal correctness). AI lead rule: you don’t “finish prompting” — you ship prompts behind eval gates and iterate with evidence. Day 5–7: Set the operating model + drive the first slice to demo readiness Goal Make the pilot safe to run, not just build. Define runbooks (wrong answer investigation, “not found” investigation, dependency outage behavior). Define go-live checklist (auth, gating, audit logs, eval threshold, dashboards). Demo the vertical slice internally to stakeholders and capture feedback. Important: A pilot without monitoring, audit logs, and a support owner is a “prototype,” not enterprise delivery. 2) The AI Lead Document Pack (aligned to this project) 2.1 Decision Record (template) This is the single most important artifact to prevent scope drift. Title: Exec Doc Q&A Pilot — Decision Record (v1) 1) Pilot Cohort - Access group: docqa-pilot-execs@company.com - Access group: docqa-pilot-eas@company.com - Pilot champion: (name) 2) Approved Corpus - Source: (Drive/SharePoint/etc.) - Locations: (folder IDs / site URLs) - Time window: last 6 months - Exclusions: HR, Legal, customer PII-heavy corpora 3) Success Metrics (Pilot) - EA time saved: baseline measured week 0 → target +30% improvement - Citation correctness: >= X on golden set - Adoption: weekly active users >= Y 4) Go-live Gate (Pilot) - All access controls enforced - Audit logging active - Golden set passes thresholds - Monitoring dashboards live - Named support owner 5) Owners / Contacts - Business owner: - Data owner: - Security/IAM: - Privacy/Risk: - AI lead: 2.2 Architecture Review Pack (HLD) — what it must contain System diagram + trust boundaries (where identity is verified, where data is stored, where LLM is called) Identity + access model: SSO, group gating, corpus gating, tenant/user mapping Data flow: what is ingested, stored, indexed, retrieved, and sent to the LLM Threats & mitigations: leakage, prompt injection, sensitive logs, exfil Operational view: metrics/logs/traces, failure modes, runbook ownership Architecture review purpose: approval to build (early) and approval to go-live (later). 2.3 ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) for this project ADR-001 — “Cited answers only; refuse without evidence.” ADR-002 — “Tenant isolation strategy (tenant_id/user_id; DB backstop).” ADR-003 — “Pilot uses corpus allowlist; per-doc ACLs in phase 2.” ADR-004 — “Model boundary: send only retrieved snippets; redact sensitive patterns.” ADR-005 — “Evaluation gates required for prompt/retrieval changes.” 2.4 EA/Ops Co-Design Notes + Output Contract What counts as “proof”: snippet + link, optional timestamp Answer length and tone suitable for executive briefings Refusal rules (“not found” behavior) Examples of good questions vs bad questions 2.5 Golden Set + Rubric (evaluation pack) You build this from real EA/Ops questions. It becomes your go-live gate. Golden Set entry example: - Question: "What did Chandima mention about no meeting on 1 Dec?" - Expected evidence: "Exec Forum Minutes 2024-12-01" section "Agenda changes" - Score: - Citation correctness (0/1/2) - Groundedness (0/1/2) - Refusal correctness (0/1) - Helpfulness (0/1) Lead-level move: every prompt/retrieval change runs the golden set and compares metrics. 2.6 Runbooks + Go-live checklist Runbook: “Wrong answer” → check citations → check retrieved chunks → check ingestion freshness Runbook: “Not found” → verify corpus boundaries → verify metadata → verify index update Checklist: access control enforced, audit logs written, eval thresholds met, dashboards live 3) Who writes what (team of 5) Artifact / Workstream Primary owner Support Decision record, ADRs, eval gates AI Lead Business owner, EM Architecture review pack AI Lead Security/IAM, EM, senior engineer Golden set + rubric AI Lead EA rep, Ops rep, SME Ingestion & metadata Data engineers (2) AI lead (schema), data owners Backend/auth/audit Software engineers (2) Security/IAM, AI lead (requirements) Runbooks + dashboards EM / senior engineer AI lead (what to measure), Ops 4) Release gates (what must be true before pilot users get access) Auth gate: only allowed org group can access Corpus gate: retrieval restricted to approved doc sets Citation gate: answers contain citations or refuse Leakage gate: cross-user/cross-corpus tests pass Audit gate: every answer logs user + cited sources Eval gate: golden set meets threshold Ops gate: dashboards + runbook + support owner exist Enterprise truth: “Working” is not enough. It must be measurable, auditable, and operable. 5) AI Lead checklist (copy/paste) ☐ Decision record published and agreed ☐ Approvals tracker created with named owners ☐ Architecture review pack drafted and review booked ☐ ADRs created for key choices ☐ EA/Ops co-design session completed ☐ Golden set + rubric created ☐ Sprint backlog created + vertical slice milestone defined ☐ Runbooks drafted + go-live checklist defined ☐ Pilot comms/training outline assigned to business owner/EA Result: by the end of week 1, you have a governable plan + measurable gates + build momentum. Week-one evidence pack Produce a filled-out Decision Record, an Architecture Review Pack outline, and a 30-question Golden Set grounded in the meeting-notes scenario. Together they connect governance decisions to measurable model behavior.

title: Architecture Reference Design
label: 6. Architecture reference design
part: Part I - Enterprise AI Delivery Lifecycle
headings: 0. Components in the setup
1. How users “connect” to the React frontend
2. User login (OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE)
3. React calls FastAPI (authenticated)
4. FastAPI validates the token (stateless and scalable)
5. How multi-tenancy is enforced (the important part)
6. Defense-in-depth: database-level isolation
7. Concurrency: multiple users at the same time
8. Where to store tokens (important practical note)
Summary you can say in interviews
description: Here is a clean, realistic reference design featuring:
text: Here is a clean, realistic reference design featuring: React frontend (hosted) FastAPI backend running on GKE Multi-tenancy (each user only sees their tenant’s data) This describes the “industry standard” flow using OIDC/OAuth2 + JWT. 0. Components in the setup Frontend React app hosted on Cloud Storage + CDN or Cloud Run. Identity Provider (IdP) OIDC provider: Google Identity, Auth0, Okta, Entra ID, etc. Backend FastAPI pods on GKE exposed via Ingress. Data Postgres (shared DB) with tenant_id column. 1. How users “connect” to the React frontend User types https://app.example.com DNS → CDN / hosting Browser downloads static files: index.html, JS bundles, CSS React app boots in the browser At this point, the user is not authenticated yet — they’ve only loaded a public website. 2. User login (OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE) When user clicks “Sign in”: React redirects user to the IdP login page User logs in (password/SSO/MFA) IdP redirects back to your React app with an authorization code React exchanges the code for tokens: ID token (who the user is) Access token (JWT used to call your API) Optional refresh token (to renew) Key point: the access token is what your backend uses to identify the user and their tenant. Where is the tenant? Two common patterns: tenant_id is a claim inside the JWT (best for multi-tenant SaaS) or backend looks up tenant_id from sub (user id) in your DB In production, many do both: claim for speed + DB as source of truth. 3. React calls FastAPI (authenticated) React calls: GET https://api.example.com/v1/chat with header: Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Ingress routes to FastAPI service in GKE. 4. FastAPI validates the token (stateless and scalable) Backend does JWT verification: Validate signature using the IdP’s JWKS Validate: iss (issuer), aud (audience), exp (expiry) Extract claims: sub (user_id), tenant_id (or org_id), roles/groups This is fast and works with thousands of concurrent users because verification is stateless. Minimal FastAPI pattern from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer, HTTPAuthorizationCredentials auth_scheme = HTTPBearer() def verify_jwt(creds: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(auth_scheme)): token = creds.credentials # 1) verify signature using JWKS # 2) validate iss/aud/exp # 3) return claims dict claims = {"sub": "user123", "tenant_id": "tenantA"} # toy return claims def tenant_context(claims=Depends(verify_jwt)): if "tenant_id" not in claims: raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="No tenant") return {"user_id": claims["sub"], "tenant_id": claims["tenant_id"]} Now every route can safely depend on tenant_context. 5. How multi-tenancy is enforced (the important part) Industry standard rule: Every data access must be scoped by tenant_id (and often user_id too). A) Shared database (toy example) Your tables include tenant_id: documents(tenant_id, doc_id, text, ...) chunks(tenant_id, chunk_id, embedding_ref, ...) Query example: SELECT doc_id, title, text, created_at FROM documents WHERE tenant_id = :tenant_id AND doc_id = :doc_id; B) Vector search (Elastic/OpenSearch) Every retrieval query includes a filter: tenant_id = tenantA So even if embeddings are shared in one index, retrieval is tenant-scoped. 6. Defense-in-depth: database-level isolation Even good teams eventually ship a bug. Industry standard is to add a backstop. Postgres Row-Level Security (RLS) Enable RLS on tables Policy: user can only see rows where tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id') Then in FastAPI, set it per request (session): SET app.tenant_id = 'tenantA'; Now, even if a developer forgets a WHERE tenant_id = ..., Postgres blocks it. 7. Concurrency: multiple users at the same time This just works if you follow the above patterns because: React is client-side; users are isolated by browser sessions Backend is stateless; each request carries its token Tenant context is derived per request Data stores enforce tenant boundaries 8. Where to store tokens (important practical note) Option 1: Tokens in memory SPA-friendly. Less risk of XSS token theft if you’re careful. Needs refresh flow. Option 2: httpOnly secure cookie Backend sets cookie after login exchange (BFF pattern). Reduces token exposure in JS. Requires CSRF protections. Summary you can say in interviews “Users authenticate via OIDC. The React app obtains an access token (JWT) and calls the FastAPI API. The backend verifies the JWT and extracts tenant_id/user_id, then enforces multi-tenancy by scoping every DB and vector-search query to that tenant. For defense-in-depth we enable Postgres Row Level Security so cross-tenant access is blocked even if a query is missing filters. Because each request is stateless and carries identity, it scales naturally to many concurrent users.” Architecture extension The next vertical slice adds Elastic retrieval, prompt assembly, and the Azure OpenAI call. Apply the tenant and corpus filter inside retrieval, re-check authorization before fetching source documents, and preserve the same identity in citations and audit events so context cannot cross users.

title: HLD Service Selection (GCP): Exec Document Q&A Pilot
label: 7. HLD and service selection
part: Part I - Enterprise AI Delivery Lifecycle
headings: 1) HLD decision principles (what we decide now vs later)
2) Reference architecture (GCP-aligned)
3) GCP service choices (what we pick, why, alternatives, and constraints)
4) Enterprise delays & critical path (what usually takes longest)
5) How to present this in an architecture review
description: This tutorial converts our service-selection discussion into a High-Level Design section you can drop into an Architecture Review Pack. It uses concrete GCP services, includes alternatives considered, and highlights e...
text: This tutorial converts our service-selection discussion into a High-Level Design section you can drop into an Architecture Review Pack. It uses concrete GCP services, includes alternatives considered, and highlights enterprise/internal delays (approvals, patterns, gates) that often dominate timelines. HLD decision principles Reference architecture Service choices (with alternatives) Enterprise delays & critical path How to present in review 1) HLD decision principles (what we decide now vs later) Decide at HLD Major components and trust boundaries Security posture (identity, access enforcement, secrets) Data boundary: what can go to the LLM Core services that create long lead-time dependencies Audit/observability requirements Defer to LLD Exact schemas, chunk sizing, prompt templates Fine-grained retry/backoff parameters Exact IAM role bindings per resource (unless forced) Exact SLOs (propose targets at HLD, finalize later) Rule of thumb: if it affects security/privacy, cost materially, operability, or requires another team’s provisioning, it must be decided (or at least bounded) at HLD. 2) Reference architecture (GCP-aligned) Request path (query time) User signs in via Google Workspace (OIDC) → SPA gets access_token. SPA calls backend API with Authorization: Bearer .... Backend validates JWT, maps to user_id/tenant_id, enforces group/corpus gates. Backend retrieves chunks (strict filters) → packs context → calls LLM → returns answer with citations. Backend writes audit logs (user, tenant, docs cited, timings). Ingestion path (offline) Document discovered/uploaded → event published. Worker extracts text + metadata → stores canonical record. Embeddings/index written to retrieval system with tenant/corpus metadata. Core HLD principle: access control is enforced in the backend and data layers, not in the browser. 3) GCP service choices (what we pick, why, alternatives, and constraints) 3.1 End-user Identity (Google Workspace SSO) Quick concept: What is an “Org allowlist”? An Org allowlist is a “front door” rule that answers: “Is this person allowed to use our application at all?” This is separate from tenant isolation (“what data can you access once inside?”). Authentication (Google login) proves who you are. Org allowlist decides whether you’re allowed to enter. Tenant isolation decides what you can see after you enter. Where it happens (two common places) In enterprises, you usually implement the allowlist in one of these places: Option A — At the IdP (preferred when available) You configure access rules at the Identity Provider (Google Workspace / your IdP) so only approved users can complete login for this application. How: use Google/IdP app access controls or group-based assignment (only members can use the app). Effect: users outside the group often cannot complete sign-in for this app (blocked earlier). Benefit: “blocked at the door” before tokens are issued for your app. Option B — In your application server (common and reliable) Your backend (FastAPI) enforces the allowlist on every request by checking group membership (or a local allowlist) after validating the JWT. How: verify token → read identity → check “is user in approved org group?” Effect: user can log in, but your API returns 403 Forbidden if not allowed. Benefit: uniform enforcement even if IdP-side restrictions are incomplete. Enterprise best practice: use both when possible. IdP-side gating reduces exposure and noise; app-side gating guarantees enforcement and supports richer rules (e.g., per-tenant mapping). How it looks in our project (Google Workspace group) We define a Google Group like docqa-users@company.com. Only members are allowed to use the product. Policy (conceptual): 1) Verify JWT (signature, issuer, audience, expiry) 2) Extract stable identity (issuer + sub, and email if present) 3) Check org allowlist: - if NOT in docqa-users@company.com → 403 "not allowed" - if IN group → continue 4) Map user → tenant_id (domain or DB lookup) 5) Enforce tenant/corpus filters on retrieval + data access Why it exists (common reasons) Security & governance: limit exposure to approved users only. Privacy: reduce risk by restricting who can query sensitive corpora. Pilot control: roll out to a small cohort first (execs + EAs), then expand. Cost control: LLM usage is expensive—control who can generate traffic. Don’t confuse this with GCP IAM End users typically do not need GCP IAM permissions. They access documents through the application. The backend uses its own service identity (service account / workload identity) to access GCS, DB, secrets, etc. Org allowlist = “Can this user use the app?” Cloud IAM = “Can this principal access GCP resources (buckets, secrets, projects)?” Capability Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives considered Enterprise constraints / delays Login + tokens Google Workspace OIDC (Auth Code + PKCE in SPA) Standard enterprise SSO; stateless API validation Identity Platform; custom IdP; IAP in front of app Token audience/issuer alignment; group claim policy; approval for group gating approach Org allowlist Google Groups gating (e.g., docqa-users@company.com) Simple “allowed to use product” control App-local allowlist; IAP access policy Group ownership, membership governance, and audit rules HLD note: group gating answers “who can use the app”; tenant isolation answers “what data can they access.” They are related but not the same. 3.2 Frontend hosting (React) Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives Delays / internal patterns Cloud Run (frontend service) Easy rollout; supports rewrites/headers and enterprise networking patterns if needed Cloud Storage + Cloud CDN (static); Firebase Hosting DNS/cert/WAF approvals can be longer than development 3.3 Backend compute (FastAPI) Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives Delays / internal patterns GKE (Kubernetes) Enterprise standard for regulated workloads; consistent policy enforcement; supports internal services Cloud Run (faster to ship); MIG on GCE Landing zone onboarding, hardened node pools, image scanning gates, network policies, mesh requirements HLD articulation: “GKE is chosen not because it’s trendy, but because it matches enterprise platform patterns and controls.” 3.4 Canonical store (metadata + system of record) Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives Delays / internal patterns Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL) Clear system-of-record; relational metadata; supports backstop controls (e.g., RLS) if needed AlloyDB (scale/perf); Firestore (not ideal for relational workloads) Private IP setup; KMS key approvals; DBA access model; backups/retention policies 3.5 Object storage (raw docs + extracted artifacts) Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives Delays / internal patterns Cloud Storage (GCS) Durable, cheap, standard; fits ingestion pipeline and artifact storage Filestore (rare); third-party storage (vendor risk) Uniform bucket-level access, retention policies, VPC-SC restrictions, data residency constraints 3.6 Retrieval / Semantic Search (vector + strict metadata filters) At HLD, you choose one path for the pilot and document the fallback/phase-2 alternative. The key requirement is strict filtering (tenant/corpus) to avoid leakage. Option When we choose it Why Tradeoffs Delays / internal patterns Option A: Vertex AI Search / Agent Builder Pilot needs speed and managed operations Managed retrieval; fast path; less ops burden Less low-level control; feature fit must be validated Service enablement approvals; data classification rules; integration reviews Option B: OpenSearch/Elasticsearch on GKE Need maximum control or org already runs search platform Full control: hybrid search, filters, scoring, tuning Higher ops cost; patching/backups/sizing required Platform onboarding queue; cluster hardening; storage class decisions; backup standards HLD best practice: choose the simplest option that satisfies strict filtering and governance. “Perfect retrieval” is not required for pilot, but “safe retrieval” is. 3.7 Async ingestion orchestration (durable retries) Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives Delays / internal patterns Pub/Sub + Cloud Tasks (or Workflows if needed) Durable eventing + retries; survives restarts; rate limiting GKE-native queues; scheduler jobs; best-effort background tasks IAM approvals for topics/subscriptions; DLQ standards; audit logging for processing events HLD note: FastAPI background tasks are fine for light best-effort work, but ingestion needs persistence and retries. 3.8 Secrets and keys Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives Delays / internal patterns Secret Manager + Cloud KMS (policy-driven) Rotation, audit, separation of duties; enterprise standard Kubernetes secrets (often restricted); third-party vault Access approval queue; rotation policy alignment; KMS key provisioning in approved region/project 3.9 LLM boundary (external provider calls) Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives Delays / internal patterns Backend on GKE calls external LLM via HTTPS (data minimised) Supports chosen model; keeps enforcement central; can redact/pack context Vertex AI (Gemini) to keep boundary within GCP; multi-provider routing Egress allowlisting/proxy; legal/compliance review of provider; data residency policy checks HLD statement to include: “Only retrieved snippets are sent to the model. No raw document dumps. Logs never include full snippets.” 3.10 Observability and audit Chosen (HLD) Why Alternatives Delays / internal patterns Cloud Logging + Cloud Monitoring + Cloud Trace (optional: BigQuery for long-term audit analytics) Required for enterprise support and governance; standard GCP tooling Splunk/Datadog (if org standard); custom ELK Retention policy approvals; sensitive logging rules; SIEM integration lead time Audit minimum (per request): who asked, which tenant, what sources were cited, timings, and outcome (answer/refusal). 4) Enterprise delays & critical path (what usually takes longest) In banks/airlines, “time to pilot” is often gated by approvals and provisioning, not coding. HLD should explicitly call out the critical path so stakeholders understand sequencing. Workstream What causes delay How the AI lead reduces risk Landing zone / projects Dev/stage/prod project creation, org policies, shared VPC attachment Request early; align with platform team templates; keep pilot in one approved project if allowed Networking Private egress, DNS, firewall rules, proxy requirements Document endpoints early; ask for a standard pattern; avoid custom exceptions IAM / service identities Least-privilege reviews, approvals, periodic reviews Provide role matrix; use standard roles; limit resources touched in pilot Data owner approval Corpus sign-off, classification review, explicit exclusions Propose a bounded corpus; provide an exclusion list; show audit controls Security/privacy review Threat model, logging policy, model boundary policy Bring a short threat model + mitigations; demonstrate “cite or refuse”; propose redaction policy HLD maturity signal: You’re not surprised by these delays — you plan around them and assign owners. 5) How to present this in an architecture review Recommended presentation structure Start with trust boundaries (what data leaves the boundary to the model) Show identity and access enforcement (group gate + tenant/corpus gates) Declare the chosen services with 1–2 sentences of why List alternatives considered and why not now End with risks + mitigations and the approval asks Reviewer-friendly line: “We are optimising for a safe pilot. Where a managed service reduces operational risk, we choose it. Where strict filtering and control are essential, we use a search platform that enforces metadata filters.” Example “Decision statement” format (copy/paste) Decision Chosen Why Alternatives Phase-2 note Retrieval layer Vertex AI Search (pilot) Fast to ship; managed ops; meets strict filtering needs (to be validated) OpenSearch on GKE Move to OpenSearch if advanced tuning is required HLD deliverable Turn the decisions in this chapter into an Architecture Review Pack containing the HLD sections, system and trust-boundary diagrams, decision tables, risks, assumptions, and phase-two alternatives.

title: After HLD: What You Do Next (AI Lead Under an AI Head)
label: 8. After HLD: next steps
part: Part I - Enterprise AI Delivery Lifecycle
headings: 1) Mental model: what changes after HLD
2) The next sequence (what you do, step-by-step)
3) Artifacts you produce after HLD (practical set)
4) Up-managing your AI Head (your manager)
5) Quick checklist (post-HLD)
description: You’ve written the High-Level Design (HLD) for the Exec Document Q&A pilot. Now you move from “design” into alignment → approvals → delivery readiness. This tutorial explains the next steps, the artifacts you produce,...
text: You’ve written the High-Level Design (HLD) for the Exec Document Q&A pilot. Now you move from “design” into alignment → approvals → delivery readiness. This tutorial explains the next steps, the artifacts you produce, and how to manage upwards when you have an AI Head. Mental model Next sequence Artifacts Up-managing your AI Head Checklist 1) Mental model: what changes after HLD HLD is the point where the system becomes reviewable. The next phase is about making it approvable and buildable. Before (HLD) Boxes & arrows + trust boundaries Core service choices + alternatives Key risks + mitigations Open questions After (execution-ready) Architecture review approval (or approval with conditions) LLD tasks and sprint backlog Provisioning tickets in flight (IAM, networking, data access) Vertical slice milestone defined Lead-level framing: after HLD, your job is to remove surprises and unblock dependencies before the team hits them. 2) The next sequence (what you do, step-by-step) Step 1 — Socialise the HLD before formal review (24–72 hours) Goal Prevent reviewers from seeing the design for the first time in the meeting. Send HLD to: Security/IAM, Platform (GKE), Data Owner, Privacy/Risk, EM. Ask for comments focused on: trust boundaries, data-to-LLM rules, audit logging, access enforcement, retention. Update HLD and produce a short “Open Questions / Decisions Needed” list. Why this matters: formal review time is scarce. Pre-alignment increases approval likelihood dramatically. Step 2 — Run the Architecture Review (and capture approval conditions) Goal Get “Approved to build pilot” + clear conditions to satisfy. Bring: HLD (service choices + alternatives + trust boundaries) ADRs (why we chose key patterns) Threat model summary (top risks + mitigations) Draft go-live gates: audit + eval + leakage tests Leave with: Approval outcome: approved / approved with conditions / rejected Action items, owners, and deadlines Any required controls (e.g., redaction policy, log schema, data classification constraints) Enterprise reality: “approved with conditions” is common. Capture conditions precisely and put them in your tracker. Step 3 — Convert HLD into LLD tasks + sprint plan (buildable backlog) Goal Turn boxes-and-arrows into implementable stories with owners. What you do: Define epics: Auth/gating, ingestion, retrieval, prompting/citations, audit/observability, eval harness. Define the vertical slice milestone (end-to-end thin slice early). Write acceptance criteria (must include safety gates, not just “it works”). Vertical slice example: ingest sample docs → retrieve with corpus/tenant filters → answer with citations → write audit log → run golden set. Step 4 — Start provisioning & dependency tickets immediately Goal Avoid “blocked by approvals” mid-sprint. GKE: namespaces, workload identity/service accounts, CI/CD access, image scanning gates Data: Cloud SQL instance + private connectivity + roles, GCS buckets + retention/IAM Async: Pub/Sub topics/subscriptions + DLQ, Cloud Tasks queues Security: Secret Manager secrets + KMS keys, logging retention rules Egress: allowlist/proxy approval for the LLM endpoint Lead-level behavior: treat provisioning as part of delivery, not “someone else will do it.” Step 5 — Engineering kickoff (internal) to start delivery Goal Align the team on “what good looks like” and reduce rework. Confirm vertical slice scope Agree API contracts (e.g., bootstrap identity, query endpoint) Agree evaluation gates (golden set baseline + regression runs) Agree “Definition of Done” includes logs/tests/dashboards 3) Artifacts you produce after HLD (practical set) Artifact Purpose What it contains (minimum) Architecture Review Pack Approval to build Trust boundaries, identity/access model, data flows, service choices, risks+mitigations ADR set Record “why” Cited-only, tenant isolation, corpus gate, model boundary, eval gates Approval Conditions Tracker Make conditions actionable Condition, owner, due date, evidence required, status Sprint Backlog Make work buildable Epics/stories, owners, acceptance criteria, dependencies Dependency/Provisioning Tickets Unblock infra IAM, networking, secrets, DB, buckets, topics, egress 4) Up-managing your AI Head (your manager) Your AI Head doesn’t need every detail. They need confidence that risks are controlled and delivery is on track. The best tool is a short, consistent weekly update. Weekly “AI Lead pack” (1 page): Status: what shipped, what’s demoable Approvals: what’s done, what’s blocked, who owns it Top 3 risks: and mitigation plan Decisions/escalations needed: exactly what you need from them Next week plan: vertical slice milestones Lead-level signal: don’t bring problems without options. Bring “risk + options + recommended path + what you need from leadership.” 5) Quick checklist (post-HLD) ☐ HLD socialised with Security/Platform/Data Owner/Privacy before review ☐ Architecture review booked and pack sent ahead of time ☐ ADRs drafted for key decisions ☐ Review outcome captured with explicit conditions and owners ☐ Backlog created with vertical slice milestone and acceptance criteria ☐ Provisioning tickets raised (IAM, DB, storage, pubsub/tasks, secrets, egress) ☐ Team engineering kickoff completed ☐ Weekly AI Head update pack started Outcome: you exit the “design phase” with approvals in motion, engineering unblocked, and stakeholders aligned. Planning artifacts Maintain an Approval Conditions Tracker and a first-two- sprint backlog for the document Q&A pilot. Order the backlog around a thin vertical slice before adding breadth.
