description: This tutorial shows how to run an enterprise architecture review for the Exec Document Q&A pilot and how to walk out with a clear approval outcome and actionable conditions. It is written for an AI Lead who must align...
text: This tutorial shows how to run an enterprise architecture review for the Exec Document Q&A pilot and how to walk out with a clear approval outcome and actionable conditions. It is written for an AI Lead who must align Security, Platform, Data Owners, and Engineering. Goal and outcomes Who attends Preparation checklist What to bring Recommended agenda Questions reviewers will ask Capturing approval conditions Post-review artifacts Templates you can copy 1) Goal and outcomes Goal Get Approved to build pilot (or Approved with conditions) and leave with explicit controls to satisfy. You want to leave with Approval outcome: approved / approved with conditions / rejected Action items with owners + due dates Required controls: redaction rules, log schema, data classification constraints, etc. Decision log: what was decided and why What “success” looks like Reviewers agree the trust boundary is safe (LLM data minimised) Access control is clear: org allowlist + tenant/corpus gates Audit and observability are adequate for production governance Pilot scope is bounded and safe Lead-level framing: the review is not about “is LLM cool?”. It’s about risk-managed delivery: identity, data boundaries, auditability, and operability. 2) Who attends (typical enterprise roles) Adjust to your org, but a good minimum set is: Architecture/Platform (GKE, networking, landing zone patterns) Security/IAM (identity, group gating, service accounts, secrets) Privacy/Risk (data classification, retention, external model boundary) Data Owner / Business Owner (corpus approval, acceptable use) Engineering Manager (delivery plan, support model, runbooks) AI Lead (you) and optionally AI Head (exec sponsor / escalation) Tip: If your AI Head is not present, confirm they support the risk posture and pilot scope beforehand. The review goes smoother when leadership alignment is obvious. 3) Preparation checklist (the difference between “approval” and “rework”) Objective Remove surprises before the meeting. Share the pack 48–72 hours prior. Do 1:1 pre-reads with Security and Platform (15–30 mins each) to surface blockers early. Confirm data classification allowed for pilot corpus (even a “pilot-only” constraint is fine). Confirm “what goes to the LLM” is explicitly stated and minimised. Bring your draft go-live gates (audit + eval + leakage tests) to show operational maturity. Common failure mode: reviewers first learn that “documents might be sent to an external model” during the meeting. Always state boundaries upfront. 4) What to bring (minimum review pack) The meeting works best when all inputs are concise and anchored on risk controls. Here is the practical minimum: Bring What it is Why reviewers care Minimum content HLD High-level architecture + service choices Trust boundaries, data flows, major services Diagrams, service selection (with alternatives), identity model, data flow ADRs Decision records (“why we chose X”) Prevents re-litigating decisions later Tenant isolation, cited-only answers, model boundary, retrieval choice, eval gates Threat model summary Top risks + mitigations Security & privacy posture Cross-tenant leakage, injection, exfiltration, logging/PII, access abuse Draft go-live gates Release criteria Operational readiness & governance Audit logging fields, evaluation thresholds, leakage tests, rollback plan Shortcut: If time is tight, prioritise (1) trust boundary, (2) identity/access enforcement, (3) audit/evals. 5) Recommended review agenda (60 minutes) 5 min — Purpose and decision asks (what approvals you need today) 10 min — Architecture overview (diagrams + trust boundaries) 10 min — Identity & access (Workspace OIDC, org allowlist, tenant/corpus isolation) 10 min — Data flows & model boundary (what is stored, what is sent to LLM, what is logged) 10 min — Threat model top risks (and mitigations) 10 min — Go-live gates (audit, evals, leakage tests, runbooks) 5 min — Decisions + conditions (capture outcome + owners) Good review behavior: move quickly from “what it is” to “how we prevent bad outcomes”. 6) Questions reviewers will ask (be ready) Security / IAM How do you validate tokens and gate access? Where is tenant/corpus enforced? How do service accounts access Cloud SQL/GCS/Secret Manager? What is logged? Do logs contain sensitive content? Privacy / Risk What data leaves GCP to the LLM provider? What data classifications are allowed in the pilot? What’s retention policy (docs, embeddings, logs)? How do you prevent “prompt injection” from documents? Platform / Architecture Why GKE vs Cloud Run? What’s the platform standard? How will this be operated (monitoring, alerts, runbooks)? How do you handle dependency failures (retrieval/LLM down)? Business / Data owners Who owns the documents? Who approves inclusion/exclusion? What’s the success metric for the pilot? How do we prove answers are grounded/cited? 7) Capturing approval conditions (this is the most important output) Enterprises often approve with conditions. Your job is to turn those conditions into trackable work with owners and evidence required. Technique: re-state each condition in the meeting in plain language and confirm agreement: “So we’re approved provided we do X, Y, Z. Owner A, due date B. Evidence is C.” Example conditions (common for GenAI) Redaction policy for sensitive patterns before sending to LLM Logging schema that excludes raw document content but captures citations + metadata Data classification constraints for pilot corpus (“only internal restricted, no secret/regulated”) Leakage tests that prove tenant/corpus filters work Evaluation gates (accuracy/citation correctness thresholds) Runbook + on-call ownership Condition tracker template (copy/paste) Condition Owner Due Evidence required Status Define and implement redaction rules before model calls AI Lead YYYY-MM-DD PR + tests + example before/after Open Audit log schema approved by Security (no raw snippets) Security + Eng YYYY-MM-DD Signed-off schema + sample logs Open Leakage test suite (cross-tenant retrieval must return 0) Data/Eng YYYY-MM-DD CI test results + report Open Anti-pattern: leaving with “Security wants some logging controls” without an owner and measurable evidence. 8) Post-review artifacts (what you send out) Decision summary (1 page): outcome + approved scope + key decisions Condition tracker: conditions, owners, dates, evidence Action items list: meeting minutes with explicit assignments Updated HLD/ADRs: incorporate agreed changes Go-live gate checklist: what must be true before pilot launch Operational tip: send the summary within 24 hours while the meeting context is fresh. 9) Templates you can copy (email + meeting close) Meeting close script (30 seconds) “To close: our outcome is [approved / approved with conditions / rejected]. Conditions are [A, B, C] with owners [X, Y, Z] and due dates [d1, d2, d3]. Evidence required is [e1, e2, e3]. I’ll circulate notes and the tracker today.” Follow-up email skeleton Subject: Architecture Review Outcome — Exec Doc Q&A Pilot Outcome: Approved / Approved with conditions / Rejected Approved scope: Pilot cohort + allowed corpora + allowed data classifications Conditions: (link to tracker) Action items: owners + due dates Next checkpoint: date for condition review / go-live readiness review Go-live gate The review outcome should feed a single checklist covering audit evidence, model evaluation, cross-tenant leakage tests, operational runbooks, rollback, and approval-condition closure for this executive document Q&A architecture.

title: Step 3: Convert HLD into LLD Tasks and a Sprint-Ready Plan
label: 10. HLD to LLD and sprint plan
part: Part I - Enterprise AI Delivery Lifecycle
headings: 1) Planning principles (enterprise reality)
2) Define epics (map directly to your HLD boxes)
3) Define the vertical slice milestone (the most important planning move)
4) Turn epics into buildable stories (how to slice work)
5) Acceptance criteria (include safety gates, not just “it works”)
6) Assign work to 5 direct reports (a practical team shape)
7) Example sprint plan (2 sprints to a vertical slice)
8) Definition of Done (what “complete” means in this org)
description: You have an approved (or conditionally approved) HLD for the Exec Document Q&A (cited RAG) pilot. Now your job as AI Lead is to translate “boxes and arrows” into implementable stories with clear owners, a vertical sli...
text: You have an approved (or conditionally approved) HLD for the Exec Document Q&A (cited RAG) pilot. Now your job as AI Lead is to translate “boxes and arrows” into implementable stories with clear owners, a vertical slice milestone, and acceptance criteria that include safety gates — not just “it works”. This guide assumes you lead 5 AI/ML/Software engineers in a large enterprise environment. Planning principles Define epics Vertical slice milestone Write buildable stories Acceptance criteria (incl. safety) Assign work to 5 engineers Example sprint plan (2 sprints) Definition of Done 1) Planning principles (enterprise reality) What makes a backlog “buildable” Every item has an owner, inputs, outputs, and acceptance criteria Dependencies are explicit (IAM, networking, data access, secrets) Work is sliced end-to-end (vertical), not by layers only Safety gates are included as first-class requirements Common failure modes Only building “the model part” without operability/audit Stories too large (“build retrieval system”) → unclear progress Security conditions treated as “later” → late rework Dependencies discovered mid-sprint → blocked delivery Lead-level mantra: “We deliver a safe end-to-end slice early, then improve quality and scale.” 2) Define epics (map directly to your HLD boxes) Start by creating epics that mirror the architecture. For this project, a clean set is: Epic A — Auth & gating: OIDC validation, org allowlist, tenant mapping, bootstrap endpoint Epic B — Ingestion pipeline: intake event, extraction, canonical store, indexing Epic C — Retrieval: strict tenant/corpus filters, ranking, chunk fetch Epic D — Prompting & citations: context packing, citation format, refusal rules Epic E — Audit & observability: structured logs, traces, dashboards, runbook hooks Epic F — Evaluation harness: golden set, citation correctness checks, regression gate in CI/CD Tip: If your architecture review produced “approval conditions”, create one epic or track lane for each condition so nothing gets lost. 3) Define the vertical slice milestone (the most important planning move) A vertical slice is a thin, end-to-end path that proves the system works safely with real constraints. It is not “production ready”, but it is real and demoable. Vertical slice (Exec Doc Q&A) — definition: One user logs in (Workspace OIDC) → backend validates → returns identity One small approved corpus (e.g., 10 meeting notes) is ingested Query retrieves tenant/corpus-filtered chunks LLM returns an answer with citations (or refuses) Audit log is written (no sensitive snippet dumps) Golden set eval runs and produces a simple report Anti-pattern: building “ingestion” for weeks before any end-to-end query works. Your team should be able to run a demo early. 4) Turn epics into buildable stories (how to slice work) Each story should be deliverable in 1–4 days by one engineer and have clear testable outputs. Use a consistent story template: Story field What to write Title Verb + object (e.g., “Implement /auth/bootstrap identity endpoint”) Goal What capability is enabled and for whom Inputs Request format, upstream data, required secrets Outputs Response format, side effects (DB rows, logs, events) Acceptance criteria Functional + safety + observability tests Dependencies IAM, networking, platform tickets, approvals Example story breakdown (one epic) Auth/gating: “Verify JWT”, “Check org allowlist”, “Map tenant”, “Provision user”, “Return /me” Retrieval: “Index schema includes tenant/corpus tags”, “Search with filters”, “Fetch chunks” Prompting: “Format citations”, “Refuse when insufficient context”, “Redact patterns” 5) Acceptance criteria (include safety gates, not just “it works”) In GenAI, acceptance criteria must include correctness, leakage prevention, and governance. Use the “3-layer” criteria pattern: Functional Endpoint works for happy path Correct request/response schema Handles expected error cases Safety & security Tenant/corpus filters enforced Prompt injection mitigations applied Refusal behavior when evidence is missing Operability Structured logs with request_id/user/tenant Metrics for latency and failure codes Tracing across retrieval + LLM call Evidence Unit tests + integration test runs Golden set eval report updated Demo script for stakeholders Key acceptance gate: “Cross-tenant retrieval attempt returns zero results (and logs an audit event).” 6) Assign work to 5 direct reports (a practical team shape) With 5 engineers, assign ownership by stream but ensure the vertical slice comes together. A common structure: Engineer (example) Primary stream Deliverables Eng 1 Auth & identity /auth/bootstrap, tenant mapping, org allowlist gate, user provisioning Eng 2 Ingestion Pub/Sub/Tasks wiring, extractor stub, canonical store writes, index writes Eng 3 Retrieval Strict filters, top-k search, chunk fetch, ranking tuning hooks Eng 4 Prompting & citations Context packing, citation format, refusal rules, redaction hooks Eng 5 Evals + observability Golden set harness, citation correctness checks, dashboards/alerts, runbook skeleton Your role: manage integration points (contracts, schemas), sequencing, and keep “approval conditions” tracked. You should also reserve time for cross-cutting reviews and stakeholder updates. 7) Example sprint plan (2 sprints to a vertical slice) Example assumes 2-week sprints. The goal is a demoable vertical slice by the end of Sprint 1 or early Sprint 2. Sprint 1 — Vertical slice foundations (end-to-end demo) Epic Stories (examples) Acceptance focus Auth/gating /auth/bootstrap validates JWT; org allowlist check; tenant mapping; user row create-if-missing 403 if not allowed; stable user mapping; audit log entry Ingestion Ingest 10 sample docs into canonical store; write minimal index entries with tenant/corpus tags Repeatable ingestion; no cross-tenant tags; basic error handling Retrieval Search endpoint with strict tenant/corpus filters; returns chunk IDs and text Cross-tenant search returns 0; latency baseline measured Prompting/citations RAG prompt template; citations required; refusal when insufficient evidence No uncited answers; refusal cases tested Obs/audit Structured log schema; request_id; traces across retrieval + LLM No raw snippets in logs; dashboard stub exists Evals Golden set (10–20 Qs); basic evaluator: citation presence + answer groundedness checklist Eval report produced in CI; baseline recorded Sprint 2 — Quality + safety hardening (pilot-ready) Improve retrieval quality (hybrid ranking, chunking refinements) Add stronger leakage tests and prompt injection tests Add redaction rules and validate policy compliance Expand eval set + add regression gates (must not degrade) Operational readiness: alerts, runbook, on-call handoff 8) Definition of Done (what “complete” means in this org) Define DoD once and apply to every story. This prevents “works on my machine” delivery. Code merged with tests (unit + at least one integration test) Observability: logs/metrics/traces updated for the feature Security: tenant/corpus enforcement verified (test case included) Documentation: README snippet or runbook note updated Demoable: a curl/script or Postman request exists Lead-level improvement: add a “safety test” checkbox to every story by default. Backlog scale A realistic first-two-sprint backlog contains roughly 20–40 stories with owners and acceptance criteria spanning GKE, Cloud SQL, GCS, Pub/Sub or Cloud Tasks, and the selected retrieval service (Vertex AI Search or OpenSearch).

description: This tutorial expands Step 4 and Step 5 for your multi-tenant Document Q&A system on GCP. It answers: which exact services you provision, why GKE / Pub/Sub / Cloud Tasks, what latency targets are acceptable, and how t...
text: This tutorial expands Step 4 and Step 5 for your multi-tenant Document Q&A system on GCP. It answers: which exact services you provision, why GKE / Pub/Sub / Cloud Tasks, what latency targets are acceptable, and how to handle 1000s of simultaneous users in a large enterprise. 1) Concrete reference architecture (GCP services) Capability Concrete GCP implementation Notes (bank/enterprise friendly) Frontend Cloud Run (React static via CDN or server-render), behind HTTPS LB Public entry, simple scaling; no direct access to data stores API backend GKE (private cluster) running FastAPI, multiple replicas Strong network controls, sidecars, private egress, platform patterns Object storage Cloud Storage (GCS) buckets (raw docs + processed artifacts) Retention policies, CMEK (KMS), uniform bucket-level access Canonical store Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL (tenants, users, documents, chunks metadata) Private IP + IAM DB auth where possible; RLS optional backstop Async pipeline Pub/Sub for events + Cloud Tasks for controlled retries to workers Pub/Sub for fan-out; Tasks for rate-limited HTTP execution + DLQ Document extraction Option A: Document AI (OCR/forms) called by an ingestion worker Best for scans/PDFs; keep outputs minimal and stored internally Search / vectors (Your design) Elasticsearch/OpenSearch hosted/managed or in-cluster Must enforce tenant/corpus filters; isolate indices or filter fields Secrets Secret Manager + CMEK KMS keys Rotation + least privilege; avoid secrets baked into images Observability Cloud Logging + Cloud Monitoring + Cloud Trace Structured logs + trace correlation IDs; retention controls Egress to external LLM Private egress via NAT + egress proxy / allowlist + DLP/redaction hooks Network allowlisting + audit + bounded payload rules Key boundary: Human users authenticate to your app (OIDC token). Your workloads authenticate to GCP using workload identity + service accounts. End users do not get GCP IAM access to buckets/DB. 2) Document extraction tooling: where implemented and why Extraction is almost never done in the interactive API path. It is an async worker responsibility. The normal pattern: User uploads document → stored in gs://raw-docs Upload emits an event (Pub/Sub) → ingestion worker picks it up Worker performs extraction (Document AI / libraries) → stores canonical text in Cloud SQL + processed text in GCS Worker generates chunks + embeddings → writes to vector store (with strict tenant/corpus tags) Option A (common): Document AI Best when you have PDFs, scans, mixed layouts, forms Managed OCR quality tends to beat DIY OCR Worker calls Document AI API; you store only needed output Option B: Self-managed extractors Apache Tika / unstructured / custom parsers in a worker container Good for Office docs / HTML / text-heavy content More operational burden (libs, CVEs, memory spikes) Enterprise-friendly practice: “extract → store canonical text internally → index” and keep extraction strictly async with retries and DLQs. 3) Why GKE for the backend (and what Cloud Run would change) Why choose GKE (common in banks) Private cluster + tighter network isolation patterns Sidecars (proxies, policy agents), service mesh (if required) More predictable performance under heavy concurrency Consistent “platform standard” if the org runs many services on GKE When Cloud Run is acceptable Faster initial delivery, simpler operations Great for stateless HTTP services Still supports service identities, private networking (with setup) Less flexibility for complex in-cluster patterns Decision framing: In a large org, you usually align with the platform team’s “golden path”. If the enterprise runs private GKE landing zones, GKE reduces approval friction. 4) Why Pub/Sub + Cloud Tasks (and what they solve) Pub/Sub: event distribution (fan-out) “Something happened” messaging (document uploaded, extraction complete) Multiple consumers can subscribe (indexer, audit, notifications) High throughput and decoupling Cloud Tasks: controlled execution (rate + retries) Push a specific HTTP job to a worker endpoint Built-in retry + scheduling + DLQ patterns Enforce per-queue throughput (useful for external API limits) Typical pattern: Pub/Sub announces the event; Cloud Tasks is used for the “do work” step when you need strict retry, backoff, and rate control. What about Kafka? Acceptable in some orgs, but usually heavier to operate. If your enterprise already has it, it’s a viable alternative. Otherwise Pub/Sub is the GCP-native path. 5) Latency targets: what’s acceptable and how to meet it You should define SLOs separately for interactive query and async ingestion. Concrete targets that work for exec Q&A: Path Target (p50 / p95) How you hit it /query (interactive) p50: 2–4s, p95: 6–10s Async I/O, fast retrieval (sub-second), bounded context size, caching, LLM timeouts Retrieval alone p50: 100–300ms, p95: < 800ms Tenant-filtered indices, warm caches, limit top_k, avoid expensive rescoring LLM call alone p50: 1–3s, p95: 5–8s Streaming responses, concurrency limits, fallback/timeout, smaller prompts Ingestion (async) Minutes are fine (SLO: < 15 min typical) Worker autoscale, retries, DLQ, document size limits, batch processing Practical trick: Stream the LLM answer to the UI so the user “sees progress” even if p95 is high. It improves perceived latency. 6) Handling 1000s of simultaneous users (GKE + FastAPI + external LLM constraints) At scale, your true bottleneck is often the LLM endpoint, not FastAPI itself. Your strategy is: keep the API stateless and fast, and protect downstream dependencies. 6.1 API layer (FastAPI on GKE) — what actually scales Stateless replicas: multiple pods behind a load balancer; each request carries its identity. Async I/O: use async clients for DB/search/LLM so threads aren’t blocked waiting on network. Connection pooling: DB and HTTP clients pooled per pod; avoid per-request reconnects. Timeouts + circuit breakers: fail fast when LLM/retrieval is degraded. 6.2 Downstream protection (what keeps you stable) Rate limits & fairness Per-tenant concurrency caps (avoid one tenant consuming all capacity) Global cap for LLM calls (protect the quota) Queueing for overflow (return 429 / retry-after when needed) Degradation strategies If retrieval slow → lower top_k / skip re-rank If LLM slow → shorter prompt / cheaper model / refusal with guidance If dependency down → return “try again” with tracking ID Key point: “1000s of users” is fine for stateless HTTP + retrieval. The hard part is controlling LLM concurrency and ensuring tenant fairness. 7) Step 4: Provisioning & dependency tickets (what to raise, exactly) Goal Avoid being blocked mid-sprint. Treat provisioning as part of delivery. Area Ticket examples (concrete) Why it matters GKE Create namespace docqa; create KSA + map to GSA (workload identity); set pod security standards; enable image scanning gate in CI/CD Everything else depends on the runtime identity and security posture Data Cloud SQL Postgres (private IP) + IAM/roles; GCS buckets: raw-docs, processed-text; retention + UBLA + CMEK Data stores are often the slowest approvals in enterprises Async Pub/Sub topic doc-uploaded; subscription for ingestion worker; DLQ topic; Cloud Tasks queues extract, index with rate limits Reliable ingestion requires retryable, auditable async plumbing Security Secret Manager secrets (DB creds / API keys); KMS keys; log retention policy; audit log schema sign-off Without this, you’ll fail review conditions late Egress External egress allowlist to LLM endpoint; egress proxy approval; NAT/IP ranges; DLP/redaction controls External calls are a common compliance blocker—start early Lead technique: Every ticket should specify: service name, data classification, identity (GSA), network path, and evidence needed for approval. 8) Step 5: Engineering kickoff (internal) — make “good” unambiguous Goal Align the team on scope, contracts, evaluation gates, and Definition of Done. Kickoff checklist Confirm vertical slice: the exact demo you will deliver at end of Sprint 1 API contracts: /auth/bootstrap, /query, /ingest (request/response + error codes) Evaluation gates: golden set baseline, citation correctness checks, regression threshold Definition of Done: includes tests + logs/metrics/traces + safety checks Integration points: schema for docs/chunks, tenant/corpus tag format, log schema Best practice: write the vertical slice as a single end-to-end “demo script” (login → ingest sample → ask question → see citations → check audit log entry). Common rework source: engineers implement in parallel without agreed contracts. Freeze the first version of schemas and endpoints early. 9) Quick “acceptable alternatives” cheat sheet (if approvals block you) Need Preferred Acceptable alternative (for pilot) Runtime platform GKE private cluster Cloud Run (if allowed by platform/security), then migrate later Async jobs Pub/Sub + Cloud Tasks Pub/Sub only (simpler), but less fine-grained rate limiting for HTTP work Extraction Document AI Basic parser for text/PDF-only corpus (limit scope to reduce risk) Search/vectors OpenSearch/Elastic w/ filters Postgres + pgvector for pilot (lower scale, simpler ops) if acceptable Leadership message: “We can deliver a safe vertical slice with reduced scope while approvals for the full target stack complete.”

title: FastAPI & Uvicorn Basics
label: 1. FastAPI and Uvicorn basics
headings: Definitions
Why FastAPI + Uvicorn
Mini Tutorial: HTTP Methods
The Common HTTP Methods
A Quick Mental Model for Your Project
description: A modern Python web framework for building APIs. You write endpoint functions with Python type hints, and FastAPI uses them to validate requests, serialize responses, and generate interactive API docs automatically.
text: Definitions FastAPI A modern Python web framework for building APIs. You write endpoint functions with Python type hints, and FastAPI uses them to validate requests, serialize responses, and generate interactive API docs automatically. Uvicorn A fast ASGI server. It’s the program that actually runs your FastAPI app and handles incoming network connections (HTTP/WebSockets), passing requests into your app and sending responses back out. ASGI Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface: a standard way for an async Python web app (FastAPI/Starlette) to communicate with an async web server (Uvicorn). Why FastAPI + Uvicorn FastAPI gives you the API framework (routing, validation, docs, dependency injection). Uvicorn gives you the server runtime to serve it efficiently. ASGI is the glue that enables async concurrency and things like WebSockets (useful for real-time apps). Mini Tutorial: HTTP Methods (GET / POST / PUT / PATCH / DELETE) + “safe” + “idempotent” (FastAPI context) Anatomy of an HTTP Request Method (GET/POST/PUT/…): the intent URL (e.g. /documents/123): the target resource Headers (e.g. Authorization) Body (optional JSON): the data you send Why there are different HTTP methods HTTP has different methods because they communicate the intent of a request in a standardized way: Safety: Some requests are meant to be read-only (GET) vs change data (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE). Retries: Some operations are designed to be safe to repeat (PUT/DELETE are typically idempotent), which matters when networks fail. Caching: Reads (GET) can be cached by browsers/CDNs/proxies; writes usually aren’t. Tooling & clarity: The method + URL together form a clear contract (GET /documents/123 vs DELETE /documents/123), which helps docs, clients, gateways, and debugging. Concepts What “safe” means A safe method should not change server state. Safe: GET, HEAD Not safe: POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE Why it matters: systems may prefetch, cache, or retry safe requests more freely because they shouldn’t cause side effects. What “idempotent” means An idempotent method means repeating the same request leads to the same final server state. Idempotent: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE (PATCH is often idempotent if it “sets fields”, but not always) Usually not idempotent: POST (repeating can create duplicates) Why it matters: when a client times out, it might retry. Retrying idempotent operations is safer. The Common HTTP Methods (What they mean + when to use) GET “Give me data” (read-only) Meaning: Retrieve a resource (or list/search results) Safe: yes Idempotent: yes Cacheable: often Use for: fetching documents, listing, searching with simple query params Example: GET /documents/123 Client call curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ http://localhost:8000/documents/123 FastAPI @app.get("/documents/{doc_id}") def get_document(doc_id: int): return {"id": doc_id, "title": "Example"} POST “Create or perform an action” Meaning: Submit data to create something or run a server action Safe: ❌ Idempotent: ❌ (usually) Cacheable: usually ❌ Use for: creating resources (POST /documents) or “commands” like Q&A query (POST /query) Example: POST /query with a question in JSON Client call curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/query \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"question":"What does my policy say about refunds?"}' FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel class QueryRequest(BaseModel): question: str @app.post("/query") def query(req: QueryRequest): return {"answer": "Mock answer", "question": req.question} PUT “Replace this resource completely” Meaning: Set the resource at this URL to exactly this representation Safe: ❌ Idempotent: yes (repeat = same final state) Use for: full replacement updates Example: PUT /documents/123 with full document fields Client call curl -X PUT http://localhost:8000/documents/123 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"title":"New title","content":"Full content"}' PATCH “Update part of this resource” Meaning: Modify only certain fields Safe: ❌ Idempotent: depends (often yes if it “sets” fields) Use for: small updates like renaming a document Example: PATCH /documents/123 with {"title":"Renamed"} Client call curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/documents/123 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"title":"Renamed"}' DELETE “Remove this resource” Meaning: Delete the resource at this URL Safe: ❌ Idempotent: yes (deleting twice still ends “deleted”) Use for: deleting documents, records, jobs Example: DELETE /documents/123 Client call curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8000/documents/123 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" A Quick Mental Model for Your Project Use GET for fetching: document list/details, status checks. Use POST for actions: your Q&A /query is naturally POST (complex body, not a simple “resource fetch”). Use PUT/PATCH for updating document metadata or settings. Use DELETE to remove a document or ingestion entry. Chapter transition The next chapters separate HTTP method semantics from parameter placement, then map /documents/{id}, ?limit=, headers, and JSON request models into typed FastAPI function arguments.

title: HTTP methods (the “verbs” of the web) — beginner friendly
label: 2. HTTP methods
headings: Core ideas you should know
How this connects to Pydantic: method, URL, and body are separate jobs
Quick table (print-this-in-your-brain)
Widely used methods (you’ll use these 99% of the time)
Common but less used (still important)
Rare / niche methods (you’ll see them sometimes)
Practical mapping to REST-style endpoints
The “PUT vs POST feels same” confusion (quick intuition)
What an HTTP request looks like
How FastAPI “decodes” the message
description: HTTP methods tell the server (and intermediaries like browsers, proxies, CDNs) what you intend to do with a URL: read, create, replace, patch, delete. That intent unlocks important behavior like caching, retries, idem...
text: HTTP methods tell the server (and intermediaries like browsers, proxies, CDNs) what you intend to do with a URL: read, create, replace, patch, delete. That intent unlocks important behavior like caching, retries, idempotency, and clearer security controls. Core ideas Method to Python contract Quick table Widely used (⭐) Less used but important Rare / niche REST-style mapping PUT vs POST confusion HTTP request shape How FastAPI decodes Quick takeaway GET read (safe) POST create or run an action PUT replace full resource PATCH partial update DELETE remove You’ll use the ⭐ methods 99% of the time. Core ideas you should know These concepts explain why method choice matters (caching, retries, correctness). Safe vs unsafe Safe means: “should not change server state” (read-only). Safe: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS Unsafe: POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE Idempotent vs non-idempotent Idempotent means: repeating the same request leads to the same final state as doing it once. Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS Often non-idempotent: POST (and sometimes PATCH) Cacheable (common in practice) GET is commonly cacheable Others are usually not cached unless explicitly configured Beginner rule: Pick the method that matches intent first. Then think about safety, idempotency, caching, and security. Method + URL = contract How this connects to Pydantic: method, URL, and body are separate jobs A clean backend design separates three questions. First, the HTTP method says the intent: are we reading, creating, replacing, patching, or deleting? Second, the URL says which resource or collection the intent applies to. Third, if the request has a JSON body, a Pydantic model says the exact shape of that body. Flow to remember: METHOD + URL chooses the endpoint. path/query/header values become function parameters. JSON body becomes a Pydantic model instance when you declare one. Request part Example Who handles it in FastAPI? Method + path POST /orders The route decorator: @app.post("/orders") Path parameter /users/42 A typed argument: user_id: int Query parameter ?limit=20 A typed argument with a default: limit: int = 20 Header Authorization: Bearer ... Header(...) or a security dependency JSON body {"items": [...]} A Pydantic model such as CreateOrderRequest This means Pydantic is not a replacement for HTTP methods. It is the next layer down. The method tells the server what the client is trying to do; Pydantic validates the structured data the client sends while doing it. Quick table (print-this-in-your-brain) ⭐ = widely used. Most APIs are mostly these 5. Method Intent Safe? Idempotent? Commonly cacheable? Body typical? ⭐ GET Read data Yes Yes Often Usually no ⭐ POST Create / run action No No (by default) Usually no Often yes ⭐ PUT Replace full resource (or create at known URL) No Yes Usually no Often yes ⭐ PATCH Partial update No Depends Usually no Often yes ⭐ DELETE Remove resource No Yes (in intent) Usually no Usually no HEAD Like GET, but headers only Yes Yes Often No OPTIONS Discover what’s allowed Yes Yes Usually no No Widely used methods (you’ll use these 99% of the time) Think of a URL like a noun (resource). Methods are verbs. GET = read POST = create/action PUT = replace PATCH = partial DELETE = remove Inline SVG “image”: self-contained, no external assets. ⭐ GET — read Use when: fetching data (read-only). Example: GET /users/42 → return user 42 Safe Idempotent Commonly cacheable Full request message GET /users/42?include=orders HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/json FastAPI from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI() @app.get("/users/{user_id}") def get_user(user_id: int, include: str | None = None): return {"user_id": user_id, "include": include} Beginner tip: If you can bookmark it, refresh it, or share the URL and it still makes sense, it’s probably a GET. ⭐ POST — create or “do an action” Use when: Creating a new resource under a collection (POST /orders) Triggering an operation that doesn’t map cleanly to CRUD (POST /reports/run) Example: POST /orders with body {"items": [...]} → creates a new order Unsafe Not idempotent by default Body usually contains the “create/action” input Full request message POST /orders HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: Bearer <token> Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json { "items": [{"sku": "ABC", "qty": 2}] } FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel class OrderItem(BaseModel): sku: str qty: int class CreateOrderRequest(BaseModel): items: list[OrderItem] @app.post("/orders") def create_order(payload: CreateOrderRequest): return {"created": True, "order_id": 123, "items": payload.items} The method POST says this is a create/action request. The Pydantic model CreateOrderRequest says what the JSON body must contain. Those are two different parts of the same API contract. ⭐ PUT — replace (or create at a known URL) Use when: you want the resource at a URL to become exactly what you send. Example: PUT /users/42 with a full user object → replaces user 42 Unsafe Idempotent Body usually contains the full resource state Full request message PUT /users/42 HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: Bearer <token> Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json { "id": 42, "name": "Asha", "email": "asha@example.com" } Common beginner bug: Using PUT with a partial body. By intent, PUT is “replace the full resource”, so missing fields might get wiped unless you implement merge behavior. ⭐ PATCH — partial update Use when: updating only some fields. Example: PATCH /users/42 with {"email": "new@x.com"} Unsafe Idempotency depends on design Body contains only changed fields (usually) Example PATCH request message PATCH /users/42 HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: Bearer <token> Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json { "email": "new@x.com" } Idempotency note: A patch like “set email to X” is usually idempotent. A patch like “increment login_count by 1” is not. ⭐ DELETE — remove Use when: deleting a resource. Example: DELETE /users/42 Unsafe Idempotent in intent Beginner intuition: Deleting twice should still end “deleted”. The second delete often returns 404 or 204 depending on API design. Common but less used (still important) HEAD — like GET, but only headers Use when: you want metadata without downloading the body. Example: check if a file changed using ETag/Last-Modified. OPTIONS — “what’s allowed here?” Use when: discovering supported methods/headers. Most common real-world use: CORS preflight (browser checks if it can call your API cross-origin). If you ever see a browser sending an OPTIONS request before your real request, that’s usually CORS, not “your frontend being weird”. Rare / niche methods (you’ll see them sometimes) TRACE — diagnostic (often disabled) Often disabled for security reasons. CONNECT — tunneling (proxies + HTTPS) Used to establish a tunnel through an HTTP proxy (common in corporate networks). Practical mapping to REST-style endpoints Collections vs single resources Type Method Example Meaning Collection GET GET /items List/search items Collection POST POST /items Create a new item (server assigns ID) Single resource GET GET /items/{id} Read one item Single resource PUT PUT /items/{id} Replace item (or create if not exists) Single resource PATCH PATCH /items/{id} Partial update Single resource DELETE DELETE /items/{id} Delete The “PUT vs POST feels same” confusion (quick intuition) POST = “You decide what happens” Think: “Here’s something; you decide what happens (often create a new thing).” The server usually chooses the new ID. PUT = “Make this URL have this exact content” Think: “Make /users/42 look exactly like this payload.” You’re targeting a specific URL. If you repeat the same request: Repeating PUT should converge to the same final state (idempotent). Repeating POST can create duplicates unless you add idempotency keys. What an HTTP request looks like A client talks to your FastAPI backend by sending an HTTP request message: METHOD /path?query=string HTTP/1.1 Header-Name: value Authorization: Bearer <token> Content-Type: application/json { "optional": "body" } METHOD: intent (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) /path: which resource (e.g. /documents/123) ?query=…: options/filters (e.g. ?limit=20) Headers: metadata (auth token, content type) Body: payload (often JSON; usually only for POST/PUT/PATCH) How FastAPI “decodes” the message FastAPI turns parts of the HTTP message into Python values using type hints: Path params → function args (e.g. user_id: int) Query params → function args (e.g. limit: int = 20) Headers → via Header(...) or security dependencies JSON body → Pydantic models (request schemas) If types don’t match, FastAPI returns a 422 validation error automatically. Next step: read the FastAPI request mapping chapter to see one HTTP message become Python function arguments, then the Pydantic chapter to understand how JSON bodies become validated Python objects.

description: The HTTP chapter separated method, URL, headers, and body. This chapter follows one request through FastAPI and shows exactly how each part becomes a typed Python value. The Pydantic chapter then explains the body mod...
text: The HTTP chapter separated method, URL, headers, and body. This chapter follows one request through FastAPI and shows exactly how each part becomes a typed Python value. The Pydantic chapter then explains the body model in depth. 1) The endpoint declares the contract from typing import Annotated from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, Query from pydantic import BaseModel, Field app = FastAPI() class QueryReq(BaseModel): question: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=2_000) class QueryResponse(BaseModel): collection_id: str q: str top_k: int auth_header: str | None @app.post( "/collections/{collection_id}/query", response_model=QueryResponse, ) def query( collection_id: str, req: QueryReq, top_k: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=50)] = 5, authorization: Annotated[str | None, Header()] = None, ) -> QueryResponse: return QueryResponse( collection_id=collection_id, q=req.question, top_k=top_k, auth_header=authorization, ) The route decorator and function signature together form the boundary contract. FastAPI inspects the signature once when the application starts and builds validation plus OpenAPI metadata from it. 2) A real HTTP request message (what the client sends) POST /collections/policies/query?top_k=10 HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: Bearer abc.def.ghi Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json {"question": "What does my policy say about refunds?"} There are five separate inputs here: method, path template, path parameter, query parameter, header, and JSON body. FastAPI does not merge them into one undifferentiated dictionary. Visual: one request, several typed sources HTTP message route POST /collections/policies/query query top_k=10 header Authorization: Bearer ... body {"question": "..."} FastAPI route match extract convert validate Python arguments collection_id = "policies" top_k = 10 authorization = "Bearer ..." req = QueryReq(...) 3) How FastAPI maps that message into your function arguments A) Method + path decide which function runs Method = POST Path = /query So FastAPI matches @app.post("/collections/{collection_id}/query") and selects query(...). A GET request to the same path would not match this route. B) The path segment becomes collection_id The route template names one dynamic segment: {collection_id}. The actual URL supplies policies, so FastAPI sets: collection_id = "policies" If the annotation were collection_id: UUID or collection_id: int, FastAPI would validate and convert the segment before calling the function. C) Query string becomes top_k From the first line: ?top_k=10 FastAPI finds top_k="10" in the query string Converts "10" → 10 because you typed it as int Checks ge=1 and le=50 If it wasn’t provided, it would use the default 5 Result: top_k = 10 D) Header becomes authorization From the headers: Authorization: Bearer abc.def.ghi Because you wrote: authorization: str | None = Header(None) FastAPI reads the Authorization header and sets: authorization = "Bearer abc.def.ghi" If the header was missing, it would be None. E) JSON body becomes req From the body: { "question": "What does my policy say about refunds?" } Because req is a Pydantic model (QueryReq), FastAPI: parses the JSON into a dict validates it matches QueryReq (must have question: str) constructs a Python object: req = QueryReq(question="What does my policy say about refunds?") So inside your function: req is not “the raw request” req is a validated object built from the JSON body you access fields like req.question 4) What FastAPI effectively calls (conceptually) query( collection_id="policies", req=QueryReq(question="What does my policy say about refunds?"), top_k=10, authorization="Bearer abc.def.ghi", ) This is a mental model, not literal generated source code. FastAPI also resolves dependencies, handles async/sync execution, and builds an HTTP response around the return value. Summary: That’s the whole mapping: query params → normal args, headers → Header(...) args, JSON body → Pydantic model arg (req), and the method+path choose the endpoint. 5) How FastAPI decides where a parameter comes from DeclarationSourceExample Name appears in the route templatePathcollection_id: str Simple scalar with no path matchQuery by defaulttop_k: int = 5 Header(...)Headerauthorization Cookie(...)CookieApplication session cookie Body(...) or Pydantic modelRequest bodyreq: QueryReq Depends(...)Dependency graphVerified identity, database session, service Form(...) / File(...)Form or multipart bodyLogin form or uploaded file Use explicit helpers when ambiguity would make the contract harder to read. In production, authentication normally becomes a security dependency rather than a raw optional string: from fastapi import Depends def query( collection_id: str, req: QueryReq, identity: Identity = Depends(get_verified_identity), top_k: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=50)] = 5, ) -> QueryResponse: ... 6) Invalid input stops before business logic If top_k=abc, if top_k=1000, or if the JSON body omits question, FastAPI does not call query(). Validation produces a structured 422 Unprocessable Content response that identifies the source and field path. { "detail": [ { "type": "less_than_equal", "loc": ["query", "top_k"], "msg": "Input should be less than or equal to 50", "input": "1000" } ] } Malformed JSON is also a client-input error. Authentication failures should be 401; authenticated callers without permission should receive 403; a hidden or absent resource is commonly 404. Do not turn all client errors into 500. 7) The return value travels back through a response contract response_model=QueryResponse validates and serializes the returned data. It also filters undeclared fields, which helps prevent internal values from leaking into the API response. FastAPI uses the request and response models to generate OpenAPI documentation. HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json { "collection_id": "policies", "q": "What does my policy say about refunds?", "top_k": 10, "auth_header": "Bearer abc.def.ghi" } Next conceptual step This chapter treated QueryReq as a black box that validates a body. The next chapter opens that box, beginning with ordinary Python classes and dataclasses before deriving Pydantic models, constraints, aliases, serialization, settings, and API contracts.
