description: FastAPI uses Pydantic because web applications live at the boundary between untyped external data and typed Python code. This chapter starts from ordinary Python classes, moves through dataclasses, then shows why Pyda...
text: FastAPI uses Pydantic because web applications live at the boundary between untyped external data and typed Python code. This chapter starts from ordinary Python classes, moves through dataclasses, then shows why Pydantic became the standard way to validate JSON, serialize objects, manage settings, and enforce structured LLM outputs. Where this fits in the book Chapter 3 showed how FastAPI maps HTTP requests into function arguments. This chapter explains the data model layer behind that mapping. After this, the concurrency, authentication, tenancy, and integration chapters can rely on one consistent idea: external data must be validated at the boundary and converted into explicit Python objects before business logic touches it. 1) Start with Python Objects: Class Variables, Instance Variables, and __init__ Before Pydantic makes sense, the reader needs a clear mental model of a normal Python object. A class is the blueprint. An instance is one concrete object built from that blueprint. Variables can live in either place, and that difference matters when you model API data. class User: species = "human" # class variable: shared by the class def __init__(self, user_id: int, name: str): self.user_id = user_id # instance variable: belongs to this object self.name = name # instance variable: belongs to this object alice = User(1, "Alice") bob = User(2, "Bob") print(alice.name) # Alice print(bob.name) # Bob print(User.species) # human __init__ is the initializer that runs after Python creates a new object. It is where ordinary classes usually copy constructor arguments onto self. In the example above, alice.name and bob.name are different because each instance has its own name attribute. Precise wording: __init__ creates or assigns instance variables on self. A class variable belongs to the class object itself and is shared by instances unless an instance overrides that attribute with its own value. Why class variables can surprise you Class variables are useful for constants, shared configuration, registries, or metadata. They are dangerous when you accidentally use them for per-object state, especially with mutable values such as lists or dictionaries. class BadCart: items: list[str] = [] # shared class-level list, not per-cart state cart_a = BadCart() cart_b = BadCart() cart_a.items.append("keyboard") print(cart_b.items) # ["keyboard"] # cart_b sees cart_a's item because the list is shared The correct plain-class version creates the mutable list inside __init__, so every instance gets its own list. class Cart: def __init__(self): self.items: list[str] = [] cart_a = Cart() cart_b = Cart() cart_a.items.append("keyboard") print(cart_b.items) # [] What @classmethod is actually for A class method receives the class as cls instead of receiving one instance as self. It does not make class variables belong to an instance. It is most often used for alternate constructors, factories, and logic that should respect subclasses. class User: default_active = True def __init__(self, user_id: int, name: str, active: bool): self.user_id = user_id self.name = name self.active = active @classmethod def from_dict(cls, data: dict) -> "User": active = data.get("active", cls.default_active) if isinstance(active, str): active = active.lower() if active in {"true", "1", "yes"}: active = True elif active in {"false", "0", "no"}: active = False else: raise ValueError("active must be true or false") return cls( user_id=int(data["user_id"]), name=str(data["name"]), active=active, ) user = User.from_dict({"user_id": "123", "name": "Alice"}) print(user.active) # True This example is already moving toward structured data modeling. We are manually doing conversion, defaults, and object construction inside from_dict. That works for tiny examples, but it becomes repetitive and error-prone when payloads are nested, fields are optional, constraints matter, error messages must be precise, and OpenAPI schema needs to be generated. 2) The Data Problem Before Pydantic JSON has fewer types than Python JSON is the common language of HTTP APIs, browser clients, queues, config files, and many LLM tool calls. It has only a small set of data types: JSON typeExamplePython usually wants string"Alice"str, sometimes datetime, EmailStr, UUID, Enum number30, 19.99int, float, Decimal booleantrue, falsebool nullnullNone, only if the field is nullable array["Python", "FastAPI"]list[str], tuple, set object{"city": "Sydney"}nested model, typed dict, dictionary That mismatch explains why validation belongs at the API boundary. JSON does not know what a Python datetime, UUID, enum, or domain object is. Your code has to decide what to accept, what to convert, what to reject, and what error to return. Plain Python classes hold data but do not validate input class User: def __init__(self, id: int, name: str, active: bool = True): self.id = id self.name = name self.active = active user = User(id="123", name=42, active="yes") print(user.id, user.name, user.active) # "123" 42 "yes" # type hints did not validate anything at runtime Python type hints help editors, static type checkers, and humans. They do not automatically validate runtime values. Without extra code, the constructor accepts whatever the caller passes. Manual validation quickly becomes repetitive You can write validation yourself inside __init__ or a @classmethod factory, but every model then needs its own parsing, conversion, defaults, error messages, and nested-object handling. class User: def __init__(self, id: int, name: str, active: bool = True): if not isinstance(id, int): raise TypeError("id must be an integer") if not isinstance(name, str): raise TypeError("name must be a string") if not isinstance(active, bool): raise TypeError("active must be a boolean") self.id = id self.name = name self.active = active @classmethod def from_json_dict(cls, data: dict) -> "User": active = data.get("active", True) if isinstance(active, str): active = active.lower() if active in {"true", "1", "yes"}: active = True elif active in {"false", "0", "no"}: active = False else: raise ValueError("active must be true or false") return cls( id=int(data["id"]), name=str(data["name"]), active=active, ) This is the bridge to Pydantic: the industry-standard version should keep the readable class shape, but make validation, conversion, error reporting, schema generation, and nested parsing consistent instead of hand-written in every constructor. 3) Dataclasses: The First Improvement Python dataclasses are the natural next step after a hand-written __init__. They let you describe the data fields once, then Python generates the repetitive object methods for you. from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class User: id: int name: str roles: list[str] = field(default_factory=list) user = User(id="123", name=42) print(user) # User(id='123', name=42, roles=[]) The annotation syntax looks similar to a Pydantic model, but at this stage it is still just Python dataclass machinery. The type hints define the fields used to generate methods; they do not automatically validate runtime values. Generated methodWhat the dataclass gives you __init__Creates an initializer with parameters for the declared fields. __repr__Returns a readable string representation such as User(id=...). __eq__Compares two instances by field values. __hash__Generated only when the class is immutable/frozen enough to be hashable. __post_init__Optional hook that runs after __init__ for extra setup or manual validation. Class variables in dataclasses: use ClassVar If a value belongs to the class and should not be treated as an instance field, annotate it with ClassVar. This is how you keep constants or shared metadata out of the generated __init__. from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import ClassVar @dataclass class User: species: ClassVar[str] = "Homo sapiens" # not part of __init__ name: str age: int user = User(name="Alice", age=30) print(user.species) # Homo sapiens Mutable defaults: use default_factory The same shared-mutable-value problem exists in dataclass-style modeling. If each instance should get its own list, dictionary, or set, create it with a factory. from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Team: members: list[str] = field(default_factory=list) team_a = Team() team_b = Team() team_a.members.append("Alice") print(team_a.members) # ["Alice"] print(team_b.members) # [] This is the same idea as avoiding mutable default arguments in functions: def add_name(name: str, names: list[str] = []): # avoid this names.append(name) return names The list is created once when the function is defined, not once per call. Dataclasses force you toward default_factory because per-instance state should be created per instance. Dataclasses still do not validate input types Dataclasses solve boilerplate, representation, equality, and mutable default setup, but they still do not validate types by default. id="123" and name=42 are accepted because dataclasses are data containers, not runtime validators. You can add manual checks in __post_init__, but then you are back to writing custom validation logic for every class. from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class User: id: int name: str def __post_init__(self): if not isinstance(self.id, int): raise TypeError("id must be an integer") if not isinstance(self.name, str): raise TypeError("name must be a string") Industry distinction: use a dataclass when data is already trusted and you want a lightweight internal container. Use Pydantic when data crosses a boundary: HTTP request, queue event, file, environment variable, third-party API response, database document, or LLM output. 4) Why Pydantic Exists Most backend bugs at API boundaries are not caused by complicated algorithms. They are caused by ordinary shape mismatches: The client sends "age": "30" but Python code expects age: int. The frontend uses personalEmail but Python code should use personal_email. A required field is missing, but the function assumes it exists. A nested payload has the correct outer shape but invalid inner objects. An LLM returns text that looks like JSON but is not the contract your code promised to handle. Pydantic was introduced to solve this boundary problem using Python type annotations. It gives you a class that still feels like normal Python, but it adds runtime validation, conversion, error reporting, JSON schema generation, serialization, and integration hooks used by frameworks such as FastAPI. Core mental model: Pydantic turns unreliable outside data into reliable inside objects. Your API should accept dictionaries/JSON at the boundary, validate them once, then pass typed objects through the rest of the system. Visual: boundary validation External data JSON, form, env vars LLM output, API response Pydantic model validate + convert report precise errors generate schema/docs Python object known fields known types invalid input becomes a structured validation error 5) Pydantic Models: Dataclass Ergonomics + Runtime Validation A Pydantic model is a class that inherits from BaseModel. It uses annotations like a dataclass, generates a constructor like a dataclass, but also validates and converts data at runtime. In Pydantic language, the class is usually called a model. Inheritance is what gives the class its extra behavior: BaseModel reads the annotations, builds model fields, creates validation logic, and adds methods for deserialization, serialization, error reporting, and schema generation. from pydantic import BaseModel class User(BaseModel): id: int name: str active: bool = True roles: list[str] = [] user = User(id="123", name="Alice", active="true") print(user) # id=123 name='Alice' active=True roles=[] Several important things happened: "123" became 123 because the field is int. "true" became True because the field is bool. The model has a clear set of fields: id, name, active, roles. Pydantic handles mutable defaults safely by copying them per instance. That default conversion behavior is useful for APIs because JSON, query parameters, forms, environment variables, and CSV values often arrive as strings. If you want no conversion, use strict mode, covered below. Three common ways to create or deserialize a model The deck uses an important flow here: once the model exists, there are three practical ways data enters it. from pydantic import BaseModel class User(BaseModel): name: str age: int # 1) Constructor: common when values are already in Python code u1 = User(name="Alice Smith", age=30) # 2) model_validate: validate a Python dict/object, common after JSON parsing payload = {"name": "Bob Jones", "age": "25"} u2 = User.model_validate(payload) # 3) model_validate_json: validate raw JSON text directly json_str = '{"name": "Carol Lee", "age": 27}' u3 = User.model_validate_json(json_str) All three paths produce a User instance. The difference is where the raw data starts: already-keyword arguments, a Python dictionary, or a JSON string. Why Pydantic fields are written in the class body This is the part that can feel strange if you just learned ordinary class variables. In a normal class, roles = [] in the class body is a shared class variable. In a Pydantic BaseModel, annotated fields in the class body are treated as model-field declarations. Pydantic reads those annotations when the class is created and builds its own validation and construction logic. class User(BaseModel): id: int # model field declaration name: str # model field declaration roles: list[str] = [] # Pydantic copies this safely per instance alice = User(id=1, name="Alice") bob = User(id=2, name="Bob") alice.roles.append("admin") print(bob.roles) # [] So the syntax looks class-level, but the meaning is not the same as an ordinary mutable class variable. Pydantic uses the class definition as a schema for constructing validated instances. If you want the explicit style that also works in dataclasses, use Field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults. 6) Validation Errors Are Part of the Contract Good validation is not just "reject bad data." It should tell the caller exactly what failed, where it failed, and why. from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError class User(BaseModel): id: int name: str try: User(id="not-a-number", name=123) except ValidationError as exc: print(exc.errors()) The error payload contains locations such as ("id",), an error message, an error type, and the bad input. FastAPI turns this into an HTTP 422 response for request-body validation failures. [ { "type": "int_parsing", "loc": ["id"], "msg": "Input should be a valid integer, unable to parse string as an integer", "input": "not-a-number" } ] 7) Required, Optional, Nullable, and Defaults This is one of the most important Pydantic topics because Python developers often mix up "optional" and "nullable." from pydantic import BaseModel class Customer(BaseModel): id: int # required, cannot be missing name: str # required, cannot be missing age: int | None # required, but may be null/None nickname: str | None = None # optional and nullable country: str = "AU" # optional, default used if missing DeclarationMay be missing?May be None?Meaning name: strNoNoRequired non-null string age: int | NoneNoYesRequired key, value may be null nickname: str | None = NoneYesYesOptional key, null/default allowed country: str = "AU"YesNoOptional key with non-null default API design rule: do not write age: int = None. If None is valid, say so in the type: age: int | None = None. If None is not valid, use a real default or make the field required. 8) Field Constraints with Field Type annotations describe the broad shape. Field describes constraints, aliases, examples, and metadata for JSON schema/OpenAPI. from decimal import Decimal from pydantic import BaseModel, Field class Product(BaseModel): sku: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=32, pattern=r"^[A-Z0-9-]+$") name: str = Field(min_length=1) price: Decimal = Field(gt=0, max_digits=10, decimal_places=2) tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list, max_length=10) product = Product(sku="SKU-100", name="Keyboard", price="129.95") print(product.price) # Decimal('129.95') Use constraints for domain rules that can be stated locally on one field: minimum length, maximum length, numeric range, regex/pattern, decimal precision, default factories, examples, and descriptions. 9) Coercion Mode vs Strict Mode Pydantic's default behavior is intentionally practical: it tries to convert compatible values. This is commonly called lax mode or coercive validation. That is the normal API mode because external data often arrives as strings. from pydantic import BaseModel class SearchParams(BaseModel): top_k: int include_archived: bool = False params = SearchParams(top_k="10", include_archived="false") print(params) # top_k=10 include_archived=False A product payload shows the same idea across several JSON-compatible types: from pydantic import BaseModel class Product(BaseModel): name: str price: float in_stock: bool product = Product.model_validate({ "name": "Keyboard", "price": "19.99", # str -> float "in_stock": "true", # str -> bool }) Lax mode does not mean "anything becomes anything." Pydantic v2 is more careful than older examples: for example, an integer is not automatically accepted as a string field unless you explicitly configure that behavior. For money movement, security policy, compliance checks, or any place where conversion could hide a bug, use strict validation. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError class StrictSearchParams(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True) top_k: int include_archived: bool = False try: StrictSearchParams(top_k="10") except ValidationError as exc: print(exc.errors()[0]["msg"]) # Input should be a valid integer You can also make selected fields strict instead of making the whole model strict. from pydantic import BaseModel, Field class Payment(BaseModel): amount_cents: int = Field(strict=True, gt=0) currency: str 10) Aliases: JSON camelCase and Python snake_case External APIs often use camelCase. Python code should use snake_case. Pydantic aliases let you support both without leaking JSON naming conventions into internal code. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field class UserProfile(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True) user_id: str = Field(alias="userId") personal_email: str = Field(alias="personalEmail") payload = {"userId": "u_123", "personalEmail": "alice@example.com"} profile = UserProfile.model_validate(payload) print(profile.personal_email) # alice@example.com print(profile.model_dump(by_alias=True)) # {'userId': 'u_123', 'personalEmail': 'alice@example.com'} In real systems, aliases are a contract boundary. Internal code should speak Python. External JSON should speak the API contract. Alias generator for large APIs from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict def to_camel(name: str) -> str: first, *rest = name.split("_") return first + "".join(word.capitalize() for word in rest) class ApiModel(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict( alias_generator=to_camel, validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True, ) class Account(ApiModel): account_id: str billing_email: str account = Account.model_validate({"accountId": "a_1", "billingEmail": "ops@example.com"}) print(account.model_dump(by_alias=True)) Pydantic also provides common alias helpers. If your whole API uses camelCase, prefer a shared base model instead of repeating Field(alias=...) everywhere. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict from pydantic.alias_generators import to_camel class ApiModel(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict( alias_generator=to_camel, validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True, ) class User(ApiModel): first_name: str user = User.model_validate({"firstName": "Alice"}) print(user.model_dump(by_alias=True)) # {'firstName': 'Alice'} print(user.model_dump()) # {'first_name': 'Alice'} Older examples: you may see populate_by_name=True in Pydantic v2 material. For current v2 code, prefer the more explicit pair validate_by_name=True and validate_by_alias=True. 11) Nested Models Real JSON payloads are rarely flat. A model can contain other models, lists of models, dictionaries of models, enums, and constrained fields. from enum import Enum from pydantic import BaseModel, Field class Plan(str, Enum): FREE = "free" TEAM = "team" ENTERPRISE = "enterprise" class Address(BaseModel): line1: str city: str country: str = "AU" class Organisation(BaseModel): org_id: str plan: Plan billing_address: Address admins: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list) org = Organisation.model_validate({ "org_id": "org_123", "plan": "enterprise", "billing_address": {"line1": "1 Market St", "city": "Sydney"}, "admins": ["alice@example.com", "bob@example.com"], }) print(org.billing_address.city) # Sydney If a nested field fails, the error path points to the nested location, such as billing_address.city or admins.1. That makes validation errors actionable for both frontend engineers and API clients. 12) Validators: Field-Level and Model-Level Rules Use built-in types and Field constraints first. Add validators when the rule is domain-specific or depends on multiple fields. Field validators from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator class Signup(BaseModel): email: str display_name: str @field_validator("email") @classmethod def email_must_look_valid(cls, value: str) -> str: value = value.strip().lower() if "@" not in value: raise ValueError("email must contain @") return value signup = Signup(email=" ALICE@EXAMPLE.COM ", display_name="Alice") print(signup.email) # alice@example.com Model validators Use a model validator when the rule needs more than one field. from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator class DateRange(BaseModel): start_day: int end_day: int @model_validator(mode="after") def end_must_not_precede_start(self): if self.end_day < self.start_day: raise ValueError("end_day must be greater than or equal to start_day") return self Pydantic v1 to v2 naming: older notes and examples often use @validator, @root_validator, .dict(), .json(), and parse_raw(). In modern Pydantic v2, prefer @field_validator, @model_validator, model_dump(), model_dump_json(), model_validate(), and model_validate_json(). FastAPI compatibility: current FastAPI development is on Pydantic v2. FastAPI 0.128.0 removed support for importing models through pydantic.v1. Treat v1 syntax as migration material, not a pattern for new endpoints, and test framework/Pydantic upgrades together because request validation and generated OpenAPI are part of the API contract. 13) Model Configuration: Class-Level Behavior for Fields Configuration controls model-wide behavior. In Pydantic v2, use model_config = ConfigDict(...). This is where you set behavior for the model as a whole. Use Field(...) when the rule belongs to one field; use model_config when the rule belongs to all fields or the model contract. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field class SecurePayload(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict( extra="forbid", str_strip_whitespace=True, validate_assignment=True, frozen=False, ) tenant_id: str = Field(min_length=1) user_id: str = Field(min_length=1) payload = SecurePayload(tenant_id=" acme ", user_id=" u_123 ") print(payload.tenant_id) # acme ConfigWhy it matters extra="forbid"Reject unknown fields instead of silently ignoring them. Good for security-sensitive APIs. extra="ignore"Ignore unknown fields. Useful when consuming third-party APIs that add fields over time. extra="allow"Keep unknown fields. Useful for flexible metadata, but avoid it for core contracts. strict=TrueDisable broad coercion. Good when conversion could hide defects. validate_default=TrueValidate default values too, instead of trusting them silently. validate_assignment=TrueValidate when fields are changed after model creation. frozen=TrueMake models immutable after creation. Useful for config and value objects. str_strip_whitespace=TrueNormalize incoming strings at the boundary. Extra fields: the default is usually ignore, but sensitive APIs should forbid By default, Pydantic v2 ignores unknown fields. That is useful when consuming external APIs that may add fields over time. For your own security-sensitive request contracts, prefer extra="forbid" so a misspelled or unexpected field becomes a validation error. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError class Model(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid") field1: int try: Model(field1=10, field2=20) except ValidationError as exc: print(exc.errors()[0]["type"]) # extra_forbidden Validate defaults when defaults can be wrong Defaults are usually trusted. If a default itself might violate the declared type or constraints, set validate_default=True. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError class Model(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(validate_default=True) field1: int | None = None # Valid because the type explicitly allows None. Model() class BadDefault(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(validate_default=True) field1: int = None try: BadDefault() except ValidationError as exc: print(exc.errors()[0]["msg"]) # Input should be a valid integer Validate assignment when objects are modified after creation Without assignment validation, Pydantic validates during construction but does not automatically check every later attribute assignment. Enable validate_assignment=True when models remain mutable but must stay valid. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError class Model(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(validate_assignment=True) field: int m = Model(field=1) try: m.field = "hello" except ValidationError as exc: print(exc.errors()[0]["msg"]) Use frozen models when mutation should be blocked frozen=True makes the model immutable after construction. This is useful for configuration objects, value objects, and contracts where later mutation would make reasoning harder. from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError class Model(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True) field: int m = Model(field=10) try: m.field = 20 except ValidationError as exc: print(exc.errors()[0]["msg"]) # Instance is frozen 14) Deserialization and Serialization Deserialization means turning external data into Python objects. Serialization means turning Python objects back into dictionaries or JSON. Validate a Python dictionary from pydantic import BaseModel class User(BaseModel): id: int name: str data = {"id": "123", "name": "Alice"} user = User.model_validate(data) Validate JSON text json_data = '{"id": "123", "name": "Alice"}' user = User.model_validate_json(json_data) Serialize to a Python dictionary or JSON string print(user.model_dump()) # {'id': 123, 'name': 'Alice'} print(user.model_dump_json()) # {"id":123,"name":"Alice"} model_dump(mode="python") may include Python-native objects such as datetime and Decimal. Use mode="json" or model_dump_json() when preparing data for JSON responses, logs, queues, or cache entries. 15) JSON Schema and OpenAPI Pydantic can produce JSON Schema from your model. FastAPI uses that schema to generate OpenAPI documentation and request/response examples. from pydantic import BaseModel, Field class CreateTicket(BaseModel): title: str = Field(min_length=3, examples=["Reset my VPN access"]) priority: int = Field(ge=1, le=5, description="1 is highest priority") print(CreateTicket.model_json_schema()) This is why FastAPI can show a form-like documentation page for your request body: the Pydantic model is both runtime validation and machine-readable API contract. 16) TypeAdapter: Validate a Type Without Creating a Model Sometimes you do not need a named model. You just need to validate list[int], dict[str, Decimal], or list[SomeModel]. Use TypeAdapter. from pydantic import BaseModel, TypeAdapter class Item(BaseModel): id: int name: str adapter = TypeAdapter(list[Item]) items = adapter.validate_python([ {"id": "1", "name": "Keyboard"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Mouse"}, ]) print(items) # [Item(id=1, name='Keyboard'), Item(id=2, name='Mouse')] TypeAdapter is useful for validating lists from files, queue batches, third-party responses, and LLM output arrays without inventing a wrapper model. 17) Settings Management with pydantic-settings In Pydantic v2, settings moved to the separate pydantic-settings package. Use it to read environment variables, .env files, and secrets into a typed object. pip install pydantic-settings from pydantic import Field from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict class Settings(BaseSettings): model_config = SettingsConfigDict( env_file=".env", env_prefix="APP_", extra="ignore", ) app_name: str = "tutorial-api" debug: bool = False database_url: str jwt_audience: str = Field(default="tutorial-api") settings = Settings() print(settings.database_url) With env_prefix="APP_", Pydantic reads variables such as APP_DATABASE_URL, APP_DEBUG, and APP_JWT_AUDIENCE. This follows twelve-factor application practice: configuration belongs in the environment, not hard-coded in source files. Do not log settings objects blindly. If a settings model contains secrets, mark them as SecretStr or keep logging focused on non-sensitive fields. 18) FastAPI Integration: Request and Response Contracts FastAPI uses Pydantic models in two directions: Request models validate data coming into your endpoint. Response models define and filter data leaving your endpoint. from decimal import Decimal from fastapi import FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field app = FastAPI() class CreateProductRequest(BaseModel): sku: str = Field(min_length=3) name: str price: Decimal = Field(gt=0) class ProductResponse(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True) sku: str name: str price: Decimal @app.post("/products", response_model=ProductResponse) def create_product(req: CreateProductRequest): # req is already validated here. product = save_product(req) # response_model controls what leaves the API. return product response_model is not just documentation. It prevents accidental data leaks by shaping the returned object. If your internal object has cost_price, supplier_token, or other private fields, they are not included unless the response model declares them. 19) External API and Queue Message Validation Pydantic is not only for incoming HTTP requests. Use it whenever your system receives data it did not create. from datetime import datetime from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field class PaymentEvent(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid") event_id: str tenant_id: str amount_cents: int = Field(gt=0) occurred_at: datetime def handle_message(raw_json: str) -> None: event = PaymentEvent.model_validate_json(raw_json) process_payment_event(event) This pattern is useful for Pub/Sub messages, Kafka events, webhook payloads, cron job inputs, uploaded JSON files, and service-to-service responses. 20) LLM Output Validation Pydantic gained renewed importance with LLM systems because model outputs are probabilistic. Even when you ask for JSON, you still need to validate the shape before using it in application code. from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError class SupportTriage(BaseModel): category: str confidence: float = Field(ge=0, le=1) summary: str = Field(min_length=1) next_action: str raw_llm_json = ''' { "category": "account_access", "confidence": 0.87, "summary": "User cannot access VPN after password reset.", "next_action": "route_to_identity_team" } ''' try: triage = SupportTriage.model_validate_json(raw_llm_json) except ValidationError as exc: # Retry, ask the model to repair, or send to human review. raise print(triage.next_action) In production LLM workflows, Pydantic is a guardrail, not a guarantee. It checks structure and local constraints. You still need business-rule validation, authorization checks, rate limits, audit logs, and human review for high-risk actions. 21) Pydantic Dataclasses Pydantic can also validate dataclasses. This is useful when you prefer dataclass style but want Pydantic validation on construction. from pydantic import ConfigDict, ValidationError from pydantic.dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass(config=ConfigDict(validate_assignment=True)) class Job: job_id: int queue: str job = Job(job_id="42", queue="email") print(job.job_id) # 42 try: job.job_id = "not-an-int" except ValidationError as exc: print(exc.errors()[0]["msg"]) Use this when integrating with dataclass-heavy code. For API contracts, settings, and OpenAPI integration, BaseModel is still the usual choice. 22) Practical Design Patterns Separate input, domain, and output models Do not use one giant model for every layer. API inputs, internal domain objects, database records, and API responses have different responsibilities. from pydantic import BaseModel, Field class CreateUserRequest(BaseModel): email: str display_name: str = Field(min_length=1) class UserRecord(BaseModel): user_id: str tenant_id: str email: str display_name: str password_hash: str class UserResponse(BaseModel): user_id: str email: str display_name: str This avoids two common mistakes: accepting fields the client should not control, and returning fields the client should never see. Validate at boundaries, not everywhere Validate when data enters the system. Inside the system, pass typed objects. Repeated validation in every function makes code noisy and hides the real trust boundary. Prefer explicit models over unstructured dictionaries # Weak boundary def create_ticket(payload: dict) -> dict: return {"title": payload["title"], "priority": int(payload["priority"])} # Strong boundary class CreateTicket(BaseModel): title: str priority: int = Field(ge=1, le=5) def create_ticket(payload: CreateTicket) -> dict: return {"title": payload.title, "priority": payload.priority} 23) Common Pitfalls PitfallBetter approach Using dict for every payloadCreate named models for important contracts. Confusing optional with nullableUse T | None only when None is valid. Letting extra fields pass through sensitive APIsUse extra="forbid" for strict input contracts. Using one model for create/update/response/databaseSplit models by responsibility. Trusting LLM JSON without validationValidate with a model or TypeAdapter, then apply business checks. Teaching v1 decorators in new codeUse v2 methods: field_validator, model_validator, model_dump. Logging secrets from settingsUse secret types and controlled logging. 24) End-to-End Example: API Payload, Alias, Validation, and Response This example combines the pieces: JSON aliases, strict API shape, field constraints, model-level validation, and response shaping. from decimal import Decimal from fastapi import FastAPI from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, model_validator app = FastAPI() class PurchaseRequest(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict( extra="forbid", validate_by_name=True, validate_by_alias=True, ) tenant_id: str = Field(alias="tenantId", min_length=1) user_id: str = Field(alias="userId", min_length=1) sku: str = Field(min_length=3) quantity: int = Field(alias="qty", gt=0, le=100) unit_price: Decimal = Field(alias="unitPrice", gt=0) @model_validator(mode="after") def total_must_be_reasonable(self): total = self.quantity * self.unit_price if total > Decimal("50000"): raise ValueError("purchase requires manual approval") return self class PurchaseResponse(BaseModel): purchase_id: str = Field(alias="purchaseId") status: str total: Decimal @app.post("/purchase", response_model=PurchaseResponse) def create_purchase(req: PurchaseRequest): total = req.quantity * req.unit_price return { "purchaseId": "po_123", "status": "accepted", "total": total, } The endpoint can now rely on req.tenant_id, req.user_id, req.quantity, and req.unit_price having already passed the declared contract. The external JSON can still use tenantId, userId, qty, and unitPrice. 25) Decision Guide NeedUse Internal trusted data containerdataclass HTTP request/response contractBaseModel Environment configurationpydantic-settings BaseSettings Validate a list/dict/primitive type directlyTypeAdapter Use dataclass syntax but add validationpydantic.dataclasses.dataclass Strict financial/security dataConfigDict(strict=True) or strict fields Frontend camelCase with Python snake_caseField(alias=...) or alias_generator LLM structured outputBaseModel or TypeAdapter plus business-rule checks 26) What to Remember Plain classes and dataclasses organize data but do not validate runtime input by default. Pydantic models are boundary contracts: validate, convert, serialize, and document data. Default Pydantic mode is practical and coercive; use strict mode where conversion is risky. Optional means "may be missing" only when there is a default. Nullable means the type includes None. Aliases let external JSON use camelCase while Python remains snake_case. Use v2 APIs in new code: model_validate, model_dump, field_validator, model_validator, and ConfigDict. Pydantic is also useful beyond FastAPI: settings, webhooks, queues, external APIs, files, and LLM output validation. Official references Pydantic documentation Pydantic v2 migration guide FastAPI: migrate from Pydantic v1 to v2 FastAPI request body models

title: FastAPI Concurrency and Per-Request User Isolation
label: 5. Concurrency and user isolation
headings: 1. What happens when 1000 users hit your API
2. Why async lets one server handle lots of traffic
3. Concurrency vs. Parallelism
4. How FastAPI keeps users separate (Per-Request Identity)
5. Critical Rule: No Global State
6. Tenant isolation must survive every boundary
7. Backpressure is part of concurrency design
8. Cancellation, disconnects, and observability
description: How one service keeps many in-flight requests efficient without mixing user or tenant state.
text: How one service keeps many in-flight requests efficient without mixing user or tenant state. Where this fits The preceding chapter established typed request boundaries with Pydantic. This chapter follows several validated requests while they execute at the same time. The next chapter moves slow work into durable background jobs without losing the same identity and tenant context. Concurrent requests sharing an event loop while retaining separate state Alice and Bob have independent request contexts. When one request awaits I/O, the event loop advances the other. Both calls reach tenant-scoped repositories. Alice request tenant-acme Bob request tenant-north Uvicorn event loop run A until await run B while A waits resume A when ready Scoped repository call WHERE tenant_id = tenant-acme Scoped repository call WHERE tenant_id = tenant-north Concurrency interleaves execution; it does not merge local variables. Isolation fails only when application code stores request-specific data in shared state or omits tenant filters. 1. What happens when 1000 users hit your API When thousands of users call your FastAPI endpoint simultaneously, Uvicorn (the ASGI server) accepts the connections. Within each worker process, the ASGI application handles each active request in its own in-flight task and request scope. For every single request, FastAPI: Matches the method + path (e.g., POST /query) to the correct function. Parses headers, query parameters, and the body specific to that request. Calls your function with fresh arguments. Key Concept: Each user request triggers an independent function call. Function arguments and local variables belong to that invocation. They are safe to interleave because Request A does not reuse Request B's Python stack frame. This is request isolation, not authorization: your code must still verify the caller and scope every data operation. 2. Why async lets one server handle lots of traffic Most API operations are I/O-bound: waiting for database queries, Elasticsearch results, or external APIs (like Azure OpenAI). If your endpoint is defined with async def and uses await for I/O, the event loop can pause a waiting request (Request A) and process others (Request B, C) in the meantime. This allows a single process to handle thousands of concurrent connections efficiently. @app.post("/query") async def query(): chunks = await es_search(...) # waiting -> event loop runs other requests answer = await call_openai(...) # waiting -> event loop runs other requests return {"answer": answer} Important: If you use blocking code (like time.sleep() or a synchronous HTTP client) inside async def, you freeze the event loop and kill concurrency. async def helps only when the libraries underneath it are asynchronous and the function reaches an await. A synchronous FastAPI endpoint is normally run in a thread pool, which is useful for blocking libraries but has finite capacity. CPU-heavy inference, image processing, and large dataframe work should use a separate process, worker service, or batch platform rather than occupying the API event loop. 3. Concurrency vs. Parallelism It is important to distinguish between these two scaling mechanisms: A) Async Concurrency (Recommended for I/O) One process + one event loop. Thousands of “tasks” can be in flight. Best when you await I/O operations. B) Parallelism (Workers) (Multi-process) Run multiple Uvicorn worker processes. Each process has its own event loop. Utilizes multiple CPU cores. Production systems usually combine both mechanisms: asynchronous I/O inside each worker, several workers or container replicas for CPU capacity and resilience, and a load balancer in front. Worker count is not a substitute for sizing database and HTTP connection pools; every replica can multiply downstream connections. 4. How FastAPI keeps users separate (Per-Request Identity) FastAPI does not “assign a user to a thread.” Instead, every HTTP request is isolated. User identity is derived from the request itself (usually via a JWT in the Authorization header), and your code uses this identity to scope data access. Concrete Example Two users hit the same endpoint at the same time, but get different results. from typing import Annotated from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException, status from pydantic import BaseModel app = FastAPI() class QueryReq(BaseModel): question: str class Identity(BaseModel): tenant_id: str user_id: str # Dependency to extract identity from a verified bearer token def get_identity( authorization: Annotated[str | None, Header()] = None, ) -> Identity: if not authorization or not authorization.startswith("Bearer "): raise HTTPException( status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED, detail="Missing bearer token", ) token = authorization.removeprefix("Bearer ").strip() # Verify signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and required claims. claims = verify_and_decode_jwt(token) return Identity(tenant_id=claims["tenant_id"], user_id=claims["sub"]) @app.post("/query") async def query( req: QueryReq, ident: Annotated[Identity, Depends(get_identity)], ): # The repository requires tenant_id; callers cannot "forget" the filter. chunks = await search_repository.search( tenant_id=ident.tenant_id, question=req.question, ) return {"user_id": ident.user_id, "chunks": chunks} User A Request Authorization: Bearer <verified JWT for Alice> FastAPI calls: ident=Identity(tenant_id="tenant-1", ...) User B Request Authorization: Bearer <verified JWT for Bob> FastAPI calls: ident=Identity(tenant_id="tenant-2", ...) Same code, same route — but different identity → tenants stay isolated. 5. Critical Rule: No Global State Never use global variables for per-user state. Globals are shared across all requests in a process. CURRENT_USER = None # unsafe: shared across requests in this process Instead, keep per-user/per-request data in: Function local variables (ident, req) Dependencies (Depends(get_identity)) request.state (middleware context) Module-level objects are not automatically wrong. Immutable configuration, database pool objects, HTTP clients, and model clients are normally shared. The unsafe pattern is putting mutable request data such as current_user, tenant_id, or a partially built response in them. 6. Tenant isolation must survive every boundary A verified identity is only the starting point. Carry the derived tenant and user identifiers through every call that can read, cache, enqueue, or store data. BoundaryIsolation ruleTypical backstop Repository / SQLRequire tenant_id in the method signature and query predicate.Row-level security and composite constraints. Search indexAdd a non-optional tenant filter to every query.Separate index/namespace for higher-risk tenants. CacheInclude tenant and authorization-relevant version data in the key.Short TTL and explicit invalidation. Object storageDerive the allowed prefix from trusted request context, never from an unchecked body field.Separate buckets or policy conditions where appropriate. Background jobPersist tenant, initiating user, authorization snapshot/version, and job ID.Worker-side re-authorization for sensitive effects. 7. Backpressure is part of concurrency design Accepting more concurrent requests than downstream systems can serve creates a queue inside your application. Latency rises, retries multiply the load, and eventually everything times out. Bound concurrency deliberately: Set connection-pool limits for databases and outbound HTTP clients. Use explicit connect, read, write, and pool-acquisition timeouts. Use a semaphore or worker queue around scarce downstream capacity. Return 429 Too Many Requests for caller-specific rate limits and 503 Service Unavailable when shared capacity is temporarily exhausted. Retry only transient failures, with exponential backoff and jitter; Chapter 6 develops that policy. 8. Cancellation, disconnects, and observability A client can disconnect while work is still running. Cooperative asynchronous libraries can receive cancellation, but an external side effect may already have happened. Use idempotency keys for effects, keep request deadlines shorter than infrastructure deadlines, and move work that must finish after disconnect into a durable job. Logs and traces should include a request ID, tenant ID, subject or internal user ID, route, downstream dependency, and latency. Do not log bearer tokens, raw secrets, or unnecessary personal data. A load test is incomplete unless it also checks cross-tenant leakage and downstream pool saturation. Operational test Run Alice and Bob requests concurrently, deliberately delay one downstream call, and assert that each response, cache key, SQL query, trace, and queued message retains the correct tenant.

title: Background Jobs, Idempotency, and Retries in FastAPI
label: 6. Background tasks and retries
headings: 1) Why slow work should not run inside the request
2) Separate best-effort background callbacks from durable jobs
3) First implementation: see the complete interaction with BackgroundTasks
4) Return job state without crossing tenant boundaries
5) Idempotency means one logical effect, not merely one HTTP response
6) Retry only failures that can plausibly succeed later
7) Retry steps, not an opaque whole workflow
8) Durable production pattern: transaction, queue, worker
9) Failure, cancellation, and dead-letter handling
10) Observability and operational controls
description: The concurrency chapter kept independent HTTP requests from blocking one another. This chapter handles a different problem: work that should outlive the request itself. We will move document ingestion into a job, make...
text: The concurrency chapter kept independent HTTP requests from blocking one another. This chapter handles a different problem: work that should outlive the request itself. We will move document ingestion into a job, make job creation safe to retry, retry only transient downstream failures, and preserve tenant identity from submission through completion. The target interaction POST /ingest accepts work quickly and returns 202 Accepted with a job_id. A worker performs the expensive extraction, embedding, and indexing. The client polls GET /jobs/{job_id} or receives a notification later. 1) Why slow work should not run inside the request A normal HTTP request has a limited time budget. A reverse proxy, load balancer, browser, or mobile client may time out even though the server is still extracting a document. If the client retries, the server may start the same expensive operation twice. Document ingestion is a good running example because it usually contains several independently fallible steps: Persist the upload or object reference. Extract and normalize text. Split text into chunks. Call an embedding service. Write vectors and metadata to an index. Mark the document ready for retrieval. The request should record the intent to perform those steps, not remain open until every step finishes. Visual: request lifecycle and job lifecycle are different Client POST /ingest FastAPI validate + enqueue Job store / queue queued, attempt 0 Worker extract → embed → index Job status succeeded / failed persist atomically 202 + job_id immediately 2) Separate best-effort background callbacks from durable jobs FastAPI's BackgroundTasks schedules a callable after the response is sent. It is useful for short, non-critical work such as a small audit write or cache cleanup when losing that work is acceptable. It is not a durable queue. The callback runs in the application process. A restart, deployment, crash, autoscaling event, or process termination can lose the task. Long callbacks also consume the same application's resources. Work typeAppropriate mechanismReason Short, best-effort action after a responseFastAPI BackgroundTasksSimple and local; loss is acceptable. Document ingestion, email delivery, webhook, media processingDurable queue plus workerSurvives restarts and supports retries, visibility, and dead-letter handling. Multi-step workflow with waits or compensationWorkflow engine or orchestratorPersists step state and long-running control flow. Periodic workScheduler that enqueues a durable jobSeparates schedule ownership from execution. Cloud Tasks, Pub/Sub with a subscriber, Celery or RQ with a durable broker, and managed workflow services are common choices. The exact product matters less than the guarantees you require: persistence, delivery semantics, retry policy, visibility timeout or lease, concurrency control, and a dead-letter path. 3) First implementation: see the complete interaction with BackgroundTasks The following in-memory version is deliberately small. It demonstrates the HTTP contract, idempotency key, identity propagation, and state transitions. The production section immediately afterward replaces its unsafe storage assumptions. from threading import Lock from typing import Annotated, Literal from uuid import uuid4 import time from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException, status from pydantic import BaseModel, Field app = FastAPI() class Identity(BaseModel): tenant_id: str user_id: str def get_identity() -> Identity: # Teaching stand-in. Production verifies a bearer token and maps claims. return Identity(tenant_id="tenant-acme", user_id="user-123") class IngestRequest(BaseModel): document_uri: str class IngestResponse(BaseModel): job_id: str status: Literal["queued"] class JobView(BaseModel): job_id: str document_uri: str status: Literal["queued", "running", "succeeded", "failed"] error: str | None = None # Teaching-only process memory. Production uses a database + durable queue. JOBS: dict[str, dict] = {} IDEMPOTENCY: dict[tuple[str, str], IngestResponse] = {} STORE_LOCK = Lock() def ingest_job(job_id: str) -> None: try: JOBS[job_id]["status"] = "running" time.sleep(2) # stand-in for extract -> embed -> index JOBS[job_id]["status"] = "succeeded" except Exception as exc: JOBS[job_id]["status"] = "failed" JOBS[job_id]["error"] = str(exc) @app.post( "/ingest", response_model=IngestResponse, status_code=status.HTTP_202_ACCEPTED, ) def ingest( payload: IngestRequest, background: BackgroundTasks, identity: Annotated[Identity, Depends(get_identity)], idempotency_key: Annotated[str, Header(alias="Idempotency-Key")], ) -> IngestResponse: store_key = (identity.tenant_id, idempotency_key) # The lock makes the teaching store's check-and-create atomic in one process. with STORE_LOCK: if previous := IDEMPOTENCY.get(store_key): return previous job_id = str(uuid4()) response = IngestResponse(job_id=job_id, status="queued") JOBS[job_id] = { "job_id": job_id, "tenant_id": identity.tenant_id, "user_id": identity.user_id, "document_uri": payload.document_uri, "status": "queued", "error": None, } IDEMPOTENCY[store_key] = response background.add_task(ingest_job, job_id) return response The client supplies the same idempotency key every time it retries the same logical submission: POST /ingest HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: Bearer <access-token> Idempotency-Key: 9c2f9f2f-9bd8-4d1e-8b45-4a338f89f9a0 Content-Type: application/json {"document_uri": "gs://tenant-acme/inbox/report.pdf"} HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted Content-Type: application/json Location: /jobs/b6d0b2e4-3fbd-4ab7-87fb-02f911c4c21e {"job_id": "b6d0b2e4-3fbd-4ab7-87fb-02f911c4c21e", "status": "queued"} Concurrency detail: “look up the key, then insert” must be one atomic operation. A Python dictionary and lock only protect one teaching process. In production, enforce a database unique constraint on a key such as (tenant_id, operation, idempotency_key) and commit the idempotency record with the job record in one transaction. 4) Return job state without crossing tenant boundaries A job_id is an identifier, not authorization. Every status read, cancel operation, artifact download, and retry must check the tenant from the verified request identity against the tenant stored on the job. @app.get("/jobs/{job_id}", response_model=JobView) def get_job( job_id: str, identity: Annotated[Identity, Depends(get_identity)], ) -> JobView: job = JOBS.get(job_id) # Returning 404 for both cases avoids revealing another tenant's job IDs. if job is None or job["tenant_id"] != identity.tenant_id: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Job not found") return JobView.model_validate(job) For user-owned jobs, add a user_id check too. For shared tenant jobs, authorize by role or permission. The worker must also scope every database read, object-store path, vector-index namespace, and emitted event using the job's persisted tenant context. 5) Idempotency means one logical effect, not merely one HTTP response An idempotency record should normally retain: tenant or principal scope; operation name and idempotency key; a hash of the normalized request payload; the created resource or job ID; the original status code and response body; creation time, expiry policy, and processing state. If the same key arrives with a different payload hash, reject it with a conflict rather than silently returning an unrelated response. Keep the retention period at least as long as the maximum client retry window. Delivery semantics Most practical queues are at least once: a worker may receive the same message more than once. “Exactly once” business behavior is therefore built from idempotent consumers, unique constraints, conditional writes, and deduplication, not from assuming the queue will never redeliver. 6) Retry only failures that can plausibly succeed later Retries help transient faults such as timeouts, connection resets, rate limits, and temporary service unavailability. They make permanent faults worse by adding latency and load. FailureRetry?Typical handling Timeout, connection reset, HTTP 502/503/504UsuallyBounded exponential backoff with jitter. HTTP 429UsuallyRespect Retry-After; apply rate limiting. HTTP 401Only after credential refreshRefresh once; repeated 401 is permanent for this attempt. HTTP 403NoFix authorization or policy. HTTP 400/422 or schema validation errorNoCorrect the request or quarantine the message. Not foundContext dependentRetry only when eventual consistency is expected and bounded. A small retry helper with exponential backoff and jitter from collections.abc import Callable from random import uniform from time import sleep from typing import TypeVar T = TypeVar("T") class TransientError(Exception): pass def retry_transient( operation: Callable[[], T], *, attempts: int = 4, base_delay: float = 0.25, max_delay: float = 4.0, ) -> T: last_error: TransientError | None = None for attempt in range(attempts): try: return operation() except TransientError as exc: last_error = exc if attempt == attempts - 1: break cap = min(max_delay, base_delay * (2 ** attempt)) sleep(uniform(0, cap)) # full jitter prevents synchronized retries assert last_error is not None raise last_error A production HTTP client library or queue normally provides retry hooks. Use those rather than maintaining a general retry framework yourself, but keep the same policy questions explicit: which exceptions, how many attempts, what deadline, whether the operation is idempotent, and how Retry-After is handled. 7) Retry steps, not an opaque whole workflow The original ingestion example called two flaky dependencies. Keep those steps independently observable and idempotent: def call_search_index(job: dict) -> None: # Use a deterministic document ID so a retry overwrites/upserts, # rather than creating duplicate indexed documents. ... def call_embedding_service(job: dict) -> list[list[float]]: # A pure request is safe to repeat; cache by content hash when useful. ... def run_ingestion(job_id: str) -> None: job = load_job(job_id) mark_running(job_id) try: vectors = retry_transient(lambda: call_embedding_service(job)) retry_transient(lambda: call_search_index({**job, "vectors": vectors})) mark_succeeded(job_id) except TransientError as exc: mark_failed(job_id, code="retries_exhausted", detail=str(exc)) raise Checkpointing matters for expensive workflows. If extraction succeeded but indexing failed, a retry should resume at indexing when possible rather than repeat the upload and extraction. Store step state and immutable input references so a worker can reconstruct the attempt. 8) Durable production pattern: transaction, queue, worker The central reliability problem is a dual write: what if the API commits the job row but crashes before publishing to the queue, or publishes to the queue but fails before committing the job row? The transactional outbox pattern solves this when the job database and broker cannot share one transaction: In one database transaction, insert the job, idempotency record, and an outbox event. Commit once. A relay publishes unsent outbox rows to the queue. After publish succeeds, mark the outbox row sent. The worker consumes idempotently because relay or broker delivery can repeat. API transaction ├─ jobs(job_id, tenant_id, status="queued", ...) ├─ idempotency(tenant_id, key, request_hash, job_id, ...) └─ outbox(event_id, type="ingest.requested", payload, sent_at=NULL) Outbox relay → durable queue → worker → status/artifacts Some managed task queues let the API create the task directly with a deterministic task name and provide adequate deduplication for your use case. Document the chosen guarantee rather than assuming every queue behaves the same. 9) Failure, cancellation, and dead-letter handling A job state machine should make terminal and non-terminal states explicit. A practical minimum is queued, running, succeeded, failed, and canceled. Add retry_scheduled or step-level states only when operators need them. After retries are exhausted, move or route the message to a dead-letter queue and mark the job failed with a stable error code. Make cancellation cooperative: set cancel_requested and let workers stop between safe steps. Do not expose internal stack traces to clients; preserve them in restricted logs. Define whether operators can replay a failed job and whether replay creates a new attempt or a new job. Use a lease or visibility timeout so abandoned work can be redelivered after a worker crash. 10) Observability and operational controls Every log, metric, and trace should carry job_id, tenant_id, attempt number, step name, and correlation or trace ID. Useful metrics include queue age, processing duration, retry count, success rate, dead-letter volume, and jobs stuck in a non-terminal state. What to remember BackgroundTasks is for short best-effort callbacks, not durable ingestion. Return 202 Accepted and a job resource when work continues after the request. Make the idempotency check and job creation atomic and tenant-scoped. Assume at-least-once delivery and make workers and side effects idempotent. Retry transient failures with bounded backoff and jitter; do not retry validation or authorization failures. Persist tenant and user context on the job and re-authorize every status or artifact read. Use an outbox or equivalent mechanism when database state and queue publication must agree. The next chapter begins the authentication sequence. It explains how the request identity persisted on a job is established through SSO, OAuth 2.0, and OpenID Connect.

title: SSO, OAuth 2.0, and OpenID Connect: The Identity Primer
label: 7. SSO, OAuth 2.0, and OIDC primer
headings: 1) Start with the problem: applications should not collect every password
2) SSO is an outcome, not a token format
3) OAuth 2.0 delegates access to an API
4) OIDC adds a standard authentication result
5) Keep ID tokens, access tokens, refresh tokens, and sessions separate
6) Why Authorization Code with PKCE is the default teaching flow
7) Authentication is not application authorization
8) Common mistakes and the correct mental model
9) The flow you will implement next
description: Authentication terminology feels confusing because several layers happen during one click on “Sign in.” This chapter separates the user experience, delegation protocol, identity protocol, browser session, and API auth...
text: Authentication terminology feels confusing because several layers happen during one click on “Sign in.” This chapter separates the user experience, delegation protocol, identity protocol, browser session, and API authorization before the next chapter implements the complete flow in React and FastAPI. The three-sentence model SSO is the experience: authenticate once with a trusted identity provider and use more than one application without entering credentials again. OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization: a client obtains an access token that lets it call a resource server within an approved scope. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds authentication: it standardizes how a client learns which user authenticated, principally through an ID token with identity claims. 1) Start with the problem: applications should not collect every password Suppose your company has ten internal applications. Without federation, every application could create its own username and password database. That produces ten password stores, ten account-recovery processes, and ten opportunities to implement authentication badly. A better design delegates authentication to an identity provider (IdP), such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google Identity, Okta, or an internal standards-compliant provider. The application redirects the user to the IdP. The IdP handles credentials, passkeys, MFA, risk checks, and account policy, then returns a cryptographically verifiable result to the application. Visual: one sign-in, separate trust boundaries User browser Client app React or BFF Identity provider login + consent Resource API FastAPI OIDC request access token The IdP authenticates the user. The API still makes its own authorization decision for each request. 2) SSO is an outcome, not a token format Single sign-on means the user can move between trusted applications without repeatedly entering credentials. It is an experience created by a shared IdP session and federation protocols. SSO is not itself an API protocol and does not tell your FastAPI endpoint which records the caller may access. When the user signs in to App A, the IdP may create its own secure browser session. Later, App B redirects the same browser to the IdP. The IdP recognizes its session, may skip the credential prompt, and completes a new authorization flow for App B. Each application still receives tokens intended for that application; one universal token should not be replayed everywhere. 3) OAuth 2.0 delegates access to an API OAuth separates four roles. Keeping these roles distinct prevents most terminology mistakes: OAuth roleIn this book's exampleResponsibility Resource ownerThe signed-in userOwns or is authorized to act on protected data. ClientReact app or backend-for-frontendRequests delegated access; it is not the API being protected. Authorization serverThe IdPAuthenticates, obtains consent/policy approval, and issues tokens. Resource serverFastAPIValidates an access token and authorizes the requested operation. The client asks for scopes such as documents:read. The authorization server may issue an access token. The client sends that token to the API using Authorization: Bearer <access-token>. The API validates the token's signature or introspection result, issuer, audience, expiry, and relevant authorization claims before serving data. OAuth alone is not a login protocol. An access token is addressed to a resource server and represents delegated API access. Treating arbitrary access-token contents as a portable user profile couples the client to one provider and can create token-substitution vulnerabilities. 4) OIDC adds a standard authentication result OpenID Connect is an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. The client requests the openid scope. After the user authenticates, the client receives an ID token intended for the client. The ID token says who authenticated, which issuer authenticated them, which client it was issued to, and when that authentication result expires. { "iss": "https://idp.example.com", "sub": "00u123stable-subject", "aud": "web-client-id", "exp": 1785400000, "iat": 1785396400, "nonce": "request-bound-random-value", "email": "alice@example.com" } The durable external identity key is normally the pair (iss, sub). Email addresses can change, be recycled, or be absent. Store the issuer and subject when mapping the external identity to your internal user_id. 5) Keep ID tokens, access tokens, refresh tokens, and sessions separate CredentialIntended recipientPrimary purposeWhere it should go ID tokenThe clientAuthentication result and identity claims.Client sign-in processing; not as the general API credential. Access tokenThe API named by its audience/resourceAuthorize API calls within scopes and policy.Authorization: Bearer ... to that resource server. Refresh tokenThe authorized clientObtain new access tokens without another full sign-in.Prefer a confidential backend or other protected storage; rotate and revoke. Application session cookieYour web application/BFFMaintain the app's local browser session.Secure, HttpOnly, appropriately scoped cookie. A backend-for-frontend (BFF) can keep OAuth tokens server-side and give the browser only a hardened session cookie. A pure SPA can use Authorization Code with PKCE, but must account for browser token-theft risk and should avoid persistent storage when the architecture allows it. 6) Why Authorization Code with PKCE is the default teaching flow The browser does not receive tokens directly from the authorization endpoint. It receives a short-lived, single-use authorization code. The client then exchanges that code at the token endpoint. PKCE binds the code to a secret value created for that particular authorization attempt: The client generates a random code_verifier. It sends a derived code_challenge with the authorization request. The IdP authenticates the user and redirects back with a code. The client sends the original verifier when exchanging the code. The authorization server checks that the verifier matches the earlier challenge before issuing tokens. PKCE limits the usefulness of a stolen authorization code. It does not replace redirect-URI validation, state for request correlation and CSRF defense, OIDC nonce validation, TLS, or secure token storage. 7) Authentication is not application authorization After token validation, your application still decides what the caller may do. A valid login does not automatically grant access to every tenant, document, or administrative operation. Imagine a company building with a receptionist. OAuth 2.0 is a visitor pass that grants access to specific rooms: it is delegated authorization. OIDC adds a verified identity badge: the client can establish who signed in. Your application policy is the door controller for each room: it checks tenant membership, role, ownership, and operation. Scopes express what an access token permits at an API boundary. Roles and groups are organizational inputs. Tenant membership and resource ownership are application data. Your authorization layer may combine all of them, but they are not interchangeable. 8) Common mistakes and the correct mental model MistakeCorrection “OAuth logs the user in.”OAuth delegates API access; OIDC standardizes authentication on top of it. “SSO means one token works for every app.”SSO normally reuses the IdP session while issuing audience-specific results to each client/resource. “The API should accept the ID token.”The API normally accepts an access token whose audience/resource identifies that API. “Email is the user ID.”Use the issuer and subject as the external stable key; treat email as a mutable attribute. “A valid token means the request is authorized.”Token validation authenticates the credential; application policy still authorizes the operation and resource. “JWT validation means decoding the payload.”Decoding is not trust. Verify signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and required claims. 9) The flow you will implement next Browser Client app Identity provider FastAPI | | | | | click sign in | | | |----------------->| authorize + PKCE | | | |---------------------->| | | authenticate / consent | | |<---------------------------------------->| | | | code + state | | | |<----------------------| | | | code + verifier | | | |---------------------->| | | | ID token + access token | | |<----------------------| | | | Authorization: Bearer access_token | | |-------------------------------------------->| | | validate token + authorize resource | Standards note OAuth 2.1 is a consolidation of modern OAuth practice, but it remains an Internet-Draft rather than a replacement RFC at the time of this edition. Production designs should follow the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, use Authorization Code with PKCE, and avoid the implicit and resource-owner-password grants. Continue to OIDC + OAuth2 + PKCE in FastAPI, where this vocabulary becomes a concrete message sequence, token-validation dependency, and stable user/tenant mapping.
