description: This is the same story end-to-end: how a React SPA securely obtains an access_token (PKCE), and how FastAPI validates that token and maps it to tenant_id + user_id per request.
text: This is the same story end-to-end: how a React SPA securely obtains an access_token (PKCE), and how FastAPI validates that token and maps it to tenant_id + user_id per request. Acronyms (quick reference) IdP: Identity Provider (e.g., Google Identity, Auth0, Okta, Entra ID) OAuth2: OAuth 2.0 (authorization framework; how clients get tokens to call APIs) OIDC: OpenID Connect (authentication layer on top of OAuth2; adds login + identity claims) PKCE: Proof Key for Code Exchange (protects authorization-code flow for public clients like SPAs) JWT: JSON Web Token (self-contained, signed token format commonly used for access tokens) JWKS: JSON Web Key Set (IdP endpoint that publishes public signing keys for JWT verification) SPA: Single Page Application (React running in the browser) JWT & JWKS (the missing piece) The confusion usually comes from not separating two steps: (1) token issuance (frontend ↔ IdP) vs (2) token validation (backend verifying the token). JWT (JSON Web Token) A JWT is a compact token format commonly used for access_token. It is typically signed so APIs can verify it hasn’t been tampered with. It usually contains claims (e.g., sub, iss, aud, exp) inside the token payload. JWT structure (conceptual): header.payload.signature - header: metadata (often includes "kid" = key id) - payload: claims (sub, iss, aud, exp, ...) - signature: proves the IdP signed it with its private key JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) A JWKS is the IdP’s published set of public keys. Your backend uses these public keys to verify the JWT signature. The backend typically fetches JWKS from a well-known IdP URL, caches it, and refreshes periodically (key rotation). The JWT header often includes kid so the backend can pick the correct public key from the JWKS. Where they come into the picture: The IdP issues an access_token (often a JWT). Then the backend validates the token signature using the IdP’s JWKS. This is why the backend usually does not need to call the IdP “to ask who the user is” on every request. Bearer token per request OAuth2 vs OIDC What PKCE is One-time setup Message sequence Backend validation JWKS fetch/cache User registration & access Mapping Token to Identity Why it scales Bearer token per request (how FastAPI identifies callers) Your backend identifies the user (and tenant) because every request carries: Authorization: Bearer <token> The key questions are: How does the frontend generate <token> securely? How does the backend trust it? OAuth2 vs OIDC (in this story) OAuth2 How the client obtains an access token to call an API. OIDC Adds authentication (“login”) and identity info (ID token + claims) on top of OAuth2. In practice: The React app uses OIDC to sign in with an IdP (e.g., Google Workspace). The React app uses the resulting access token as the Bearer token when calling FastAPI. What PKCE is (and why you need it) The problem PKCE solves A React SPA is a public client: it cannot safely store a permanent client secret in the browser. Without protection, an attacker who steals the authorization code could exchange it for tokens. PKCE in one sentence PKCE (“Proof Key for Code Exchange”) makes the authorization code usable only by the same client instance that started the login. How PKCE works (simple) React generates a random secret string: code_verifier React hashes it into code_challenge React sends code_challenge during the login redirect Later, when exchanging the authorization code for tokens, React must present the original code_verifier The IdP checks the verifier matches the earlier challenge Result: If someone stole the authorization code but doesn’t have the verifier, they can’t get tokens. Important boundary: PKCE is between the frontend and the IdP. Your FastAPI backend does not perform PKCE. What you must set up first (one-time) On the Identity Provider (e.g., Google Identity / Workspace) Create an OAuth client for your SPA You get a client_id Set redirect URI (e.g., https://app.example.com/callback) Choose scopes (typical: openid email profile) On FastAPI (what the backend “keeps”) The backend remains stateless and does not store per-user sessions. It keeps: Trusted issuer(s) (who is allowed to mint tokens) Expected audience (token must be intended for your API/client) Access to the IdP’s public signing keys (JWKS), usually cached That’s enough to validate tokens for any user on any request. Concrete message sequence (OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE) 1) React redirects user to the IdP /authorize (includes PKCE challenge) GET https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth? response_type=code& client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID& redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fcallback& scope=openid%20email%20profile& state=RANDOM_STATE& code_challenge=PKCE_CHALLENGE& code_challenge_method=S256 response_type=code → request an authorization code scope=openid ... → OIDC login + identity code_challenge → PKCE protection 2) IdP redirects back with the authorization code GET https://app.example.com/callback?code=AUTH_CODE&state=RANDOM_STATE 3) React exchanges code for tokens at /token (includes PKCE verifier) POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded grant_type=authorization_code& code=AUTH_CODE& redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fcallback& client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID& code_verifier=PKCE_VERIFIER 4) IdP returns tokens { "token_type": "Bearer", "access_token": "....", "id_token": "....", "expires_in": 3600, "scope": "openid email profile" } Now the frontend can call your API. The API call to FastAPI (per user, per request) POST /query HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: Bearer <access_token_for_user_742> Content-Type: application/json { "question": "..." } How the backend knows the token is “correct” FastAPI doesn’t “trust the browser”. It trusts the IdP’s signature + standard token checks. Does the backend call the IdP on every request? Usually no. With JWT access tokens, the backend verifies the signature locally using the IdP’s public keys (from JWKS), plus it checks standard claims (iss, aud, exp). The backend may fetch JWKS occasionally (and cache it), not per request. What “signature verification using JWKS” means The IdP signs the JWT with its private key when issuing the token. The backend reads the token header (often containing kid). The backend selects the matching public key from the cached JWKS. The backend verifies the JWT signature. If it matches, the token was minted by the IdP and wasn’t altered. How the backend gets JWKS, where it caches it, and when it refreshes Where does JWKS come from? In OIDC, the IdP exposes a discovery document at /.well-known/openid-configuration. That JSON includes a jwks_uri URL. Where is it cached? Most APIs cache JWKS in memory inside each running process (each Uvicorn worker / each GKE pod). That means: Pod A caches keys in Pod A memory (Pod B has its own cache). On restart/rollout, the cache is empty and re-fetched on first request (or warm-up). When does it refresh? Common triggers: TTL expiry (e.g., refresh every 5–60 minutes). Unknown kid (IdP rotated keys; refetch JWKS and retry once). Startup warm-up (optional: fetch once at boot so first request is fast). Practical note: caching is an optimization; correctness comes from signature verification + claim checks. Key rotation is why “refetch on unknown kid” is a standard pattern. From a Verified Identity to Application Access A valid token proves that the configured issuer authenticated a subject; it does not automatically grant that subject access to your application. The API still needs a local onboarding and authorization decision. Validate the token completely before reading identity claims. Build the stable external key from (iss, sub), not email or the token string. Look up or idempotently create the local user in one database transaction. Require an invitation, approved domain policy, or administrator action before creating tenant membership. Load current roles and permissions from your application policy store. Do not equate email domain with authorization. A verified domain can be one onboarding signal, but a user can change address, leave an organization, or belong to several tenants. Persist an explicit membership and check its current status on protected requests. How the Backend Maps a Dynamic Token to a Stable User ID The backend does not identify a user by the literal Bearer token string (because tokens change over time). Instead, it uses a 3-step mapping for every single request: 1) Validate the Bearer token The token is usually a JWT signed by your Identity Provider (e.g., Google). FastAPI verifies the signature using the IdP’s public keys (JWKS) and checks basic claims like: exp (not expired) iss (issued by the expected IdP) aud (intended for your app/API) If any check fails, the request is rejected (401). 2) Extract a stable user identifier → user_id After validation, FastAPI reads the token’s claims (the payload). The sub (subject) claim is typically the stable unique identifier for the user at that IdP. user_id = claims["sub"] 3) Derive or look up the tenant → tenant_id The backend then determines which tenant that user belongs to, using one of these common strategies: Claim-based: If the token includes a tenant/org claim (e.g. tenant_id, tid, org_id), use it directly. Database mapping (most common): Store a user table keyed by (iss, sub). Look up (claims["iss"], claims["sub"]) to find the tenant_id. If not found, you can optionally provision the user and assign a tenant. Domain mapping (common for Google Workspace): Use the email claim and map the domain to a tenant (e.g., alice@acme.com → tenant “acme”). Key idea: Tokens rotate, but sub (plus iss) is stable. The mapping is always: token → validated claims → stable user key → tenant. Anti-pattern: don’t store “current user” in a global variable and don’t treat the token value as a permanent user identifier. Tokens are short-lived and will naturally differ across time and devices. Why the Pattern Scales Each API instance can validate a JWT locally with cached public keys, so token verification does not require a network round trip to the IdP for every request. Because identity is reconstructed from the request, any healthy FastAPI worker can handle the next call; no sticky session or process-global “current user” is required. LayerScale mechanismCorrectness requirement JWT verificationPer-process JWKS cacheIssuer, audience, time, signature, and algorithm checks on every request User mappingIndexed lookup on (iss, sub)Unique constraint and idempotent provisioning Tenant authorizationShort-lived policy cache where justifiedTenant membership remains explicit and revocable API computeStateless horizontal replicasRequest-scoped identity and no mutable global user state Local JWT validation trades immediate token revocation for low-latency verification. Keep access tokens short-lived, revoke sessions or refresh tokens at the authorization server, and re-check high-risk application permissions at the point of action.

title: First Login and User Provisioning
label: 9. First login and user provisioning
headings: 1. New User Sign-In Flow (React + Google OIDC + FastAPI)
2. Example FastAPI Endpoint for User Provisioning
3. Where "Registration" Actually Lives
4. Choose a Provisioning Policy Explicitly
5. Make First Login Race-Safe
6. Sign-In Is Ongoing Reconciliation
description: Authentication proves an external identity; provisioning creates the application account, tenant membership, and starting authorization state.
text: Authentication proves an external identity; provisioning creates the application account, tenant membership, and starting authorization state. Where this fits The preceding chapters established OIDC Authorization Code with PKCE and API token validation. This chapter begins after a token has been validated. It explains just-in-time provisioning without confusing an identity-provider account, an application user, and a tenant membership. Assume the organisation's Google Workspace policy already allows this person to authenticate. That permission does not by itself grant access to this application or any tenant data. First-login authentication and provisioning state machine The browser authenticates with the identity provider, the API validates a token, then an atomic bootstrap either returns an existing user or creates an allowed tenant membership. Browser Auth Code + PKCE Identity provider authenticate identity FastAPI boundary verify iss, aud, exp, sub Existing user refresh last login New identity policy + atomic upsert or deny found not found Identity verification precedes provisioning. The create-or-return step must be atomic because two browser requests can arrive for the same first login. 1. New User Sign-In Flow (React + Google OIDC + FastAPI) Key idea: The login page doesn't "register" the user with Google—Google already knows them. Your app "registers" the user by provisioning a record in your database the first time your backend sees a valid identity. User clicks "Sign in with Google" React starts OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE by redirecting the browser to Google's authorization endpoint. Outcome: user authenticates with Google (SSO). The registered client completes the code exchange In a browser-only public-client design, React can exchange the authorization code using its PKCE verifier and keep tokens in memory. In a backend-for-frontend design, the backend completes the exchange and gives the browser an HTTP-only session cookie. The credential sent to your API must be an access token issued for that API's audience. An OIDC ID token describes the login result for its client; it is not a general-purpose API bearer token. A Google-only application may instead validate the login at its backend and mint an application session. React calls a bootstrap endpoint on your API Right after login, the frontend calls something like: POST /auth/bootstrap for an operation that may create or update application records, then GET /me for later read-only profile retrieval. with: Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Purpose: let the backend validate the token and decide what to do with this identity. FastAPI validates token and extracts stable identity Backend verifies the token (signature + issuer/audience/expiry), then reads claims like: sub → stable user identifier at this IdP email and email_verified → optional policy inputs, never the stable primary key Backend checks if the user already exists in your DB Backend looks up by a stable key like (issuer, sub) (best practice), optionally storing email too. Case A: user exists Return user profile + tenant info. Frontend proceeds normally. Case B: user is new This is where "registration" happens (provisioning). 2. Example FastAPI Endpoint for User Provisioning This endpoint is the bootstrap call that validates the Bearer token, looks up the user, creates the DB row if missing, and returns user details. The code below is a teaching scaffold. The industry-standard version verifies the token against JWKS/OIDC discovery, stores users in a real database with a unique constraint on (issuer, subject), performs the create-or-return logic in a transaction/upsert, and records audit fields such as created_at and last_login_at. from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, HTTPBearer from pydantic import BaseModel from datetime import datetime, timezone app = FastAPI() bearer = HTTPBearer(auto_error=True) class BootstrapResponse(BaseModel): user_id: str tenant_id: str is_new_user: bool # --- Teaching-only in-memory store (production: Postgres/Cloud SQL) --- USERS_BY_ISS_SUB: dict[tuple[str, str], dict] = {} # key = (issuer, sub) # --- Teaching-only token verifier (production: JWT/JWKS validation) --- def verify_and_decode_access_token(token: str) -> dict: """ Production implementation: - verify JWT signature using Google JWKS - check issuer (iss), audience (aud), expiry (exp) - optionally check nonce/azp/scopes depending on token type This teaching version returns mock claims so you see where they come from. """ # demo-alice-token is only a classroom stand-in for an already-verified JWT. if token == "demo-alice-token": return { "iss": "https://accounts.google.com", "sub": "user-A-sub", "email": "alice@acme.com", "email_verified": True, } raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid/expired token") def map_email_to_tenant_id(email: str) -> str: """ Example tenant mapping policy: email domain -> tenant. (Alternative policies: invite-only lookup, explicit claim, etc.) """ domain = email.split("@")[-1].lower() if domain == "acme.com": return "tenant-acme" raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="No tenant mapping for this user") @app.post("/auth/bootstrap", response_model=BootstrapResponse) def auth_bootstrap(creds: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(bearer)): # 1) Extract raw token from "Authorization: Bearer <token>" token = creds.credentials # 2) Validate + decode -> claims (iss/sub/email) claims = verify_and_decode_access_token(token) issuer = claims["iss"] sub = claims["sub"] email = claims.get("email", "") if not claims.get("email_verified", False): raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Verified email required") # 3) Look up user by stable key (issuer, sub) key = (issuer, sub) existing = USERS_BY_ISS_SUB.get(key) if existing: # User already provisioned return BootstrapResponse( user_id=existing["user_id"], tenant_id=existing["tenant_id"], is_new_user=False, ) # 4) New user -> determine tenant_id (domain/invite/etc.) tenant_id = map_email_to_tenant_id(email) # 5) "Register" user in DB (provision) user_row = { "user_id": f"db-user-{sub}", # in real DB: UUID "tenant_id": tenant_id, "issuer": issuer, "sub": sub, "email": email, "created_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(), } USERS_BY_ISS_SUB[key] = user_row return BootstrapResponse( user_id=user_row["user_id"], tenant_id=user_row["tenant_id"], is_new_user=True, ) Provision the user (your app's "registration") The backend creates the required records: Determine tenant_id Domain mapping: alice@acme.com → tenant "acme" or invite-only: user must already be linked to a tenant or self-serve tenant creation (first user creates tenant) Create user row Store: issuer, sub, email, tenant_id, timestamps Optional defaults Preferences, empty workspace, default roles, etc. Backend returns a bootstrap response Example: { "user_id": "…", "tenant_id": "…", "is_new_user": true } React can now show an onboarding / "upload documents" screen. 3. Where "Registration" Actually Lives Google authenticates the user. Your backend decides whether the identity is allowed and attaches it to a tenant. "Registration" = your DB provisioning, not creating credentials. 4. Choose a Provisioning Policy Explicitly PolicyHow a new identity becomes a userUse when Invite onlyA pending invitation already binds an email or subject to a tenant and initial role.Controlled B2B and regulated applications. Just in time (JIT)A verified identity that satisfies policy is created during first login.Managed workforce domains with clear admission rules. SCIM / directory syncAn identity-management system creates, updates, and disables users before login.Enterprise lifecycle automation and rapid deprovisioning. Self-service tenant creationThe first allowed user creates a tenant and becomes its initial administrator.SaaS onboarding with abuse controls and verification. Domain mapping such as @acme.com → tenant-acme is a teaching example, not a universal policy. Use it only with a verified email, an owned-domain registry, and an explicit business rule. Invitations or directory-managed membership are safer when the same domain can contain people who must not share application data. 5. Make First Login Race-Safe Browsers retry, users double-click, and multiple tabs can call bootstrap simultaneously. An in-memory check followed by an insert is not sufficient in production. Put a unique constraint on (issuer, subject) and perform an upsert or transaction: INSERT INTO app_user (issuer, subject, email, status, created_at) VALUES (:issuer, :subject, :email, 'active', CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) ON CONFLICT (issuer, subject) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email, last_login_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP RETURNING user_id, status; Tenant membership should have its own unique key, such as (tenant_id, user_id). Keeping identity and membership separate supports users who legitimately belong to more than one tenant and avoids treating tenant data as an attribute permanently embedded in the identity-provider account. 6. Sign-In Is Ongoing Reconciliation The second login is not simply "do nothing." Update safe profile metadata such as display name, verified email, and last_login_at; evaluate whether the application user or membership is suspended; and apply current authorization policy. Never silently reactivate a locally disabled user merely because the identity provider authenticated them. Use (iss, sub) as the external identity key; email addresses can change or be reassigned. Model user status and membership status separately: invited, active, suspended, or removed. Decide whether group and role changes are read on every login, synchronized by SCIM, or maintained locally. Record provisioning, membership changes, denial reasons, and the policy version in an audit trail. Define deprovisioning and session revocation; login is only one part of the account lifecycle. Correct mental model The identity provider owns credentials and authentication. Your application owns admission, the internal user record, tenant memberships, roles, and data authorization.

title: Authentication: Tokens, OAuth, and API Security
label: 10. Authentication deep dive
headings: 1) Big picture: who talks to whom?
2) Bearer tokens (Authorization: Bearer ...)
3) API keys: when they fit (and when they don’t)
4) Opaque vs JWT access tokens
5) Opaque tokens: introspection flow (client + server both talk to auth server)
6) JWT tokens: JWKS + public key caching (server “keeps the public key”)
7) “Gmail authenticator”: Google OIDC login (client still talks to Google)
8) PKCE: why it exists and when you use it
9) Why an /authorize endpoint might be POST
10) MCP: authenticating MCP servers and forwarding headers
11) SQL Server auth: username/password vs Windows/SSO
12) Practical security checklist
Putting it all together (one-page mental model)
description: A practical, end-to-end guide to: API keys, Bearer tokens, OAuth/OIDC (PKCE), JWT vs opaque tokens (introspection), Google (Gmail) login verification with JWKS, and how this ties into MCP servers and SQL Server access.
text: A practical, end-to-end guide to: API keys, Bearer tokens, OAuth/OIDC (PKCE), JWT vs opaque tokens (introspection), Google (Gmail) login verification with JWKS, and how this ties into MCP servers and SQL Server access. Contents 1) Big picture: who talks to whom? 2) Bearer tokens (Authorization: Bearer ...) 3) API keys: when they fit (and when they don’t) 4) Opaque vs JWT access tokens 5) Opaque tokens: introspection flow 6) JWT tokens: JWKS + public key caching 7) “Gmail authenticator”: Google OIDC login 8) PKCE: why it exists and when you use it 9) Why an /authorize endpoint might be POST 10) MCP: authenticating MCP servers and forwarding headers 11) SQL Server auth: username/password vs Windows/SSO 12) Practical security checklist 1) Big picture: who talks to whom? Almost every authentication setup can be described with three roles: Client: your app, script, frontend, or service making requests Resource Server: the API you want to call (your MCP server, your web API, etc.) Authorization Server / Identity Provider: issues tokens (your auth server, Google, Entra ID, etc.) (A) Client authenticates with Auth Server → gets token (B) Client calls Resource Server → sends token in headers (C) Resource Server validates token → grants/denies access Critical idea: A bearer token is like a “keycard”. Whoever holds it can use it. So you must protect it in transit and at rest (HTTPS, secure storage). (RFC 6750) Reference: RFC 6750 Bearer Token Usage. Sources: RFC 6750 Bearer Token Usage and general OAuth usage. 2) Bearer tokens (Authorization: Bearer ...) A bearer token is sent on every request to a protected API using an HTTP header: Authorization: Bearer <token>. Source: RFC 6750 bearer token scheme. What the server does with a bearer token Extract token from the Authorization header Validate it (either by introspection call or signature verification) Check claims/scopes/roles (authorization) Allow or deny the request Why this is common: it works the same for browsers, mobile, services, and “agent” calls. 3) API keys: when they fit (and when they don’t) An “auth key” often means an API key: a static secret like X-API-Key: .... It’s simple, but it’s usually a service identity, not a user identity. ApproachGood forWeakness API key (static) Internal service-to-service, quick prototypes Often long-lived; hard per-user auth; higher blast radius if leaked Token (short-lived) User-level identity, scopes, auditability, safer rotation More moving parts (issuer + validation) Common hybrid pattern: use an API key to authenticate to an auth server, then exchange it for a short-lived bearer token. 4) Opaque vs JWT access tokens Bearer tokens can be: opaque strings (random-looking) or structured JWTs. The difference is how the resource server validates them. Token typeWhat it looks likeHow server validatesTradeoff Opaque token Random string Call auth server (introspection) Easy revocation, but adds network hop JWT header.payload.signature Verify signature locally using public key No hop per request, but revocation is harder (use short expiry/rotation) Sources: bearer tokens can be opaque or structured; introspection is defined by RFC 7662. 5) Opaque tokens: introspection flow (client + server both talk to auth server) This is the “both client and server access auth server” pattern you asked about: 1) Client → Auth Server: POST /token (login / credentials) → gets opaque access_token 2) Client → Resource Server: Authorization: Bearer access_token 3) Resource Server → Auth Server: POST /introspect (is token active? scopes?) 4) Resource Server → Client: allow/deny Token introspection spec: resource server queries auth server about token state (RFC 7662). Example endpoints (like our demo) # Auth server: POST /token -> returns {"access_token": "...", "expires_in": 3600} POST /introspect -> returns {"active": true, "sub": "demo", "scope": "sql:read"} Why people choose this: easy centralized revocation and policy checks (auth server is source of truth). Production tip: add caching at the resource server (cache introspection results briefly) to reduce auth server load. 6) JWT tokens: JWKS + public key caching (server “keeps the public key”) When the access token is a JWT, the server can validate it locally using a public key. But the key might rotate, so the server usually downloads keys from a JWKS endpoint. Startup (or periodic): 1) GET /.well-known/openid-configuration → find jwks_uri 2) GET jwks_uri → cache public keys keyed by "kid" Per request: 3) Read JWT header.kid → pick matching public key 4) Verify signature + validate claims (iss, aud, exp) OIDC Discovery defines the well-known configuration and includes jwks_uri; verification relies on keys. See the OpenID Connect Discovery specification. Why this is faster than introspection No network call to auth server per request (after keys are cached) Works even if auth server is temporarily down (until keys expire/rotate) Tradeoff: immediate revocation is harder. Typical mitigations: short token lifetimes + key rotation + occasional back-channel checks. 7) “Gmail authenticator”: Google OIDC login (client still talks to Google) If “auth server is Gmail” means “users sign in with their Google account”, you’re using OpenID Connect (OIDC) on top of OAuth 2.0. Google issues an ID token (a signed JWT) and optionally access tokens. Google documents its OpenID Connect implementation and server-side token verification in the Google Identity OIDC guide. Key point you asked: even if your server caches Google’s public keys, the client still must talk to Google to obtain the token (login/consent). Caching keys only removes server→Google calls on each request. What your resource server validates (minimum) iss (issuer) is Google aud (audience) matches your Google OAuth client ID exp not expired signature matches a Google public key from JWKS OIDC Core defines claims such as iss, aud, and exp; see the OpenID Connect Core specification. 8) PKCE: why it exists and when you use it PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) protects the OAuth authorization code flow against code interception attacks for public clients (mobile apps, SPAs, desktop apps). (RFC 7636) PKCE is defined in RFC 7636. 1) Client generates code_verifier (secret) and code_challenge (hash) 2) Client → /authorize includes code_challenge 3) Client receives authorization code 4) Client → /token sends authorization code + code_verifier 5) Auth server checks verifier matches challenge, then issues tokens Modern direction: The active OAuth 2.1 Internet-Draft requires PKCE for authorization-code clients. It is a draft, not a published RFC; use RFC 9700 as the finalized OAuth 2.0 security best-current-practice baseline. See the active OAuth 2.1 Internet-Draft and RFC 9700: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice. 9) Why an /authorize endpoint might be POST In the classic OAuth/OIDC web flow, /authorize is often reached via a browser navigation (commonly a GET with query parameters). But you may see POST in practice because: Form submissions: login pages submit credentials and consent forms via POST, and then the server continues the authorization flow. Reducing sensitive data in URLs: some systems avoid putting large or sensitive request data in query strings. OIDC response mode “form_post”: the authorization response can be returned to the client via an HTTP form POST. OIDC Core defines the overall authorization behavior; response modes such as form_post are specified separately by OpenID. Important: Whether your /authorize is GET or POST is a design choice / framework detail. The security requirements (PKCE, redirect URI validation, HTTPS, etc.) matter much more than the verb itself. 10) MCP: authenticating MCP servers and forwarding headers For MCP, the same authentication patterns apply: protect your MCP server and require a token (or API key) on its HTTP endpoint. When an LLM (via OpenAI’s tool integration) calls your remote MCP server, you typically pass credentials in HTTP headers. What you do in practice Your client obtains a token (from your auth server, Google OIDC, etc.) Your client configures the MCP tool with headers containing that token The MCP server middleware checks Authorization: Bearer ... on every request OpenAI docs cover MCP integration, tool filtering with allowed_tools, and MCP tool usage via the Responses API. Example: bearer token on MCP calls # Client sets headers when connecting: headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"} # MCP server checks Authorization header for every /mcp request # (then validates via introspection or JWT verification) Safety practice you discussed: avoid passing secrets as tool arguments; prefer headers or OAuth. Also restrict which tools the model can use (e.g., read-only) with allowed_tools. OpenAI MCP tool guidance covers filtering tools with allowed_tools. 11) SQL Server auth: username/password vs Windows/SSO This is separate from your API/MCP authentication. This is how your software authenticates to the database itself. SQL Server commonly supports: Windows Authentication (Integrated / Active Directory): the OS/AD vouches for the identity; SQL Server doesn’t handle passwords directly. SQL Server Authentication: database-level username/password (“SQL login”). Microsoft Learn explains SQL Server authentication modes and when to choose Windows authentication or SQL Server authentication. How it looks in connection configuration # SQL authentication (username/password in connection string) DRIVER={ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server}; SERVER=host,1433; DATABASE=MyDb; UID=${DB_USER}; PWD=${DB_PASSWORD_FROM_SECRET_MANAGER}; Encrypt=yes; TrustServerCertificate=no; # Windows integrated authentication (varies by environment) # Often includes Integrated Security / Trusted_Connection # DRIVER=...;SERVER=...;DATABASE=...;Trusted_Connection=yes; Industry standard: prefer managed identity / Active Directory authentication where possible. If you must use SQL username/password, store the password in a secret manager, rotate it, require encrypted transport, and validate the server certificate instead of using TrustServerCertificate=yes. Don’t confuse the layers: Your API/MCP auth controls “who can call the server”. DB auth controls “what the server process is allowed to do in the database”. In production, you usually use a service identity with least privilege for DB access. 12) Practical security checklist Transport & storage Always use HTTPS/TLS for bearer tokens (possession = access). (RFC 6750) Don’t log tokens; avoid putting them in URLs; store securely. Bearer token security considerations are covered in RFC 6750. Token validation Opaque tokens: implement introspection (RFC 7662) and consider caching. JWT tokens: verify signature + claims; fetch JWKS via OIDC discovery; refresh on unknown kid. Always validate aud and iss for OIDC tokens. Token introspection is defined in RFC 7662; JWT validation commonly combines OIDC Discovery and OIDC Core. OAuth/OIDC hygiene Use PKCE for authorization-code clients. (RFC 7636; RFC 9700) Use exact redirect URI matching and avoid the implicit grant. (RFC 9700) Do not use the resource-owner password credentials grant; prefer browser-based authorization or workload credentials appropriate to the caller. See RFC 7636 for PKCE, RFC 9700 for the finalized security BCP, and the OAuth 2.1 draft for consolidation work still in progress. MCP-specific hygiene Use least-privilege tool exposure (e.g., read-only tools) via allowed_tools. Prefer headers/OAuth rather than passing secrets in tool arguments. OpenAI’s MCP tool guidance covers tool filtering and MCP tool usage. Putting it all together (one-page mental model) Your user logs in (or your service authenticates) → gets a token (Bearer) Your app calls your protected API/MCP server with Authorization: Bearer ... Your API validates token either via RFC 7662 introspection (opaque) or JWT verification (JWKS) Your API uses DB credentials (separate layer) to query SQL Server Your API returns response Implementation decision Choose the validation path from both token format and caller type: opaque tokens require introspection; JWT access tokens use issuer metadata and JWKS; Google OIDC identifies the user but the API must still receive an access token intended for its audience. Browser and mobile public clients use Authorization Code with PKCE, while backend services use an approved workload flow or token exchange.

title: Modern Auth Additions: Passkeys, DPoP, mTLS, Token Exchange
label: 11. Passkeys, DPoP, mTLS, and token exchange
headings: 1) Passkeys / WebAuthn — replacing passwords for human login
2) DPoP — sender‑constrained access tokens (RFC 9449)
3) mTLS — sender‑constrained tokens for service‑to‑service (RFC 8705)
4) OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) — propagating the user downstream
5) Quick decision matrix
6) Reading list (specs)
description: A passkey is a WebAuthn credential bound to the user's device (or a synced keychain like iCloud Keychain / Google Password Manager / 1Password). Instead of typing a password, the browser uses public‑key cryptography o...
text: Why this chapter exists Chapters 6–9 in this Part cover the bedrock — bearer tokens, OAuth2, OIDC, PKCE, JWT vs opaque, JWKS. This 2026 supplement covers four controls now commonly assessed in enterprise designs. It uses RFC 9700 as the finalized OAuth 2.0 security baseline; OAuth 2.1 remains an active Internet-Draft. This chapter is a focused supplement, not a replacement. 1) Passkeys / WebAuthn — replacing passwords for human login A passkey is a WebAuthn credential bound to the user's device (or a synced keychain like iCloud Keychain / Google Password Manager / 1Password). Instead of typing a password, the browser uses public‑key cryptography over a challenge issued by your server. The private key never leaves the authenticator; only a signed assertion comes back. Why prefer passkeys over passwords (and even over TOTP) Phishing‑resistant: the credential is bound to your origin (rp.id), so a fake site cannot trigger a usable signature. No shared secret on the server: you store only a public key. A database breach exposes nothing reusable. Less dependence on password reset: a synced passkey can follow the user through the platform credential provider. Device-bound credentials, lost authenticators, account takeover, and bootstrap for a new device still require an explicit recovery and re-enrolment policy. Where it sits relative to OIDC You typically still use OIDC for SSO across apps; passkeys replace the password step at the Identity Provider. Major identity providers, including Google, GitHub, Microsoft Entra, Okta, and Auth0, support passkeys in their current authentication offerings, although enrolment, recovery, and passwordless-policy options differ. The downstream OAuth2/OIDC flow is unchanged from Chapter 7. Minimal server skeleton (FastAPI + py_webauthn) # pip install webauthn fastapi from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException from webauthn import ( generate_registration_options, verify_registration_response, generate_authentication_options, verify_authentication_response, ) from webauthn.helpers.structs import ( PublicKeyCredentialDescriptor, AuthenticatorSelectionCriteria, UserVerificationRequirement, ) app = FastAPI() RP_ID = "example.com" RP_NAME = "Example Corp" ORIGIN = "https://example.com" USERS = {} # user_id -> {"name": ..., "credentials": [...]} CHALLENGES = {} # user_id -> current challenge bytes @app.post("/webauthn/register/options") def reg_options(user_id: str, username: str): opts = generate_registration_options( rp_id=RP_ID, rp_name=RP_NAME, user_id=user_id.encode(), user_name=username, authenticator_selection=AuthenticatorSelectionCriteria( user_verification=UserVerificationRequirement.PREFERRED, resident_key="required", # creates a discoverable passkey ), ) CHALLENGES[user_id] = opts.challenge USERS.setdefault(user_id, {"name": username, "credentials": []}) return opts # browser calls navigator.credentials.create() with this @app.post("/webauthn/register/verify") def reg_verify(user_id: str, attestation: dict): verification = verify_registration_response( credential=attestation, expected_challenge=CHALLENGES[user_id], expected_origin=ORIGIN, expected_rp_id=RP_ID, ) USERS[user_id]["credentials"].append({ "id": verification.credential_id, "public_key": verification.credential_public_key, "sign_count": verification.sign_count, }) return {"ok": True} The login side is symmetric: you call generate_authentication_options(...), send the resulting challenge to the browser, and verify the assertion with the public key you stored at registration. The skeleton omits production state management A WebAuthn challenge must be random, one-time, short-lived, and bound to the intended user or anonymous ceremony session. Consume it atomically after verification. Store credentials durably, validate user-verification policy, update the signature counter where the authenticator supplies one, rate-limit ceremonies, and design recovery so it is not weaker than the passkey. Production reality Almost no one writes the server primitives by hand anymore. In an enterprise stack you turn passkeys on at the IdP (Entra / Okta / Auth0 / Keycloak) and your FastAPI app keeps using OIDC unchanged. The snippet above is for understanding what the IdP does. 2) DPoP — sender‑constrained access tokens (RFC 9449) A plain bearer token (Chapter 9) is like cash: whoever holds it can spend it. If a token leaks via logs, a misconfigured proxy, or an XSS bug, the attacker gets full access until expiry. DPoP (Demonstrating Proof‑of‑Possession) binds the token to a key pair the client holds, so a stolen token is useless without the private key. How a DPoP request looks POST /api/v1/orders HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Authorization: DPoP eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...<access_token> DPoP: eyJ0eXAiOiJkcG9wK2p3dCIsImFsZyI6IkVTMjU2In0.<proof_jwt> Two headers are sent: Authorization: the access token, prefixed with DPoP instead of Bearer. DPoP: a short‑lived JWT, signed with the client's private key, whose payload includes the HTTP method (htm), request URL (htu), issued-at time (iat), and unique proof ID (jti). A protected-resource proof also includes a hash of the access token (ath). A nonce is included when the authorization or resource server has issued one; it is not present in every proof. At token issuance, the AS records the JWK thumbprint of the client's public key inside the access token's cnf.jkt claim. The resource server verifies that the DPoP proof was signed by that exact key, that the htm/htu match this request, that jti has not been replayed during the acceptance window, and that the proof is fresh. Validating DPoP in FastAPI (sketch) import base64, hashlib, time, jwt # PyJWT from fastapi import Header, HTTPException, Request from jwt import PyJWK def b64url(value: bytes) -> str: return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(value).rstrip(b"=").decode() async def require_dpop( request: Request, authorization: str = Header(...), dpop: str = Header(...), ): if not authorization.startswith("DPoP "): raise HTTPException(401, "Expected DPoP scheme") access_token = authorization.removeprefix("DPoP ") # 1) Inspect the JOSE header, but never let it choose any algorithm. header = jwt.get_unverified_header(dpop) if header.get("typ") != "dpop+jwt" or header.get("alg") != "ES256": raise HTTPException(401, "unsupported DPoP header") public_jwk = header.get("jwk", {}) if not public_jwk or "d" in public_jwk: raise HTTPException(401, "invalid public JWK") # 2) Verify with a server allowlist and require protocol claims. proof_key = PyJWK.from_dict(public_jwk, algorithm="ES256").key proof = jwt.decode( dpop, proof_key, algorithms=["ES256"], options={"verify_aud": False}, require=["htm", "htu", "iat", "jti"], ) # 3) Bind to the externally visible canonical request URI and method. if proof["htm"].upper() != request.method: raise HTTPException(401, "htm mismatch") if proof["htu"] != canonical_public_uri(request): raise HTTPException(401, "htu mismatch") if abs(time.time() - proof["iat"]) > 60: raise HTTPException(401, "stale proof") if not await replay_cache.mark_once(proof["jti"], ttl_seconds=120): raise HTTPException(401, "replayed proof") # 4) Bind proof to this access token. ath_expected = b64url(hashlib.sha256(access_token.encode()).digest()) if proof.get("ath") != ath_expected: raise HTTPException(401, "ath mismatch") # 5) Validate access token normally, then compare its key thumbprint. claims = verify_access_token(access_token) # signature, iss, aud, exp if claims.get("cnf", {}).get("jkt") != jwk_thumbprint(public_jwk): raise HTTPException(401, "token not bound to this key") # 6) If the server issued a DPoP-Nonce, verify proof["nonce"] here. return claims This remains a teaching sketch: use an authorization-server/resource-server library that implements RFC 9449 where possible. Behind a reverse proxy, construct canonical_public_uri only from trusted forwarding configuration; accepting arbitrary Forwarded headers lets a client choose the value you compare. DPoP reduces bearer-token replay, but it does not protect a client whose private key and token are both stolen by XSS, malware, or a compromised runtime. When to adopt DPoP Public clients (SPAs, mobile apps) that cannot be issued mTLS certs. High‑sensitivity APIs (payments, admin) where bearer leakage is unacceptable. MCP servers that accept tokens forwarded from a host — see Part III. 3) mTLS — sender‑constrained tokens for service‑to‑service (RFC 8705) For workload‑to‑workload calls inside your platform (Chapter 10 / 11), mutual TLS is another sender-constraining mechanism. The calling service presents an X.509 client certificate during the TLS handshake. In the specific RFC 8705 OAuth profile, the authorization server binds an issued access token to the certificate's hash through cnf.x5t#S256. The flow Workload requests a token from the AS over mTLS. AS records the SHA‑256 thumbprint of the client cert in cnf.x5t#S256. Workload calls the resource server also over mTLS with the same cert. Resource server verifies that the cert hash from the TLS layer matches the cnf.x5t#S256 claim in the token. Where it fits in your reference architecture This is a strong match for the “workload identity” boundary already covered in Chapter 10 (end‑user vs workload identity) and Chapter 11 (GCP workload identity). SPIFFE/SPIRE can issue X.509 SVIDs, and a service mesh such as Istio can enforce transport mTLS. That does not automatically turn an OAuth token into an RFC 8705 certificate-bound token: the authorization server and resource server must explicitly implement the RFC 8705 binding and compare it with the certificate authenticated at the protected endpoint. 4) OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) — propagating the user downstream The classic question from Chapter 10: "My user calls FastAPI with their OIDC token. FastAPI then calls a downstream API that needs the user's identity, not FastAPI's. How do I forward identity safely?" A standards-based option is OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange. FastAPI asks the authorization server to exchange the inbound user token for a new, downstream-audience token with narrower scope: POST /oauth/token HTTP/1.1 Host: idp.example.com Authorization: Basic <FastAPI client credentials> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange &subject_token=<the inbound user access token> &subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token &audience=https://crm.example.com &scope=crm.read If the authorization server's policy permits the exchange, it returns a new access token whose: sub and delegated-subject semantics follow the authorization server's policy rather than being assumed to copy unchanged, aud is the downstream API, act can record FastAPI as the current actor when the authorization server represents delegation that way, allowing the downstream API to audit “subject X via service Y.” Anti‑pattern alert Forwarding the inbound user token verbatim to a downstream API is the most common mistake. It works, but the downstream API now sees a token whose aud claim is your service, which a good resource server will reject. Token exchange (RFC 8693) is one standards-based fix when both authorization and resource servers support it. Microsoft Entra's on-behalf-of (OBO) flow addresses the same delegation problem through its provider-specific contract. 5) Quick decision matrix BoundaryUseWhy Human → Browser → Your app OIDC + Passkeys at the IdP, PKCE for the app Phishing‑resistant, no passwords stored. Browser/SPA/mobile → Your API OIDC + DPoP access tokens Token-only replay is blocked; full client compromise remains in scope. Workload → Workload (inside platform) mTLS + cert‑bound tokens (cnf.x5t#S256) Strong binding when the OAuth and TLS layers implement RFC 8705 together. Workload → Workload (across orgs) Workload Identity Federation (Chapter 11) + signed JWT assertion No long‑lived secrets to rotate. Your API → Downstream API on user's behalf Token exchange (RFC 8693) / OBO Preserves user identity, narrows audience, records the actor. 6) Reading list (specs) WebAuthn Level 3 RFC 9449 — OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) RFC 8705 — OAuth 2.0 Mutual-TLS Client Authentication and Certificate-Bound Access Tokens RFC 8693 — OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange RFC 9700 — OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice OAuth 2.1 — active Internet-Draft, not yet an RFC

title: Tenant Identity vs IAM vs Workload Identity (GCP)
label: 12. End-user vs workload identity
headings: The 3-lane model (memorize this)
Scenario 1 — A normal end user uses your app (tenant isolation)
Scenario 2 — An internal employee sees buckets in the GCP Console (IAM)
Scenario 3 — Only users in an org group can use the app (allowlist gating)
How all three show up in one request (the full picture)
How Bearer token maps to user_id and tenant_id
How a service account is used to write to a bucket (workload identity)
FastAPI examples (clean + simple)
Common mistakes (and the fix)
description: This tutorial fixes the #1 enterprise confusion: tenant isolation (your SaaS data boundaries) is not the same thing as Cloud IAM (who can see/use GCP resources) and not the same thing as org group gating (who is allow...
text: This tutorial fixes the #1 enterprise confusion: tenant isolation (your SaaS data boundaries) is not the same thing as Cloud IAM (who can see/use GCP resources) and not the same thing as org group gating (who is allowed to use the app at all). We’ll explain all three using your multi-tenant Doc Q&A app as the running example. Reading path This chapter is the primary explanation of the three-lane identity model. Chapter 13 applies the same model to AD/Workspace group gating and tenant bootstrap policy; Chapter 14 implements the workload-identity lane on GCP. Acronyms The 3-lane model Scenario 1: Tenant isolation Scenario 2: GCP Console (IAM) Scenario 3: Org allowlist (groups) One request: how they combine Bearer token → user_id/tenant_id Service account → bucket/secrets FastAPI examples Common mistakes Acronyms (quick) Tenant: a customer org (Company A vs Company B) User: a human inside a tenant (Alice, Bob) OIDC: login tokens from your IdP (Google Workspace) JWT: token format often used for access tokens IAM: GCP permissions to GCP resources (buckets, projects, secrets) Service account: “machine identity” your backend runs as Workload Identity: how GKE/Cloud Run give pods/services service-account credentials without storing keys Org allowlist / group gating: “only members of Group X can use this app” The 3-lane model (memorize this) Lane A — End-user identity Who is calling? Comes in the HTTP request as Authorization: Bearer .... Used to derive user_id and tenant_id. Lane B — App authorization What can they see? Your code enforces tenant isolation (DB filters, search filters, RLS backstop). Lane C — Workload identity (IAM) What can the service access? The backend’s service account permissions to GCS, Secret Manager, Cloud SQL, logs. Org allowlist (gating) Who is allowed in at all? Often based on Workspace/AD groups. Checked during bootstrap/login. Shortcut: Tenant isolation protects customer data inside your app. IAM protects cloud resources. Group gating protects who can even use the app. Scenario 1 — A normal end user uses your app (tenant isolation) Goal Thousands of users can hit the same API, but each user can only access their tenant’s documents. What makes this work User logs in with Google Workspace → frontend receives an access token. Frontend calls your API with: Authorization: Bearer <token> Backend validates token, extracts user_id and maps to tenant_id. Every DB/search call is scoped: WHERE tenant_id = ... Key point: The user does not need GCP Console access. They are not an IAM principal for your cloud resources. Scenario 2 — An internal employee sees buckets in the GCP Console (IAM) Goal Some employees can see/modify buckets and projects in the GCP Console; others can’t. What controls visibility Employee signs into GCP Console with their corporate identity. GCP checks IAM bindings (direct user or group membership). Console shows resources they have permission to list/access. Common confusion: “I can’t see the bucket in console, so tenant isolation must be broken.” No — console visibility is IAM. Tenant isolation is your app’s logic + DB policies. Scenario 3 — Only users in an org group can use the app (allowlist gating) Goal Only users in a particular org group (e.g., “DocQA-Users”) can use the app at all. Where it’s enforced User logs in and obtains a token (OIDC). Frontend calls a bootstrap endpoint like GET /me or POST /auth/bootstrap. Backend verifies the token, then checks: “Is this user in allowed group(s)?” If not allowed → return 403. If allowed → map to tenant and proceed. Group gating answers: “Can you use the product?” Tenant isolation answers: “Which tenant’s data can you access once inside?” How all three show up in one request (the full picture) Think of it as three independent checks that happen in different places. Lane A (OIDC token): Identify caller → user_id, claims, email. Org gate: Is the user allowed group(s)? If no → 403. Lane B (tenant isolation): Determine tenant_id → scope DB/search to that tenant only. Lane C (workload IAM): Backend service account reads secrets / reads & writes to GCS / logs. POST /query HTTP/1.1 Authorization: Bearer <user_access_token> Content-Type: application/json { "question": "What did Chandima mention on 1 Dec?" } How Bearer token maps to user_id and tenant_id Why the token string itself is not the identity Access tokens rotate (expiry, refresh, re-login). The backend does not “recognize” a user by comparing token strings. Instead it validates the token and extracts a stable identity claim. Typical mapping logic Verify token (signature + issuer + audience + expiry). Extract stable user key (usually sub, combined with iss). Derive tenant from: a claim (e.g., tid/tenant_id) or a DB lookup (issuer+sub → tenant_id) or a policy mapping (email domain → tenant) for B2B setups. Best practice: store users keyed by (issuer, sub) in your DB. That stays stable even when tokens change. How a service account is used to write to a bucket (workload identity) What’s happening Your backend runs as a service account (machine identity). That service account is granted IAM permissions on a bucket (e.g., write objects). When your code calls the GCS SDK, it automatically obtains a short-lived access token for that service account. Key idea: The backend uses its own service identity to reach GCS/Secret Manager — not the end user’s token. The end-user token only decides which tenant path/object the backend is allowed to touch. Important: If you let end users access buckets directly via IAM, you are mixing “cloud control plane identity” with “app tenancy”. Most SaaS designs avoid this — users access files through your API (or via signed URLs), while the backend holds storage permissions. FastAPI examples (clean + simple) 1) End-user identity dependency (Bearer → claims → user_id/tenant_id) This is intentionally small: validate token, then map to tenant. In real code your JWT verification can use JWKS. from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, HTTPException from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, HTTPBearer from pydantic import BaseModel app = FastAPI() bearer = HTTPBearer(auto_error=True) class Identity(BaseModel): user_id: str tenant_id: str email: str | None = None def verify_jwt_and_get_claims(token: str) -> dict: # In production: verify signature (JWKS), iss/aud/exp checks. # Here: pretend token is valid and return decoded claims. return {"sub": "user-123", "iss": "https://accounts.google.com", "email": "alice@acme.com"} def map_claims_to_tenant(claims: dict) -> str: # Example: domain-based tenant mapping (toy). email = claims.get("email") or "" if "@" not in email: raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="No tenant mapping") return email.split("@", 1)[1] # "acme.com" def require_allowed_group(claims: dict) -> None: # Example gate. In real life you would check group membership via claims or directory lookup. # If user is not in allowed group(s), block the app. allowed = True if not allowed: raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Not allowed to use the app") def get_identity(creds: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(bearer)) -> Identity: claims = verify_jwt_and_get_claims(creds.credentials) require_allowed_group(claims) user_id = claims["sub"] tenant_id = map_claims_to_tenant(claims) return Identity(user_id=user_id, tenant_id=tenant_id, email=claims.get("email")) @app.get("/me") def me(ident: Identity = Depends(get_identity)): return ident 2) Workload identity in code (service account → Secret Manager / GCS) No keys in code. The SDK picks up the pod/service’s identity automatically. # pip install google-cloud-secret-manager google-cloud-storage from google.cloud import secretmanager, storage def read_secret_value(secret_resource_name: str) -> str: # Uses workload identity (service account) behind the scenes. client = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient() resp = client.access_secret_version(request={"name": secret_resource_name}) return resp.payload.data.decode("utf-8") def write_tenant_object(bucket: str, tenant_id: str, object_name: str, data: bytes) -> None: # Uses workload identity; IAM decides if this service account can write. gcs = storage.Client() b = gcs.bucket(bucket) # App tenancy decides *where* we write (tenant prefix). blob = b.blob(f"{tenant_id}/{object_name}") blob.upload_from_string(data) Separation of duties: IAM answers “can the service write to this bucket at all?” Tenant isolation answers “which tenant prefix/object is allowed for this request?” Common mistakes (and the fix) ❌ Mistake 1: “Tenant = IAM” Wrong: “If IAM is correct, tenants are isolated.” Right: IAM is cloud infra permissions. Tenant isolation is your app filtering + DB policy (RLS as backstop). ❌ Mistake 2: Passing user tokens to cloud APIs Wrong: backend calls Secret Manager with the user’s Bearer token. Right: backend calls cloud APIs using its service account. User token only controls tenant scoping and app permissions. ❌ Mistake 3: Losing tenant context in async/background work Wrong: enqueue a job without storing tenant_id. Right: persist tenant_id with the job and enforce tenant checks when the job runs. Bank-grade habit: add an audit record for “who requested what” (end-user identity) and “which workload executed it” (service identity). Identity rule to carry forward Preserve both actors in every sensitive audit event: the end user who requested the action and the workload identity that executed it. Authorization uses the user's application permissions; cloud API access uses the workload's IAM permissions.

headings: The one-sentence mental model
Scenario 1 — Normal end user uses your app (tenant isolation)
Scenario 2 — Internal employee sees buckets in GCP Console (IAM)
Scenario 3 — App is accessible only to an AD group (org allowlist gate)
Scenario 3 has two enforcement methods
How all three fit together (the “3-lane model”)
Common mistakes (and fixes)
Bootstrap decision tree (the exact order)
description: You’re dealing with three different “who are you / what can you access” systems that often get mixed up:
text: You’re dealing with three different “who are you / what can you access” systems that often get mixed up: Application tenancy (tenant_id, user_id) → your SaaS data isolation Cloud IAM → who can see/use GCP resources (Console, buckets, secrets) Org group gating (AD/Workspace groups) → who is allowed to use your app at all They can interact, but they’re not the same thing. How this chapter relates to Chapter 10 Chapter 10 owns the core three-lane model: end-user identity, application authorization, and workload identity/IAM. This chapter keeps the same concepts but rearranges them around the enterprise policy question: tenant bootstrap, AD/Workspace group gating, and common operational mistakes. The one-sentence mental model IAM controls access to GCP resources (projects, buckets, secrets). Tenancy controls access to your app’s data (documents, rows, search results). AD/Group gating controls who can even use the app (coarse allowlist), before tenancy even matters. Three distinct identity and authorization lanes User authentication enters an application gate, tenant authorization scopes data, and workload identity accesses cloud services. Lane A: end-user identity OIDC login -> access token -> verified (issuer, subject) Who initiated this request? Lane B: application authorization group gate -> tenant membership -> role -> row/search/object filter Which application data is allowed? Lane C: workload identity service account -> IAM role -> Cloud SQL, Storage, Secret Manager, queues Which infrastructure calls may execute? A request may involve all three lanes, but no lane substitutes for another. Preserve both the requesting user and executing workload in the audit record. Scenario 1 — Normal end user uses your app (tenant isolation) Goal User can only access their tenant’s documents, even though all tenants share the same backend + databases. Step-by-step User signs in with Google Workspace React uses OIDC (Auth Code + PKCE). React receives an access token This is the user’s “proof” for your API. React calls your backend Every call includes: Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Backend validates token signature + issuer + audience + expiry. Backend maps token → identity user_id = claims["sub"] tenant_id = mapping(...) (domain mapping or DB lookup) Backend scopes all data access by tenant DB queries: WHERE tenant_id = ... Search queries: tenant filter Jobs: store tenant_id and enforce later What this means Tenant isolation is enforced inside your app + DB/search rules. 🚫 End users do not need GCP Console access or IAM permissions. Scenario 2 — Internal employee sees buckets in GCP Console (IAM) Goal Some employees can see/modify certain buckets/projects, others cannot. Step-by-step Employee logs into GCP Console They are a human principal. GCP checks IAM bindings Example: group:platform-admins@company.com has roles/storage.admin on a project. Console shows only permitted resources If they lack storage.buckets.list or equivalent permissions, the bucket won’t show / access denied. What this means Console visibility = Cloud IAM (users/groups/roles on org/folder/project/bucket). 🚫 This is unrelated to your app’s tenant_id. The GCP Console is the cloud control plane, not your SaaS tenancy system. Scenario 3 — App is accessible only to an AD group (org allowlist gate) Goal Only users in an org group (from Active Directory) can use the app at all. Step-by-step AD group exists e.g. DocQA-Users Group is synced/federated into Google Workspace e.g. Google Group: docqa-users@company.com User signs in with Google (OIDC) React calls /auth/bootstrap (or /me) with: Authorization: Bearer <access_token> Backend checks two things: token is valid user is in docqa-users@company.com If allowed: backend does tenant mapping + provisioning determine tenant_id create user row if missing return identity What this means Group gating answers: “Can you use the app at all?” Tenancy answers: “Which tenant’s data can you access?” 🚫 Group gating is not tenancy. 🚫 Group gating is not IAM. Scenario 3 has two enforcement methods Method A — Backend enforces group membership (app-level gate) How it works The backend validates the token and calls an org directory/groups API (or uses cached membership) to answer: “Is alice@company.com in docqa-users@company.com?” Not a member → 403 Member → proceed to tenant mapping + provisioning Why you’d choose it Your backend remains the “source of truth” for access. You can combine it naturally with onboarding/provisioning logic. Works even if you change gateways or hosting. Trade-offs Backend needs permission to check group membership. You usually cache membership in DB to avoid checking on every request. Method B — Edge/gateway enforces group membership (Apigee/IAP-style) How it works An edge layer sits in front of your backend. It verifies the caller identity and enforces a policy: “must be in allowed group” If user is not allowed, the request never reaches FastAPI. Why you’d choose it Strong perimeter: reduces backend exposure. Central policy for multiple services: auth, rate limits, quotas, logging. Trade-offs More moving parts. You still typically keep backend checks as a backstop (especially for provisioning + tenant mapping). Best-practice combo Edge gate = front door protection Backend gate = final authority + tenant mapping + provisioning (Defense in depth) How all three fit together (the “3-lane model”) Lane A — End-user identity (OIDC token) Comes from Google login Arrives as Authorization: Bearer ... Used to derive user_id/tenant_id Lane B — Application authorization (tenant isolation) DB/search filtering rules using tenant_id RLS is a backstop, not the primary identity mechanism Lane C — Workload identity (service account IAM) Backend runs as a service account IAM grants that service account access to infra: Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage, Secret Manager, logging, queues Not tied to the human user Common mistakes (and fixes) Mistake 1: “Tenant = IAM” No. Tenant is inside your app; IAM is for GCP resources. Fix: keep end users out of IAM; enforce tenancy in app/DB/search. Mistake 2: “If user is in AD group, they’re tenant X” Not necessarily. Group is a coarse gate; tenant mapping is separate. Fix: group check first, tenant mapping second. Mistake 3: “Users should access buckets directly via IAM” Usually no for SaaS customers. Fix: users access files via your API (or signed URLs); backend uses service account to talk to storage. Bootstrap decision tree (the exact order) /auth/bootstrap (or /me): Verify token (signature, iss, aud, exp) Check org allowlist (AD/Workspace group) → if fail: 403 Map to tenant_id (domain mapping or DB lookup) → if fail: 403 Provision user if missing (issuer+sub key, store tenant_id) Return {user_id, tenant_id, is_new_user} Typed FastAPI bootstrap boundary Keep verification, group lookup, tenant mapping, and persistence behind separate interfaces. This makes each policy independently testable and prevents the route from trusting unverified claims. from typing import Annotated from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException, status from pydantic import BaseModel app = FastAPI() class VerifiedIdentity(BaseModel): issuer: str subject: str email: str email_verified: bool class BootstrapResponse(BaseModel): user_id: str tenant_id: str is_new_user: bool async def require_identity( authorization: Annotated[str | None, Header()] = None, ) -> VerifiedIdentity: token = extract_bearer_token(authorization) claims = await token_verifier.verify( token, expected_issuer=settings.issuer, expected_audience=settings.api_audience, ) return VerifiedIdentity( issuer=claims["iss"], subject=claims["sub"], email=claims["email"], email_verified=claims.get("email_verified", False), ) @app.post("/auth/bootstrap", response_model=BootstrapResponse) async def bootstrap( identity: Annotated[VerifiedIdentity, Depends(require_identity)], ) -> BootstrapResponse: if not identity.email_verified: raise HTTPException( status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, detail="A verified organization email is required", ) allowed = await directory.is_group_member( email=identity.email, group="docqa-users@company.com", ) if not allowed: raise HTTPException( status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, detail="User is not in the application access group", ) tenant_id = await tenant_directory.resolve_membership( issuer=identity.issuer, subject=identity.subject, email=identity.email, ) if tenant_id is None: raise HTTPException( status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, detail="No active tenant membership", ) user, created = await users.upsert_external_identity( issuer=identity.issuer, subject=identity.subject, verified_email=identity.email, tenant_id=tenant_id, ) return BootstrapResponse( user_id=user.id, tenant_id=tenant_id, is_new_user=created, ) Concurrency requirement Enforce a database uniqueness constraint on (issuer, subject) and perform the lookup/upsert in one transaction. Two first requests can arrive concurrently; an in-process “check then insert” is not sufficient across workers or replicas.
