description: Begin by organizing your Google Cloud resources under a single Organization (especially if you have Google Workspace). Under the organization, use Folders and Projects to separate concerns. A common approach is one pr...
text: Project Setup Begin by organizing your Google Cloud resources under a single Organization (especially if you have Google Workspace). Under the organization, use Folders and Projects to separate concerns. A common approach is one project per environment (e.g. myapp-dev, myapp-prod). This isolates IAM boundaries and billing by environment. For example: Create a project for production and one for development: gcloud projects create myapp-prod --name="MyApp Production" --organization=ORG_ID gcloud projects create myapp-dev --name="MyApp Development" --organization=ORG_ID Link each project to a billing account: gcloud billing projects link myapp-prod --billing-account=BILLING_ACCOUNT_ID gcloud billing projects link myapp-dev --billing-account=BILLING_ACCOUNT_ID (You can list billing accounts via gcloud billing accounts list.) Optionally, use Folders to group projects (e.g. Network, Platform, Services folders). Folders allow applying policies to multiple projects, and projects segregate environments and teams. A project can contain one or more VPC networks. Google Cloud may create a default network for a new standalone project, unless an organization policy suppresses it, but production platforms should create and manage their network topology explicitly. You can use separate custom VPCs per project or a centrally governed Shared VPC host project. For example, create a custom VPC in the prod project: gcloud compute networks create my-vpc --project=myapp-prod --subnet-mode=custom gcloud compute networks subnets create subnet-us --project=myapp-prod \ --network=my-vpc --region=us-central1 --range=10.10.0.0/16 If using Shared VPC, set up one “host” project containing the VPC, and attach service projects (e.g. myapp-prod) to it. Configure firewall rules to allow only necessary traffic (for example, allow public HTTPS only to the external load balancer, allow Google health-check ranges to backend services, and keep database traffic private). These are separate controls: Private Google Access lets resources without external IP addresses reach supported Google APIs, while Cloud SQL private IP requires private services access or the currently supported Private Service Connect design. Enabling one does not configure the other. Finally, tag and label your projects and resources for clarity (e.g. env=prod). At the org level, enforce policies (such as disabling default-credential grants) so that service accounts must have only the permissions you grant. IAM and Service Accounts Use IAM roles and service accounts with least privilege. For each project, create Google service accounts (GSAs) for the workloads and grant them only needed roles. For example: Cloud Run frontend: Create a service account (e.g. frontend-sa@myapp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com) and give it only the roles needed (e.g. roles/storage.objectViewer if it reads from Cloud Storage, or other roles for backend calls). Assign this SA to the Cloud Run service with --service-account=frontend-sa@.... Avoid using the default Compute Engine SA broadly; instead use user-managed SAs with minimal permissions. GKE backend: Create a Google SA (e.g. backend-sa@myapp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com) for the FastAPI pods. Grant it roles like roles/cloudsql.client (to access Cloud SQL) and roles/logging.logWriter. For example: gcloud iam service-accounts create backend-sa --display-name="Backend Service Account" gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding myapp-prod \ --member="serviceAccount:backend-sa@myapp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \ --role="roles/cloudsql.client" gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding myapp-prod \ --member="serviceAccount:backend-sa@myapp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \ --role="roles/logging.logWriter" Workload Identity Federation for GKE: Enable it so pods can obtain short-lived Google credentials without service-account key files. When creating the GKE cluster, use --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog. GKE creates the workload identity pool PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog for the project. Then choose one of two authorization patterns: Direct resource access, preferred when the target API supports federated principals: grant the Kubernetes workload principal the required role directly on the resource or project. IAM service-account impersonation, for compatibility: allow a Kubernetes ServiceAccount (KSA) to impersonate a Google service account (GSA), then annotate the KSA with that GSA. A direct grant for default/backend-ksa looks like this: PROJECT_ID=myapp-prod PROJECT_NUMBER="$(gcloud projects describe "$PROJECT_ID" --format='value(projectNumber)')" gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding "$PROJECT_ID" \ --role="roles/logging.logWriter" \ --member="principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${PROJECT_NUMBER}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${PROJECT_ID}.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/default/sa/backend-ksa" If a service requires GSA impersonation, the IAM binding and KSA annotation are both required: gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \ backend-sa@myapp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role="roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser" \ --member="serviceAccount:myapp-prod.svc.id.goog[default/backend-ksa]" apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: backend-ksa namespace: default annotations: iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: backend-sa@myapp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com Then deploy the KSA and set serviceAccountName: backend-ksa on the Pod. The annotation alone is not an authorization grant: the roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser binding above is what permits impersonation. Google client libraries use Application Default Credentials (ADC), and the GKE metadata server exchanges the KSA token for short-lived credentials. Cloud Run authentication to GCP: Cloud Run uses its service identity (the Google SA you assign) to call other Google Cloud services. By default Cloud Run will fetch tokens from its metadata server and use ADC. Ensure the Cloud Run SA has the right roles (for example roles/storage.objectViewer to read static objects, roles/storage.objectUser to write objects, and roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator only if it truly needs to mint tokens). As above, use a user-managed SA and avoid broad roles like Editor or project-wide Storage Admin unless there is a specific operational reason. Remember to use Google Groups to manage user access to projects. Assign IAM roles to groups (e.g. “NetworkAdmin”, “DevOps”, “AppDeveloper”) rather than individual users. Authentication with Google Identity (OIDC) To authenticate end-users, use Google’s OAuth2/OpenID Connect. First, create OAuth 2.0 credentials in your project: in the Cloud Console go to APIs & Services > Credentials > Create > OAuth Client ID. Choose “Web application” and set your React app’s origin and redirect URI (e.g. https://myapp.example.com and https://myapp.example.com/oauth2callback). This gives you a Client ID. In your React frontend, use Google Identity Services or another maintained OAuth/OIDC library to implement the authorization code flow with PKCE. The authorization endpoint returns a short-lived authorization code; the client or a backend-for-frontend exchanges that code at the token endpoint. With scope=openid email profile, the token response can include an ID token that describes the authenticated user. For higher-sensitivity applications, a backend-for-frontend can perform the exchange and establish an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie so browser JavaScript does not retain long-lived tokens. An ID token is evidence of authentication for the OAuth client; it is not a general-purpose access token for arbitrary APIs. Validate it at the login/session boundary, then establish your own application session. If your API directly accepts Google-issued access tokens, validate their intended audience and scopes using the resource-server rules for that API. The following ID-token check is appropriate at a sign-in endpoint: from google.oauth2 import id_token from google.auth.transport import requests try: # TOKEN is the ID token string from the client, and CLIENT_ID is your OAuth 2.0 client ID id_info = id_token.verify_oauth2_token(TOKEN, requests.Request(), CLIENT_ID) # The token is valid. You can trust id_info['sub'], id_info['email'], etc. except ValueError: # Invalid token raise Unauthorized() The verify_oauth2_token call checks the token’s signature, issuer (https://accounts.google.com or Google’s equivalent issuer form), audience, and lifetime. If valid, id_info contains the user’s Google identity. Use the stable sub claim as the external identity key; treat email as mutable display/contact data, and enforce hosted-domain policy explicitly if your application requires it. The backend can then create its own session without handling the user’s Google password. Key points: Local ID-token verification does not require the obsolete Google+ API. Configure the OAuth consent screen and the correct web OAuth client, use that client ID as the expected audience, register exact origins and redirect URIs, and use maintained Google Identity/OAuth libraries rather than writing the protocol by hand. Data Storage Design For application data, choose managed GCP services: Relational data (Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL): Cloud SQL is a fully managed PostgreSQL database (with high availability, automated backups, patching). Create a Cloud SQL instance in your project: gcloud sql instances create my-postgres --database-version=POSTGRES_15 \ --tier=db-f1-micro --region=us-central1 --network=my-vpc gcloud sql databases create mydb --instance=my-postgres Grant the workload principal or impersonated GSA the Cloud SQL Client role so it can open an authorized connection through the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or a connector. On GKE, you can also use private IP after configuring the required private network connection. Keep the layers separate: Workload Identity supplies Google credentials for the connector and Cloud SQL control plane; roles/cloudsql.client does not by itself log into PostgreSQL. The database still authenticates a database user with a password, or you explicitly enable Cloud SQL IAM database authentication and use a connector/proxy flow that supports it. Why not alternatives? We prefer Cloud SQL over a self-hosted database because it offloads operations to Google (automated failover, backups, scaling). Compared to NoSQL options like Firestore or Firebase RTDB, Postgres offers strong consistency and complex relational queries. BigQuery is purely analytic (not suited for OLTP). (If you needed wide-column or global scale, Cloud Spanner could be considered, but it’s more complex and costly.) File/object storage (Cloud Storage): For user-uploaded files, static assets, or backups, use Cloud Storage buckets. It is a durable managed object store, but replication and data residency depend on the bucket location you choose: region, dual-region, or multi-region. Select that location deliberately rather than assuming every bucket is globally replicated. Example: gcloud storage buckets create gs://myapp-prod-files \ --project=myapp-prod \ --location=us-central1 \ --uniform-bucket-level-access Then grant your backend SA a Storage role (e.g. roles/storage.objectAdmin) on that bucket. In code you can use the Cloud Storage client, which under the hood uses Workload Identity for auth: from google.cloud import storage client = storage.Client() bucket = client.bucket('myapp-prod-files') blob = bucket.blob('somefile.png') blob.upload_from_filename('localfile.png') Why not alternatives? Cloud Storage is simpler and cheaper for large blobs than, say, storing files in a SQL database. It replaces running a custom file server. We don’t use Firestore or Firebase for file storage. (You could store small JSON data in Firestore, but it is not transactional SQL.) Cloud Storage integrates with other GCP tools (logging, CDN, etc.) and automatically handles encryption and scaling. Using Workload Identity, both Cloud SQL and Cloud Storage access are secured without embedding keys. The KSA mapping ensures the Pod’s Google SA (with its IAM roles) is used by the Google client libraries. Deployment Architecture Our frontend is a React Single-Page App; our backend is a FastAPI microservice. Frontend on Cloud Run For a purely static React SPA, Cloud Storage + Cloud CDN, Firebase Hosting, or a managed static host is often the simplest industry-standard deployment. Use Cloud Run when you want a containerized frontend, SSR, a backend-for-frontend, or the same release controls as the rest of your services. If you do containerize the SPA, use reproducible installs and a non-root runtime image: # Build stage FROM node:lts-bookworm-slim AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci COPY . . RUN npm run build # Serve with nginx as a non-root user; pin image digests in production. FROM nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:stable-alpine COPY --from=builder /app/build /usr/share/nginx/html Build and push the container image. New GCP projects usually use Artifact Registry rather than the older Container Registry-style gcr.io path: REGION=us-central1 PROJECT_ID=myapp-prod REPOSITORY=app-images TAG=2026-05-17 gcloud artifacts repositories create "$REPOSITORY" \ --repository-format=docker \ --location="$REGION" docker build -t "$REGION-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/$REPOSITORY/react-frontend:$TAG" . docker push "$REGION-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/$REPOSITORY/react-frontend:$TAG" For production, prefer immutable version tags or image digests over latest. That makes rollbacks and audit trails much easier. Deploy it to Cloud Run: gcloud run deploy react-frontend \ --image us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/myapp-prod/app-images/react-frontend:2026-05-17 \ --region us-central1 \ --platform managed \ --allow-unauthenticated \ --service-account=frontend-sa@myapp-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com --allow-unauthenticated is appropriate for a public marketing site or public SPA shell. For internal/admin frontends, remove it and put Cloud Run behind IAM, Identity-Aware Proxy, or your enterprise IdP. Cloud Run automatically provisions an HTTPS endpoint for you (for example https://react-frontend-abcd1234-uc.a.run.app). It only serves over HTTPS – HTTP is redirected to HTTPS by default. If you want a custom domain (e.g. www.myapp.com), you can map it in Cloud Run settings. Set environment variables on the Cloud Run service for any configuration (e.g. the backend API URL or OAuth client ID). Cloud Run containers use the assigned service account (frontend-sa@…) as their identity when calling other GCP services. Backend on GKE Create a GKE cluster for the FastAPI service. For example, a Standard cluster with Workload Identity and alias IPs: gcloud container clusters create my-cluster \ --region us-central1 \ --workload-pool=myapp-prod.svc.id.goog \ --num-nodes=3 \ --machine-type=e2-standard-4 \ --enable-ip-alias This sets up my-cluster with a default node pool of 3 VMs. The --workload-pool flag enables Workload Identity Federation. You could also use a GKE Autopilot cluster (which has WI on by default) to avoid managing nodes at all. You can add more node pools if desired. For example, to separate workloads: gcloud container node-pools create backend-pool \ --cluster=my-cluster \ --num-nodes=2 \ --machine-type=e2-medium \ --node-labels=role=backend Use node pools to apply different machine types or taints. Always enable IP alias (--enable-ip-alias) to allow private pod ranges. Deploy your FastAPI app as a Kubernetes Deployment + Service. For example: apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: { name: fastapi-deployment } spec: replicas: 2 selector: { matchLabels: { app: fastapi } } template: metadata: { labels: { app: fastapi } } spec: serviceAccountName: backend-ksa containers: - name: fastapi image: us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/myapp-prod/app-images/fastapi-backend:2026-05-17 ports: [ { containerPort: 80 } ] apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: { name: fastapi-service } spec: selector: { app: fastapi } ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: 80 } ] These expose the app on port 80 internally. Note the serviceAccountName: backend-ksa (the K8s SA we annotated earlier); this ensures the pod assumes the Google service account identity. Ingress and Load Balancing To expose the backend publicly, create a Kubernetes Ingress (which uses an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer): apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: fastapi-ingress annotations: kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "gce" spec: rules: - host: api.myapp.com http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: fastapi-service port: { number: 80 } When applied, GKE can provision an external Application Load Balancer with a public IP. The Ingress alone does not automatically prove domain ownership or create a certificate. Reserve the address, point DNS at it, and configure a Google-managed certificate (or Certificate Manager) using the supported GKE annotation/Gateway design. Wait for the certificate to become active before enforcing HTTPS. Make sure the backend permits Google health checks; in a Shared VPC, coordinate the required firewall policy with the host-project administrators. A browser-hosted SPA normally calls the public GKE endpoint directly. If Cloud Run is acting as an SSR service or backend-for-frontend, it can call that endpoint over HTTPS. For private connectivity, use an internal load balancer and Cloud Run VPC egress. Prefer Direct VPC egress where it is supported; use a Serverless VPC Access connector when its compatibility or topology is required. Observability and Scaling Enable Cloud Logging and Monitoring on the cluster (this is on by default in GKE). Export logs via the Kubernetes Logging agent or use aggregated sinks. Define uptime checks and alerts in Cloud Monitoring (for example, an alert if the health endpoint of your service fails). Use horizontal pod autoscaling on the FastAPI Deployment if needed (kubectl autoscale deploy fastapi-deployment --cpu-percent=70 --min=1 --max=5). Networking and Resource Governance VPC and Subnets: Use a custom VPC (or Shared VPC host) with appropriately sized subnets. Enable Private Google Access when private workloads need supported Google APIs without external IP addresses. Configure Cloud SQL private IP separately through private services access or the supported Private Service Connect topology. The GKE metadata server is link-local and governed separately. Use hierarchical firewall policies for organization/folder defaults while allowing required DNS, metadata, health-check, control-plane, and application traffic. If using Shared VPC, the host project owns the network and service projects attach workloads to it. Project-level Security: Disable overly broad Org policies like automatic Editor grants for default SAs. Regularly audit IAM policies (Cloud IAM Recommender can surface over-privileged identities). Use Google Groups for role assignments (e.g. “DevOps” group with Compute Admin on dev, but Cloud SQL Client on prod). Networking Security: Consider enabling VPC Service Controls if you need to protect against data exfiltration from managed services. At a minimum, configure Kubernetes Network Policies to restrict traffic between pods if you run multiple services. Cost and Billing: Since billing is at the project level, use separate projects (or folders) per environment to track costs. Use billing reports or Cloud Billing budget alerts to monitor spend. Tag resources (with labels like env=prod) and set up budgets per tag. Regularly clean up unused resources (old node pools, images, volumes) to control costs. Consider using Cloud Budgets with alerts on 50%/75%/90% spend thresholds. VPC Quotas and Limits: Use VPC native clusters (alias IP) to avoid exhaustion of IPs. Plan subnet sizes for pods and services, anticipating scale. For example, if you expect 100 Pods per node pool, allocate a /14 for pod range. Use Cloud NAT if your nodes need to access the Internet without external IPs. DNS and TLS: Use Cloud DNS (or your provider) for domain names. For Cloud Run, GKE Ingress, or Gateway, use the product’s supported Google-managed certificate integration or Certificate Manager. “ACM” commonly refers to AWS Certificate Manager and is not the Google Cloud product name. By following these steps and best practices, you’ll have a robust GCP foundation: isolated projects and IAM, secure service identities (Workload Identity) for accessing Cloud SQL and Storage, user login via Google OIDC in the React app, and autoscaled deployments of your frontend and backend on Cloud Run and GKE. All communication is over HTTPS, and data access from code is locked down to specific service accounts with minimal privileges. This architecture is production-ready and scalable for an enterprise SaaS with Google Workspace authentication. Official references Workload Identity Federation for GKE: concepts and credential flow GKE: configure workload access to Google Cloud APIs Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL: connect from GKE Cloud Storage bucket locations GKE: secure traffic with managed certificates Cloud Run: Direct VPC egress and VPC connectors

title: Calling External Services Across Cloud Trust Boundaries
label: 15. Cross-cloud service integration
headings: 1. Option A: API Key Stored in GCP Secret Manager
2. Option B: Microsoft Entra Workload Identity Federation
3. How This Relates to Service Accounts
4. Reliability Rules Shared by Both Options
5. Data Governance and Observability
6. Decision Summary
Official References
description: A GCP workload calling Azure OpenAI needs an Azure-accepted credential, a bounded network client, and a clear data-governance contract.
text: A GCP workload calling Azure OpenAI needs an Azure-accepted credential, a bounded network client, and a clear data-governance contract. Where this fits Chapter 12 separated end-user identity, application authorization, and workload identity. This chapter follows the workload across a cloud boundary. The end user's bearer token still authorizes the application request, but the backend uses its own credential to call Azure. Two supported authentication paths from GCP to Azure OpenAI A GKE workload can read an API key from Secret Manager or exchange a Google-issued workload token with Microsoft Entra. Either credential is then used to call Azure OpenAI. GKE backend Google workload identity GCP Secret Manager versioned Azure API key Microsoft Entra ID federated token exchange Azure OpenAI API key or Entra bearer token read secret api-key external assertion short-lived token The two paths solve the same authentication problem with different operational tradeoffs. Neither sends the end user's token to Azure as the backend credential. There are two production patterns. Choose from policy and operational requirements rather than assuming that the most complex option is always best. QuestionAPI key in Secret ManagerEntra workload federation Long-lived Azure credentialYes; rotate and version it.No; exchange a trusted external assertion for a short-lived token. Initial setupLower.Higher: app registration, federated credential, RBAC, and token exchange. Runtime dependenciesGCP IAM + Secret Manager + Azure endpoint.Google token issuer + Entra token endpoint + Azure endpoint. Best fitSmaller systems with mature secret rotation.Higher-assurance systems that prohibit static cross-cloud credentials. 1. Option A: API Key Stored in GCP Secret Manager Flow Your backend (running on GKE) authenticates to GCP Secret Manager using its GCP service account (Workload Identity). It reads the Azure OpenAI API key from Secret Manager. It calls Azure OpenAI with: api-key: <key> header (typical for Azure OpenAI) Why choose this Easiest to implement No Azure identity federation complexity Common and reliable What you “associate” 1) Store the secret Secret: azure-openai-api-key 2) Grant your backend service account access to read it IAM: give backend-sa@... role roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor on that secret. 3) In code: load once, reuse the HTTP client, and call Azure import os from contextlib import asynccontextmanager import httpx from fastapi import FastAPI, Request from google.cloud import secretmanager def read_secret(secret_id: str, version: str) -> str: client = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient() name = ( f"projects/{os.environ['GCP_PROJECT']}/secrets/" f"{secret_id}/versions/{version}" ) response = client.access_secret_version(request={"name": name}) return response.payload.data.decode("utf-8") class AzureOpenAIClient: def __init__(self, *, api_key: str, endpoint: str, deployment: str): self._deployment = deployment self._http = httpx.AsyncClient( base_url=endpoint.rstrip("/"), headers={"api-key": api_key}, timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=5.0, read=60.0, write=15.0, pool=5.0), limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=100, max_keepalive_connections=20), ) async def create_response(self, prompt: str) -> dict: response = await self._http.post( "/openai/v1/responses", json={"model": self._deployment, "input": prompt}, ) response.raise_for_status() return response.json() async def close(self) -> None: await self._http.aclose() @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app: FastAPI): # Secret access is synchronous, but startup completes before requests run. # Pin a deployed version so rollback is deterministic. api_key = read_secret( "azure-openai-api-key", os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_KEY_VERSION"], ) app.state.azure_openai = AzureOpenAIClient( api_key=api_key, endpoint=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT"], deployment=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT"], ) yield await app.state.azure_openai.close() app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan) @app.post("/generate") async def generate(request: Request, prompt: str) -> dict: return await request.app.state.azure_openai.create_response(prompt) Microsoft Foundry exposes several API surfaces. The example uses the current OpenAI-compatible /openai/v1/responses shape. Older deployment-scoped routes use an explicit api-version query parameter. Treat endpoint paths, supported models, and API versions as deployed configuration checked against the current Azure documentation. Reading Secret Manager on every model call adds latency and another failure point. Load a pinned version at startup, inject a mounted secret through your platform, or use a controlled refresh mechanism. Rotate by creating a new secret version, deploying the new version reference, verifying it, and then disabling the old version. 2. Option B: Microsoft Entra Workload Identity Federation Flow Your backend runs as a specific Kubernetes/Google service account through Workload Identity Federation for GKE. The workload obtains a Google-signed OIDC assertion with the audience expected by the Entra federated credential. Microsoft Entra validates the assertion's issuer, subject, audience, and signature against the configured trust. The workload exchanges that assertion for a short-lived Entra access token scoped to Azure AI. It calls Azure OpenAI with Authorization: Bearer <access_token>. What must be configured Create an Entra app registration (or supported managed identity) and its service principal. Add a federated identity credential whose issuer, subject, and audience exactly match the Google assertion. Microsoft's Google Cloud example uses issuer https://accounts.google.com, the Google service account's unique ID as subject, and api://AzureADTokenExchange as audience. Assign only the Azure role required for inference, commonly Cognitive Services OpenAI User, at the narrowest useful scope. Configure the workload with the Entra tenant ID, application client ID, Azure scope, endpoint, and model deployment; none of these values is a secret. # Protocol-level outline. Production code should use a supported credential # library or a well-tested exchange component rather than duplicating OAuth. external_assertion = obtain_google_oidc_assertion( audience="api://AzureADTokenExchange" ) token_response = await http.post( f"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant_id}/oauth2/v2.0/token", data={ "client_id": entra_client_id, "grant_type": "client_credentials", "scope": "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default", "client_assertion_type": ( "urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer" ), "client_assertion": external_assertion, }, ) token_response.raise_for_status() azure_access_token = token_response.json()["access_token"] result = await http.post( f"{azure_endpoint}/openai/v1/responses", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {azure_access_token}"}, json={"model": deployment, "input": prompt}, ) Why choose this No long-lived API keys Short-lived tokens, easier to rotate Stronger enterprise security posture Tradeoffs More setup (Azure app registration, federated identity config, token exchange logic) Slightly more moving parts than API keys 3. How This Relates to Service Accounts Important: Your GCP service account gives you permission to read GCP secrets/logs/etc. Azure doesn’t care about GCP service accounts. Azure cares about Azure identity (or API keys). So you either: use GCP SA → read API key → call Azure (Option A), or configure federation so your workload can mint Azure tokens (Option B) 4. Reliability Rules Shared by Both Options Reuse clients and connections: create one bounded HTTP client per process, not one client per request. Set phase-specific timeouts: connect, pool acquisition, write, and read can fail for different reasons. Retry selectively: retry connection failures, selected 429 responses, and selected 5xx responses with server guidance, exponential backoff, jitter, and a strict attempt budget. Do not retry ordinary 400/401/403 errors unchanged. Bound concurrency: use connection limits, rate limits, and admission control so Azure throttling does not become an internal retry storm. Preserve deadlines: an outbound timeout must fit inside the remaining inbound request deadline. Make effects idempotent: model inference is normally read-like, but tool calls or downstream writes triggered from a response need explicit idempotency controls. 5. Data Governance and Observability Authentication answers whether the workload may call Azure. It does not decide whether the prompt may contain a customer's data. Before crossing the boundary, classify the payload and enforce residency, retention, encryption, private networking/egress, content logging, and contractual requirements. Send only the fields required for the model task; redact secrets and unnecessary personal data. Log request IDs, tenant IDs, deployment names, token counts, latency, status class, retry count, and policy decisions, but never credentials or full sensitive prompts by default. Separate caller authorization from provider credentials in traces so audit records show both the initiating user and executing workload. Alert on authentication failures, sustained throttling, latency percentiles, model/deployment drift, and unusual per-tenant usage. 6. Decision Summary Choose the simplest option that satisfies policy Use a versioned Secret Manager API key when your organization accepts managed static credentials and can rotate them reliably. Use Entra federation when eliminating long-lived cross-cloud secrets justifies the extra trust configuration and token-exchange dependency. Official References Microsoft Entra: create trust with an external identity provider Microsoft Foundry Models: Responses REST reference Microsoft Foundry: use the Responses API Google Cloud Secret Manager best practices

title: GitHub Governance: Rulesets, Actions Workflows, Runners, and Enforcement
label: 16. GitHub governance and CI
headings: 1) The admin mental model (the “plumbing”) most important
2) Git vs GitHub governance (what each can/can’t enforce)
3) Workflows and actions (how GitHub knows what to run)
4) Status checks (what the ruleset actually reads)
5) Rulesets (what they enforce and why they don’t “run tools”)
6) Required checks vs Required workflows (enterprise scale)
7) Aqua/Trivy example (scan workflow + merge enforcement)
8) Push controls (naming, direct pushes, secrets)
9) Runners (hosted vs self-hosted) and runner security
10) Enterprise-wide patterns (recommended setup)
11) Troubleshooting as an admin
12) Copy/paste templates
description: A practical admin guide explaining what runs, who runs it, where it runs, and how GitHub blocks merges/pushes when policy is not satisfied.
text: A practical admin guide explaining what runs, who runs it, where it runs, and how GitHub blocks merges/pushes when policy is not satisfied. Contents 1) The admin mental model (the “plumbing”) 2) Git vs GitHub governance (what each can/can’t enforce) 3) Workflows and actions (how GitHub knows what to run) 4) Status checks (what the ruleset actually reads) 5) Rulesets (what they enforce and why they don’t “run tools”) 6) Required checks vs Required workflows (enterprise scale) 7) Aqua/Trivy example (scan workflow + merge enforcement) 8) Push controls (naming, direct pushes, secrets) 9) Runners (hosted vs self-hosted) and runner security 10) Enterprise-wide patterns (recommended setup) 11) Troubleshooting as an admin 12) Copy/paste templates 1) The admin mental model (the “plumbing”) most important Think of GitHub governance like a gated building: workflows produce evidence (passes/fails) and rulesets are the bouncer. The bouncer does not do the inspection themselves; they only check the evidence before letting someone in. Four building blocks you should memorize: Workflow: the script that defines what to do (run tests, scan code, etc.) and when to do it. Runner: the machine that executes workflow jobs. Status check: the recorded outcome from the workflow job (pass/fail) attached to a commit/PR. Ruleset: the policy gate that blocks merge/push if conditions aren’t met. Key clarification: If you type aqua-trivy-scan into a ruleset, you are not “turning on Aqua”. You are saying: “I expect a check with this name to exist and be passing.” Someone/something must create that check—usually a workflow file in the repository or a GitHub App integration. Admin perspective: Your job is to ensure (1) the right workflows exist and run on the right events, and (2) the ruleset requires the correct checks and restricts bypass. 2) Git vs GitHub governance (what each can/can’t enforce) This matters because people often say “Git should block X”. In reality: Git is the version control system, while GitHub is the policy and automation platform. Git (alone) Git controls commits/branches and lets you push/fetch. It can run optional local hooks, but those are not reliable for enforcement because users can bypass them. Git itself does not understand “tests passed” or “scan passed” across a company. Good for: history, branching, collaboration primitives. Not good for: enterprise policy enforcement of scans/tests. GitHub (platform) GitHub adds PRs, reviews, checks, and enforcement. This is where administrators set rules and apply them across repositories. PR process: reviews, approvals, merge strategies. Automation: GitHub Actions workflows. Governance: rulesets, required checks/workflows, branch restrictions. 3) Workflows and actions (how GitHub knows what to run) GitHub Actions is configured by YAML files stored in the repository at .github/workflows/*.yml. GitHub watches for specific events (like PR updates or pushes). When an event occurs, GitHub checks: “Do I have any workflows whose on: section matches this event?” If yes, those workflows are scheduled to run. Workflow anatomy TermPlain EnglishWhy admins care Workflow A set of jobs triggered by events. Defines what will run (or not run) for a PR/push. Job Runs on one runner; contains steps. Each job produces a check result; required checks often match job names. Step One action call (uses) or one shell command (run). Steps are where tools run; failures here fail the job/check. Action Reusable unit referenced via uses: owner/repo@ref. This is how you “bring in” scanners like Trivy/Aqua into workflows. Runner The compute that executes the job. Admins control runner availability, security, and who can use them. “How is that container/tool found?” (your earlier question) In a workflow, a line such as uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 is an explicit pointer to an Action repository and immutable commit. GitHub fetches that action and runs it. If the action is Docker-based, its own action.yml defines the container image. If it is composite-based, it runs commands directly on the runner (often installing Trivy and executing it). Keep a version comment such as # v0.36.0 beside the SHA so update tools and reviewers retain context. GitHub can enforce full-length SHA pins at repository or organization level. Use Dependabot or another reviewed update process to advance those SHAs, and restrict which actions are allowed through organization or enterprise policy. 4) Status checks (what the ruleset actually reads) A status check is a named pass/fail result attached to a commit and shown on the PR. When a job finishes, GitHub records the result. Rulesets don’t inspect your code; they simply check whether the required check names are present and successful. How check names are typically formed The UI usually shows checks as <workflow name> / <job name>. Example: workflow name aqua-trivy-scan with job name scan → check appears as aqua-trivy-scan / scan. Why admins often get “stuck” They require aqua-trivy-scan but the real check is aqua-trivy-scan / scan. The workflow doesn’t run on pull_request, so PRs never get that check. Actions are disabled by org policy, so checks never run. The check exists, but the job is “skipped” due to workflow conditions. Admin practice: always read the PR “Checks” list and copy the exact check name to your ruleset. 5) Rulesets (what they enforce and why they don’t “run tools”) A ruleset is a server-side enforcement policy attached to branch targets (e.g., main or release/*). It can block pushes, block merges, require approvals, require checks, and more. But it does not run scanners or execute workflows; it only evaluates the recorded states of checks and PR requirements. Rulesets can enforce Require PRs (no direct merge) Require approvals / code owners Require status checks to pass Restrict direct pushes / force pushes Restrict branch creation/updates (naming patterns) Rulesets cannot do by themselves Install tools like Aqua/Trivy Decide what to run without workflows or required-workflow feature Produce a check result without something executing What this means for your “Aqua enforcement” requirement You must have a workflow (or required workflow) that performs the Aqua scan and fails if policy is violated. Then the ruleset requires the check to be green before merge. 6) Required checks vs Required workflows (enterprise scale) There are two ways to enforce scanning outcomes with rulesets. They look similar but behave differently: Required checks (most common) You list a check name (e.g., aqua-trivy-scan / scan) and GitHub blocks merges until that check is successful. This relies on each repo (or a shared reusable workflow) producing the same check name. Pros: simple, widely used, clear in PR UI. Cons: requires standardization; check name drift causes broken merges. Required workflows (better for enterprise governance) Instead of requiring a “name that must appear”, you require a specific workflow to run. This is useful when you want centralized enforcement and fewer per-repo variations. Pros: less drift; admins can enforce a standard baseline. Cons: still requires Actions to be enabled and configured for the targeted repos. Practical admin advice: use required workflows for the baseline (security + compliance), and required checks for additional repo-specific checks. 7) Aqua/Trivy example (scan workflow + merge enforcement) Below is a concrete “end-to-end” example: the workflow produces a scan check, and the ruleset blocks merges if it fails. The workflow must fail when policy is violated; that failure becomes the red status check. 7.1 Workflow: run Trivy (Aqua) and fail on HIGH/CRITICAL Create: .github/workflows/aqua-trivy-scan.yml name: aqua-trivy-scan on: pull_request: push: branches: [ "main" ] permissions: contents: read jobs: scan: name: scan runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 steps: - name: Checkout uses: actions/checkout@de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd # v6.0.2 - name: Trivy filesystem scan (fail on HIGH/CRITICAL) uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0 with: scan-type: fs scan-ref: . severity: HIGH,CRITICAL ignore-unfixed: true format: table exit-code: 1 Why the SHA pin is a security control, not cosmetic Aqua's March 2026 advisory records a temporary compromise in which many historical trivy-action tags were force-pushed to malicious commits. Versions before 0.35.0 are listed as affected; the older v0.24.0 example previously shown in this chapter must not be restored. A full commit SHA cannot move when a tag moves. If the affected action ran during the advisory's exposure window, follow the vendor's incident-response guidance and rotate any credentials available to that job. What check appears in the PR? Typically: aqua-trivy-scan / scan. That is the string you require in the ruleset. 7.2 Ruleset: block merge to main unless the scan check is green Create/edit a ruleset targeting branch: main. Enable “Require a pull request”. Enable “Require status checks to pass”. Select aqua-trivy-scan / scan as a required check. Disable direct pushes to main (recommended). Why must the workflow exist? Because the ruleset only checks for the recorded status check. If there is no workflow producing aqua-trivy-scan / scan, the ruleset has no green check to verify—merge stays blocked. 8) Push controls (naming, direct pushes, secrets) “Push-time enforcement” means blocking a push before it lands in the repository history. GitHub can do this strongly for a few categories; for heavier scans, the common pattern is merge gating. Strong push-time controls Block direct pushes to protected branches (via ruleset). Branch naming restrictions (allow only certain patterns). Secret push protection (block pushes containing detected secrets). Why not push-gate everything? Many scans take time (minutes). Push rejection must be near-instant and synchronous. Therefore, organizations usually enforce “heavy scanning” at merge time (required checks) and keep push-time controls for fast, deterministic rules (naming, protected branches, secret push protection). Branch naming enforcement example As an admin, you typically allow only patterns like: feature/* bugfix/* hotfix/* chore/* release/* Note: In GitHub, rulesets often work by targeting patterns and restricting create/update. You configure allowed patterns by restricting broadly and explicitly permitting specific patterns (depending on your chosen ruleset approach). 9) Runners (hosted vs self-hosted) and runner security A runner is the execution environment for jobs. If someone can run code on a runner, they effectively execute arbitrary commands in that environment. That’s why runner governance (which repos can use which runners) is a core admin responsibility. GitHub-hosted runners GitHub manages them; they are generally ephemeral and reset between jobs. This reduces persistence risk. Great default for most repos and for consistent environments. Select a specific image such as runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 when reproducibility matters; ubuntu-latest is convenient but can move. Minimal operational work for admins Self-hosted runners You manage the machines (VMs/on-prem/Kubernetes). Choose these when you need strict network access, specialized tools, or compliance controls. However, you must treat them as sensitive and isolate them from untrusted workloads. Select with labels: runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64, secure] Admins should use runner groups to restrict usage Self-hosted runner security (short, practical) Use runner groups and allow only selected repos. Keep a “secure” runner group for sensitive repos; do not allow broad access. Prefer ephemeral runners (one job → destroy) for high-security posture. Do not allow fork PRs or untrusted code to run on sensitive runners. Minimize secrets exposure; assume workflow-exposed secrets can be exfiltrated. 10) Enterprise-wide patterns (recommended setup) Enterprise governance works best when you standardize: workflow names, job names, required checks, and who can bypass rulesets. Your goal is to make compliance “boring” and predictable. Recommended enterprise baseline Enterprise ruleset applied to protected branches (e.g., main, release/*). Require PR + require approvals (optional based on policy). Require checks: tests + scan checks (aqua-trivy-scan / scan). Block direct pushes to protected branches. Branch naming restriction (limit branch creation/update patterns). Secret push protection enabled org/enterprise-wide. Full-length action SHA policy enabled, with automated update PRs and review. CODEOWNERS review required for .github/workflows/ and governance files. Scaling tip: required workflows If you can use required workflows, centralize the baseline scanning workflow so every repo gets the same scanning behavior and check naming. This reduces drift and makes rulesets more stable. Cloud deployments: OIDC instead of stored cloud keys Give the job id-token: write, exchange GitHub's short-lived OIDC token with the cloud provider, and constrain the provider trust policy by aud and sub. Do not trust every workflow in an organization. Where appropriate, also bind the reusable workflow through job_workflow_ref, repository ID, environment, or custom repository-property claims. Repositories created after July 15, 2026 use GitHub's immutable default sub format containing owner and repository IDs; older repositories keep the name-based format until opted in. Migrate the cloud trust policy before opting in so deployments do not fail. Build provenance: artifact attestations For release binaries and images, generate a GitHub artifact attestation after the build and verify it at promotion or deployment. The workflow needs id-token: write, attestations: write, and least-privilege access to the artifact or package. artifact-metadata: write is additionally required when publishing storage records to the linked artifacts page. An attestation proves where and how an artifact was built; it does not replace tests, vulnerability scanning, or review. 11) Troubleshooting as an admin Problem: “Ruleset requires Aqua scan but no check appears” Does the repo contain .github/workflows/aqua-trivy-scan.yml? Does it trigger on pull_request (not only on push)? Are GitHub Actions enabled at org/enterprise level for that repo? Does the workflow have conditions that skip it for some branches? Is the job failing before it reports a check (syntax errors, permission errors, runner issues)? Problem: “I required aqua-trivy-scan but merges still blocked” Confirm the exact check name shown on PR (often aqua-trivy-scan / scan). Require the exact name in the ruleset. Ensure the check is not “skipped” or “neutral” for PRs. Problem: “Self-hosted runner never picks up jobs” Is the runner online and registered? Does the workflow use the runner’s labels in runs-on? Is the runner in a runner group that allows this repository? Do org policies restrict runner usage? 12) Copy/paste templates 12.1 Minimal workflow skeleton name: example-workflow on: pull_request: permissions: contents: read jobs: job1: name: job1 runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd # v6.0.2 - run: echo "hello" 12.2 Standardized Aqua/Trivy scan workflow (recommended naming) name: aqua-trivy-scan on: pull_request: push: branches: [ "main" ] permissions: contents: read jobs: scan: name: scan runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd # v6.0.2 - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0 with: scan-type: fs scan-ref: . severity: HIGH,CRITICAL exit-code: 1 12.3 Self-hosted runner selector runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64, secure-runner] Final admin summary: Workflows define what runs (.github/workflows). Runners execute jobs (runs-on). Jobs produce named checks (workflow / job). Rulesets enforce policy by requiring those checks and restricting push/merge behavior. 12.4 Supply-chain verification checklist Resolve the release tag from the action's official repository and verify that the SHA belongs to that repository, not a fork. Review automated SHA-update PRs and the action's release/security notes before merging. Keep the default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions read-only and elevate only the job permissions that are required. Never check out untrusted pull-request code in a privileged pull_request_target job. Record and verify artifact attestations for promoted release artifacts. Scope. This chapter focuses on GitHub administration: rulesets, workflows/actions, runners, and enforcement behavior. Convert the enterprise baseline into a rollout matrix keyed by enterprise, organization, repository class, and branch pattern, with owners and exception-expiry dates. Official references: Secure use of GitHub Actions · GitHub Actions OIDC claims · Artifact attestations · Trivy 2026 security advisory

text: How modern AI applications connect to tools, data, and other agents. Chapters 1–4 are the MCP track: from first principles, through discovery + remote + auth, into a concrete enterprise pattern, and finally the protocol's 2025-to-2026 evolution. Chapter 5 covers stable A2A 1.0 for multi-agent collaboration. Chapter 6 is a self-contained JavaScript/TypeScript primer used by Chapter 7's LangChain → LangGraph → Flowise journey. Prerequisites Comfortable with Python and HTTP basics. Part II Chapters 1–3 (FastAPI & Uvicorn, HTTP methods, request mapping) are recommended before the MCP track. The auth deep‑dive (Part II Ch. 7–11) makes Chapters 2 and 4 easier to follow. What changed after the first MCP examples The 2025 protocol family introduced Streamable HTTP, protected-resource authorization, elicitation, structured tool output, and resource links. The 2026-07-28 core then removed protocol sessions and the mandatory initialize handshake, added server/discover, moved tasks to an extension, and made continuation input explicit. Chapter 4 teaches this evolution without mixing the wire formats. MCP reading path Chapter 1 is the beginner local example. Chapter 2 is the primary MCP technical chapter: components, discovery, remote servers, auth, token acquisition, validation, and best practices. Chapter 3 applies the same concepts to an enterprise FastAPI-to-Salesforce pattern. Chapter 4 is not a replacement for the earlier chapters; it preserves the 2025 foundation and then maps it to the current stateless protocol. Chapters in order MCP fundamentals — tools, resources, prompts (DB example) MCP discovery, remote servers, authentication MCP enterprise pattern (FastAPI host → MCP → Salesforce) MCP protocol evolution — 2025 foundations to the 2026 stateless core A2A 1.0 — discovery, delegation, and task lifecycle JavaScript & TypeScript primer LangChain → LangGraph → Flowise

label: 1. MCP fundamentals
headings: What MCP is
Why MCP Exists: The Problem It Solves
MCP Architecture: How the Pieces Fit Together
What MCP is used for
Why This Pattern Matters: Key Benefits
MCP components (the 3 primitives)
Example 1: Single User Lookup (Simple)

Summary: Why MCP Matters
description: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for an "AI host" (an app that uses an LLM) to connect to external capabilities through MCP servers.
text:
Where this fits This chapter is the beginner MCP introduction using a local database-style example. The complete technical treatment of MCP discovery, remote servers, authentication, token validation, and best practices lives in Chapter 2. Protocol version boundary Tools, resources, prompts, schemas, host policy, and the decorator examples remain the durable concepts. The current MCP 2026-07-28 wire protocol is stateless: each request carries version/capability metadata and the server implements server/discover; there is no mandatory initialize handshake or protocol session. High-level adapters may hide those messages or still expose a 2025 compatibility API. Pin mutually compatible client, adapter, and server releases, and use Chapter 4 for the exact current wire model. What MCP is MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for an "AI host" (an app that uses an LLM) to connect to external capabilities through MCP servers. Instead of hard-coding integrations (DB, CRM, ticketing, etc.) inside every app, you run a server that publishes capabilities in a consistent shape. The host connects as an MCP client, discovers what the server offers, and then uses those capabilities to answer user questions (often with an LLM making decisions). The Key Insight: MCP provides a unified framework so the agent doesn't need to learn every system's custom API—it just talks MCP. Why MCP Exists: The Problem It Solves Without MCP Every connector looks different: Different endpoints, auth mechanisms, and payload shapes Agents must hardcode provider-specific logic Hard to secure and audit consistently Hard to swap systems (e.g., DB vendor changes) without changing agent logic Example of the Problem: Without MCP, if you want user data, you might need to know: Is it GET https://api.vendor.com/users?email=...? Or SELECT user_id, email, plan FROM users WHERE email = :email? Or sdk.users.get(email)? Each requires different code, different error handling, different security patterns. With MCP: Unified Abstraction MCP standardizes the interface. Whether the tool internally: calls an HTTP API, runs a database query, invokes a SaaS SDK, reads from a file system, publishes to a message queue, The agent always does: call_tool("tool_name", {"arg": "value"}) One-Sentence Summary: MCP standardizes how agents discover safe context (resources), learn correct workflows (prompts), and execute controlled operations (tools), so underlying HTTP/DB/SaaS operations become consistent and auditable. MCP Architecture: How the Pieces Fit Together Three Main Components: 1. MCP Server Exposes Tools / Resources / Prompts Enforces its own security policies Hides implementation details (DB, HTTP, SDK) 2. MCP Client (your app) Connects to the server Fetches prompts and resources Calls tools Feeds content to the LLM 3. LLM / Agent Reads the prompt + policy + schema Decides which tool to call and with what arguments Never directly touches the DB/API—only through tools Important: MCP is not "replacing HTTP." MCP is a standard protocol on top of whatever the server uses internally. The MCP server might call HTTP APIs, databases, SDKs, etc., but the MCP client always speaks MCP. What MCP is used for MCP is used when you want an LLM-powered system to: Discover what it can do (what tools exist, what resources exist, what prompts exist) Invoke actions safely (call a tool to fetch data or perform operations) Fetch reference context reliably (read policies/schemas/config as resources) Reuse standard workflows (prompts that encode "how to do this safely") In short: MCP helps you build tool-using LLM apps without reinventing a connector interface for every integration. Why This Pattern Matters: Key Benefits 1. Separation of Concerns: Read vs. Write Resources are safe, cacheable "reference documents" for the agent. Tools are the only things that touch live data (DB/API), so you can lock them down and audit them. This prevents the "LLM invents SQL" problem and makes governance easier. 2. Reduced Coupling and Increased Portability You can replace the server implementation (DB → HTTP API → different vendor) without changing: the agent logic the client tool-calling logic ...as long as the MCP tool contract remains stable. 3. Improved Security Posture In enterprise setups, you want: Strict tool allowlists Input schemas and validation Auditing of tool calls Minimal exfiltration surface MCP naturally fits this because the LLM can't "reach into the DB" directly—only through defined tools. 4. Standardized Workflows Prompts standardize agent behavior across many clients. They teach the agent the safe/recommended sequence of operations. MCP components (the 3 primitives) 1) Tools = "do something" A Tool is a callable function exposed by the server. Input: arguments (e.g., user_id) Output: structured data (e.g., dict/JSON) Use for: database reads, API calls, computations, actions In this tutorial: db_get_user_profile(user_id) db_get_subscription(user_id) 2) Resources = "read something" A Resource is read-only content, addressed by a URI. Input: a URI like db://tooling/guide Output: text or JSON content Use for: tool guides, schemas, policy text, reference docs In this tutorial: db://tooling/guide (instructions for when to call which tool) 3) Prompts = "how to think / workflow templates" A Prompt is a server-provided template that returns structured messages (system/user) to feed to an LLM. Input: parameters (e.g., question, user_id) Output: "messages" that guide the LLM reliably In this tutorial: account_assistant(question, user_id) returns a workflow telling the LLM: read the guide resource, choose the correct tool(s), summarize results. Example 1: Single User Lookup (Simple) User asks: "Confirm my name and what plan I'm on." The LLM should: call db_get_user_profile(user_id) for name/email call db_get_subscription(user_id) for plan/renewal combine them into a single answer We'll expose: 2 tools (two "DB reads") 1 resource (a read-only tool guide) 1 prompt (a standard workflow template) Part A — MCP Server (Tools + Resource + Prompt) Save as: mcp_db_server.py mcp_db_server.py # pip install "mcp[cli]" from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP from mcp.server.fastmcp.prompts import base # This creates an MCP server instance. # "json_response=True" means tool outputs can be structured JSON. mcp = FastMCP("DBMCP", stateless_http=True, json_response=True) # ============================================================ # RESOURCE: read-only context # ============================================================ # URI: db://tooling/guide # The client reads this via session.read_resource("db://tooling/guide") # # Think of this as "documentation the LLM can read": # - what tools exist # - when to use which tool # - rules (like "user_id must come from host identity") @mcp.resource("db://tooling/guide") def tooling_guide() -> str: # Returned value is just text (could also be JSON). # The MCP client will receive it as resource contents. return ( "Tool guide:
" "- Use db_get_user_profile(user_id) for: name, email, profile.
" "- Use db_get_subscription(user_id) for: plan, billing, renew, payment.

" "Rules:
" "- user_id must come from the host identity, not from user text.
" "- If question asks for both profile + plan, call BOTH tools.
" ) # ============================================================ # PROMPT: reusable workflow template # ============================================================ # Name: account_assistant (the function name is the prompt name) # # The client calls this via session.get_prompt("account_assistant", arguments={...}) # The server returns structured messages (system/user) suitable for an LLM. # # This is NOT a tool call. It does not read DB. It provides instructions. @mcp.prompt(title="Account assistant") def account_assistant(question: str, user_id: str) -> list[base.Message]: return [ base.SystemMessage( "You are an account assistant.
" "Workflow:
" "1) Read resource db://tooling/guide
" "2) Decide which tool(s) to call
" "3) Call the tool(s)
" "4) Summarize results briefly
" ), base.UserMessage( # This is the actual user task formatted in a consistent way. f"user_id={user_id}
question={question}" ), ] # ============================================================ # TOOL 1: action (DB read) - profile # ============================================================ # Tools are invoked by the client as: tools/call with name + arguments. @mcp.tool() async def db_get_user_profile(user_id: str) -> dict: # In real life: query your database. # Here: mocked data. return { "user_id": user_id, "full_name": "Alice Example", "email": "alice@bank.com", } # ============================================================ # TOOL 2: action (DB read) - subscription # ============================================================ @mcp.tool() async def db_get_subscription(user_id: str) -> dict: # In real life: query your database. # Here: mocked data. return { "user_id": user_id, "plan": "Pro", "renews_at": "2026-01-10", } if __name__ == "__main__": # Run the MCP server over Streamable HTTP (network server). # Your MCP client will connect to http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp (default). mcp.run(transport="streamable-http") Run it: python mcp_db_server.py Part B — MCP Client + LangChain LLM (uses Prompt + Resource + Tools) Save as: mcp_client_langchain.py mcp_client_langchain.py # pip install langchain langchain-openai langchain-mcp-adapters mcp # export OPENAI_API_KEY="..." # export OPENAI_MODEL="a currently supported tool-capable model" import asyncio import os from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage from langchain_mcp_adapters.client import MultiServerMCPClient from langchain_mcp_adapters.resources import load_mcp_resources from langchain_mcp_adapters.prompts import load_mcp_prompt MCP_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp" # IMPORTANT: this is host-derived identity (from your auth system in real life). # The user/LLM should not be allowed to choose it. USER_ID = "u_742" async def main(): # ------------------------------------------------------------ # 1) Connect to MCP server # ------------------------------------------------------------ mcp_client = MultiServerMCPClient({ "db": {"transport": "http", "url": MCP_URL} }) # ------------------------------------------------------------ # 2) Load server tools -> LangChain tools # ------------------------------------------------------------ # tools is a list of LangChain Tool wrappers. # Example: # tools[0].name == "db_get_user_profile" # tools[1].name == "db_get_subscription" tools = await mcp_client.get_tools() # Create a tool-capable LLM and bind these tools so it can request tool calls. llm = ChatOpenAI(model=os.environ["OPENAI_MODEL"], temperature=0).bind_tools(tools) question = "Confirm my name and what plan I'm on." # ------------------------------------------------------------ # 3) Pull Resource + Prompt from MCP server # ------------------------------------------------------------ async with mcp_client.session("db") as session: # 3A) Read the Resource (guide/policy text) # blobs is a list of Blob objects returned by the adapter. # Since we ask for 1 URI, blobs typically contains exactly 1 element. blobs = await load_mcp_resources(session, uris=["db://tooling/guide"]) # guide_text is a plain string extracted from the Blob: # example: # "Tool guide:
- Use db_get_user_profile(user_id) for: ...
..." guide_text = blobs[0].as_string() if blobs else "" # 3B) Get the Prompt (server-defined messages for the LLM) # prompt_msgs is a list of LangChain message objects. # typically something like: # [SystemMessage("...workflow..."), HumanMessage("user_id=... question=...")] prompt_msgs = await load_mcp_prompt( session, "account_assistant", arguments={"question": question, "user_id": USER_ID} ) # ------------------------------------------------------------ # 4) Build the messages we send to the LLM # ------------------------------------------------------------ messages = [] # Add the resource guide as system context. # This lets the LLM learn "which tool to use for which question". if guide_text.strip(): messages.append(SystemMessage(content="(MCP Resource) Tool guide:
" + guide_text)) # Add the server-defined prompt messages (workflow template). messages.extend(prompt_msgs) # ------------------------------------------------------------ # 5) Agent loop: ask LLM, run tool calls, feed results back # ------------------------------------------------------------ while True: # Ask the LLM for the next step ai_msg = await llm.ainvoke(messages) messages.append(ai_msg) # If the LLM requests tool calls, they appear here. # Example tool_calls: # [ # {"name":"db_get_user_profile","args":{"user_id":"u_742"}}, # {"name":"db_get_subscription","args":{"user_id":"u_742"}} # ] tool_calls = getattr(ai_msg, "tool_calls", None) # If no tool calls, the model produced a final natural-language answer. if not tool_calls: print("
FINAL ANSWER:") print(ai_msg.content) break # Execute each tool call the model requested for tc in tool_calls: tool_name = tc["name"] # string: which tool to run tool_args = tc["args"] # dict: arguments for that tool # SAFETY: force user_id from host, not from the model. # Even if the model tried to pass a different user_id, we override it. if "user_id" in tool_args: tool_args["user_id"] = USER_ID # Find the tool object by name tool = next(t for t in tools if t.name == tool_name) # Run the tool. tool_result is usually a dict returned by the MCP tool. # Example: # {"user_id":"u_742","full_name":"Alice Example","email":"alice@bank.com"} tool_result = await tool.ainvoke(tool_args) # Feed tool output back to the LLM as system context. messages.append(SystemMessage(content=f"(Tool result) {tool_name}: {tool_result}")) if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) Run it: python mcp_client_langchain.py Example 2: Multi-Tool Router (Advanced) This example demonstrates the power of MCP's unified framework with: 2 tools: profile lookup and orders lookup 2 prompts: workflow for each tool 3 resources: shared policy and separate schemas LLM routing: agent chooses which tool to call based on the question Server Code (Multiple Tools + Resources + Prompts) mcp_server_advanced.py # filepath: examples/mcp_server_advanced.py # pip install "mcp[cli]" from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP mcp = FastMCP("Bank-DB-MCP", stateless_http=True, json_response=True) # ------------------------- # RESOURCES (read-only) # ------------------------- @mcp.resource("db://policy/access") def policy_access() -> str: return ( "POLICY:
" "- Only allow lookups by email (no bulk export).
" "- Return only permitted fields.
" "- If request is ambiguous, ask a clarifying question.
" ) @mcp.resource("db://schema/user_profile") def schema_user_profile() -> str: return ( "SCHEMA user_profile:
" "- email: string (unique)
" "- full_name: string
" "- tier: enum(silver|gold|platinum)
" "- status: enum(active|suspended)
" "Permitted output fields: email, full_name, tier, status
" ) @mcp.resource("db://schema/user_orders") def schema_user_orders() -> str: return ( "SCHEMA user_orders:
" "- email: string
" "- orders: list of { order_id: string, total: number, state: string }
" "Permitted output fields: email, orders
" ) # ------------------------- # PROMPTS (server workflows) # ------------------------- @mcp.prompt() def workflow_user_profile() -> str: return ( "WORKFLOW: User Profile Lookup
" "1) Read db://policy/access
" "2) Read db://schema/user_profile
" "3) Call tool db_get_user_profile with {"email": "..."}
" "4) Return ONLY permitted fields.
" ) @mcp.prompt() def workflow_user_orders() -> str: return ( "WORKFLOW: User Orders Lookup
" "1) Read db://policy/access
" "2) Read db://schema/user_orders
" "3) Call tool db_get_user_orders with {"email": "..."}
" "4) Return ONLY permitted fields.
" ) # ------------------------- # TOOLS (actions) # ------------------------- @mcp.tool() def db_get_user_profile(email: str) -> dict: # Unified interface: whether this internally calls HTTP, SQL, or SDK, # the client always uses: call_tool("db_get_user_profile", {"email": "..."}) fake_profiles = { "alice@bank.com": { "email": "alice@bank.com", "full_name": "Alice Chen", "tier": "gold", "status": "active" }, "bob@bank.com": { "email": "bob@bank.com", "full_name": "Bob Singh", "tier": "silver", "status": "suspended" }, } return fake_profiles.get(email) or {"error": "not_found"} @mcp.tool() def db_get_user_orders(email: str) -> dict: fake_orders = { "alice@bank.com": { "email": "alice@bank.com", "orders": [ {"order_id": "A1001", "total": 129.50, "state": "PAID"}, {"order_id": "A1002", "total": 58.00, "state": "REFUNDED"}, ], } } return fake_orders.get(email) or {"error": "not_found"} if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run(transport="streamable-http") Client Code (LLM Router + Multiple Resources) mcp_client_advanced.py # filepath: examples/mcp_client_advanced.py # pip install mcp import asyncio import json import re from typing import Any, Dict, Literal, TypedDict from mcp import ClientSession from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamable_http_client MCP_URL = "http://localhost:8000/mcp" class ToolDecision(TypedDict): tool_name: Literal["db_get_user_profile", "db_get_user_orders"] arguments: Dict[str, Any] prompt_to_use: Literal["workflow_user_profile", "workflow_user_orders"] def extract_email(text: str) -> str | None: m = re.search(r"[\w\.-]+@[\w\.-]+\.\w+", text) return m.group(0) if m else None def llm_choose_tool( user_question: str, workflow_profile: str, workflow_orders: str, policy_text: str, schema_profile: str, schema_orders: str, ) -> ToolDecision: """ This simulates what GPT would do: - reads workflows + policy + schemas - picks the right tool - returns a structured decision In production, replace this with a real LLM call that outputs JSON. """ email = extract_email(user_question) or "alice@bank.com" # Minimal routing logic (standing in for LLM reasoning) if "order" in user_question.lower() or "purchase" in user_question.lower(): return { "tool_name": "db_get_user_orders", "arguments": {"email": email}, "prompt_to_use": "workflow_user_orders" } else: return { "tool_name": "db_get_user_profile", "arguments": {"email": email}, "prompt_to_use": "workflow_user_profile" } async def main(): user_question = "Show me the orders for alice@bank.com" async with streamable_http_client(MCP_URL) as (read, write, _): async with ClientSession(read, write) as session: await session.initialize() # 1) Discover server-provided workflows (prompts) p_profile = await session.get_prompt("workflow_user_profile") p_orders = await session.get_prompt("workflow_user_orders") workflow_profile = json.dumps(p_profile, indent=2, default=str) workflow_orders = json.dumps(p_orders, indent=2, default=str) # 2) Read shared policy + schemas (resources) r_policy = await session.read_resource("db://policy/access") r_schema_profile = await session.read_resource("db://schema/user_profile") r_schema_orders = await session.read_resource("db://schema/user_orders") policy_text = json.dumps(r_policy, indent=2, default=str) schema_profile = json.dumps(r_schema_profile, indent=2, default=str) schema_orders = json.dumps(r_schema_orders, indent=2, default=str) # 3) LLM chooses which tool to call decision = llm_choose_tool( user_question=user_question, workflow_profile=workflow_profile, workflow_orders=workflow_orders, policy_text=policy_text, schema_profile=schema_profile, schema_orders=schema_orders, ) print("
--- TOOL DECISION (what GPT would output) ---") print(json.dumps(decision, indent=2)) # 4) Client executes the chosen tool via MCP tool_name = decision["tool_name"] args = decision["arguments"] result = await session.call_tool(tool_name, arguments=args) print("
--- TOOL RESULT (from MCP server) ---") print(result.structuredContent or {"content": result.content}) if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) Expected Output: --- TOOL DECISION (what GPT would output) --- { "tool_name": "db_get_user_orders", "arguments": { "email": "alice@bank.com" }, "prompt_to_use": "workflow_user_orders" } --- TOOL RESULT (from MCP server) --- { "email": "alice@bank.com", "orders": [ {"order_id": "A1001", "total": 129.5, "state": "PAID"}, {"order_id": "A1002", "total": 58.0, "state": "REFUNDED"} ] } Key Takeaway from Example 2: Even if db_get_user_profile internally becomes GET https://internal-api/profile?email=..., the client still calls it as call_tool("db_get_user_profile", {"email": ...}) That's the unified abstraction MCP provides. What you should observe When you run the client: The LLM reads the resource (tool guide) and sees that: name/email → db_get_user_profile plan/renew → db_get_subscription The LLM reads the prompt (workflow) which tells it to: read the guide, call tools, summarize The LLM will typically call both tools for the combined question. You'll see a final answer like: Expected Output: "Your name is Alice Example and your email is alice@bank.com. Your plan is Pro and it renews on 2026-01-10." Summary: Why MCP Matters MCP gives a unified "capabilities interface" To the agent/client, tools look like callable functions, resources look like URIs you can read, and prompts look like workflow templates—regardless of the underlying implementation. MCP separates "read-only context" from "actions" This is a big safety and design win. Resources are safe, audit-friendly, and cacheable. Tools are gated, validated, and permissioned. MCP reduces coupling and increases portability You can replace the server implementation without changing the agent logic or client tool-calling logic, as long as the MCP tool contract remains stable. MCP improves security posture The LLM can't "reach into the DB" directly—only through defined, auditable tools with strict allowlists and input schemas. Integration exercise: Run the relevant list_* operations against a real MCP server, replace the example tool/resource/prompt names with the discovered contracts, and add one test for each capability before enabling it for a model.
