text:
This chapter connects MCP basics (resources, prompts, tools) to server/client code, how remote MCP servers are used by LLMs (OpenAI-style analogy), and how authentication fits in (self-hosted Identity Provider, Bearer tokens, PKCE, introspection vs JWKS). Reading path This is the primary MCP technical chapter. Chapter 1 is the beginner local example, Chapter 3 is the enterprise application, and Chapter 4 explains the protocol's 2025-to-2026 evolution. For OAuth/OIDC/JWT theory, use Part II Chapter 10. Current protocol versus compatibility SDKs The normative protocol in this chapter is MCP 2026-07-28. It uses stateless, self-contained requests, optional up-front server/discover, and per-request _meta. The explicit ClientSession.initialize() example later in the chapter is retained and labelled as the older 2025-compatible Python SDK shape because deployed clients and adapters may still negotiate that version. Table of contents 1) What MCP is (and what it isn’t) 2) Core MCP components: resources, prompts, tools 3) Discovery: how a client finds resources/prompts/tools 4) Server tutorial: a simple MCP “shop” server in Python 5) Client tutorial: list resources/prompts/tools and call them 6) Remote MCP servers and “mcp.shop” style analogy 7) Using a remote MCP server from an LLM (OpenAI analogy) 8) Authentication & Identity Providers in MCP 9) Self-hosted IdP + Bearer token + middleware validation 10) How the client gets tokens (PKCE, client credentials, token exchange) 11) How the server validates tokens (introspection vs JWKS) 12) Practical best practices (tool allow-list, least privilege, CORS) 12) Best practices and troubleshooting 1) What MCP is (and what it isn’t) MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard interface for connecting an AI host (the app that runs the model) to external capabilities offered by servers. Those capabilities usually fall into three buckets: ResourcesPromptsTools. User ↔ Host App (LLM) ↔ MCP Server(s) The host app is in control: it decides what context to provide to the LLM and which tools the LLM is allowed to call. The MCP server is “just” a capability provider. Important: MCP is not “the LLM calling the Internet by itself.” In well-designed systems, the LLM proposes actions, but the host executes calls and enforces policy. That is exactly how you keep things safe and predictable. 1.1 Beginner mental model (the 3 roles) (1) User asks a question ↓ (2) Host app (your code) decides what to do ↓ (3) Host talks to MCP server(s) for data/actions ↓ (4) Host feeds results back to the LLM and the user Beginners often think “the model calls the tool”. In reality, the host is the component that makes network calls and enforces policy (allow-lists, rate limits, auth headers). 1.2 Key MCP terms (quick glossary) Term Beginner explanation Example Host Your app that runs the LLM and enforces policy. A Python service using an LLM SDK. MCP Server A capability provider that exposes resources/prompts/tools. A “shop” server exposing inventory_check. Transport How messages move between host and server (stdio or HTTP). Streamable HTTP at /mcp. Discovery Listing what exists (tools/resources/prompts) before using them. list_tools() then call_tool(). Stateless vs stateful Whether the server expects a durable session per client. Stateless HTTP is simplest to scale. 2) Core MCP components: resources, prompts, tools Here’s a conceptual mapping that makes MCP intuitive: Component What it is What the host typically does with it Example in a “shop” domain Resources Named/URI-addressed context objects (data you want the model to read). Fetch and inject into the LLM’s context (or summarize first). shop://catalog, shop://schema Prompts Reusable prompt templates or workflows published by the server. Present to user or internally use as standard instructions. “Write a purchase summary for SKU + quantity” Tools Callable functions with structured inputs/outputs. Can have side effects. Allow the model to call them (with restrictions), then return results back to the model. inventory_check(sku, qty), create_order(sku, qty) Quick rule: If something is read-only or “context,” make it a Resource. If it’s a reusable instruction, make it a Prompt. If it changes state (writes, creates, sends), make it a Tool. 3) Discovery: how a client finds resources/prompts/tools Discovery is the step that confused you earlier (“where is mcp_call? how does discovery happen?”). The answer is: the host connects to the server and asks for the catalogs. Typical host flow (high-level): Connect to MCP server transport (stdio, local HTTP, remote HTTP) Discover/select the protocol version, or let a compatible SDK negotiate it List tools (names + input and optional output schema) List prompts (names + args) List resources (URIs + metadata) After discovery, the host can do two important policy steps: Tool allow-list: choose which tools the model may call (e.g., only read-only tools in production). Context selection: decide which resources to inject (to avoid over-sharing or prompt bloat). Discovery doesn’t mean the model automatically sees everything. The host chooses what to show and what to enable. 3.1 Transports (how MCP messages travel) MCP is a protocol. It can be carried over different transports. Beginners usually start with Streamable HTTP (easy to deploy) or stdio (great for local tools). Common transports: stdio: host spawns the server process and communicates via stdin/stdout (local only). HTTP: server runs as a web app; host calls it over the network (local or remote). Remote servers usually use HTTP because it works across machines and supports standard web controls (auth, rate limits, logs). 3.2 Version discovery: current protocol and historical handshake In the 2025 protocol family, initialize() was the handshake where client and server negotiated version and capabilities before normal calls. MCP 2026-07-28 removed that handshake and protocol-level sessions. A current server implements server/discover; each ordinary request then carries its selected protocol version, client capabilities, and client identity in params._meta. The request must be processable without remembering a previous connection. 3.3 Tool schemas: why structured inputs matter Tools are not “free-form strings”. Each tool has a schema (think: a mini API contract). That lets the host validate inputs before calling and gives the LLM a clear structure to follow. Beginner rule: If you can’t describe a tool’s inputs/outputs as JSON, the tool is probably too vague. Split it into smaller tools. 4) Server tutorial: a simple MCP “shop” server in Python This server has: 2 resources (catalog and schema), 1 prompt (purchase summary prompt), and 2 tools (inventory check and create order). This is a toy example but it demonstrates the full pattern: read context (resources), reuse instructions (prompt), perform actions (tools). # server.py from typing import TypedDict, Optional from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP # Create the MCP server mcp = FastMCP( "MiniShop MCP", stateless_http=True, json_response=True, ) # In-memory demo data CATALOG = { "SKU-APPLE": {"name": "Apple", "price": 1.50, "stock": 12}, "SKU-CHAIR": {"name": "Chair", "price": 49.00, "stock": 0}, } # ---------------------- # RESOURCES # ---------------------- @mcp.resource("shop://catalog") def catalog_snapshot() -> str: import json return json.dumps(CATALOG, indent=2) @mcp.resource("shop://schema") def schema_doc() -> str: return """Data shapes: - Catalog item: { name: string, price: number, stock: number } - Order request: { sku: string, qty: number } - Order result: { order_id: string, status: 'created'|'rejected', reason?: string } """ # ---------------------- # PROMPTS # ---------------------- @mcp.prompt(title="Purchase Summary") def purchase_summary_prompt(sku: str, qty: int) -> str: item = CATALOG.get(sku) if not item: return f"Write a polite message: SKU {sku} does not exist." return f"""Write a short purchase summary for the user. Item: {item['name']} ({sku}) Quantity: {qty} Unit price: ${item['price']} Mention stock status and alternatives if stock is low/zero. """ # ---------------------- # TOOLS # ---------------------- class InventoryResult(TypedDict): sku: str requested: int available: int can_fulfill: bool @mcp.tool() def inventory_check(sku: str, qty: int) -> InventoryResult: item = CATALOG.get(sku, {"stock": 0}) available = int(item["stock"]) return { "sku": sku, "requested": qty, "available": available, "can_fulfill": available >= qty, } class OrderResult(TypedDict, total=False): order_id: str status: str # "created" | "rejected" reason: Optional[str] @mcp.tool() def create_order(sku: str, qty: int) -> OrderResult: check = inventory_check(sku, qty) if not check["can_fulfill"]: return {"status": "rejected", "reason": "Insufficient stock"} # Side effect: reserve stock CATALOG[sku]["stock"] -= qty import uuid return {"status": "created", "order_id": f"ord_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"} # ---------------------- # Expose as a Streamable HTTP MCP app # ---------------------- app = mcp.streamable_http_app() # Run with: uvicorn server:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 What you just built Resources are readable by URI (catalog/schema) Prompt provides a reusable instruction template Tools enable actions (inventory check, create order) In a real deployment, your resources might be “database schema”, “latest sales report”, “customer profile”. Tools might be “run SQL”, “create ticket”, “approve order”. 5) Client tutorial: list resources/prompts/tools and call them The client is the “host brain” that: (1) discovers what the server provides, and then (2) reads resources or calls tools. This client uses MCP’s streamable HTTP client transport. You can adapt the same pattern for stdio or other supported transports. Compatibility example: the code below is the stateful-looking Python SDK interface used with the 2025 protocol family. Its initialize() call is not part of the 2026-07-28 wire protocol. Do not infer that a current server may keep hidden per-client state. Use an SDK release that explicitly supports the protocol version selected by your server; do not delete this example if you maintain older deployments. # client.py import asyncio from mcp.client.session import ClientSession from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamable_http_client MCP_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp" async def main(): async with streamable_http_client(MCP_URL) as (read, write): async with ClientSession(read, write) as session: await session.initialize() # 1) Discover tools tools = await session.list_tools() print("
TOOLS:") for t in tools: print("-", t.name, ":", t.description) # 2) Discover resources resources = await session.list_resources() print("
RESOURCES:") for r in resources: print("-", r.uri) # 3) Read a resource catalog = await session.read_resource("shop://catalog") print("
CATALOG RESOURCE CONTENT:
", catalog.contents[0].text) # 4) Discover prompts prompts = await session.list_prompts() print("
PROMPTS:") for p in prompts: print("-", p.name) # 5) Call tools inv = await session.call_tool("inventory_check", {"sku": "SKU-APPLE", "qty": 2}) print("
INVENTORY CHECK RESULT:
", inv.content[0].text) order = await session.call_tool("create_order", {"sku": "SKU-APPLE", "qty": 2}) print("
CREATE ORDER RESULT:
", order.content[0].text) if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) How to run the client # In another terminal (server already running): python client.py You should see the discovered TOOLS/RESOURCES/PROMPTS, the catalog resource content, and the JSON-ish tool results. What you should notice in this client Discovery is explicit: you call list_tools, list_resources, list_prompts. Resources are read with read_resource(uri) and returned as content blocks. Tools are invoked with call_tool(name, args_dict). Prompts appear in discovery; many hosts surface them to users as “recipes”. Connection to what we discussed earlier: This is the MCP equivalent of “passing dictionaries” in LangChain: tool calls are structured dict inputs, and tool results become structured outputs that the host can feed back to the LLM. The same client flow on MCP 2026-07-28 The host may call server/discover, selects a mutually supported version, and sends tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list, and later calls as independent requests. Each request repeats protocol and capability metadata. Application continuity uses explicit server-minted handles in tool arguments, not Mcp-Session-Id or connection affinity. See Chapter 4 for complete JSON-RPC and Streamable HTTP shapes. 6) Remote MCP servers and the “mcp.shop” analogy Everything you did above works the same when the server is remote. The only differences are: The MCP URL becomes something like https://mcp.shop.example/mcp You must add auth (almost always) You should add operational controls: rate limits, logs, monitoring, timeouts Example “mcp.shop” capabilities Resources: shop://catalog, shop://shipping_zones, shop://return_policy Tools: search_products, inventory_check, create_order, track_order Prompts: “Recommend products”, “Write an invoice summary”, “Draft a customer confirmation message” Remote MCP should be treated like a production API: authentication, authorization, and least-privilege tool exposure become the main concerns. 7) Using a remote MCP server from an LLM (OpenAI analogy) You said: “I use OpenAI and my own client with an LLM — the LLM is actually invoking the server.” The accurate picture is: LLM proposes a tool call ↓ Your host/client executes the tool call (HTTP request to MCP server) ↓ MCP server returns tool result ↓ Host/client sends tool result back to the LLM as context So the LLM isn’t holding sockets or managing auth. Your host is. The LLM “decides” which tool to use (within the boundaries you allow). Conceptual OpenAI-style configuration The exact API fields can differ by SDK/version, but the concept is always: configure an MCP tool with a URL, restrict tools, attach headers. # Conceptual OpenAI host wiring for a remote MCP server tools = [ { "type": "mcp", "server_label": "mcp.shop", "server_url": "https://mcp.shop.example/mcp", "allowed_tools": ["inventory_check", "create_order"], "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer <token>"} } ] Safety levers you should always use: allowed_tools: start minimal (read-only), expand carefully. server-side authorization: don’t rely on “the model will behave”. 8) Authentication & Identity Providers in MCP MCP runs over HTTP. So authentication looks exactly like a typical API: Client obtains an access token from an Identity Provider (IdP) Client sends Authorization: Bearer <token> to the MCP server Server middleware validates token and attaches identity/scopes to request context Tools enforce authorization (scopes/roles) before doing side effects “Authentication” answers who are you? “Authorization” answers what are you allowed to do? Middleware usually handles authentication; tool handlers should handle authorization. 9) Self-hosted IdP + Bearer token + middleware validation This is the pattern you asked about: “client gets bearer token from auth server; server validates it.” We’ll show two validation approaches: Opaque token validated by calling IdP introspection endpoint JWT validated locally using public keys fetched from IdP (JWKS) 9.1 Opaque token path (introspection) Client → IdP: standards-based OAuth flow → access_token (opaque or JWT) Client → MCP: Authorization: Bearer access_token MCP → IdP: POST /introspect (token) → active? claims? scopes? MCP → allow/deny 9.2 Server middleware example (introspection) This middleware sits in front of /mcp and rejects requests without a valid token. # middleware_snippet.py (conceptual) auth = request.headers.get("authorization", "") if not auth.startswith("Bearer "): return JSONResponse({"detail": "Missing Bearer token"}, status_code=401) token = auth.split(" ", 1)[1].strip() r = await client.post( IDP_INTROSPECT_URL, data={"token": token}, auth=(INTROSPECTION_CLIENT_ID, INTROSPECTION_CLIENT_SECRET), timeout=5, ) r.raise_for_status() data = r.json() if not data.get("active"): return JSONResponse({"detail": "Invalid token"}, status_code=401) request.state.sub = data.get("sub") request.state.scope = data.get("scope", "") Once identity is attached to request.state, your tools can enforce permissions: e.g., order:write required to call create_order. 10) How clients get tokens: PKCE, client credentials, and token exchange You asked two key questions: “In this case we don’t use an auth key just username/password — can we use an auth key and why?” “Client has to access Google server to get bearer token still? Is this PKCE?” 10.1 Confidential clients and services If your client is a backend service, CLI running in a managed environment, or trusted machine workload, use a standards-based OAuth pattern rather than passing user passwords around: Authorization Code + PKCE when a human user is signing in. Client Credentials or workload identity federation for service-to-service calls. Token Exchange when a host service must call MCP on behalf of an already-authenticated user. Where API keys fit: API keys can still be useful for legacy integrations, bootstrap, or low-risk service identification, but they are not the preferred way to represent end-user identity. Prefer OAuth tokens with issuer, audience, expiry, and scopes. 10.2 Public clients (cannot keep secrets): PKCE In browsers/mobile apps, secrets can be extracted. PKCE exists to secure the authorization code flow for these clients. The client must talk to the IdP (Google or your IdP) to obtain the token—yes, that’s required. The server keeping a public key does not remove the need for the client to obtain the token; it only makes server-side validation faster. Public client (SPA/mobile) gets token from IdP via PKCE → then calls MCP server with Authorization: Bearer token 11) Server validation: introspection vs JWKS (public key retrieval at start) 11.1 Introspection (opaque tokens) Opaque tokens are validated by calling the IdP (or cached results). This is simple and supports immediate revocation. 11.2 JWKS (JWT tokens) If your IdP issues JWTs, your MCP server can validate locally. It needs public keys. The usual pattern is: On startup, fetch IdP discovery document (or configure JWKS URL directly) Fetch JWKS and cache keys keyed by kid For each request, read the JWT header.kid and choose key to verify signature Validate claims: issuer (iss), audience (aud), expiry (exp) Refresh keys on cache expiration or unknown kid Answering your earlier question: “How server gets the public key at start?” — it fetches the JWKS from the IdP and caches it. It may refresh periodically or when it sees an unknown key id (kid). 12) Best practices & troubleshooting 12.1 Always separate “tool selection” from “tool execution” Let the model suggest which tool to call, but enforce policy in the host: allowed tool list, argument validation, rate limits, and safe defaults. 12.2 Validate inputs server-side Treat MCP tool calls like API requests. Validate types, lengths, SKU formats, and scope permissions. Don’t trust that the model will always supply correct values. 12.3 Limit data exposure via resources Just because a resource exists doesn’t mean it should be offered to all callers. Consider per-user resource filtering (e.g., only their own catalog segment or their own orders). 12.4 CORS (browser hosts) If a browser-based host calls your MCP server cross-origin, you must configure CORS properly. Expect OPTIONS preflight if you use Authorization headers. Industry standard: do not use wildcard CORS with credentialed requests. Allow only the exact host origins you operate, return only the methods/headers required, and keep authorization enforcement on the server even when CORS blocks browsers. One-sentence summary: MCP defines how capabilities are exposed; your host decides what the model can use; authentication and middleware make remote access safe. Final end-to-end picture 1) Host connects to MCP server and discovers tools/resources/prompts 2) Host obtains bearer token from IdP (PKCE for public clients; client credentials or token exchange for services) 3) Host calls MCP server with Authorization: Bearer token 4) MCP middleware validates token (introspection or JWT+JWKS public key) 5) Host lets model call allow-listed tools; executes calls; returns results to model 6) Tools enforce scopes and perform actions (DB, APIs, etc.) Official references MCP 2026-07-28 specification Key changes from the 2025 protocol family server/discover reference

headings: Part A — MCP Salesforce Server
Part B — FastAPI Host Endpoint
What Changed: The "Auth Story"
Environment Variables Required
Summary: Why This Architecture Matters
description: With Authentication and MCP Primitives: Tools / Resources / Prompts
text:
With Authentication and MCP Primitives: Tools / Resources / Prompts Current implementation boundary The architecture and authorization boundaries are protocol-version independent. For MCP 2026-07-28, deploy the HTTP server statelessly and use client/server releases that explicitly support that version. Some high-level fastmcp APIs shown here can also target the 2025 protocol family; do not assume a library class name proves wire-level compatibility. Three Separate Auth Boundaries in Your Bank-Style Setup 1. User → FastAPI (your app auth) User logs in with Google Workspace (OIDC). React calls FastAPI with Authorization: Bearer <user_access_token>. 2. FastAPI → MCP server (service-to-service auth) internal boundary Your FastAPI backend calls the MCP server using a separate internal Bearer token (or OAuth/JWT/mTLS in real prod). This prevents "anyone who can reach the MCP URL" from using it. 3. MCP server → Salesforce (downstream service auth) MCP server authenticates to Salesforce as an integration identity (service-level) using OAuth JWT Bearer flow. Part A — MCP Salesforce Server Components: Auth Middleware + Resource + Prompt + Tool FastMCP Features Used: Middleware: Intercept requests for authentication Resources: Read-only URIs for policies/schemas/guardrails Prompts: Server-defined templates to guide clients/agents consistently Tools: Executable actions that interact with external systems Save as: mcp_salesforce_server.py mcp_salesforce_server.py # pip install fastmcp httpx PyJWT cryptography cachetools import os import re import time from typing import Any, Dict, Optional, TypedDict import httpx import jwt from cachetools import TTLCache from fastmcp import FastMCP from fastmcp.exceptions import ToolError from fastmcp.server.dependencies import get_http_headers from fastmcp.server.middleware import Middleware, MiddlewareContext mcp = FastMCP( "DocQA-Salesforce-MCP", stateless_http=True, json_response=True, ) # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 1) SERVICE-TO-SERVICE AUTH (FastAPI -> MCP) # MCP server requires: Authorization: Bearer <MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN> # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN = os.environ["MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN"] class ServiceAuthMiddleware(Middleware): async def on_request(self, context: MiddlewareContext, call_next): # Runs for MCP "request" messages (list tools, call tool, read resource, get prompt, etc.) headers = get_http_headers() auth = headers.get("authorization") or headers.get("Authorization") if not auth or not auth.startswith("Bearer "): raise ToolError("Unauthorized: missing Bearer token to call MCP server") token = auth.removeprefix("Bearer ").strip() if token != MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN: raise ToolError("Unauthorized: invalid MCP service token") return await call_next(context) mcp.add_middleware(ServiceAuthMiddleware()) # FastMCP middleware registration # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 2) SALESFORCE SERVICE-LEVEL AUTH (MCP -> Salesforce) # OAuth JWT Bearer flow to get access_token. # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- SF_LOGIN_URL = os.environ.get("SF_LOGIN_URL", "https://login.salesforce.com").rstrip("/") SF_CLIENT_ID = os.environ["SF_CLIENT_ID"] # Connected App consumer key SF_USERNAME = os.environ["SF_USERNAME"] # Integration user username SF_PRIVATE_KEY = os.environ["SF_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM"] # PEM private key SF_API_VERSION = os.environ.get("SF_API_VERSION", "v67.0") # Summer '26; configure and test explicitly _token_cache: TTLCache[str, Dict[str, Any]] = TTLCache(maxsize=1, ttl=14 * 60) # ~14 min cache def _build_jwt_assertion() -> str: now = int(time.time()) payload = { "iss": SF_CLIENT_ID, "sub": SF_USERNAME, "aud": SF_LOGIN_URL, "exp": now + 180, # short-lived assertion } return jwt.encode(payload, SF_PRIVATE_KEY, algorithm="RS256") async def _get_salesforce_token() -> tuple[str, str]: cached = _token_cache.get("sf_token") if cached: return cached["access_token"], cached["instance_url"] token_url = f"{SF_LOGIN_URL}/services/oauth2/token" data = { "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer", "assertion": _build_jwt_assertion(), } async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client: r = await client.post(token_url, data=data) if r.status_code != 200: raise RuntimeError(f"Salesforce token error: {r.status_code} {r.text}") tok = r.json() _token_cache["sf_token"] = { "access_token": tok["access_token"], "instance_url": tok["instance_url"], } return tok["access_token"], tok["instance_url"] # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 3) RESOURCE: publish a "bank-safe SOQL policy" as read-only context # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- @mcp.resource("resource://salesforce/soql_policy") def soql_policy() -> str: return ( "BANK POLICY:
" "- Only SELECT queries
" "- LIMIT required (<= 50)
" "- No write keywords (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/UPSERT/MERGE)
" "- Require allowlisted objects and fields in production
" ) # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 4) PROMPT: a reusable instruction template clients/agents can fetch # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- @mcp.prompt def salesforce_safe_query_prompt() -> str: return ( "You are generating Salesforce SOQL for a banking environment.
" "Follow the SOQL policy from resource://salesforce/soql_policy.
" "Always include LIMIT <= 50. Only SELECT.
" ) # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- # 5) TOOL: execute SOQL (after validation) via Salesforce Query REST endpoint # /services/data/vXX.X/query?q=<soql> # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- def _validate_soql_bank_safe(soql: str) -> None: s = soql.strip() if not re.match(r"(?is)^select\s", s): raise ValueError("Only SELECT queries are allowed") if re.search(r"(?is) (insert|update|delete|upsert|merge|drop) ", s): raise ValueError("Write operations are not allowed") m = re.search(r"(?is) limit\s+(\d+) ", s) if not m: raise ValueError("LIMIT is required") if int(m.group(1)) > 50: raise ValueError("LIMIT too high (max 50)") async def _sf_query(instance_url: str, access_token: str, soql: str) -> Dict[str, Any]: url = f"{instance_url}/services/data/{SF_API_VERSION}/query" headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {access_token}"} async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=15) as client: r = await client.get(url, headers=headers, params={"q": soql}) if r.status_code == 401: # token expired/invalid -> clear cache and retry once _token_cache.pop("sf_token", None) access_token, instance_url = await _get_salesforce_token() headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {access_token}" r = await client.get(url, headers=headers, params={"q": soql}) if r.status_code != 200: raise RuntimeError(f"Query error: {r.status_code} {r.text}") return r.json() @mcp.tool() async def sf_execute_soql(soql: str) -> Dict[str, Any]: """ Executes SOQL under the integration user's permissions. """ _validate_soql_bank_safe(soql) access_token, instance_url = await _get_salesforce_token() return await _sf_query(instance_url, access_token, soql) if __name__ == "__main__": # Streamable HTTP is the common production transport. mcp.run(transport="streamable-http") Part B — FastAPI Host Endpoint Calls MCP with Service Authentication Key Feature: FastMCP's Streamable HTTP client transport supports custom headers (or a BearerAuth helper) for service-to-service authentication. Save as: main.py main.py # pip install fastapi uvicorn fastmcp pydantic import os from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException from pydantic import BaseModel from fastmcp import Client from fastmcp.client.transports import StreamableHttpTransport app = FastAPI() MCP_SF_URL = os.environ["MCP_SF_URL"] # e.g. https://mcp-salesforce.internal/mcp MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN = os.environ["MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN"] # short-lived OAuth access token from client credentials/token exchange class SoqlReq(BaseModel): soql: str async def get_identity(): # Production: verify OIDC Bearer token, map groups/roles, and return claims. return {"email": "alice@bank.com", "roles": ["salesforce.query.read"]} @app.post("/admin/salesforce/query") async def admin_salesforce_query(req: SoqlReq, ident=Depends(get_identity)): # Bank rule: free-form query text is privileged and should usually be # replaced by named, parameterized tools. If kept, gate it by role/scope. if "salesforce.query.read" not in ident.get("roles", []): raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Missing salesforce.query.read") # Service-to-service auth to MCP server (NOT the end-user token) transport = StreamableHttpTransport( url=MCP_SF_URL, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN}"}, ) mcp_client = Client(transport) async with mcp_client: # Optional: read policy/prompt for debugging or to feed an agent policy = await mcp_client.read_resource("resource://salesforce/soql_policy") prompt = await mcp_client.get_prompt("salesforce_safe_query_prompt") # Actual tool call res = await mcp_client.call_tool("sf_execute_soql", {"soql": req.soql}) return { "policy": policy.content, # what the server says is allowed "prompt": prompt.messages, # how the server wants queries generated "result": res, } What Changed: The "Auth Story" Key Security Improvements FastAPI doesn't just "call the MCP URL." It must present an MCP service token (or OAuth/JWT/mTLS in stricter setups). The MCP server enforces that token in middleware before allowing any MCP operation (tools/resources/prompts/listing). Only after that does the MCP tool do Salesforce service-level auth (JWT Bearer) and run SOQL via Salesforce's Query REST endpoint. Authentication Flow User (Google OIDC) ↓ FastAPI (User token validated) ↓ MCP Server (Service token validated in middleware) ↓ Salesforce (OAuth JWT Bearer flow) Next Level Security: To tighten the bank-safe boundary, the client must never send arbitrary SOQL. It sends only validated parameters, such as an email address, while the MCP server constructs a fixed allowlisted query internally. Environment Variables Required MCP Server (mcp_salesforce_server.py): MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN - Short-lived OAuth token for FastAPI → MCP auth SF_CLIENT_ID - Salesforce Connected App consumer key SF_USERNAME - Integration user username SF_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM - PEM private key for JWT signing SF_LOGIN_URL - (Optional) Default: https://login.salesforce.com SF_API_VERSION - (Optional) Example default: v67.0 (Summer '26); pin a version supported by your org and regression-test upgrades FastAPI Host (main.py): MCP_SF_URL - MCP server URL (e.g., http://mcp-salesforce.internal/mcp) MCP_SERVICE_TOKEN - Short-lived OAuth token, preferably obtained at startup or per request from the IdP Summary: Why This Architecture Matters Defense in Depth: User Authentication: Validates end-user identity via Google OIDC Service Authentication: Prevents unauthorized access to MCP server Downstream Authentication: Secures integration with Salesforce Query Validation: Enforces bank-safe SOQL policies at MCP layer Resource Policies: Provides read-only context for LLM agents Prompt Templates: Standardizes agent behavior across clients Result: A secure, auditable system where each layer has its own authentication boundary and the MCP server acts as a controlled gateway to sensitive operations. Official references: MCP 2026-07-28 specification · Salesforce Summer '26 / API 67.0 · Salesforce API end-of-life policy

description: The earlier chapters establish MCP's durable mental model: a host contains clients, clients connect to servers, and servers expose tools, resources, and prompts. This chapter adds the version dimension. MCP changed su...
text: The earlier chapters establish MCP's durable mental model: a host contains clients, clients connect to servers, and servers expose tools, resources, and prompts. This chapter adds the version dimension. MCP changed substantially during 2025 and again in the 2026-07-28 specification. The capability model remains recognizable, but connection state, discovery, subscriptions, server requests, tasks, and registration changed. Read the version before copying a wire example. The 2025 session-based protocol and the 2026 stateless protocol are both explained because existing systems may still implement either one. A production client should negotiate or explicitly select the protocol version; it should never combine fields from the two eras. MCP evolution from two-endpoint HTTP to stateless requests A timeline showing HTTP plus SSE, 2025 Streamable HTTP with sessions, and the 2026 stateless protocol. Early HTTP transport POST /messages GET /sse two coordinated endpoints 2025 foundation POST or GET /mcp initialize + session ID Streamable HTTP 2026 current core server/discover self-contained request explicit state handles Stable concepts: JSON-RPC, tools, resources, prompts, consent, and authorization MCP kept its capability model while moving transport and conversational context out of implicit connection state. 1) What stays stable across versions MCP standardizes how an AI application discovers and invokes external capabilities. All versions in this chapter use JSON-RPC 2.0 messages and preserve three server-facing primitives: PrimitivePurposeTypical example Tool Perform an operation with typed arguments. orders/create or weather/get Resource Expose addressable context that can be read on demand. doc://contracts/acme-msa Prompt Publish a reusable, parameterized message template or workflow. A code-review or incident-triage prompt The host still owns the trust decision. A tool description is not proof that the tool is safe; the host must authenticate the server, constrain what can be called, validate arguments, obtain appropriate user consent, and render results as untrusted content. 2) The two protocol eras Concern2025 protocol family2026-07-28 core Context Negotiated during initialize; optionally tied to Mcp-Session-Id. Every request is self-contained; protocol version and capabilities travel in _meta. Discovery Initialization and feature-specific list calls. server/discover advertises versions, capabilities, and server identity. Server notifications A transport-level GET stream and resource subscribe/unsubscribe calls. subscriptions/listen is an explicit long-lived request. More client input Server-initiated requests such as elicitation/create. An input_required result asks the client to retry with input responses. Long-running tasks Introduced experimentally in the core. Moved to the official io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension. Compatibility rule The 2025 sections below are not disposable history. They explain why Streamable HTTP, protected-resource metadata, structured output, and resource links exist. When implementing, however, use the message shapes for the version your client and server actually select. 3) The current stateless request model 3.1 Discovery replaces the mandatory handshake In the current protocol, a server must implement server/discover. A client may call it before other methods to choose a supported version and inspect capabilities, or it may optimistically send another request and handle an unsupported-version error. { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": "discover-1", "method": "server/discover", "params": { "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28", "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "book-example-host", "version": "1.0.0" }, "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {} } } } A successful result includes resultType: "complete", supported protocol versions, server capabilities, server identity metadata, and cache hints. Discovery is useful for up-front negotiation, but it does not create a session. 3.2 Every request carries its own protocol context { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 42, "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "quote", "arguments": {"symbol": "ACME"}, "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28", "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {}, "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "book-example-host", "version": "1.0.0" } } } } The server must be able to process this request without remembering an earlier initialize call, connection, conversation, or process. If an application needs state across calls, the server returns an explicit identifier, such as task_7f12 or checkout_session_91, and the client passes that handle in later arguments. Why statelessness matters Any healthy instance can process the next request. Load balancers no longer need sticky sessions, a reconnect does not erase hidden protocol state, and task or conversation identity is visible in application data rather than inferred from a socket. 3.3 Result types make continuation explicit Every current result has a resultType. Ordinary final responses use "complete". A response that needs more information uses "input_required". Clients talking to an older server treat a missing resultType as "complete" for backward compatibility. 4) Transport evolution: HTTP+SSE to Streamable HTTP 4.1 Before Streamable HTTP Early remote MCP examples exposed two coordinated endpoints: POST /messages carried client-to-server requests and GET /sse held a Server-Sent Events channel for server-to-client messages. Deployments had to coordinate two endpoints, preserve connection affinity, and survive load-balancer idle timeouts. 4.2 The 2025 Streamable HTTP model The 2025-03-26 family introduced one endpoint, commonly /mcp: POST /mcp accepted a JSON-RPC request and returned either one JSON response or an SSE response stream containing the result and request-scoped progress. GET /mcp could open an independent SSE stream for notifications such as resource changes, sampling, or elicitation. The initialize response could issue Mcp-Session-Id, and later requests sent the negotiated MCP-Protocol-Version. This was a major improvement over the two-endpoint HTTP+SSE transport, and many deployed clients still use it. It is also the context in which calls such as mcp.run(transport="streamable-http") first appeared in SDK examples. 4.3 The 2026 Streamable HTTP model Streamable HTTP remains, but the protocol-level session and GET notification stream do not. The current model uses: self-contained POST requests with required protocol metadata; the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name request headers for HTTP routing consistency; request-scoped response streams for progress and log notifications; subscriptions/listen when a client explicitly wants selected change notifications; a new request ID when retrying after a broken in-flight response stream. HTTP boundary security Validate the Origin header to defend against DNS rebinding, bind local-only servers to loopback, require HTTPS and authentication for remote servers, and never treat CORS as authorization. 5) Authorization: protected resources and least privilege A simple bearer-token middleware is useful for learning. Production remote MCP uses the protocol's OAuth profile and the same resource-server principles developed in Part II: The MCP server is the protected resource. Its /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource metadata identifies trusted authorization servers. Public clients use Authorization Code with PKCE. OAuth 2.1 remains an Internet-Draft, so treat "OAuth 2.1" as a modern profile: follow the current OAuth security best practices and avoid implicit and password grants. The client includes a resource indicator so the access token is minted for this MCP resource rather than silently replayed at another server. The server validates JWTs with issuer metadata and JWKS, or validates opaque tokens through introspection. It checks issuer, audience/resource, expiry, and required scopes. Authorization-server issuer binding matters: credentials issued by one authorization server must not be reused at another. The 2025 guidance used Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) for clients unknown to the authorization server. In the current specification it is deprecated in favor of Client ID Metadata Documents, although DCR remains a compatibility path for authorization servers that do not yet support the replacement. End-user versus workload identity DPoP can sender-constrain a public-client token; mTLS is common between workloads; token exchange is the cleanest way for a host to obtain a downstream token that represents an authorized user delegation. Do not forward an upstream access token merely because both services accept JWTs. 6) From elicitation to multi-round-trip requests 6.1 The 2025 elicitation model A tool sometimes needs a missing parameter, clarification, or confirmation. The 2025 protocol introduced elicitation/create, a server-initiated request routed through the host to the user: # Historical 2025-style conceptual FastMCP API @mcp.tool() async def book_flight(ctx, origin: str, destination: str) -> dict: if not origin: response = await ctx.elicit( message="Which city should I book the flight from?", schema={ "type": "object", "properties": {"origin": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["origin"], }, ) if response.action != "accept": return {"error": "user_declined"} origin = response.content["origin"] return await reserve(origin, destination) The host displayed the prompt, validated the structured response, and returned an accept, decline, or cancel outcome. This established a clean human-in-the-loop contract for sensitive tools. 6.2 The 2026 MRTR model The current protocol removes server-initiated requests from the core transport. Instead, the server returns an InputRequiredResult. Its inputRequests describe the required elicitation, sampling, or roots input. The client gathers the information and retries the original method with inputResponses. { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 42, "result": { "resultType": "input_required", "inputRequests": [ { "requestId": "origin-city", "type": "elicitation", "message": "Which city should I book the flight from?" } ] } } The exact schema should come from the selected SDK and protocol version. The important mental shift is that the server does not call backward over an assumed session: it returns a continuation requirement, and the client explicitly resumes the operation. 7) Structured tool output Plain text is useful for a human, but fragile for application code. Structured output lets a tool declare a JSON Schema and return machine-ready data in structuredContent, optionally alongside a readable content rendering: @mcp.tool( output_schema={ "type": "object", "properties": { "price": {"type": "number"}, "currency": {"type": "string"}, }, "required": ["price", "currency"], "additionalProperties": False, }, ) def quote(symbol: str) -> dict: return {"price": 142.55, "currency": "USD"} The host can render the result as a chart, badge, form, or JSON view without asking the language model to re-parse prose. Current MCP accepts JSON Schema 2020-12 by default and permits a full JSON value in structuredContent. Validators should bound schema depth and composition complexity, and they must not automatically fetch arbitrary network $ref targets. 8) Resource links keep large data out of the immediate context A search result, PDF, or table dump can consume the model's context before the model knows whether it is relevant. A tool can return a typed resource link instead: { "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "I found three matching contracts." }, { "type": "resource_link", "uri": "doc://contracts/2024-Q4/acme-msa.pdf", "mimeType": "application/pdf", "name": "Acme MSA (2024-Q4)" } ] } The model receives a compact handle. The host can fetch the referenced resource with resources/read only when needed and only after applying authorization and size limits. A URI is a reference, not evidence that the target is safe: defend against SSRF, disallowed schemes, oversized content, and cross-tenant access. 9) Operational changes worth remembering FeatureCurrent guidanceReason JSON-RPC batching Use one request per call; batching was removed in 2025-06-18. Clear request lifecycle and streaming semantics. Progress Keep request-scoped progress on that request's response stream. Avoid cross-request ambiguity. Change notifications Use subscriptions/listen and opt into specific notification types. Subscriptions become explicit request state. Tasks Use the official tasks extension, with tasks/get polling and tasks/update for later input. Durable work evolves independently of the core. Roots, sampling, logging Existing implementations may support them, but new implementations should follow the documented migration paths because these features are deprecated. Reduce connection-coupled client features. Tool annotations Treat read-only, destructive, idempotent, and open-world hints as untrusted metadata. The host still enforces policy and consent. Caching Honor ttlMs and cacheScope on cacheable list/read results. Reduce polling without leaking private results through shared caches. Tracing Propagate traceparent, tracestate, and baggage in _meta. Trace one operation across host, server, and downstream systems. 10) Migration checklist Older design2025 improvementCurrent destination /messages plus /sse One Streamable HTTP /mcp endpoint Keep Streamable HTTP, remove the independent GET stream, and use subscriptions/listen. Implicit connection assumptions initialize plus optional Mcp-Session-Id Per-request version and capabilities in _meta; explicit application handles. Ad hoc feature detection Initialization capabilities server/discover plus per-request capability declaration. Custom bearer authentication Protected Resource Metadata, PKCE, and resource indicators Retain the resource-server model; prefer Client ID Metadata Documents over new DCR integrations. Plain-text-only tool result Output schema and structuredContent Use JSON Schema 2020-12 and bounded validation. Inline large blobs resource_link Keep links compact and fetch with authorization and network-safety controls. Fail when information is missing elicitation/create Return input_required and resume through MRTR. Chapter transition The next chapter moves from connecting one host to capabilities toward collaboration between autonomous agents. MCP and A2A overlap at the system boundary, but they solve different primary problems: MCP exposes context and operations; A2A delegates stateful work to another agent. Official references MCP 2026-07-28 specification MCP 2026-07-28 key changes server/discover reference

description: The previous chapters used MCP to expose tools and context to an AI host. A2A addresses the next boundary: one autonomous agent delegates work to another autonomous agent without depending on the other agent's interna...
text: The previous chapters used MCP to expose tools and context to an AI host. A2A addresses the next boundary: one autonomous agent delegates work to another autonomous agent without depending on the other agent's internal framework, memory, model, or tools. We will build the idea from a simple message into discovery, task state, multi-turn input, artifacts, streaming, security, and a purchasing-concierge implementation. Contents 1) What A2A is (the mental model) 2) Why A2A exists (problems it solves) 3) Core concepts and vocabulary 4) Agent discovery via AgentCard 5) Skills: how agents advertise capability 6) Tasks, status, and long-running work 7) Messages, parts, and artifacts 8) Interaction models: sync vs streaming vs async 9) Orchestration patterns (concierge, hub, mesh) 10) A full concrete scenario: Purchasing Concierge + Inventory + Approval 11) Practical JSON examples (AgentCard + task lifecycle) 12) Security and authentication (what you must implement) 13) Minimal Python implementation (server + concierge client) 14) Operational checklist (retries, idempotency, observability) 1) What A2A is (the mental model) A2A is a standard way for agents, rather than only tools, to communicate with each other over a network. The important word is “agents”: each participant is allowed to be autonomous, stateful, long-running, and potentially opaque internally. A2A does not require agents to share their chain-of-thought, private memory, or internal tools. Instead, they collaborate via a shared external protocol. An agent wants help → it finds another agent → it delegates work as a Task → it receives Messages and Artifacts → it continues / completes the Task. One-line mental model: A2A is structured messages, discoverable capabilities, and a durable task lifecycle for collaboration across vendors, frameworks, and deployments. Version used in this chapter The normative examples target stable A2A 1.0. The protocol defines one canonical data model and three standard bindings: JSONRPC, GRPC, and HTTP+JSON. The HTTP+JSON examples send A2A-Version: 1.0 and use application/a2a+json. A2A delegation model A concierge discovers two specialist agents, delegates tasks, receives status updates, and combines artifacts. Concierge owns user journey Inventory agent stock + quote artifact Approval agent input + decision artifact Final plan composed artifacts message + task message + task status + artifact status + artifact The delegating agent does not need the specialists' private reasoning; it needs trustworthy discovery metadata and explicit task outputs. 2) Why A2A exists (problems it solves) Problem 1: Agents live in silos One team builds an agent with Framework A, another team builds a specialist agent with Framework B, a third vendor provides a hosted agent. Without a common “language,” collaboration becomes bespoke glue code. Problem 2: Work is long-running and multi-turn Real workflows have approvals, waiting on humans, retries, partial progress, streaming updates, and artifacts (files, forms, structured outputs). Problem 3: You need discovery If an agent is going to delegate, it must discover capabilities: “Who can do inventory checks?” “Who can approve spending?” “What modalities do they accept?” Problem 4: Enterprises need governance Identity, authentication, authorization, audit logs, versioning, and safe handling of files/URLs must be aligned with typical enterprise security practices. A2A is not “a prompt format.” It’s a collaboration protocol with discovery, structured data, and lifecycle. 3) Core concepts and vocabulary These are the A2A building blocks you should hold in your head: Concept Meaning Why it matters Agent A network service that can accept tasks and return results. Agents are peers: each can delegate to another agent. AgentCard A machine-readable “business card” that describes an agent's interfaces, skills, modalities, capabilities, and security requirements. Enables discovery and safe routing. Skill A declared capability like “check_inventory” or “approve_purchase”. Used to choose the right agent for a subtask. Task The core unit of delegated work with an id, contextId, status, optional history, and artifacts. Supports long-running work and human-in-the-loop. Message A communication unit inside a task (request, update, clarification, final answer). Multi-turn interactions without leaking internal state. Part A piece of message or artifact content containing exactly one of text, raw bytes, a URL, or structured data. Enables multi-modality and structured payloads. Artifact An output object produced by the task (report, file, decision record, structured JSON). Separates “conversation” from “deliverables.” Think “project management”: a Task has a status, Messages are the discussion, and Artifacts are the deliverables. A contextId can group multiple related tasks into one continuing interaction. 4) Agent discovery via AgentCard Discovery starts with the Agent Card: a JSON document published by an A2A server at a well-known path such as /.well-known/agent-card.json. The purpose is to make it possible for other agents (or an orchestrator) to learn: Who this agent is (name/version/vendor) Where to send requests and which bindings/versions each endpoint supports What the agent can do (skills) How to authenticate (schemes, requirements) What interaction styles it supports (streaming, push notifications, extended card) Concierge agent wants “inventory check” ↓ GET well-known AgentCard for candidate agents ↓ Choose agent whose Skills match the needed work ↓ Create Task + exchange Messages/Artifacts until complete Security note: even though the AgentCard is a discovery document, you should treat it as a potentially sensitive surface and protect it appropriately (don’t embed secrets). 4.1 Interface selection is ordered, not guessed A 1.0 Agent Card can list several supportedInterfaces in preference order. A client chooses the first binding it supports and uses that interface's URL and protocol version. If the interface declares an opaque tenant routing value, the client copies it into every request for that interface. BindingBest fitStreaming HTTP+JSONREST-oriented services and browser-friendly infrastructureServer-Sent Events JSONRPCRPC-oriented clients over HTTPServer-Sent Events GRPCStrongly typed internal platforms and generated clientsgRPC server streaming Public cards must not contain credentials. When capabilities.extendedAgentCard is enabled, an authenticated client can fetch a richer card after obtaining credentials out of band. Cards may also be signed with JWS after JSON Canonicalization Scheme normalization when provenance and tamper detection are required. 5) Skills: how agents advertise capability A2A “Skills” are intentionally high-level: they describe what an agent does in a way another system can reason about. Skills are not the internal tool list, not chain-of-thought, and not implementation details. A skill typically answers: What the agent can do (“approve_purchase”, “inventory_availability”) Input modes and examples that help a router understand when the skill applies Output modes returned through artifacts Constraints (needs human approval, requires certain auth scope) Practically, your orchestrator (concierge) uses skills like a routing index: “Which agent should I hire for this sub-problem?” 6) Tasks, status, and long-running work A2A is “async-first.” That means it is designed for tasks that may take time: waiting on a human, waiting on another system, or doing multi-step reasoning. A2A 1.0 task states: StateMeaningTerminal? TASK_STATE_UNSPECIFIEDUnknown or indeterminate state; avoid creating tasks in this state.No TASK_STATE_SUBMITTEDAccepted and acknowledged.No TASK_STATE_WORKINGActively being processed.No TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIREDMore user input is required.Interrupted TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIREDAuthorization must be fulfilled through an agreed mechanism.Interrupted TASK_STATE_COMPLETEDFinished successfully; inspect artifacts for deliverables.Yes TASK_STATE_FAILEDFinished with an error.Yes TASK_STATE_CANCELEDCanceled before completion.Yes TASK_STATE_REJECTEDThe agent decided not to perform the task.Yes Earlier diagrams often called these states created, running, needs input, blocked, and succeeded. Those remain useful plain-English descriptions, but they are not the 1.0 wire values. External-system waiting is normally represented as TASK_STATE_WORKING plus a status message; user clarification and authorization have their own explicit states. Why tasks exist: If agents only did one-shot request/response, they’d fail on most real workflows. Tasks let agents coordinate across time, state, and dependencies. 7) Messages, parts, and artifacts 7.1 Messages A Message is “what we said” within an interaction: a request, clarification, follow-up, or status explanation. Every Message has a creator-assigned messageId, a role, and at least one Part. The two wire roles are ROLE_USER for client-to-agent messages and ROLE_AGENT for agent-to-client messages. contextId and taskId associate later turns with ongoing work. 7.2 Parts A Part is “what kind of content this is.” A2A is modality-agnostic. A Part contains exactly one of text, base64-encoded raw bytes, a file url, or JSON-compatible data. File metadata such as filename and media type sits beside the chosen content field. 7.3 Artifacts Artifacts are the outputs: a report, a decision, a JSON payload, an attached file reference, a filled form. Every artifact has an artifactId unique within its task and one or more Parts. The key design win is: artifacts represent deliverables; messages represent conversation. If you mix “final deliverables” and “chatty conversation” into one blob of text, you make downstream automation fragile. Artifacts fix that by making outputs explicit. Reliability boundary A task history is not guaranteed to retain every transient Message, and a disconnected stream may miss informational updates. Put durable results in Artifacts and recover current state with task operations; do not use chat messages as a guaranteed event log. 8) Interaction models: sync vs streaming vs async A2A supports multiple interaction modes so agents can choose what is appropriate: Mode When to use How it feels Synchronous Fast tasks that can complete quickly. SendMessage returns a direct Message or a completed Task. Streaming You want progress updates or partial results. SendStreamingMessage emits the initial Task or Message, then status/artifact update events. Asynchronous Long-running tasks, human-in-loop approvals, external dependencies. Receive a submitted/working Task, then poll, subscribe, or configure authenticated push notifications. A2A is built to treat “waiting” as normal. That’s why the task object and its status/history are central. The binding changes the transport shape, not the meaning. For example, HTTP+JSON uses POST /message:send, JSON-RPC invokes SendMessage, and gRPC calls the generated SendMessage method. All three carry the same canonical request and produce functionally equivalent objects. 9) Orchestration patterns In multi-agent systems, there are common architectures: Concierge (Orchestrator) Pattern One “front” agent speaks to the user and hires specialist agents for subtasks. This keeps the user experience consistent and concentrates policy + governance in one place. User ↔ Concierge ↙ ↘ Inventory Approval Hub-and-Spoke (Platform) Pattern A central platform routes tasks and enforces org-wide authentication, authorization, quotas, and auditing. Individual agents remain independent services. Agents ↔ Hub ↔ Agents Mesh (Peer-to-Peer) Pattern Agents directly discover and delegate to each other. Powerful, but harder to govern unless you add strong identity and allow-lists. Agent A ↔ Agent B ↔ Agent C ↖──────────↙ Human-in-the-Loop Variant One or more tasks become “blocked” until a human approves or provides missing information. A2A’s async-first model makes this a first-class concept. If you’re building your first system, start with the concierge pattern. It’s easiest to debug, easiest to secure, and easiest to explain. 10) Concrete scenario: Purchasing Concierge + Inventory + Approval Let’s implement the exact “why do we need this and what does it do?” story using A2A. Your user says: “Buy 20 keyboards for the team.” The concierge agent must: Find an inventory agent to check stock and pricing Find an approval agent to approve budget (human-in-loop) Return a final “approved purchase plan” to the user Agents (roles) Concierge Agent: user-facing, orchestrates subtasks Inventory Agent: checks availability, lead time, estimated cost Approval Agent: determines if purchase is allowed and records approval 10.1 Step-by-step flow (exactly what happens) Discovery: Concierge fetches AgentCards for Inventory and Approval agents. Routing: Concierge selects agents by matching required Skills. Delegate inventory task: Concierge creates a Task on Inventory agent: “Check 20 keyboards.” Inventory responds: Inventory produces an Artifact: availability + cost breakdown. Delegate approval task: Concierge creates a Task on Approval agent with the cost breakdown. Approval pauses: Approval agent returns TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED with a Message explaining which manager decision is needed. Human approves: Concierge (or UI) submits approval decision back to Approval agent. Approval completes: Approval agent transitions to TASK_STATE_COMPLETED and emits an approval Artifact (decision + approver + timestamp). Concierge finalizes: Concierge returns a final plan to the user. This is what A2A “gives you”: the structured way to discover agents, start tasks, wait safely, and collect artifacts. Without a shared protocol, each integration must invent discovery, payloads, status semantics, versioning, and long-running state. 11) A2A 1.0 wire examples: Agent Card and task lifecycle 11.1 Agent Card for the Inventory Agent This card advertises the HTTP+JSON binding first, so it is the preferred interface. The skill is intentionally descriptive: A2A routing uses names, descriptions, tags, examples, and media modes rather than a protocol-level function-argument schema. // GET https://inventory.example/.well-known/agent-card.json { "name": "Inventory Agent", "description": "Checks stock, price, and lead time for purchase requests.", "supportedInterfaces": [ { "url": "https://inventory.example/a2a/v1", "protocolBinding": "HTTP+JSON", "protocolVersion": "1.0" }, { "url": "inventory.example:443", "protocolBinding": "GRPC", "protocolVersion": "1.0" } ], "provider": { "organization": "Example Procurement Platform", "url": "https://inventory.example" }, "version": "1.0.0", "capabilities": { "streaming": true, "pushNotifications": true, "extendedAgentCard": false }, "securitySchemes": { "workloadBearer": { "httpAuthSecurityScheme": { "scheme": "Bearer", "bearerFormat": "JWT" } } }, "securityRequirements": [ {"schemes": {"workloadBearer": {"list": []}}} ], "defaultInputModes": ["text/plain", "application/json"], "defaultOutputModes": ["application/json", "text/plain"], "skills": [ { "id": "inventory.check", "name": "Inventory Check", "description": "Returns stock, unit price, back-order lead time, and estimated total for a requested item and quantity.", "tags": ["inventory", "stock", "pricing", "procurement"], "examples": [ "Check availability and price for 20 keyboards.", "{\"item\":\"keyboard\",\"quantity\":20}" ], "inputModes": ["text/plain", "application/json"], "outputModes": ["application/json"] } ] } 11.2 Send a message (Concierge to Inventory Agent) A client sends a Message; it does not directly invent a Task. The agent may return a direct response Message for trivial work or create and return a Task when lifecycle tracking is useful. POST /a2a/v1/message:send HTTP/1.1 Host: inventory.example Authorization: Bearer eyJ... Content-Type: application/a2a+json A2A-Version: 1.0 { "message": { "messageId": "msg-7f83", "role": "ROLE_USER", "parts": [ {"text": "Check availability and price for 20 keyboards."}, {"data": {"item": "keyboard", "quantity": 20}} ] }, "configuration": { "acceptedOutputModes": ["application/json"] } } 11.3 Inventory returns a completed Task and Artifact { "task": { "id": "task_123", "contextId": "purchase_8b1", "status": { "state": "TASK_STATE_COMPLETED", "timestamp": "2026-07-30T10:20:00Z" }, "artifacts": [ { "artifactId": "artifact_quote_1", "name": "Inventory quote", "parts": [ { "data": { "item": "keyboard", "quantity": 20, "available": 18, "backorderEtaDays": 7, "unitPrice": 35.0, "currency": "USD", "estimatedTotal": 700.0 } } ] } ] } } If the work takes longer, the first response can instead carry TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED or TASK_STATE_WORKING. The concierge can then get the task, subscribe to its stream, or receive authenticated push updates if the Agent Card advertises that capability. 11.4 Approval requires another turn { "task": { "id": "task_456", "contextId": "purchase_8b1", "status": { "state": "TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED", "message": { "messageId": "msg-approval-1", "role": "ROLE_AGENT", "parts": [ {"text": "Manager approval is required because the total exceeds $500."}, { "data": { "approvalForm": { "approver": "", "decision": "approve | reject" } } } ] } } } } The follow-up Message includes the same taskId so the approval agent can continue the existing Task: { "message": { "messageId": "msg-approval-2", "taskId": "task_456", "contextId": "purchase_8b1", "role": "ROLE_USER", "parts": [ { "data": { "approver": "manager-42", "decision": "approve" } } ] } } Earlier illustrative payload shape and its 1.0 mapping Early teaching examples often modeled task creation as a custom POST /a2a/tasks request with a top-level skillId, used the role requester, represented success as succeeded, and put type/data directly on an artifact: { "skillId": "inventory.check", "message": { "role": "requester", "parts": [ {"type": "data", "data": {"item": "keyboard", "quantity": 20}} ] } } { "taskId": "task_123", "status": {"state": "succeeded"}, "artifacts": [ { "type": "data", "name": "inventory_quote", "data": { "item": "keyboard", "quantity": 20, "available": 18, "backorderEtaDays": 7, "unitPrice": 35.0, "currency": "USD", "estimatedTotal": 700.0 } } ] } Those names are useful for a private REST API but are not the A2A 1.0 contract. The current mapping is: send a ROLE_USER Message, use TASK_STATE_COMPLETED for success, and place data inside an Artifact's parts array. Notice the separation: a status Message explains what the interaction needs next, while the final approval decision belongs in an explicit Artifact that downstream systems can validate and audit. 12) Security and authorization boundaries A2A intentionally relies on standard web security practices. That means: Transport security Use HTTPS for integrity and authenticity Verify the server certificate; consider mTLS between workloads Authentication Bearer tokens obtained through OAuth/OIDC are common Service-to-service credentials for private deployments Authorization Scopes/roles per skill (for example, approval:write) Don’t let “any agent” call “any skill” File/URL safety Validate file references to avoid SSRF Sanitize and validate user-provided data parts Practical governance recommendation: Use allow-lists for which agents your concierge is permitted to hire, and limit which skills can be invoked based on policy. 12.1 Discovery describes security; it does not issue credentials securitySchemes describes supported mechanisms and securityRequirements states which are required. The client obtains credentials through the appropriate out-of-band OAuth, workload, API-key, or certificate flow and transmits them through binding-specific headers or metadata on every request. The agent authenticates and authorizes each request; an Agent Card entry is not an access grant. 12.2 Authentication during a task is a state, not a credential envelope If later work needs additional authorization, the agent may transition the Task to TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED and explain the requirement in its status Message. Credentials remain out of ordinary Messages and Artifacts unless a separately negotiated extension defines a protected in-band mechanism. 12.3 Push callbacks form a second trust boundary A push notification endpoint is an inbound API. Use a high-entropy callback URL or authenticated webhook token, validate the expected Task ID, reject unknown senders, apply replay/idempotency controls, and return a 2xx response only after durable acceptance. Delivery may be duplicated, so handlers must be idempotent. 13) Mechanics-first Python simulator (server + concierge client) Below is the original minimal educational implementation, retained because writing the storage and routing mechanics by hand makes the lifecycle concrete. It publishes a card, accepts delegated work, tracks status, and returns an artifact. Boundary of the example This FastAPI service is an A2A-shaped simulator, not a compliant A2A 1.0 server: it uses the private endpoint POST /a2a/tasks and omits binding-level version negotiation, streaming events, formal error mappings, and several required fields. Use an official or maintained A2A SDK for interoperability. The simulator exists to expose the moving parts before the SDK hides them. 13.1 Specialist agent lifecycle simulator (FastAPI) # inventory_agent.py from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException from pydantic import BaseModel import uuid, time app = FastAPI(title="Inventory Agent (A2A demo)") # In-memory task store (demo only) TASKS = {} def agent_card(): return { "name": "Inventory Agent", "description": "Checks stock, price, and ETA for purchase requests.", "supportedInterfaces": [{ "url": "http://127.0.0.1:9101/a2a", "protocolBinding": "HTTP+JSON", "protocolVersion": "1.0", }], "version": "1.0.0", "capabilities": { "streaming": False, "pushNotifications": False, }, "defaultInputModes": ["text/plain", "application/json"], "defaultOutputModes": ["application/json"], "skills": [ { "id": "inventory.check", "name": "Inventory Check", "description": "Returns stock, price, ETA, and estimated total.", "tags": ["inventory", "pricing", "procurement"], "examples": ["Check availability for 20 keyboards."], } ] } # Well-known discovery document (demo path) @app.get("/.well-known/agent-card.json") def get_agent_card(): return agent_card() class CreateTask(BaseModel): skillId: str message: dict @app.post("/a2a/tasks") def create_task(body: CreateTask): if body.skillId != "inventory.check": raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Unsupported skillId") task_id = f"task_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}" # Parse the structured data part if present item = "unknown" qty = 1 for part in body.message.get("parts", []): if "data" in part: data = part.get("data", {}) item = data.get("item", item) qty = data.get("quantity", qty) # Demo logic available = 18 if item.lower() == "keyboard" else 5 unit_price = 35.0 if item.lower() == "keyboard" else 10.0 eta_days = 7 if qty > available else 0 total = float(qty) * unit_price TASKS[task_id] = { "id": task_id, "contextId": "demo-purchase", "createdAt": time.time(), "status": {"state": "TASK_STATE_COMPLETED"}, "artifacts": [{ "artifactId": f"artifact_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}", "name": "Inventory quote", "parts": [{ "data": { "item": item, "quantity": qty, "available": available, "backorderEtaDays": eta_days, "unitPrice": unit_price, "currency": "USD", "estimatedTotal": total, } }] }] } return TASKS[task_id] @app.get("/a2a/tasks/{task_id}") def get_task(task_id: str): t = TASKS.get(task_id) if not t: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Unknown task") return t # Run: # pip install fastapi uvicorn # uvicorn inventory_agent:app --port 9101 13.2 Concierge client: discover skills, create a task, read artifact # concierge.py import uuid import requests INVENTORY_BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:9101" def discover_agent(base: str) -> dict: r = requests.get(base + "/.well-known/agent-card.json", timeout=5) r.raise_for_status() return r.json() def create_inventory_task(base: str, item: str, qty: int) -> dict: payload = { "skillId": "inventory.check", "message": { "role": "ROLE_USER", "messageId": f"msg_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}", "parts": [ {"text": f"Check availability and pricing for {qty} {item}s."}, {"data": {"item": item, "quantity": qty}} ] } } r = requests.post(base + "/a2a/tasks", json=payload, timeout=10) r.raise_for_status() return r.json() if __name__ == "__main__": card = discover_agent(INVENTORY_BASE) print("Discovered agent:", card["name"], "skills=", [s["id"] for s in card["skills"]]) task = create_inventory_task(INVENTORY_BASE, "keyboard", 20) print("Task status:", task["status"]["state"]) artifact = task["artifacts"][0]["parts"][0]["data"] print("Quote artifact:", artifact) Even in this simplified demo, you can see the A2A “shape”: discover an agent (AgentCard), pick a skill, create a task, receive an artifact. The next implementation increment is to add the approval agent and model TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED before completion. 14) Operational checklist (retries, idempotency, observability) Idempotency Task creation should be safe to retry (idempotency keys) Artifact writes should be append-only or versioned Use unique Message IDs and deduplicate webhook deliveries Retries + timeouts Use bounded retries with jitter Different timeouts for: card fetch, create task, poll task Do not retry a non-idempotent operation without a stable key Observability Trace IDs per task and propagate them across agents Log skill invoked, caller identity, status transitions Correlate contextId, taskId, and messageId Safety Validate file references and URLs (SSRF defense) Keep AgentCards free of secrets Use allow-lists for which agents can be contacted Honor A2A-Version; reject unsupported versions explicitly The easiest multi-agent failures are “silent failure” and “infinite waiting.” Always implement: (1) clear status transitions, (2) timeouts, (3) explicit failure artifacts. 14.1 Concurrency and terminal-state rules Treat the Task store as a concurrent state machine. Use compare-and-set or a transactional version column so two workers cannot both advance the same Task from WORKING to conflicting outcomes. A terminal Task must not return to a non-terminal state. Cancellation is a request to stop: workers still need cooperative checks and resource cleanup. 14.2 Cache discovery, not authorization decisions Agent Cards change relatively slowly and should use normal HTTP caching with Cache-Control, ETag, and conditional requests. Cache the card, but authenticate and authorize each task operation independently. A cached declaration that a skill exists does not prove the current caller may invoke it. Summary: the complete mental model AgentCard enables discovery: who the agent is, what it can do, how to call it. Skills enable routing: choose the right specialist agent for a subtask. Tasks enable long-running collaboration: statuses, multi-turn messages, and deliverable artifacts. Messages/Parts enable structured, multi-modality communication. Artifacts are explicit outputs that downstream automation can reliably consume. Bindings change transport syntax, while the canonical Task/Message/Artifact model stays equivalent. Version and security are explicit on the boundary; agent autonomy does not bypass enterprise controls. Official reference Field names and lifecycle values in the normative examples follow the A2A 1.0 specification. Use the schema or an SDK for generated models rather than maintaining duplicate hand-written protocol classes in production.
