description: Welcome! This tutorial starts from absolute first principles: what JavaScript is, what Node.js is, and why we can run code "outside the browser". You'll learn JavaScript in a way that prepares you to write clean, comp...
text: Welcome! This tutorial starts from absolute first principles: what JavaScript is, what Node.js is, and why we can run code "outside the browser". You'll learn JavaScript in a way that prepares you to write clean, component-style code, then transition smoothly into TypeScript. No web development experience required. No HTML or CSS needed. Just pure programming fundamentals. Part 1: JavaScript Fundamentals 1. What is JavaScript? JavaScript (JS) is a programming language that lets you write instructions for a computer to execute. Originally designed for web browsers, JavaScript has evolved into a versatile language used in many contexts. You can use JavaScript in two main environments: In a web browser (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, etc.) - for interactive websites Outside the browser using Node.js - for servers, tools, and applications What is Node.js? Node.js is a runtime environment - a program you install on your computer that can execute JavaScript files directly, just like Python or Java. Key Understanding: JavaScript = The programming language (the "what") Node.js = The tool that runs JavaScript on your computer (the "how") Without Node: Your computer doesn't understand .js files With Node: You can run .js files like any other program 2. Your First "Hello World" Program Let's write and run the simplest possible JavaScript program. Step A: Create a folder named js-basics on your computer Step B: Inside that folder, create a file named hello.js Step C: Put this code inside hello.js: console.log("Hello world!"); Step D: Open a terminal in that folder and run: node hello.js You should see: Hello world! What just happened? hello.js is a text file containing JavaScript code node hello.js means "run this file using Node.js" console.log(...) prints text to the terminal/console 3. How Programs Think: Data and Instructions Every program consists of two fundamental elements: Data - Information like text, numbers, and true/false values Instructions - Commands that tell the computer what to do with that data Common Data Types in JavaScript Type Example Description String "hello" Text (must be in quotes) Number 42 Integers and decimals Boolean true or false True/false values Null null Intentionally empty value Undefined undefined Not yet assigned a value "hello" // text (string) 42 // number true // boolean (true/false) null // intentionally empty undefined // not set yet 4. Variables: Storing Data for Later Use A variable is like a labeled container that holds a value. Think of it as a named box where you can store information and retrieve it later. Using let (for values that change) let score = 0; // Initial value score = 10; // Changed value score = score + 5; // Now score is 15 console.log(score); // Prints: 15 Using const (for values that stay the same) const username = "Sam"; console.log(username); // Prints: Sam // username = "John"; // ❌ ERROR! Cannot change a const Beginner Best Practice: Always use const by default. Only use let when you genuinely need to change the value later. This prevents accidental changes and makes your code easier to understand. 5. Strings: Working with Text Strings are sequences of characters used to represent text. JavaScript offers multiple ways to work with strings. String Concatenation const first = "Ada"; const last = "Lovelace"; // Old style: using + operator console.log(first + " " + last); // Ada Lovelace // Modern style: template literals (template strings) console.log(`${first} ${last}`); // Ada Lovelace Template literals (backticks `) are the modern, preferred way. They're easier to read and allow you to embed expressions directly using ${...} syntax. More String Examples const age = 25; const message = `I am ${age} years old`; console.log(message); // I am 25 years old const calculation = `5 + 3 = ${5 + 3}`; console.log(calculation); // 5 + 3 = 8 6. Numbers and Arithmetic Operators JavaScript provides standard mathematical operators for working with numbers. const a = 10; const b = 3; console.log(a + b); // 13 (addition) console.log(a - b); // 7 (subtraction) console.log(a * b); // 30 (multiplication) console.log(a / b); // 3.333... (division) console.log(a % b); // 1 (remainder/modulo) console.log(a ** b); // 1000 (exponentiation: 10³) More Complex Operations // Order of operations follows standard math rules (PEMDAS) const result = (10 + 5) * 2; // 30 // Increment and decrement let counter = 0; counter++; // counter is now 1 counter--; // counter is now 0 again // Compound assignment let total = 10; total += 5; // Same as: total = total + 5 total *= 2; // Same as: total = total * 2 7. Making Decisions: If Statements Programs need to make choices based on conditions. The if statement lets your code take different paths depending on whether something is true or false. Basic If-Else const age = 18; if (age >= 18) { console.log("Adult"); } else { console.log("Not adult"); } Multiple Conditions const score = 85; if (score >= 90) { console.log("Grade: A"); } else if (score >= 80) { console.log("Grade: B"); } else if (score >= 70) { console.log("Grade: C"); } else { console.log("Grade: F"); } Comparison Operators Operator Meaning Example === Equal to 5 === 5 → true !== Not equal to 5 !== 3 → true > Greater than 5 > 3 → true < Less than 5 < 3 → false >= Greater or equal 5 >= 5 → true <= Less or equal 3 <= 5 → true 8. Repeating Work: Loops Loops allow you to execute code multiple times without writing the same code over and over. The For Loop Use when you know exactly how many times to repeat: // Count from 1 to 5 for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { console.log("Count:", i); } // Output: Count: 1, Count: 2, Count: 3, Count: 4, Count: 5 For Loop Anatomy: let i = 1 - Initialize counter i <= 5 - Continue while this is true i++ - Increment counter after each iteration The For...Of Loop (Easiest for Arrays) Use when you want to loop through each item in a list: const names = ["Ava", "Noah", "Mia"]; for (const name of names) { console.log("Hello,", name); } // Output: Hello, Ava // Hello, Noah // Hello, Mia While Loop Use when you don't know how many times you'll need to repeat: let count = 0; while (count < 3) { console.log("Count is:", count); count++; } 9. Functions: Reusable Blocks of Logic A function is a named set of instructions that you can run (call) whenever needed. Functions are the foundation of component-style programming. Basic Function // Define the function function add(x, y) { return x + y; } // Use (call) the function const result = add(5, 7); console.log(result); // 12 Functions with Multiple Statements function greet(name) { const message = `Hello, ${name}!`; console.log(message); return message; // Can also return the value } greet("Alice"); // Prints: Hello, Alice! Arrow Functions (Modern Syntax) // Traditional function function multiply(a, b) { return a * b; } // Arrow function (shorter syntax) const multiply = (a, b) => { return a * b; }; // Even shorter (when only returning one expression) const multiply = (a, b) => a * b; Why Functions Matter for Components: A component is essentially: Inputs - Data passed to the function (parameters) Processing - Logic inside the function Outputs - Data returned from the function Mastering functions is Step #1 toward component-style programming! 10. Objects: Grouping Related Data Objects are the #1 data structure you'll use for component inputs. They group related pieces of data together with named properties. Creating and Using Objects const settings = { model: "example-model", temperature: 0.7, maxTokens: 200 }; // Accessing object properties console.log(settings.model); // example-model console.log(settings.temperature); // 0.7 console.log(settings.maxTokens); // 200 Destructuring (Modern and Clean) Extract multiple properties at once: const { model, maxTokens } = settings; console.log(model); // example-model console.log(maxTokens); // 200 // This is the same as: const model = settings.model; const maxTokens = settings.maxTokens; Nested Objects const user = { name: "Alice", age: 30, address: { city: "New York", country: "USA" } }; console.log(user.address.city); // New York Think of destructuring as "unpacking" a config object. This pattern is everywhere in modern JavaScript and component-style code. 11. Arrays: Lists of Items Arrays store ordered lists of items - perfect for messages, inputs, results, or any collection of data. Creating and Modifying Arrays const items = ["a", "b", "c"]; // Add to end items.push("d"); console.log(items); // ["a", "b", "c", "d"] // Remove from end const last = items.pop(); console.log(last); // "d" // Access by index (starts at 0) console.log(items[0]); // "a" console.log(items[1]); // "b" Essential Array Methods const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; // map: transform each item const doubled = numbers.map(n => n * 2); console.log(doubled); // [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] // filter: keep items that match a condition const evens = numbers.filter(n => n % 2 === 0); console.log(evens); // [2, 4] // find: get first item that matches const firstBig = numbers.find(n => n > 3); console.log(firstBig); // 4 // reduce: combine all items into one value const sum = numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0); console.log(sum); // 15 Looping Through Arrays const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]; // Method 1: for...of (cleanest) for (const fruit of fruits) { console.log(fruit); } // Method 2: forEach (functional style) fruits.forEach(fruit => { console.log(fruit); }); // Method 3: traditional for loop for (let i = 0; i < fruits.length; i++) { console.log(fruits[i]); } 12. Asynchronous Programming: Waiting for Work to Complete This is the most important modern JavaScript concept. In real applications, many operations take time: Reading files from disk Making network requests (API calls) Querying databases Any operation that requires waiting Synchronous vs Asynchronous Synchronous (sync): Code runs line by line, each line waits for the previous to finish Asynchronous (async): You start an operation, let it run in the background, then handle the result when it's ready The Modern Way: async/await // Helper function that returns a Promise function wait(ms) { return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); } // Async function can use 'await' to wait for Promises async function run() { console.log("Start"); await wait(1000); // Wait 1 second console.log("After 1 second"); await wait(1000); // Wait another second console.log("After 2 seconds"); } run(); Real-World Example: Fetching Data // Simulated API call async function fetchUserData(userId) { console.log("Fetching user data..."); await wait(1000); // Simulate network delay return { id: userId, name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com" }; } async function main() { const user = await fetchUserData(123); console.log("User:", user); console.log("Email:", user.email); } main(); This skill is essential for component-style code. Almost all real-world components perform asynchronous operations. 13. Error Handling: Protecting Your Code Good code anticipates problems and handles them gracefully. The try/catch block lets you catch and handle errors. Basic Try/Catch function parseJson(text) { return JSON.parse(text); } try { const data = parseJson("{ bad json }"); console.log(data); } catch (err) { console.log("Error parsing JSON:", err.message); } With Async Functions async function fetchData(url) { try { // Simulate API call that might fail if (url === "") { throw new Error("URL cannot be empty"); } const data = await someAsyncOperation(url); return data; } catch (err) { console.error("Failed to fetch:", err.message); return null; // Return safe default } } Component-Style Error Handling: Validate inputs early and clearly Fail with helpful messages that explain what went wrong Use try/catch around risky operations Return safe defaults when appropriate 14. Modules: Organizing Code Across Files Real projects split code into multiple files. Modules let you export code from one file and import it into another. Example: Math Utilities File: math.js // Export individual functions function add(a, b) { return a + b; } function subtract(a, b) { return a - b; } function multiply(a, b) { return a * b; } // Export them module.exports = { add, subtract, multiply }; File: index.js // Import from math.js const { add, multiply } = require("./math"); console.log(add(2, 3)); // 5 console.log(multiply(4, 5)); // 20 Run it: node index.js Modern ES Modules (Alternative Syntax) File: math.mjs // Modern export syntax export function add(a, b) { return a + b; } export function multiply(a, b) { return a * b; } File: index.mjs // Modern import syntax import { add, multiply } from "./math.mjs"; console.log(add(2, 3)); console.log(multiply(4, 5)); Why This Matters: Component-style programming is all about creating reusable, modular code. Each component typically lives in its own file and exports its functionality. Part 2: TypeScript - JavaScript with Type Safety What is TypeScript? TypeScript is JavaScript plus type annotations. It helps you catch mistakes before running your code. The Problem TypeScript Solves: // JavaScript allows this mistake: const x = "10"; // x is a string console.log(x * 2); // 20 (JavaScript converts it) // But what if you didn't intend that? // TypeScript catches it: const x: number = "10"; // ❌ ERROR: Type 'string' not assignable to 'number' 1. Installing TypeScript In your project folder, run these commands: # Initialize a new Node.js project npm init -y # Install TypeScript as a development dependency npm install -D typescript # Create TypeScript configuration file npx tsc --init This creates a tsconfig.json file that configures how TypeScript compiles your code. 2. Your First TypeScript File Create a file named index.ts: const name: string = "Sam"; const age: number = 30; const isActive: boolean = true; console.log(name, age, isActive); Compile TypeScript to JavaScript: npx tsc This creates index.js. Now run it: node index.js The TypeScript Workflow: Write code in .ts files (TypeScript) Compile with npx tsc → creates .js files (JavaScript) Run the JavaScript with node 3. Essential TypeScript Types Primitive Types const enabled: boolean = true; const count: number = 5; const label: string = "hello"; const nothing: null = null; const notSet: undefined = undefined; Arrays // Array of strings const tags: string[] = ["javascript", "typescript"]; // Array of numbers const scores: number[] = [90, 85, 92]; // Alternative syntax (less common) const names: Array<string> = ["Alice", "Bob"]; Objects (The Most Important) // Define the shape with 'type' type User = { id: number; name: string; email: string; isActive: boolean; }; const user: User = { id: 1, name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com", isActive: true }; // TypeScript ensures all properties exist console.log(user.name); // valid console.log(user.age); // ❌ ERROR: Property 'age' doesn't exist Optional Properties type Settings = { model: string; temperature: number; maxTokens?: number; // ← Optional (? makes it optional) }; // This is valid (maxTokens is optional) const settings: Settings = { model: "configured-model-id", temperature: 0.7 }; 4. Functions with Types TypeScript lets you specify types for function parameters and return values. Basic Typed Function function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; } const result = add(5, 7); // valid const bad = add("5", "7"); // ❌ ERROR: Argument type 'string' not assignable Arrow Functions const multiply = (a: number, b: number): number => { return a * b; }; // Shorthand const divide = (a: number, b: number): number => a / b; Async Functions async function fetchUserName(id: number): Promise<string> { // Simulate API call await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100)); return `User_${id}`; } // Using it async function main() { const name = await fetchUserName(123); console.log(name); // name is type 'string' } main(); Promise<string> means "this async function will eventually return a string". 5. Component-Style Function Pattern This is the pattern you'll use constantly for building components. It combines everything you've learned. // Define input shape type Input = { text: string; repeat: number; }; // Define output shape type Output = { result: string; length: number; }; // Validation function function validateInput(input: Input): void { if (input.repeat < 1) { throw new Error("repeat must be at least 1"); } if (input.repeat > 100) { throw new Error("repeat cannot exceed 100"); } if (!input.text || input.text.trim() === "") { throw new Error("text cannot be empty"); } } // Main processing function export async function run(input: Input): Promise<Output> { // Step 1: Validate validateInput(input); // Step 2: Process const repeated = Array(input.repeat).fill(input.text).join(" "); // Step 3: Return structured output return { result: repeated, length: repeated.length }; } // Example usage async function example() { try { const output = await run({ text: "Hello", repeat: 3 }); console.log(output.result); // "Hello Hello Hello" console.log(output.length); // 17 } catch (err) { console.error("Error:", err.message); } } example(); This Pattern Teaches: Clean inputs - Well-defined type for what goes in Validation - Check inputs before processing Predictable output - Well-defined type for what comes out Async-ready - Can handle asynchronous operations Error handling - Fails gracefully with clear messages Exportable - Can be imported and reused in other files Advanced TypeScript Features Union Types (Multiple Possible Types) type Status = "pending" | "success" | "error"; function handleStatus(status: Status) { if (status === "pending") { console.log("Loading..."); } else if (status === "success") { console.log("Done!"); } else { console.log("Failed!"); } } handleStatus("success"); // valid handleStatus("loading"); // ❌ ERROR: Not a valid Status Interfaces (Alternative to Type) interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string; } // Interfaces can extend interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[]; } const admin: Admin = { id: 1, name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com", permissions: ["read", "write", "delete"] }; Generic Types (Reusable Type Patterns) // Generic array wrapper function wrapInArray<T>(item: T): T[] { return [item]; } const nums = wrapInArray(42); // number[] const strs = wrapInArray("hello"); // string[] // Generic API response type ApiResponse<T> = { data: T; status: number; message: string; }; const userResponse: ApiResponse<User> = { data: { id: 1, name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com" }, status: 200, message: "Success" }; Practice Path for Mastery Beginner-to-Component-Developer Roadmap Complete these exercises in order to master component-style programming: Simple Function Write a function that takes an object with { firstName, lastName } and returns { fullName } Add Validation Enhance the function to throw an error if either name is empty Make it Async Convert it to an async function that waits 500ms before returning (simulating a database lookup) Split into Modules Move the function to a separate file and import it in your main file Convert to TypeScript Add proper types for input, output, and the function signature Build a Real Component Create a "user profile" component that takes user data, validates it, and returns formatted profile information Example: Complete Component Here's a complete, real-world style component combining all concepts: // types.ts - Type definitions export type UserInput = { username: string; email: string; age?: number; }; export type ValidationResult = { isValid: boolean; errors: string[]; }; export type ProcessedUser = { username: string; email: string; age: number; createdAt: string; }; // validators.ts - Validation logic export function validateUser(input: UserInput): ValidationResult { const errors: string[] = []; if (!input.username || input.username.length < 3) { errors.push("Username must be at least 3 characters"); } if (!input.email || !input.email.includes("@")) { errors.push("Valid email is required"); } if (input.age !== undefined && (input.age < 0 || input.age > 120)) { errors.push("Age must be between 0 and 120"); } return { isValid: errors.length === 0, errors }; } // component.ts - Main component logic import { UserInput, ValidationResult, ProcessedUser } from "./types"; import { validateUser } from "./validators"; export async function processUser(input: UserInput): Promise<ProcessedUser> { // Validate input const validation = validateUser(input); if (!validation.isValid) { throw new Error(`Validation failed: ${validation.errors.join(", ")}`); } // Simulate async processing (e.g., database save) await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100)); // Return processed result return { username: input.username, email: input.email.toLowerCase(), age: input.age ?? 0, // Default to 0 if not provided createdAt: new Date().toISOString() }; } // index.ts - Usage example import { processUser } from "./component"; async function main() { try { const result = await processUser({ username: "alice123", email: "Alice@Example.com", age: 25 }); console.log("User processed:", result); } catch (err) { console.error("Failed to process user:", err.message); } } main(); Next Steps Practice building small components with clear input/output types Learn about popular frameworks that use this pattern (React, Vue, etc.) Explore Node.js libraries for file I/O, HTTP requests, and databases Study design patterns (Factory, Builder, Strategy) in TypeScript Build a complete application with multiple interconnected components Remember: The best way to learn is by building. Start small, make mistakes, and gradually increase complexity. Every expert programmer started exactly where you are now!

title: LangChain → LangGraph → Flowise
label: 7. LangChain, LangGraph, and Flowise
headings: Bridge from HTTP → “dict pipelines”
LangChain: everything is a runnable that transforms inputs → outputs
LangGraph: stateful graphs (State → partial State)
Flowise: visual applications and Agentflow V2
Extension path
description: How to think in “passing dictionaries”, building nodes, composing runnables, managing state, and then turning it into a UI flow.
text: How to think in “passing dictionaries”, building nodes, composing runnables, managing state, and then turning it into a UI flow. Table of contents Bridge from HTTP → “dict pipelines” LangChain: everything is a runnable that transforms inputs → outputs The “passing dictionaries” mental model Runnables: invoke/batch/stream + composition RunnablePassthrough + assign Custom node creation (custom runnable) Mini end-to-end chain example LangGraph: stateful graphs (State → partial State) State passing and reducers Example: “purchase request” graph (inventory + approval) Flowise: visual applications and Agentflow V2 Framework status The runnable and StateGraph examples in this chapter remain current. In LangChain v1, langchain.agents.create_agent is the standard prebuilt agent API and replaces langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent. Use raw StateGraph when you need an explicit custom workflow. Flowise Agentflow V2 is a native orchestration system with standalone nodes and Flow State; it is not merely a visual skin over LangChain. Bridge from HTTP → “dict pipelines” You already learned HTTP methods (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE). When you build LLM apps, you’ll usually expose them as HTTP endpoints too. The key connection: HTTP request body is typically JSON → in Python it becomes a dict. LangChain/LangGraph pipelines are easiest to understand as “functions that transform dictionaries”. Client JSON └─> Python dict └─> LangChain runnable pipeline (dict -> dict/string) └─> HTTP JSON response Visual: request → dict → runnable pipeline Client JSON body {...} Python dict {"question": ...} LangChain Runnable pipeline prompt | llm | parser Response JSON / text "..." parse invoke return This is the “dict pipeline” mental model: you’re always passing one structured object through transforms. LangChain: everything is a runnable that transforms inputs → outputs 1) The “passing dictionaries” mental model Think of a chain as a pipeline that receives a dictionary, adds/changes keys, and eventually returns a final output. Input dict { "user_id": "u_123", "question": "What is my total spend last month?" } Output "Your total spend last month was $1,245.40" Internally, intermediate steps might create keys like sql, rows, summary. 2) Runnables: one interface + composition A Runnable is “anything” you can call in a consistent way: one input → one output. ConceptWhat it meansWhy you care invoke(input) Run once, return output Simple request/response batch([inputs]) Run many inputs efficiently Lower cost + faster throughput stream(input) Yield partial outputs as they’re produced Great UX for chat/long responses Composition rule (LCEL): pipe output of one runnable into the next prompt_template | llm | output_parser Mentally: output = parser(llm(prompt(input))) Why this “uniform runnable” idea is powerful: Once everything speaks the same interface, you can mix-and-match prompts, models, retrievers, parsers, and custom logic like LEGO. Visual: one interface, different runtimes Runnable one input → one output uniform interface invoke batch stream Composition prompt | llm | parser mix-and-match components same call shape everywhere 3) RunnablePassthrough (and “keeping keys alive”) In real pipelines you often need to compute something new without losing the original input. That’s where “passthrough” patterns help. Typical RAG shape (conceptual) { "question": "...", "context": "<retrieved docs text>" } --> prompt --> llm --> answer RunnablePassthrough behaves like identity, and can also be used with an “assign” pattern to add keys. # Conceptual example (LangChain LCEL style) from operator import itemgetter from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough # Suppose you already have: retriever, format_docs, prompt, llm, parser setup = RunnablePassthrough.assign( context=itemgetter("question") | retriever | format_docs ) chain = setup | prompt | llm | parser result = chain.invoke({"question": "What are the top 3 products by revenue?"}) print(result) Key mental model: Passthrough keeps your dict intact, while letting you attach extra computed fields. 4) Custom node creation in LangChain (custom runnable) “Node” isn’t an official LangChain term the way it is in graph frameworks, but developers often call each pipeline step a “node”. The simplest way to create a custom node is to wrap a Python function as a runnable. from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda def normalize_question(inputs: dict) -> dict: q = inputs["question"].strip() return {**inputs, "question": q} normalize_node = RunnableLambda(normalize_question) # Now it composes like any other runnable: # normalize_node | prompt | llm | parser Rule of thumb Input and output can be strings, lists, or dicts… but dicts give you the most flexibility. Prefer “pure transforms” (no side effects) for easy debugging. If you need side effects (DB writes, HTTP calls), isolate them in a clearly-named node. 5) Mini end-to-end LangChain example (SQL helper, dict-first) Here’s a tiny pipeline that: 1) builds SQL from a question, 2) executes it, 3) summarizes rows. This is intentionally small so you can “see the dictionaries move”. from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda, RunnablePassthrough from operator import itemgetter # --- pretend implementations --- def llm_write_sql(inputs: dict) -> dict: # In practice: prompt | llm | parser q = inputs["question"] sql = "SELECT SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE order_month = :month" params = {"month": "last"} return {**inputs, "sql": sql, "params": params, "question_echo": q} def run_sql(inputs: dict) -> dict: # In practice: call your DB driver here with bound parameters, not string interpolation. rows = [{"total": 1245.40}] return {**inputs, "rows": rows} def summarize(inputs: dict) -> str: total = inputs["rows"][0]["total"] return f"Your total spend last month was ${total:,.2f}" # --- wrap as nodes --- write_sql = RunnableLambda(llm_write_sql) execute = RunnableLambda(run_sql) summarize_node = RunnableLambda(summarize) # --- keep dict, add keys, finish with a string --- chain = ( RunnablePassthrough() # starts as identity (keeps original dict) | write_sql # adds sql | execute # adds rows | summarize_node # returns final string ) print(chain.invoke({"user_id": "u_123", "question": "What is my total spend last month?"})) What you should notice: Each step either (a) returns a new dict with extra keys, or (b) returns the final answer. That’s the “passing dictionaries” idea in one page. LangGraph: stateful graphs (State → partial State) 1) State passing LangGraph is what you use when a simple linear chain becomes a workflow: branching, loops, retries, tool-calling cycles, or multi-step “agent” behavior. Core rule: Each node reads State and returns a partial update to State Visual: State → partial State updates State (shared) {"sku", "qty", "amount", ...} + intermediate keys node A returns {"in_stock": true} node B returns {"approval": "approved"} Merged State State + updates (reducers define merging) You usually define a typed state (e.g., TypedDict) and each node returns only the keys it changed. Reducers (why they exist): If multiple nodes update the same key (e.g., message history), reducers define how those updates are merged (append, overwrite, etc.). 2) Example: “purchase request” graph (inventory + approval) This mirrors the A2A story you built earlier (concierge → inventory + approval), but inside a single LangGraph workflow with shared state. Graph shape START | parse_request | check_inventory ----(out_of_stock)----> finalize | request_approval ----(rejected)-------> finalize | finalize | END Visual: branching workflow START parse_request check_inventory finalize (out_of_stock) request_approval finalize (then END) no stock in stock approved/rejected → finalize from typing import TypedDict, Literal, Optional from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END class PurchaseState(TypedDict, total=False): # input sku: str qty: int amount: float po_id: str # derived/intermediate in_stock: bool reserved: bool approval: Literal["approved", "rejected", "skipped"] reason: Optional[str] # final result: str # --- nodes --- def parse_request(state: PurchaseState) -> PurchaseState: # In real life, parse from user text. Here we assume state already has fields. return {} def check_inventory(state: PurchaseState) -> PurchaseState: # pretend inventory lookup stock_map = {"SKU-APPLE": 12, "SKU-CHAIR": 0} available = stock_map.get(state["sku"], 0) if available < state["qty"]: return {"in_stock": False, "reserved": False, "reason": f"Only {available} left"} return {"in_stock": True, "reserved": True} def request_approval(state: PurchaseState) -> PurchaseState: # pretend policy: auto-approve up to 1000 if state["amount"] <= 1000: return {"approval": "approved"} return {"approval": "rejected", "reason": "Over auto-approval limit"} def finalize(state: PurchaseState) -> PurchaseState: if not state.get("in_stock", True): return {"result": f"FAILED: out of stock ({state.get('reason')})"} if state.get("approval") == "rejected": return {"result": f"FAILED: approval rejected ({state.get('reason')})"} return {"result": "SUCCESS: reserved and approved"} # --- build graph --- g = StateGraph(PurchaseState) g.add_node("parse_request", parse_request) g.add_node("check_inventory", check_inventory) g.add_node("request_approval", request_approval) g.add_node("finalize", finalize) g.set_entry_point("parse_request") g.add_edge("parse_request", "check_inventory") # conditional branching after inventory def inventory_router(state: PurchaseState): return "finalize" if not state.get("in_stock", True) else "request_approval" g.add_conditional_edges("check_inventory", inventory_router, { "finalize": "finalize", "request_approval": "request_approval", }) # conditional branching after approval def approval_router(state: PurchaseState): return "finalize" g.add_conditional_edges("request_approval", approval_router, { "finalize": "finalize", }) g.add_edge("finalize", END) app = g.compile() print(app.invoke({"sku": "SKU-APPLE", "qty": 2, "amount": 4.50, "po_id": "PO-1001"})["result"]) print(app.invoke({"sku": "SKU-CHAIR", "qty": 1, "amount": 150.0, "po_id": "PO-2002"})["result"]) print(app.invoke({"sku": "SKU-APPLE", "qty": 1, "amount": 2500.0, "po_id": "PO-3003"})["result"]) Key difference vs LangChain chain: LangChain pipelines are typically linear transforms; LangGraph makes the “workflow control” (branching/loops) explicit and stateful. Where the current prebuilt agent fits If your workflow is the standard model → tool calls → model loop, use langchain.agents.create_agent. It is implemented on LangGraph and can add middleware for guardrails, dynamic prompts, human approval, and state. Use the raw graph above when the business process itself has named states, deterministic branches, or custom persistence semantics. import os from langchain.agents import create_agent # inventory_check is an ordinary LangChain tool defined elsewhere. agent = create_agent( model=os.environ["LANGCHAIN_MODEL"], tools=[inventory_check], system_prompt="Check inventory before promising availability.", ) result = agent.invoke({ "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Can we supply two SKU-APPLE units?"} ] }) Flowise: visual applications and Agentflow V2 Flowise is an open-source visual platform for assistants, LLM applications, and agent workflows. Its three main builder levels are Assistant for the simplest configured agent, Chatflow for single-agent/chatbot and RAG flows, and Agentflow for single- or multi-agent orchestration. A simple Chatflow can resemble the runnable pipeline above, but that mapping is only the starting point. In code (LangChain) input dict └─> prompt | llm | parser └─> output In UI (Flowise) [Prompt Node] → [LLM Node] → [Output Parser Node] (+ optional Retriever/Memory/Tools nodes) Visual: code pipeline ↔ UI nodes LangChain (code) Flowise (UI) prompt llm parser Prompt Node LLM Node Parser Node source controlled fast prototyping A simple Chatflow can map closely to a code pipeline; Agentflow V2 adds its own explicit orchestration model. How a simple Flowise flow maps to “passing dictionaries” Each node performs a configured operation such as prompting a model, retrieving documents, calling a tool, transforming data, or replying. Edges are “data flow”: output of one node becomes input to the next. Node settings in the UI become the parameters you’d pass in code (model name, temperature, prompt template, etc.). What Agentflow V2 adds Native standalone nodes: the execution graph is defined explicitly rather than delegated entirely to an external agent framework. Flow State: declare shared keys in the Start node, then let later nodes read or update those keys without threading every value through adjacent edges. Control flow: conditions, loops, routing, deterministic Tool nodes, LLM-driven Agent nodes, and reusable subflows. Human-in-the-loop: pause for approval or feedback, save a checkpoint, and resume the workflow instead of blocking a process in memory. Operations: streaming execution updates, tracing, API deployment, and workspace/security controls are part of the platform surface. Practical workflow: Decide where the maintained source of truth lives. A team may keep a Flowise Agentflow in versioned exported configuration, or implement the workflow directly in LangGraph code. Rebuilding the same flow twice creates drift. Whichever path you choose, add evaluation fixtures, approval tests, secret management, access control, tracing, and a promotion process before production. Where LangGraph shows up in UI tools LangGraph and Agentflow V2 solve overlapping orchestration problems at different abstraction and governance boundaries. LangGraph keeps the workflow in Python code with explicit state, reducers, checkpointers, and tests. Agentflow V2 exposes branches, loops, agent/tool nodes, human input, checkpoints, and Flow State in a visual platform. Choose based on ownership, deployment controls, extensibility, and testability rather than assuming one is only a prototype for the other. Rule of thumb LangChain runnables: compose deterministic transforms and model calls. LangChain create_agent: use the supported prebuilt model/tool agent loop. LangGraph: use code-first graphs for custom workflow logic, persistence, and shared state. Flowise: use Assistant, Chatflow, or Agentflow V2 when a governed visual platform is the intended runtime and authoring surface. Official references LangChain v1 changes and create_agent LangGraph v1 migration guide LangGraph Graph API Flowise official documentation Flowise Agentflow V2 Extension path Turn the LangChain mini SQL chain into a real HTTP endpoint (POST /ask) that accepts JSON dict input. Replace the fake DB function with a real SQL driver call. Add auth: JWT / API key / OAuth, just like we discussed earlier. Promote to LangGraph when you need branching (e.g., approval required only over $1000).

text: The geometric, code‑first foundations every later chapter depends on. We start with tensors, autograd, modules, and the training loop, then ask “what is a model, geometrically?” We implement linear regression and classification end-to-end in PyTorch before covering the tree/ensemble family (Random Forest, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost) — the family that still beats deep learning on tabular data. Prerequisites Python 3 fluency, basic linear algebra (vectors, matrix multiply, derivatives). No prior PyTorch needed — Chapter 1 is the on‑ramp. Read this part before Part V (Deep Learning & LLMs). What you can do after this part Train and evaluate a regression or classification model in PyTorch from scratch, and ship a tabular ML baseline using XGBoost. You can then proceed to Part V with no gaps. ML foundations spine Chapter 2 is the conceptual foundation: data points, model shapes, regression, classification, and supervised learning. Chapters 3 and 4 intentionally repeat the same fit/predict/score workflow because regression and classification differ in target type, output activation, loss, and metrics. Chapter 5 then branches to tree and ensemble methods as the tabular baseline family that often competes with or beats neural networks on structured data. Chapters in order PyTorch foundations: tensors, autograd, modules, and training Machine learning as geometry Linear regression and the training loop Linear classification (logistic regression) Trees, bagging & boosting (Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost)

title: PyTorch Foundations: Tensors, Autograd, Modules, and Training
label: 1. PyTorch foundations
headings: We start from the very beginning
Why PyTorch
Practical applications
The four objects behind every PyTorch example
Tensors: arrays with shape, dtype, and device
Autograd: gradients from a recorded computation
Modules and parameters: a model is a callable object
The smallest complete training loop
The first debugging contract: inspect shape, dtype, device, and range
How we’ll work
description: A practical journey through modern deep learning with PyTorch—from first principles to real applications.
text: Part IV • Machine Learning Foundations A practical journey through modern deep learning with PyTorch—from first principles to real applications. Deep learning has transformed how we work with data, from recognizing images and understanding language to powering recommendation engines and game-playing agents. This book is a practical journey through modern deep learning with PyTorch, designed to take you from beginner to advanced without requiring a heavy math background (though pointers to deeper theory are provided if you want them). We start from the very beginning We start from the very beginning: linear regression and the idea of a neuron as a simple nonlinear transformation of a linear model. From there, we build up to deep neural networks, then explore specialized architectures: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for images and signals Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and LSTMs for sequences and time series Best practices for time series forecasting, including what commonly goes wrong in stock prediction tutorials Why PyTorch Along the way, you’ll see how PyTorch’s automatic differentiation and rich set of prebuilt layers let you focus on ideas and experiments instead of manually deriving and coding gradients. PyTorch became popular partly because its eager, Python-first execution model was easier to inspect than the static-graph-first workflows used by Theano and early TensorFlow. Modern TensorFlow also supports eager execution; both frameworks remain capable, while this book uses PyTorch for one consistent implementation path. Practical applications The second half of the book focuses on applications that matter in practice: Natural Language Processing (NLP) and text classification Embeddings for words and other categorical data Recommender systems as used by companies like Amazon, Facebook, and Google Transfer learning with pretrained models, allowing you to leverage massive datasets like ImageNet Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for realistic image generation Reinforcement Learning (RL) for sequential decision-making and control The four objects behind every PyTorch example Later chapters introduce many architectures, but the training machinery changes very little. Hold these four objects in your head: ObjectJobTypical PyTorch form TensorStores numeric inputs, targets, parameters, and intermediate values.torch.Tensor ModelMaps an input tensor to an output tensor using learnable parameters.nn.Module LossMeasures how wrong the model output is for the target.nn.MSELoss, nn.CrossEntropyLoss OptimizerUpdates parameters using their gradients.torch.optim.SGD, AdamW Visual: the reusable training loop Input x tensor Model prediction = f(x) Loss compare to y Optimizer update parameters backward computes gradients; step changes parameters Tensors: arrays with shape, dtype, and device A tensor is a multidimensional numeric array. A scalar has no axes, a vector has one, a matrix has two, and a batch of color images often has four: [batch, channels, height, width]. import torch scalar = torch.tensor(3.0) # shape: [] vector = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]) # shape: [3] matrix = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]) # shape: [2, 2] print(matrix.shape) # torch.Size([2, 2]) print(matrix.dtype) # usually torch.float32 here print(matrix.device) # cpu, unless moved to an accelerator Shape describes axis lengths. Dtype describes numeric representation, such as float32 or int64. Device says where the storage and operation live, such as CPU, CUDA GPU, or Apple MPS. Tensors used in one operation must have compatible shapes, dtypes, and devices. device = ( "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" ) x = torch.randn(32, 10, device=device) # 32 examples, 10 features each Autograd: gradients from a recorded computation Training asks: “How should each parameter change to reduce the loss?” PyTorch records operations involving tensors that require gradients. Calling backward() applies the chain rule backward through that computation graph. w = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True) x = torch.tensor(3.0) y = w * x ** 2 y.backward() print(w.grad) # 9.0 because dy/dw = x^2 The graph is a record of operations for this forward pass, not a drawing you have to create manually. A new graph is normally built on the next pass. Gradients accumulate in .grad, which is why training loops clear them before the next backward pass. Modules and parameters: a model is a callable object nn.Module is the base class for trainable PyTorch components. It registers nested modules and parameters so the optimizer, device movement, saving, and training/evaluation modes work recursively. from torch import nn class LinearRegressor(nn.Module): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.linear = nn.Linear(in_features=1, out_features=1) def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: return self.linear(x) model = LinearRegressor() prediction = model(torch.tensor([[2.0]])) # call model(...), not forward(...) The learnable weight and bias are nn.Parameter objects. They are tensors with gradient tracking that were registered because self.linear is a child module. The smallest complete training loop This example learns the relationship y = 2x + 1. Later chapters change the data, model, and loss, but keep this loop structure. import torch from torch import nn x = torch.tensor([[0.0], [1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]) y = torch.tensor([[1.0], [3.0], [5.0], [7.0]]) model = nn.Linear(1, 1) loss_fn = nn.MSELoss() optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05) for step in range(500): model.train() prediction = model(x) # 1) forward pass loss = loss_fn(prediction, y) # 2) measure error optimizer.zero_grad() # 3) clear old gradients loss.backward() # 4) compute new gradients optimizer.step() # 5) update weight and bias model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): print(model(torch.tensor([[4.0]]))) # close to 9 model.train() and model.eval() control layers whose behavior differs by mode, such as dropout and batch normalization. torch.no_grad() disables gradient recording for this evaluation block, reducing memory and work. It does not replace eval(); the two controls solve different problems. The first debugging contract: inspect shape, dtype, device, and range Before changing an architecture, print the boundary facts. Many apparent “model problems” are tensor contract problems: print("x:", x.shape, x.dtype, x.device) print("y:", y.shape, y.dtype, y.device) print("prediction:", prediction.shape) print("finite:", torch.isfinite(loss).item()) Regression predictions and targets usually need matching floating-point shapes. Class indices for CrossEntropyLoss are normally torch.long. Do not mix CPU inputs with a GPU model. Do not silently broadcast incompatible target and prediction shapes. Check for NaN or infinity before tuning hyperparameters. How we’ll work Throughout, we will rely on PyTorch and GPU-backed environments (such as Google Colab), so you can train powerful models even if you don’t have specialized hardware. The goal is not just to show you which buttons to press, but to help you understand why the architectures work, where they fail, and how to adapt them to your own projects. Progression: The next chapter turns tensors into geometry: rows become points, model parameters define lines or separating boundaries, and loss measures how poorly that geometry fits the data. The regression chapter then implements the same loop above one line at a time. Deep Learning with PyTorch • Chapter 1

title: Machine Learning as Geometry
label: 2. Machine learning as geometry
headings: 1. Data as Points, Models as Shapes
2. Regression: Fitting Numbers
3. Classification: Separating Categories
4. Supervised Learning in One Picture
description: A concrete mental model: data become points, and learning becomes fitting (or separating) shapes in space.
text: Chapter 2 • Geometric Foundations A concrete mental model: data become points, and learning becomes fitting (or separating) shapes in space. Most descriptions of machine learning make it sound mysterious: computers “learn from experience” and “improve automatically.” In this book, we’ll use a much simpler, concrete view: Machine learning is, at its core, a geometry problem. We turn data into points in a space, then learn shapes—lines, planes, and curves—that fit or separate those points. 1. Data as Points, Models as Shapes Every machine learning problem has two parts: A geometric view of data: each example becomes a point in feature space. Features → points in space A person becomes a point with coordinates like (years of experience, age, education level, …). A patient becomes a point like (height, weight, blood pressure, …). Each example is a point in a 2D, 3D, or higher-dimensional space. Model → a geometric object In 2D: a line or curve In 3D: a plane or surface In higher dimensions: a hyperplane or more complex surface Learning means adjusting that geometric object so that it matches the data well. 2. Regression: Fitting Numbers Regression is about predicting a number: a salary, a house price, a temperature. Regression fits a shape (often a line) through a cloud of points. Example: Salary vs Experience We want to predict salary from years of experience: For each person, we record \( x \) = years of experience \( y \) = salary Each person is a point \((x, y)\) on a 2D graph. We look for a line: \[ y = mx + b \] \( m \): how much salary increases per year \( b \): salary when experience is zero The learned \( m \) and \( b \) define our model: given a new \( x \), we predict \( y \). With more features (experience, age, education, location), each person becomes a point in higher dimensions, and the model becomes a plane or hyperplane instead of a line. With nonlinear relationships, we replace straight lines with curves or more flexible surfaces—but the geometric idea is the same: we fit a shape to a cloud of points. 3. Classification: Separating Categories Classification is about predicting a category: spam/not spam, dog/cat, fraud/not fraud, at risk/not at risk. Classification learns a decision boundary that separates labeled points. Example: Cardiovascular Risk from Height and Weight We want to predict cardiovascular risk from: \( x_1 \) = height \( x_2 \) = weight We encode the label as: 0 = not at risk 1 = at risk Steps: Plot each patient as a point \((x_1, x_2)\) in 2D. Color points by label (e.g. blue = 0, green = 1). Find a line that separates the colors as well as possible. This line is a decision boundary: One side → predicted “not at risk” Other side → predicted “at risk” In problems like fraud detection, each transaction is a point in a high-dimensional space. The model learns a boundary—no longer a simple visible line, but still a geometric surface—that separates “fraud” from “not fraud”. 4. Supervised Learning in One Picture Both regression and classification are forms of supervised learning: We know the inputs (features). We know the targets (numbers or labels). We learn a function that maps inputs to targets from many examples. Geometrically: Regression → fit a line/plane/curve through points. Classification → find a boundary that separates differently labeled points. As we move to deep learning and more complex architectures, the spaces and shapes become higher-dimensional and more flexible. But the fundamental picture remains: Data are points. Models are shapes. Learning is finding the shapes that best match the points. Deep Learning with PyTorch • Concepts

description: We’ll connect the math of linear regression to a working PyTorch training loop, keeping the link between equations and code as clear as possible.
text: Chapter 3 • Linear Regression We’ll connect the math of linear regression to a working PyTorch training loop, keeping the link between equations and code as clear as possible. In the previous chapter we viewed machine learning as a geometry problem: data become points in a space; models are shapes (lines, planes, curves) that we fit or use to separate those points. In this chapter we make that concrete with the simplest possible model: linear regression in PyTorch. The linear regression picture: fit a straight line to data points. 2.1 A Simple Dataset and Notation Consider a dataset with one input feature and one target. For example: $x$: years of experience $y$: salary We have $N$ samples: $$ (x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots, (x_N, y_N). $$ Here, capital $N$ denotes the total number of samples. The input values $x_i$ and target values $y_i$ are fixed; our job is to learn a function that maps $x_i \mapsto \hat{y}_i$ so that predictions $\hat{y}_i$ are close to the true values $y_i$. In PyTorch, we store the data as tensors: import torch # Toy example x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]).view(-1, 1) # shape: (N, 1) y = torch.tensor([2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0]).view(-1, 1) # shape: (N, 1) The .view(-1, 1) reshapes the 1D tensors into column vectors of shape $(N, 1)$, which is the common shape for a single input feature and single output in PyTorch. 2.2 The Model: A Straight Line For simple linear regression, our model is a straight line: $$ \hat{y} = m x + b. $$ For each sample $i$: $$ \hat{y}_i = m x_i + b. $$ The parameters $m$ (slope) and $b$ (intercept) are unknown; these are what we want to learn from data. In PyTorch we represent this line with nn.Linear: import torch.nn as nn # One input feature, one output model = nn.Linear(in_features=1, out_features=1) This model internally stores a weight and a bias, which correspond to $m$ and $b$: print(model.weight) # corresponds roughly to m print(model.bias) # corresponds roughly to b To get predictions, we call the model like a function: y_pred = model(x) # computes y_hat = m * x + b for all samples Conceptually, this is computing all the $\hat{y}_i = m x_i + b$ at once using tensor operations. 2.3 The Loss Function: Mean Squared Error To evaluate how good a particular line is, we measure how far the predictions are from the true values. For regression, the standard choice is Mean Squared Error (MSE): $$ L(m, b) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl(y_i - \hat{y}_i\bigr)^2. $$ Substituting the model $\hat{y}_i = m x_i + b$, we can write: $$ L(m, b) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl(y_i - (m x_i + b)\bigr)^2. $$ Geometrically, $\lvert y_i - \hat{y}_i \rvert$ is the vertical distance from the point $(x_i, y_i)$ to the line. Squaring and averaging gives us a single non-negative number that is small when the line fits the data well and large when it does not. In PyTorch, we use nn.MSELoss: criterion = nn.MSELoss() y_pred = model(x) loss = criterion(y_pred, y) # scalar tensor: the MSE print(loss.item()) At this point we have everything needed to define a supervised learning problem: a model $\hat{y} = m x + b$, and a loss function $L(m, b)$ that tells us how good any particular choice of $m$ and $b$ is. 2.4 Learning as Minimizing the Loss The data $(x_i, y_i)$ are given and fixed. The variables in the loss expression are the parameters $m$ and $b$. Learning means: $$ (m^*, b^*) = \arg\min_{m, b} L(m, b). $$ In other words, we want to find the values of $m$ and $b$ that make the mean squared error as small as possible. For very simple models like this, you can derive explicit formulas for $m^*$ and $b^*$ by taking derivatives of $L$ with respect to $m$ and $b$, setting them to zero, and solving: $$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial m} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = 0. $$ The normal-equation approach is useful theory, and closed-form or direct solvers remain important for some linear models. However, this approach does not generalize cleanly to deep neural networks, where the loss depends on thousands or millions of parameters in highly nonlinear ways. For those models, we use gradient-based iterative methods. For a parameter vector $\theta$ (in our case $\theta = \{m, b\}$), classic gradient descent updates parameters as: $$ \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla_\theta L(\theta), $$ where $\eta > 0$ is the learning rate. Applied to our parameters, this becomes: $$ m \leftarrow m - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial m}, \qquad b \leftarrow b - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}. $$ PyTorch computes these derivatives automatically using automatic differentiation. Our job is to define the model, the loss, and the optimization procedure; PyTorch will handle the gradients. 2.5 The Optimizer: SGD We now need a component that takes the gradients and updates the parameters. PyTorch provides several optimizers; the simplest is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD): import torch.optim as optim learning_rate = 0.01 optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate) Here, model.parameters() returns an iterator over the model’s trainable parameters (in this case, the weight and bias). The optimizer will update these in-place, using the gradients that PyTorch computes. 2.6 The Training Loop Training consists of repeating the same sequence of steps: zeroing gradients, computing predictions, computing the loss, computing gradients, and updating parameters. Each full pass through these steps is one training iteration; when we apply this to the whole dataset repeatedly, we often call each pass through the dataset an epoch. The standard PyTorch training pattern you’ll reuse in nearly every model. A typical training loop for simple linear regression looks like this: num_epochs = 1000 for epoch in range(num_epochs): # 1. Zero out previous gradients optimizer.zero_grad() # 2. Forward pass: compute predictions y_pred = model(x) # 3. Compute the loss loss = criterion(y_pred, y) # 4. Backward pass: compute gradients dL/dm and dL/db loss.backward() # 5. Update parameters using the optimizer optimizer.step() # (Optional) monitor progress if (epoch + 1) % 100 == 0: print(f"Epoch {epoch + 1}, Loss = {loss.item():.4f}") The mapping to the math is direct: y_pred = model(x) computes all $\hat{y}_i = m x_i + b$. loss = criterion(y_pred, y) computes $L(m, b)$. loss.backward() fills in model.weight.grad and model.bias.grad with $\frac{\partial L}{\partial m}$ and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}$. optimizer.step() performs the gradient descent updates. 2.7 Getting Results Out After training, we may want to inspect predictions or plot the learned line. Since many plotting libraries expect NumPy arrays, we often convert our tensors: with torch.no_grad(): # disable gradient tracking y_pred = model(x) # final predictions x_np = x.detach().numpy() y_np = y.detach().numpy() y_pred_np = y_pred.detach().numpy() The detach() call removes tensors from the computation graph, making conversion to NumPy safe. We can then plot x_np versus y_np and y_pred_np using Matplotlib, or use them in further analysis. 2.8 Summary In this chapter we connected the geometric picture of linear regression to both its mathematical formulation and its PyTorch implementation. We started with a set of data points $(x_i, y_i)$, defined a linear model: $$ \hat{y} = m x + b, $$ and measured its performance using the mean squared error: $$ L(m, b) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl(y_i - (m x_i + b)\bigr)^2. $$ We then viewed learning as minimizing this loss with respect to the parameters $m$ and $b$: $$ (m^*, b^*) = \arg\min_{m, b} L(m, b), $$ and we implemented this using PyTorch’s tensors, nn.Linear model, nn.MSELoss loss function, and an SGD optimizer inside a training loop. This simple example is more than a toy: the same pattern—define data, define model, define loss, define optimizer, write a training loop—will reappear in every deep learning model we build with PyTorch, from basic neural networks to convolutional and recurrent architectures. Deep Learning with PyTorch • Linear Regression

text: A student-friendly chapter that explains linear decision boundaries, logistic regression, and a complete PyTorch training loop end-to-end. Diagrams are saved locally under assets/images/ch4 (downloaded from Wikimedia Commons) so the page works offline. Light theme • VSCode-like code blocks • LaTeX via KaTeX • Offline diagrams 1) The ML workflow and what happens inside fit/predict/score 2) Accuracy, error, train vs test 3) Linear decision boundaries and the logit 4) Step vs sigmoid, logistic regression 5) Training: loss, gradient descent, learning rate 6) Dataset: Breast cancer (scikit-learn) + preprocessing 7) PyTorch implementation: BCE, Adam, training loop, accuracy 8) Better logistic regression: BCEWithLogitsLoss 9) Saving/loading models (state_dict) + Colab download 10) Why logistic regression is a “neuron” 11) Train/validation/test, Kaggle, cross-validation, hyperparameters 12) Summary + exercises What you’ll build (and the math behind it) A linear classifier with logit $a = w^\top x + b$ and probability $p = \sigma(a)$. A training objective (binary cross-entropy) and a training loop that minimizes it: $$\theta^* = \arg\min_{\theta} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell\bigl(a_i(\theta), y_i\bigr).$$ Practical evaluation: accuracy on train vs test, and how to spot overfitting. Notation used throughout: $x\in\mathbb{R}^D$ (features), $y\in\{0,1\}$ (label), $w\in\mathbb{R}^D$ (weights), $b\in\mathbb{R}$ (bias). 1) The ML Workflow: What Happens Inside fitpredictscore? A typical scikit-learn-style workflow follows the same outer structure for many models: Load data into inputs \(X\) and targets \(y\). Instantiate a model (e.g., logistic regression, linear regression, etc.). Train it with something like model.fit(X, y). Make predictions with model.predict(X) (on train or on new/test data). Evaluate with model.score(X, y). Why this question matters On the surface, “linear regression” and “logistic regression” can look identical in code: you mostly change the class name. The difference is what the model computes, what loss it minimizes, and how training updates parameters. The inside of these functions is where the real meaning is. In math terms, fit is “choose parameters to minimize a loss”, predict is “run the model forward”, and score is “compute a metric”. For classification, the most common metric is accuracy. 2) Classification Accuracy and Error In binary classification (e.g., spam vs not-spam), every prediction is either correct or incorrect. $$\text{accuracy}=\frac{\#\text{correct}}{\#\text{total}}, \qquad \text{error}=\frac{\#\text{wrong}}{\#\text{total}}=1-\text{accuracy}.$$ Equivalently, using an indicator function $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$: $$\text{accuracy} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_i = y_i].$$ Train vs test accuracy You can compute accuracy on the training set and on a held-out test set: train accuracy measures how well you fit the seen data, while test accuracy estimates how well you generalize to unseen data. Note: if classes are highly imbalanced (e.g., 99% of samples are class 0), accuracy can be misleading. It’s still a good starting point, but you may later want precision/recall or ROC-AUC. 3) Geometry: Linear Decision Boundary and the Logit A linear classifier draws a boundary in feature space. For a 2D input \(x=(x_1,x_2)\), the boundary is a line: $$w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b=0.$$ This form generalizes cleanly to higher dimensions (where the boundary is a hyperplane). It also connects directly to the key scalar quantity the model computes: $$a=w^\top x + b,$$ where \(a\) is commonly called the activation or logit. Signed distance intuition The value $a = w^\top x + b$ tells you which side of the boundary you’re on. If you normalize by $\lVert w\rVert$, then $\frac{a}{\lVert w\rVert}$ is proportional to the signed distance from the point to the hyperplane. Why not just use \(y=mx+b\)? In classification, the axes are features \(x_1,x_2,\dots\). The label \(y\) is not an axis. The vector form \(w^\top x+b\) works for any number of features \(D\), not just 2. From geometry to prediction (sign test) If a point is not on the boundary, then \(a=w^\top x+b\) will be either positive or negative. One side of the hyperplane always yields \(a>0\), the other yields \(a<0\). $$\hat{y}=\begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } a>0 \\ 0 & \text{if } a\le 0 \end{cases}$$ Wikimedia diagram illustrating separating hyperplanes (used here purely as a visual intuition for linear decision boundaries). The lecture’s key idea matches the hyperplane form \(w^\top x + b = 0\). 4) Step Function vs Sigmoid: Logistic Regression The sign test is like a hard “step function.” In deep learning we prefer smooth differentiable functions, so we often map the logit \(a\) through a sigmoid: $$\sigma(a)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-a}} \in (0,1).$$ We interpret \(p=\sigma(a)\) as a probability: $$p(y=1\mid x)=\sigma(w^\top x + b).$$ A useful identity: the log-odds are linear in $x$: $$\log\frac{p}{1-p} = w^\top x + b.$$ This is one reason logistic regression is so interpretable. And convert to a class prediction by thresholding: $$\hat{y}=\mathbf{1}[p\ge 0.5].$$ Terminology you’ll see Logistic function = sigmoid function. Logit = the sigmoid input \(a=w^\top x+b\). Logistic regression = linear model + sigmoid for binary classification. Sigmoid curve from Wikimedia. It smoothly maps any real logit \(a\) to a probability in \((0,1)\). Note: \(a=0 \Rightarrow \sigma(a)=0.5\). 5) Training: Loss Functions, Gradients, and Learning Rate Regression vs classification: why the loss changes In regression, targets \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), predictions \(\hat{y}\in\mathbb{R}\), so losses like mean squared error (MSE) make sense: $$\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2.$$ In binary classification, the model outputs probabilities, and a standard loss is binary cross-entropy: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i\log(p_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right],\quad p_i=\sigma(a_i).$$ Where BCE comes from (one sentence) If you assume $y\mid x$ follows a Bernoulli distribution with probability $p=\sigma(w^\top x+b)$, then minimizing BCE is exactly minimizing the negative log-likelihood. Loss / cost / objective The lecture used these words interchangeably: they all mean “the scalar we minimize during training.” How does a model learn? PyTorch uses automatic differentiation to compute gradients of the loss with respect to parameters \(w\) and \(b\). Gradient descent updates parameters iteratively: $$w \leftarrow w - \eta \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w},\qquad b \leftarrow b - \eta \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b},$$ where \(\eta\) is the learning rate. Learning rate is a hyperparameter It is not learned by the model; you choose it (often by trial + intuition). A common starting sweep is \(10^{-1},10^{-2},10^{-3},\dots\). Gradient descent animation (Wikimedia). It shows repeated steps moving “downhill” along the loss landscape. The step size relates to the learning rate. 6) Dataset: Breast Cancer (scikit-learn) + Preprocessing The lecture uses the well-known breast cancer dataset included in scikit-learn. Loading it is a single function call (no manual download needed): Inputs: data.data \(\rightarrow X\) Targets: data.target \(\rightarrow y\) (0/1) Names: data.target_names, data.feature_names Two preprocessing steps from the lecture Train/test split so we can evaluate on unseen data. Standardization with StandardScaler: fit on train only, then transform train and test using the train mean/std. Standardization is: $$x' = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$$ computed per feature (dimension). It helps optimization because different features can start on very different scales. 7) PyTorch Implementation: Logistic Regression End-to-End We will implement the lecture’s PyTorch pipeline: load data, split, scale, build model, train with gradient descent, then evaluate accuracy. Python Load + split + scale import numpy as np from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler # 1) Load data (built into sklearn) data = load_breast_cancer() X = data.data # shape (n, D) y = data.target # shape (n,), values in {0,1} # (Optional inspection) print("X shape:", X.shape) # e.g., (569, 30) print("y shape:", y.shape) print("target names:", data.target_names) # e.g., ['malignant', 'benign'] # 2) Train/test split (test_size ~ 33% as in the lecture) X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.33, random_state=123, stratify=y ) # 3) Standardize features scaler = StandardScaler() X_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train) # fit only on train X_test = scaler.transform(X_test) # transform test using train stats n, D = X_train.shape print("train:", X_train.shape, "test:", X_test.shape) Model: Linear layer + sigmoid The lecture builds a logistic regression model as: $$p=\sigma(w^\top x+b),$$ which in PyTorch can be represented as nn.Linear(D,1) then nn.Sigmoid(), wrapped in nn.Sequential. Shape sanity check For binary classification, it’s common to keep outputs as shape $(n,1)$. That’s why the targets are reshaped with .view(-1, 1). Python Model + loss + optimizer + tensor conversion import torch import torch.nn as nn # Logistic regression = Linear + Sigmoid model = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(D, 1), nn.Sigmoid() ) # Binary cross entropy loss (for probabilities) criterion = nn.BCELoss() # Adam optimizer (common default in deep learning) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) # Convert numpy -> torch tensors (float32) X_train_t = torch.from_numpy(X_train.astype(np.float32)) X_test_t = torch.from_numpy(X_test.astype(np.float32)) # IMPORTANT in PyTorch: y should be shape (n, 1) for this setup y_train_t = torch.from_numpy(y_train.astype(np.float32)).view(-1, 1) y_test_t = torch.from_numpy(y_test.astype(np.float32)).view(-1, 1) Training loop (gradient descent with autograd) The lecture’s loop is the standard PyTorch pattern: zero gradients → forward pass → loss → backward → optimizer step. Python Train + track train/test loss (per epoch) train_losses = [] test_losses = [] epochs = 300 for epoch in range(epochs): # ---- TRAIN step ---- optimizer.zero_grad() p_train = model(X_train_t) # probabilities in (0,1) loss_train = criterion(p_train, y_train_t) loss_train.backward() optimizer.step() # ---- EVAL losses (no gradient needed) ---- with torch.no_grad(): p_test = model(X_test_t) loss_test = criterion(p_test, y_test_t) train_losses.append(loss_train.item()) test_losses.append(loss_test.item()) if (epoch+1) % 50 == 0: print(f"epoch {epoch+1:4d} train_loss={loss_train.item():.4f} test_loss={loss_test.item():.4f}") Why “test loss increasing” matters If training loss keeps decreasing but test/validation loss starts increasing, you may be overfitting (memorizing train patterns that don’t generalize). Wikimedia overfitting diagram: blue = training error, red = validation error over epochs. This matches the lecture’s explanation of monitoring loss curves to detect overfitting. Accuracy computation (and the “mean of booleans” trick) The model outputs probabilities. For predictions, round to 0/1: $$\hat{y}=\text{round}(p).$$ Then accuracy is the mean of element-wise equality: in Python, True behaves like 1 and False like 0. Python Train/test accuracy with torch.no_grad(): p_train = model(X_train_t).numpy() p_test = model(X_test_t).numpy() # probabilities -> class predictions yhat_train = np.round(p_train) yhat_test = np.round(p_test) train_acc = (yhat_train.reshape(-1) == y_train).mean() test_acc = (yhat_test.reshape(-1) == y_test).mean() print("train accuracy:", train_acc) print("test accuracy:", test_acc) Lecture exercise (kept, but made explicit) Modify the training loop to also compute accuracy each epoch (train and test), store them in arrays, and plot accuracy vs epoch. You should typically see loss go down while accuracy goes up. 8) A Better Logistic Regression in PyTorch: BCEWithLogitsLoss The lecture points out a practical numerical-stability issue: explicitly computing sigmoid uses exponentials, and BCE uses logs. PyTorch provides a stable combined loss that works directly on logits. Conceptually, it’s still the same loss, just computed in a numerically stable way. For a single logit $a$ and label $y\in\{0,1\}$, one stable form is: $$\ell(a,y)=\max(a,0) - a\,y + \log\left(1+e^{-|a|}\right).$$ Instead of computing \(p=\sigma(a)\) then BCE, we keep the model output as: $$a=w^\top x+b\quad\text{(logit)},$$ and use nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss. Python Stable version: logits + BCEWithLogitsLoss # Model now outputs logits (no Sigmoid layer!) model = nn.Linear(D, 1) # Stable combined loss criterion = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) # Training loop is the same shape, but now model(X) returns logits for epoch in range(epochs): optimizer.zero_grad() logits_train = model(X_train_t) # any real number loss_train = criterion(logits_train, y_train_t) loss_train.backward() optimizer.step() # Predictions: logits > 0 <=> sigmoid(logits) > 0.5 with torch.no_grad(): logits_test = model(X_test_t).numpy() yhat_test = (logits_test > 0).astype(np.int64).reshape(-1) Prediction rule without sigmoid Because \(\sigma(a)\ge 0.5 \iff a\ge 0\), you can classify directly using the sign of the logit: \(a>0 \Rightarrow \hat{y}=1\), else \(\hat{y}=0\). 9) Saving and Loading Models (and Downloading from Colab) The key object: state_dict In PyTorch, a model’s parameters live in an ordered dictionary returned by: $$\texttt{model.state\_dict()} \Rightarrow \{\text{weights},\text{biases},\dots\}.$$ Python Save + reload (recommended pattern) # Save torch.save(model.state_dict(), "mymodel.pt") # Recreate the same architecture (must match!) model2 = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(D, 1), nn.Sigmoid() ) # Load weights state = torch.load("mymodel.pt", map_location="cpu") model2.load_state_dict(state) model2.eval() # Verify identical accuracy (example) with torch.no_grad(): p_test2 = model2(X_test_t).numpy() yhat_test2 = np.round(p_test2).reshape(-1) print("test accuracy (reloaded):", (yhat_test2 == y_test).mean()) Colab download The lecture gave two ways: Use the Colab file browser sidebar and click “Download” on mymodel.pt. Use code: from google.colab import files; files.download("mymodel.pt"). 10) Why Logistic Regression is a “Neuron” A single neuron-like computation in deep learning is: $$a=\sum_{i=1}^{D} w_i x_i + b,\qquad \hat{y}=\sigma(a)\ \text{(then threshold)}.$$ So logistic regression has the same mathematical shape as a simple artificial neuron: a weighted sum + bias, followed by a nonlinear activation. Deep networks stack many such units, but the biology analogy should not be pushed too far; artificial neurons are engineering abstractions, not faithful biological neuron simulations. The lecture’s biological analogy: Inputs \(x_i\) correspond to signals from many incoming connections (dendrites). Weights \(w_i\) represent connection strengths (strong vs weak). The sign of \(w_i\) represents excitatory (positive) vs inhibitory (negative) influence. A threshold-like effect resembles the “all-or-nothing” firing behavior. Interpretation of weights (kept from lecture) If \(w_i\approx 0\), feature \(x_i\) has little effect on the output. If \(|w_i|\) is large, small changes in \(x_i\) strongly affect the output. The sign determines direction of influence. 11) Train / Validation / Test: Why Splits Exist (and How Kaggle Changes the Words) Why split at all? The whole point of a classifier is to work on future unseen data. If you only measure performance on past seen data, you can fool yourself. Overfitting intuition (from lecture) Complex models can fit training data extremely well but generalize poorly. We want a model that balances being expressive enough to learn patterns, but not so expressive that it memorizes noise. Local bias-variance diagram: total error is a combination of bias and variance (and irreducible noise). This supports the lecture’s “not too simple, not too complex” message. Train vs validation vs test: the naming confusion If you only split into two sets, the “test” set is effectively acting as a validation set (you are using it to validate generalization). That’s why people sometimes say “train/validation” and sometimes “train/test” for the same two-way split. Kaggle contest semantics (from the lecture) Kaggle provides a labeled “train” set and an unlabeled “test” set. You can’t compute test accuracy yourself (labels are hidden). So you split Kaggle’s train into train + validation to tune choices. Public leaderboard vs private leaderboard: private is used for final ranking to reduce overfitting to the public test feedback. Cross-validation (kept, with clean wording) A common classical ML approach is \(k\)-fold cross-validation: split data into \(k\) parts, train on \(k-1\), validate on the remaining part, repeat \(k\) times, then summarize validation performance. The lecture notes it’s less common in deep learning due to large datasets and long training times. What is validation used for? Validation performance is how you choose hyperparameters: learning rate, optimizer type, feature subsets, model architecture, number of layers/units, activation choices, etc. You can’t just “gradient descent” on architecture, so you use trial-and-error guided by validation scores. Local learning-curve diagram: training vs validation score as training data grows. This supports the lecture’s point that validation helps diagnose bias/variance issues and whether more data would help. 12) Summary + Exercises What you should now understand (directly from lecture topics) What a linear classifier is: boundary \(w^\top x+b=0\), logit \(a=w^\top x+b\). How predictions work: sign test or sigmoid + threshold. Why logistic regression is linear + sigmoid, and why “logit” matters. Why classification uses cross-entropy (binary cross entropy for two classes). The PyTorch training loop pattern: zero_grad → forward → loss → backward → step. Why scaling (StandardScaler) and train/test split matter. How to compute accuracy correctly (including the boolean-mean trick). How to save/load models using state_dict. Why BCEWithLogitsLoss is numerically safer than sigmoid + BCELoss. Train/validation/test semantics, Kaggle workflow, and what validation is for (hyperparameter tuning). Exercises (from the lecture, made precise) During training, compute train accuracy and test accuracy each epoch. Store them in arrays and plot them later (or print every N epochs). Verify: loss ↓ tends to imply accuracy ↑. Switch from nn.Sequential(Linear,Sigmoid) + BCELoss to Linear + BCEWithLogitsLoss. Confirm you get similar accuracy, and change prediction rule to (logits > 0). Experiment with learning rates \(10^{-2}, 10^{-3}, 10^{-4}\) and compare convergence behavior and final test accuracy. Image sources: SVM hyperplanes, Sigmoid, Gradient descent, Overfitting, Bias-variance, Learning curves.
