text: One-page tutorial Trees → Ensembles Impurities explained This page is a complete, friendly walkthrough of what we discussed: how decision trees split using Gini impurity and Information Gain, how Bagging (Random Forests) works, how Boosting works, a deep step-by-step of AdaBoost, and what makes XGBoost fast and powerful — including what’s sequential vs what can be parallelized. Ensembles Decision Trees Gini & Information Gain A Split Example Bagging & Random Forest Boosting Overview AdaBoost Deep Dive Gradient Boosting & XGBoost Sequential vs Parallel Random Forest vs XGBoost Cheat Sheet 1) What is an Ensemble? Big Picture Ensemble learning means we combine many simple models to create one strong model. The individual models are called base learners (often decision trees). Why does combining models help? Reduce variance: if one model is “noisy”, averaging many models smooths errors. Reduce bias: if one model is “too simple”, sequential correction can capture complex patterns. Stability: ensembles are less sensitive to small changes in data. The two main families Bagging builds many models independently and averages/votes. Boosting builds models sequentially, each correcting earlier mistakes. Key theme: Bagging focuses on variance reduction. Boosting focuses on bias reduction (and can also reduce variance with regularization). Bagging (Random Forest style) Trees trained independently (can run in parallel) Tree 1 Tree 2 Tree 3 Tree 4 → Average / Vote Boosting (AdaBoost / XGBoost style) Trees trained sequentially (each corrects previous errors) Tree 1 → Tree 2 → Tree 3 → Add weighted contributions 2) Decision Trees: How They Learn Foundation What a split really is At a node, a decision tree searches for a question like: $\text{feature}_j \le \text{threshold}$ that divides the data into two groups (left/right). The tree wants the children nodes to be more “pure” than the parent — meaning each child contains mostly one class (for classification), or reduced spread (for regression). The tree’s “greedy” rule Trees usually use a greedy strategy: pick the best split right now, then repeat inside each child node. Greedy means: it doesn’t look ahead many steps; it chooses the best local improvement. That’s why trees are fast and intuitive — but also why a single tree can be unstable. Optional: what does “best” mean in practice? “Best” means the split that most reduces a chosen impurity measure (Gini/Entropy), or for modern boosting (XGBoost) the split that most reduces the training loss (objective). The spirit is identical: choose the split that creates the most useful separation. 3) Impurity Measures: Gini and Information Gain Splitting Criteria Impurity is a number that tells you how mixed the classes are inside a node. Lower impurity = node is closer to “all one class”. Gini Impurity (CART; very common) Idea: if a node is mostly one class, it’s pure; if it’s evenly mixed, it’s impure. $$\mathrm{Gini}(\text{node}) = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2$$ Binary example: if p = 0.7 and 0.3 → Gini = 1 − (0.49 + 0.09) = 0.42 Pure node: p = 1.0 and 0.0 → Gini = 0 Entropy & Information Gain (ID3/C4.5 style) Idea: entropy measures “surprise” or uncertainty in the class label. $$\mathrm{Entropy}(\text{node}) = -\sum_k p_k\,\log_2(p_k)$$ A split is chosen by maximizing Information Gain: $$IG = \mathrm{Entropy}(\text{parent}) - \left(\frac{N_L}{N}\,\mathrm{Entropy}(L) + \frac{N_R}{N}\,\mathrm{Entropy}(R)\right)$$ How the tree uses impurity: For each candidate split, compute the children impurities, take a weighted average, then choose the split with the largest impurity reduction. Gini reduction formula (same shape as Information Gain) $$\mathrm{GiniSplit} = \frac{N_L}{N}\,\mathrm{Gini}(L) + \frac{N_R}{N}\,\mathrm{Gini}(R) \qquad \mathrm{GiniGain} = \mathrm{Gini}(\text{parent}) - \mathrm{GiniSplit}$$ 4) A Concrete Split Example (Step-by-Step) Intuition Imagine a node contains 10 training samples for binary classification (Yes/No): 6 Yes, 4 No. Parent impurity (Gini) p(Yes)=0.6, p(No)=0.4 $$\mathrm{Gini}(\text{parent}) = 1 - (0.6^2 + 0.4^2) = 1 - (0.36 + 0.16) = 0.48$$ Try a candidate split Suppose we test: $\text{Age} \le 30$ Left child: 6 samples → 5 Yes, 1 No Right child: 4 samples → 1 Yes, 3 No Child impurities $$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Gini}(L) &= 1 - \left(\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^2\right) = 1 - \frac{26}{36} = \frac{10}{36} \approx 0.2778 \\ \mathrm{Gini}(R) &= 1 - \left(\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2\right) = 1 - \frac{10}{16} = \frac{6}{16} = 0.375 \end{aligned}$$ Weighted average & gain $$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{GiniSplit} &= \frac{6}{10}\cdot 0.2778 + \frac{4}{10}\cdot 0.375 = 0.3167 \\ \mathrm{GiniGain} &= 0.48 - 0.3167 = 0.1633 \end{aligned}$$ The tree would compare this gain with all other possible splits and choose the biggest. Core takeaway: every split is “just” computing impurity before and after. Ensembles (bagging/boosting) change how trees are trained, not the basic logic of splitting. 5) Bagging and Random Forests Variance Reduction Bagging in plain words Bagging trains many trees on slightly different versions of the dataset. Each tree makes its own prediction, then we combine predictions by averaging (regression) or voting (classification). Bagging is powerful because averaging many noisy models tends to cancel out random errors. How do we get “different versions” of the data? Using bootstrap sampling: sample N points from the training set with replacement. Some points repeat, some are missing. Each tree sees a different dataset → trees become less correlated. Less correlation → averaging works better. Random Forest: Bagging + Feature Randomness Random Forest adds one more trick: at each split, it considers only a random subset of features. This makes trees even more diverse. Diversity improves the power of averaging. What split criterion is used? Usually Gini impurity for classification (CART-style), and variance/MSE for regression. In Random Forest, trees are independent, so you can train trees in parallel very easily. Common Random Forest terms n_estimators: number of trees. max_features: how many features to try at each split. OOB (out-of-bag) error: estimate accuracy using samples left out of each bootstrap. 6) Boosting Overview Bias Reduction Boosting trains trees one after another. Each new tree is trained to correct mistakes made by the current ensemble. Boosting as “learning from errors” Suppose the first model is a little better than random. It will still make mistakes on “hard” examples. Boosting increases focus on those hard examples, so the next model improves where it matters. Over many rounds, the ensemble becomes very strong. Two major boosting styles AdaBoost: reweights training examples; uses a weighted vote. Gradient Boosting / XGBoost: minimizes a loss function using gradients; adds trees as corrections. Boosting is sequential at the “tree level”: tree (t) depends on results from tree (t−1). 7) AdaBoost (Adaptive Boosting) — Deep Dive Weights + Weak Learners AdaBoost is easiest to understand if you imagine the algorithm is “turning up the volume” on points it got wrong. Those points become more important in the next round. What AdaBoost uses as base learners Most commonly: decision stumps (depth-1 trees). A stump is one split like: $\text{feature}_j \le \text{threshold}$. A stump is weak by itself, but many stumps combined can form a complex boundary. AdaBoost is typically described for binary labels: $y \in \{-1, +1\}$. (It can be extended, but binary is the cleanest story.) AdaBoost algorithm (step-by-step) Initialize weights: w_i = 1/N for i=1..N For t = 1..T: 1) Train weak learner h_t(x) using weights w_i 2) Compute weighted error: ε_t = Σ w_i * 1[y_i ≠ h_t(x_i)] 3) Compute learner weight (importance): α_t = 0.5 * ln( (1 − ε_t) / ε_t ) 4) Update sample weights: w_i ← w_i * exp( −α_t * y_i * h_t(x_i) ) (misclassified points get upweighted) 5) Normalize weights so Σ w_i = 1 Final prediction: H(x) = sign( Σ α_t * h_t(x) ) What does α mean? αt is how much we trust the stump. If a stump has low error, it gets a larger α (more voting power). $$\alpha_t = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon_t}{\varepsilon_t}\right)$$ Why weights focus on mistakes If a point is misclassified, the term $\exp(-\alpha\, y\, h(x))$ becomes exp(+α), increasing its weight. Correct points shrink by exp(−α). This is why AdaBoost can be sensitive to noise/outliers: if an outlier is repeatedly misclassified, its weight can become huge. How splitting/impurity works inside AdaBoost AdaBoost changes the “importance” of each training sample via weights. That means when the stump chooses a split, it effectively uses a weighted impurity (or weighted classification error). Weighted Gini idea (intuition) In a normal node, class probability is “count of class / total count”. In AdaBoost, it becomes “sum of weights of class / sum of all weights”. $$p_k = \frac{\sum_i w_i\,\mathbf{1}[y_i = k]}{\sum_i w_i} \qquad \mathrm{WeightedGini} = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2$$ The stump still tries to reduce impurity — but now mistakes have larger weights, so splits that fix mistakes become more attractive. Mini numeric example (why a weak learner can get high α) If ε = 0.2 (20% weighted error), then: $$\alpha = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{0.8}{0.2}\right) = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(4) \approx 0.693$$ That’s a strong positive weight, meaning the stump gets a meaningful vote. If ε approaches 0.5, α approaches 0 (weak vote). 8) Gradient Boosting and XGBoost Loss Optimization Gradient Boosting generalizes boosting by saying: “Let’s minimize a loss function (objective) by adding trees that move us in the best direction.” Gradient Boosting idea in simple steps Start with a simple prediction (like the average). Compute how wrong you are (residuals / gradients). Train a small tree to predict those errors. Add the tree (scaled by a learning rate) to improve predictions. Repeat. Additive model view: $$\hat{y}^{(t)}(x) = \hat{y}^{(t-1)}(x) + \eta\, f_t(x)$$ Here η is the learning rate (shrinkage). Smaller η usually needs more trees but improves generalization. Regression vs classification nuance: for squared-error regression, the “errors” are literal residuals. For logistic loss and other objectives, boosting fits negative gradients (pseudo-residuals), not raw label errors. What makes XGBoost special? Second-order optimization Uses gradients (g) and Hessians (h) to choose better splits. More accurate split scoring Regularization Penalizes complex trees to reduce overfitting. (Think: don’t let the model become “too wiggly”.) Better generalization Engineering for speed Histogram splits, cache efficiency, parallel computation, GPU support, distributed training. Much faster on large data How does XGBoost decide splits (vs Gini/Entropy)? Random Forest uses impurity reduction (Gini/Entropy). XGBoost uses objective reduction (loss + regularization). But conceptually, both are choosing the split that gives the “best improvement”. Split “gain” intuition (no heavy math) For a candidate split, XGBoost summarizes the node using two numbers: the sum of gradients (G) and sum of Hessians (H) in that node. It estimates how much the regularized objective improves if we split into left and right. $$\mathrm{Gain} = \frac{1}{2}\left[ \frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda} - \frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda} \right] - \gamma$$ Where λ is L2 regularization on leaf weights and γ is a penalty for creating a new split (discouraging unnecessary splits). Parallel-friendly split finding (histograms) XGBoost often uses a histogram algorithm: Bucket each feature into bins (like 256 bins). Accumulate gradient/Hessian sums per bin. Scan bins to find the best threshold. This makes split-finding fast and parallelizable across features and bins. 9) Sequential vs Parallel in Boosting (XGBoost) Important Detail Boosting is sequential across trees because tree t needs the gradients/residuals from the current model (trees 1..t−1). So you can’t train all trees at once. So how can XGBoost still be fast? Because XGBoost parallelizes within each boosting round. Think: “We can’t write Chapter 5 before Chapter 4, but many people can work in parallel on Chapter 4.” What can be parallelized inside a round? Gradient & Hessian computation per data point (independent operations). Split search across features (each feature can be evaluated separately). Histogram building (bin counts/aggregations can be parallelized). Node processing at the same depth (level-wise growth enables parallel node expansion). Distributed / multi-GPU idea Each worker computes local gradient statistics. Workers do a reduce (sum) to combine stats. Then the best split is chosen globally. Trees stay sequential, but the expensive computations inside each tree are distributed. What XGBoost does NOT parallelize Training tree (t+1) before finishing tree (t) Skipping gradient dependency (that would break boosting) 10) Random Forest vs XGBoost Practical Comparison Aspect Random Forest (Bagging) XGBoost (Boosting) Training style Independent trees (parallel) Sequential trees (each corrects errors) Main benefit Reduces variance, very robust Reduces bias strongly, often best accuracy Split criterion Gini / Entropy (classification) or MSE (regression) Objective gain using gradients & Hessians + regularization Noise sensitivity Usually more tolerant More sensitive; needs regularization/tuning Hyperparameters Fewer critical knobs More knobs; more control (and more tuning) Parallelism Across trees Within each tree / round (features, bins, nodes) Rule of thumb: If you want a strong baseline with little tuning, Random Forest is great. If you want maximum performance on tabular data and can tune/regularize, XGBoost often wins. 11) Quick Cheat Sheet Remember Fast Bagging (Random Forest) Goal: reduce variance. How: bootstrap samples + random feature subsets. Combine: vote / average. Splits: Gini/Entropy (classification). Parallel: yes, across trees. Boosting (AdaBoost / XGBoost) Goal: reduce bias by fixing errors. AdaBoost: reweight samples; weighted vote with α. Gradient Boosting: fit residuals/gradients; add trees. XGBoost: optimized objective + regularization + fast splits. Parallel: not across trees, but inside each round. If you only remember one thing: Trees split by reducing “badness” (impurity or loss). Bagging improves stability by averaging many independent trees. Boosting improves accuracy by sequentially correcting mistakes. Jump back to the top: ↑ This chapter closes the classical tabular-model path and prepares the transition to learned representations in Part V.

Feed‑forward networks (concepts, then training/debugging), CNNs (theory then PyTorch), forecasting, autoregressive baselines, RNNs with a step-by-step translation example, then Transformers & attention as the bridge from cross-attention to self-attention and GPT-style generation, followed by modern LLM alignment beyond DPO. How the chapters cluster FFN track — Chapters 1, 2 (Chapter 3 is the single-chapter reference version). CNN track — Chapters 4, 5, 6; Chapter 7 is the dropout/train-eval deep dive that expands the short dropout section in Chapter 6. The animated RNN companion gives a live narrated walkthrough before the formal RNN chapter. LLM track — Chapters 11, 12, 13: attention mechanics, decoder-only generation, fine-tuning, and alignment. If you read 1 and 2 in order, skip Chapter 3 — it repeats the same material. Use it as a single‑document reference if you ever want one long FFN article instead of the split lecture form. Sequence forecasting Ch. 8 Ch. 9 implements the AR baseline, Ch. 10 moves from recurrent hidden state into GRU/LSTM memory and encoder-decoder translation, and Ch. 11 turns that bridge into cross-attention, self-attention, and causal GPT generation. LLM adaptation and alignment Ch. 12 and Ch. 13 Ch. 12 owns SFT/PEFT/fine-tuning and introduces DPO/RLHF. Ch. 13 owns the modern ORPO/KTO/GRPO/RLAIF comparison. description: A practical tutorial built from the lecture transcript: why neural networks, how they compute, and how to train them (with PyTorch).
text: A practical tutorial built from the lecture transcript: why neural networks, how they compute, and how to train them (with PyTorch). ANN ≈ “artificial neurons” FFN = feed-forward network Forward propagation Activations: sigmoid / tanh / ReLU Softmax for multiclass Mini-batch gradient descent MNIST example Why neural nets? From a neuron to a network Forward propagation equations Activation functions Vanishing gradients Softmax & tasks Images as tensors MNIST FFN in PyTorch Sources & credits 1) Start with “Why?” and “How?” The motivation in the lecture is simple: the brain is a physical system of neurons that exchange signals. If a neuron can be approximated as a computation, then connecting many of them (in a simulation) might produce useful behavior—what we call artificial intelligence. Key idea: neural networks are powerful because they can learn hierarchies of features: simple patterns in early layers (edges), more meaningful parts in middle layers (eyes/noses), and full concepts later (faces). This “stacking” of representation is why the field is called deep learning. If you want an intuition playground, the lecture mentions TensorFlow Playground: https://playground.tensorflow.org (try changing layers/units and watch non-linear boundaries appear). 2) From logistic regression to a “neuron” A single artificial neuron is basically a linear model plus a nonlinearity. For an input vector \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\): \[ z = w^\top x + b \] \[ a = \sigma(z) \] Here \(w\) are weights, \(b\) is a bias, \(z\) is the pre-activation, and \(a\) is the activated output. In binary classification, \(\sigma\) (sigmoid) turns \(z\) into a value in \((0,1)\), interpretable as a probability. Sigmoid curve (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: File:Sigmoid-function.svg 3) Feed-forward networks: architecture & forward propagation A feed-forward neural network arranges neurons in layers, with connections flowing from input → hidden layers → output. (If connections loop back to earlier layers, that’s typically a recurrent design; the transcript contrasts these.) Vectorized layer equation For layer \(\ell\), we typically use: \[ z^{(\ell)} = W^{(\ell)} a^{(\ell-1)} + b^{(\ell)} \] \[ a^{(\ell)} = g^{(\ell)}\!\left(z^{(\ell)}\right) \] This is the same idea as the single neuron, but generalized: \(W^{(\ell)}\) is a matrix of weights, \(b^{(\ell)}\) is a bias vector, and \(g^{(\ell)}\) is an activation function applied elementwise (except for some output activations like softmax). What changes vs. linear/logistic regression? Nothing fundamental—just multiple linear transforms chained with nonlinearities. Why does that help? Without nonlinearities, stacked linear layers collapse into a single linear layer. How to read it? Think “feature → feature → feature → … → final prediction”. A 2-layer example (hidden layer + output layer) \[ a^{(1)} = g\!\left(W^{(1)}x + b^{(1)}\right) \] \[ \hat{y} = \text{(output activation)}\!\left(W^{(2)}a^{(1)} + b^{(2)}\right) \] 4) Activation functions (why they matter) The lecture emphasizes: activations are what give neural networks the ability to learn non-linear decision boundaries. Without them, you get only linear separators. Sigmoid \[ \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} \] Good for binary outputs, but can be problematic in deep networks due to small derivatives. Tanh (hyperbolic tangent) \[ \tanh(z)=\frac{e^z-e^{-z}}{e^z+e^{-z}} \] Similar “S-shape” to sigmoid, but centered around 0 (outputs in \((-1,1)\)), which often helps internal scaling. Tanh curve (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: File:Hyperbolic_Tangent.svg ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) \[ \mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z) \] The lecture’s storyline: researchers moved from “beautiful smooth” activations (sigmoid/tanh) toward ReLU because it trains deep networks more reliably in practice. ReLU “hockey stick” (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: Rectifier (neural networks) and image URL from upload.wikimedia.org. Pragmatic ML takeaway (from the transcript): experimentation beats philosophy. If you have a computer, run experiments instead of guessing outcomes in your head. 5) The vanishing gradient problem (and why ReLU helped) When training with backpropagation, gradients for earlier layers are products of many derivatives (chain rule). If these derivatives are often small, multiplying them repeatedly can make the gradient shrink toward zero for early layers—so those layers barely learn. Sigmoid derivative is small most of the time \[ \sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\bigl(1-\sigma(z)\bigr) \] The derivative peaks at \(0.25\). Repeated multiplication like \((0.25)^5 \approx 0.0009766\) shrinks fast. Sigmoid vs. sigmoid derivative (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: File:Sigmoid-derivative.png A related visualization used in discussions of vanishing gradients Diagram referenced in vanishing-gradient discussions (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: File:One-neuron recurrent network bifurcation diagram.png Historically (as mentioned in the lecture), one workaround was layer-wise pretraining (e.g., Hinton’s earlier-era approaches). Modern practice usually relies on better activations (ReLU-family), initialization, normalization, and optimizers. 6) Multiclass classification: Softmax + Cross-Entropy For \(K\) classes, the output layer produces a vector of logits \(z \in \mathbb{R}^K\). We convert logits into a probability distribution with softmax: \[ \mathrm{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}} \] This guarantees probabilities are positive and sum to 1. In practice, we usually do not apply softmax explicitly during training; we use a numerically-stable loss that combines softmax with cross-entropy. Softmax illustration (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: File:Softmax.svg Softmax illustration (English) (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: File:Softmax_en.svg Three common tasks ↔ output activations Regression: identity output (no activation): \(\hat{y}=z\) Binary classification: sigmoid output: \(\hat{y}=\sigma(z)\) Multiclass classification: softmax output: \(\hat{y}=\mathrm{softmax}(z)\) The lecture also notes: softmax can handle binary classification too (with \(K=2\)), but it’s redundant because the two probabilities always sum to 1. 7) Images as tensors (and why we “flatten” for a basic FFN) Computers store images as arrays. A color image (RGB) is typically a tensor of shape: \[ \text{image} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}, \quad C=3 \] Each pixel channel is often quantized into 256 levels (0–255). For neural networks, it’s common to scale to \([0,1]\). Grayscale is simpler MNIST digits are grayscale, so each image is \(28 \times 28\) (no RGB channels). Flattening A fully-connected FFN expects vectors. Flattening turns a \(28\times 28\) image into a vector of length \(784\): \[ x \in \mathbb{R}^{28\times 28} \;\;\longrightarrow\;\; \mathrm{vec}(x)\in \mathbb{R}^{784} \] MNIST sample digits (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: File:MnistExamples.png t-SNE embedding of MNIST (Wikimedia Commons). Source page: File:T-SNE Embedding of MNIST.png 8) MNIST feed-forward network in PyTorch (with mini-batches) The lecture’s example: MNIST has 10 classes (digits 0–9), so it’s multiclass classification. A simple FFN can look like: 784 → 128 → 10, with ReLU in the hidden layer. Model equations (as described) \[ a^{(1)} = \mathrm{ReLU}(W^{(1)}x + b^{(1)}) \] \[ z^{(2)} = W^{(2)}a^{(1)} + b^{(2)} \] \[ \hat{y} = \mathrm{softmax}(z^{(2)}) \quad \text{(conceptually; training uses cross-entropy)} \] Mini-batch gradient descent: instead of computing gradients over the entire dataset at once, we compute them on small batches. PyTorch’s DataLoader handles batching for you. PyTorch code (end-to-end) This follows the transcript’s steps: load MNIST, flatten + scale, build FFN, train with batches, evaluate, and inspect mistakes. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F from torch.utils.data import DataLoader from torchvision import datasets, transforms # 1) Data: MNIST (grayscale 28x28) # - ToTensor() scales uint8 [0,255] -> float [0,1] # - We'll flatten in the training loop (or use transforms.Lambda) transform = transforms.ToTensor() train_ds = datasets.MNIST(root="data", train=True, download=True, transform=transform) test_ds = datasets.MNIST(root="data", train=False, download=True, transform=transform) train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, num_workers=2, pin_memory=True) test_loader = DataLoader(test_ds, batch_size=256, shuffle=False, num_workers=2, pin_memory=True) device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") # 2) Model: 784 -> 128 -> 10 class FFN(nn.Module): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(28*28, 128) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(128, 10) def forward(self, x): # x: (B, 1, 28, 28) -> flatten to (B, 784) x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) x = F.relu(self.fc1(x)) logits = self.fc2(x) # raw scores (logits) return logits model = FFN().to(device) # 3) Training setup # CrossEntropyLoss = LogSoftmax + NLLLoss (numerically stable) criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss() optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1) def accuracy_from_logits(logits, y): preds = logits.argmax(dim=1) return (preds == y).float().mean().item() # 4) Train loop (mini-batch gradient descent) def train_one_epoch(): model.train() total_loss = 0.0 total_acc = 0.0 n_batches = 0 for x, y in train_loader: x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) optimizer.zero_grad() logits = model(x) loss = criterion(logits, y) loss.backward() optimizer.step() total_loss += loss.item() total_acc += accuracy_from_logits(logits, y) n_batches += 1 return total_loss / n_batches, total_acc / n_batches @torch.no_grad() def evaluate(): model.eval() total_loss = 0.0 total_acc = 0.0 n_batches = 0 for x, y in test_loader: x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) logits = model(x) loss = criterion(logits, y) total_loss += loss.item() total_acc += accuracy_from_logits(logits, y) n_batches += 1 return total_loss / n_batches, total_acc / n_batches # 5) Run training for epoch in range(1, 6): tr_loss, tr_acc = train_one_epoch() te_loss, te_acc = evaluate() print(f"epoch {epoch:02d} | train loss {tr_loss:.4f} acc {tr_acc:.4f} | test loss {te_loss:.4f} acc {te_acc:.4f}") # 6) Inspect mistakes (what the model gets wrong) @torch.no_grad() def collect_mistakes(max_items=24): model.eval() mistakes = [] for x, y in test_loader: x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) logits = model(x) preds = logits.argmax(dim=1) wrong_mask = preds != y if wrong_mask.any(): xw = x[wrong_mask].cpu() yw = y[wrong_mask].cpu() pw = preds[wrong_mask].cpu() for i in range(xw.size(0)): mistakes.append((xw[i], int(yw[i]), int(pw[i]))) if len(mistakes) >= max_items: return mistakes return mistakes mistakes = collect_mistakes() print("Collected mistakes:", len(mistakes)) Plotting training curves You can compare your runs to standard learning-curve discussions and visualizations. For example, compare whether training loss decreases smoothly, validation loss follows it, or validation loss starts rising while training loss keeps falling. You can also log your own metrics and view them in TensorBoard, Weights & Biases, or another dashboard. Common gotcha: If you use nn.CrossEntropyLoss(), do not apply softmax in your model forward pass. Cross-entropy expects raw logits. Probability nuance: softmax outputs non-negative values that sum to 1, so they are convenient class probabilities. They are not automatically well calibrated. A model can be 99% confident and still be wrong. Calibration is a separate evaluation topic, usually checked with reliability diagrams, expected calibration error, or held-out validation data. 3) Training loop patterns that scale
4) Accuracy when your data arrives in batches
5) Logits vs probabilities: why argmax is enough for predictions

description: Training at scale with mini-batches, evaluation (accuracy + confusion matrix), and a synthetic regression example for visual intuition.
text:
Training at scale with mini-batches, evaluation (accuracy + confusion matrix), and a synthetic regression example for visual intuition. Mini-batch gradient descent Argmax over logits Accuracy over DataLoader GPU device placement Confusion matrix + error analysis Synthetic data + surface fitting Mini-batches & why they work Data pipeline & transforms Training loop patterns Accuracy with batches Logits, softmax, argmax GPU: keeping tensors on one device Confusion matrix & mistakes Synthetic regression surface Hyperparameter tuning mindset Online plots used 1) Mini-batches: the practical way to train on large datasets Most training objectives are averages over a dataset. If your dataset has \(N\) samples and per-sample loss \(\ell_i(	heta)\), the empirical risk is: \[ L(	heta) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i(	heta) \] Computing \(
abla_	heta L(	heta)\) over all \(N\) samples every step is expensive. Instead, we use a mini-batch \(B\) (a small random subset) and approximate the loss and gradient: \[ \widehat{L}_B(	heta) =  rac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i\in B}\ell_i(	heta), \quad 
abla_	heta \widehat{L}_B(	heta) \approx 
abla_	heta L(	heta) \] Intuition: if batches are shuffled, each batch is a “representative sample” of the dataset. Over many steps, you still see the whole dataset, but each update is much cheaper. Optimizer behavior (Wikimedia Commons): Optimizer_Animations.gif 2) Data pipeline: datasets, transforms, and DataLoader A clean PyTorch pipeline usually has three parts: Dataset: knows how to fetch one sample \((x,y)\) Transform(s): preprocessing applied per sample DataLoader: batching, shuffling, parallel loading MNIST: why values become 0–1 only when transformed MNIST is stored as 8-bit integers (0–255). transforms.ToTensor() converts to float and scales to \([0,1]\). If you inspect raw stored tensors, you’ll see 0–255. If you iterate through the DataLoader with the transform, you’ll see 0–1. python • verify raw vs transformed MNIST ranges from torchvision import datasets, transforms train_raw = datasets.MNIST(root="data", train=True, download=True, transform=None) print("raw dtype:", train_raw.data.dtype) print("raw min/max:", int(train_raw.data.min()), int(train_raw.data.max())) # typically 0..255 train_tf = datasets.MNIST(root="data", train=True, download=True, transform=transforms.ToTensor()) x0, y0 = train_tf[0] print("transformed dtype:", x0.dtype) print("transformed min/max:", float(x0.min()), float(x0.max())) # typically 0..1 Rule of thumb: keep preprocessing inside the Dataset via transform=.... That way every training/eval pass uses the same consistent inputs. 3) Training loop patterns that scale A robust training loop separates: training mode (updates parameters) vs evaluation mode (no updates) metrics computed batch-by-batch device transfers done once per batch One update step on a batch For a batch \((x_B, y_B)\), gradient descent performs: \[ 	heta \leftarrow 	heta - \eta 
abla_	heta \widehat{L}_B(	heta) \] Canonical PyTorch “inner loop” python • canonical mini-batch update step model.train() # enables train-time behavior (e.g., dropout/bn) for x, y in train_loader: x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) optimizer.zero_grad() # clear old gradients logits = model(x) # forward pass loss = criterion(logits, y) loss.backward() # compute gradients optimizer.step() # update parameters Epoch loss: average over batches If you collect per-batch losses \(\{\widehat{L}_{B_k}\}\) in one epoch, a common summary is the mean: \[ 	ext{epoch\_loss} =  rac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K \widehat{L}_{B_k} \] This is a practical proxy for “how training is going” without doing a second full pass just to re-measure loss. 4) Accuracy when your data arrives in batches When data comes via a DataLoader, you usually can’t compute accuracy in one shot. The simple fix is to accumulate counts. \[ 	ext{accuracy} =  rac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}\{\hat{y}_i = y_i\}}{N} \] With batches, you compute “correct in this batch” and “batch size”, then add them up. python • batched accuracy over a DataLoader @torch.no_grad() def accuracy_loader(model, loader, device): model.eval() correct = 0 total = 0 for x, y in loader: x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) logits = model(x) pred = logits.argmax(dim=1) # class index correct += (pred == y).sum().item() total += y.numel() return correct / total Tip: use @torch.no_grad() in evaluation to reduce memory usage and speed things up. 5) Logits vs probabilities: why argmax is enough for predictions Many classification models output logits \(z \in \mathbb{R}^K\). Softmax converts logits into probabilities: \[ \mathrm{softmax}(z)_i =  rac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}} \] For choosing the predicted class, you almost never need the probabilities. You only need: \[ \hat{y} = \arg\max_i z_i \] Key fact: argmax(softmax(z)) == argmax(z). Exponentials preserve ordering and the denominator is shared. Softmax illustration (Wikimedia Commons): Softmax_en.svg PyTorch: get indices (classes) from logits python • logits → predicted class indices logits = model(x) # shape: (B, K) pred = torch.argmax(logits, dim=1) # shape: (B,) If you want probabilities for interpretability (e.g., confidence), you can still compute: probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1). For training with nn.CrossEntropyLoss, keep the model output as logits. 6) GPU usage: avoid “tensors on different devices” errors In PyTorch, your model parameters live on a device (CPU or GPU). Your data must be on the same device before you do operations between them. Do: • model.to(device) • x.to(device), y.to(device) each batch Don’t: • keep model on GPU and data on CPU (or vice versa) • mix tensors across devices in one computation python • device selection + consistent placement device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") model = model.to(device) for x, y in train_loader: x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) logits = model(x) ... 7) Debugging classification: confusion matrix + misclassified samples Overall accuracy hides which classes are being confused. A confusion matrix breaks errors down by class. For a \(K\)-class problem, it’s a \(K 	imes K\) table where entry \((i,j)\) counts: “true label \(i\) predicted as \(j\)”. Confusion matrix example (Wikimedia Commons): Confusion_matrix.png Collect predictions for a full DataLoader pass python • gather all predictions + labels @torch.no_grad() def collect_preds(model, loader, device): model.eval() all_pred = [] all_y = [] for x, y in loader: x = x.to(device) logits = model(x) pred = logits.argmax(dim=1).cpu() all_pred.append(pred) all_y.append(y.cpu()) return torch.cat(all_y), torch.cat(all_pred) Compute confusion matrix (two options) Option A: pure PyTorch (no extra deps) python • confusion matrix in pure torch def confusion_matrix_torch(y_true, y_pred, num_classes): cm = torch.zeros((num_classes, num_classes), dtype=torch.int64) for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred): cm[t, p] += 1 return cm y_true, y_pred = collect_preds(model, test_loader, device) cm = confusion_matrix_torch(y_true, y_pred, num_classes=10) print(cm) Option B: scikit-learn (convenient) python • confusion matrix via scikit-learn # pip install scikit-learn from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix y_true, y_pred = collect_preds(model, test_loader, device) cm = confusion_matrix(y_true.numpy(), y_pred.numpy(), labels=list(range(10))) print(cm) Find and visualize misclassified samples Once you know common confusions, actually look at examples. (The code below generates plots when you run it.) python • extract misclassified MNIST examples + plot a grid import matplotlib.pyplot as plt @torch.no_grad() def get_misclassified(model, loader, device, max_items=25): model.eval() items = [] for x, y in loader: x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) logits = model(x) pred = logits.argmax(dim=1) wrong = pred != y if wrong.any(): xw = x[wrong].cpu() yw = y[wrong].cpu() pw = pred[wrong].cpu() for i in range(xw.size(0)): items.append((xw[i], int(yw[i]), int(pw[i]))) if len(items) >= max_items: return items return items mis = get_misclassified(model, test_loader, device, max_items=16) # Plot (runs locally; not generated in this HTML) fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 4, figsize=(6, 6)) for ax, (img, y, p) in zip(axes.ravel(), mis): ax.imshow(img.squeeze(0), cmap="gray") ax.set_title(f"true={y}, pred={p}", fontsize=9) ax.axis("off") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() 8) Synthetic regression: fit a non-linear surface you can visualize Classification isn’t the only job for feed-forward nets. For regression, the output layer is typically identity (no activation), and the loss is often mean squared error (MSE). Define a “bumpy” 2D function We’ll sample \(x \in \mathbb{R}^2\) uniformly in a box and define targets: \[ y = \cos(2x_1) + \cos(3x_2) \] Example 3D surface plot (Wikimedia Commons): 3-D_surface_plot.jpg Generate data + 3D scatter (run locally) python • synthetic dataset + 3D scatter import numpy as np import torch import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D # noqa: F401 (needed for 3D) # Reproducibility torch.manual_seed(0) np.random.seed(0) N = 5000 x = (torch.rand(N, 2) * 6.0) - 3.0 # uniform in [-3, 3]^2 y = torch.cos(2.0 * x[:, 0]) + torch.cos(3.0 * x[:, 1]) y = y.unsqueeze(1) # shape (N, 1) # 3D scatter (generated when you run this) fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5)) ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d") ax.scatter(x[:,0].numpy(), x[:,1].numpy(), y[:,0].numpy(), s=3) ax.set_xlabel("x1"); ax.set_ylabel("x2"); ax.set_zlabel("y") plt.show() Model: 2 → 128 → 1 (ReLU hidden, identity output) python • regression FFN + training loop import torch.nn as nn from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") ds = TensorDataset(x, y) loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=256, shuffle=True) model = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1), ).to(device) criterion = nn.MSELoss() optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-2) def train_epochs(epochs=50): model.train() history = [] for ep in range(epochs): losses = [] for xb, yb in loader: xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device) optimizer.zero_grad() pred = model(xb) loss = criterion(pred, yb) loss.backward() optimizer.step() losses.append(loss.item()) history.append(float(np.mean(losses))) if (ep + 1) % 10 == 0: print(f"epoch {ep+1:03d} | mse {history[-1]:.6f}") return history loss_hist = train_epochs(epochs=60) Predict on a grid: meshgrid → model → reshape → surface To draw a smooth surface, you evaluate the model on a grid of \((x_1, x_2)\) points. The key is reshaping: grids are 2D, the model wants a 2-column matrix, and the output must be reshaped back to the grid. python • meshgrid predictions + 3D surface plot (run locally) @torch.no_grad() def plot_surface(model, lim=3.0, steps=80): model.eval() xs = torch.linspace(-lim, lim, steps) ys = torch.linspace(-lim, lim, steps) X, Y = torch.meshgrid(xs, ys, indexing="ij") # shapes (steps, steps) grid = torch.stack([X.reshape(-1), Y.reshape(-1)], dim=1).to(device) # (steps*steps, 2) Z = model(grid).reshape(steps, steps).cpu() # Plot import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D # noqa: F401 fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5)) ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d") ax.plot_surface(X.numpy(), Y.numpy(), Z.numpy(), linewidth=0, antialiased=True) ax.set_xlabel("x1"); ax.set_ylabel("x2"); ax.set_zlabel("pred y") plt.show() plot_surface(model) What you’re checking visually: does the learned surface match the “bumpy” cosine structure? If not, try adjusting learning rate, epochs, batch size, or hidden width. 9) Hyperparameters: a practical experimentation workflow Hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, hidden width, optimizer choice) don’t come with universal rules that always win. A reliable workflow is: Start reasonable (common defaults: Adam or SGD, moderate LR, moderate batch size) Confirm learning (loss decreases; accuracy increases) Search locally (try a small grid around current settings) Use evidence (plots/metrics) to decide next changes Minimal grid-search skeleton python • tiny hyperparameter sweep skeleton def run_experiment(lr, hidden, epochs=3): model = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(28*28, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, 10), ).to(device) opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr) crit = nn.CrossEntropyLoss() for _ in range(epochs): model.train() for x, y in train_loader: x = x.view(x.size(0), -1).to(device) y = y.to(device) opt.zero_grad() logits = model(x) loss = crit(logits, y) loss.backward() opt.step() acc = accuracy_loader(model, test_loader, device) return acc for lr in [0.3, 0.1, 0.03]: for hidden in [64, 128, 256]: acc = run_experiment(lr=lr, hidden=hidden, epochs=2) print(f"lr={lr:<5} hidden={hidden:<4} -> test acc {acc:.4f}") Goal: don’t hunt for mystical “best” defaults—build a habit of quick, disciplined experiments. Local visuals and source credits Optimizer animation (SGD variants): Optimizer_Animations.gif Softmax illustration: Softmax_en.svg Confusion matrix example: Confusion_matrix.png 3D surface plot example: 3-D_surface_plot.jpg This page serves displayed images from local assets, with source credits retained where applicable. Code blocks are formatted by the shared book styling and include copy buttons. When you run the plotting code locally, it will generate the visualizations (this HTML itself does not generate plots).

description: A student-friendly tutorial that reconstructs the lecture ideas: why neural networks exist, how they generalize linear models, why activation functions matter, how backpropagation works (chain rule!), and how this con...
text: A student-friendly tutorial that reconstructs the lecture ideas: why neural networks exist, how they generalize linear models, why activation functions matter, how backpropagation works (chain rule!), and how this connects to practical PyTorch code for multiclass image classification. Optional reference edition This chapter presents the concepts from Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 into one long reference article. If you are reading the teaching path in order, treat this as a recap/reference rather than a separate required lesson. Task types: regression · binary class · multiclass class Core math: logits · sigmoid · softmax · cross-entropy · chain rule Practical: batching · DataLoader · GPU device · confusion matrix Theme: readable light-mode, VS Code-ish code colors Contents Why & How: “can we build a brain?” From logistic regression to a neuron From one neuron to layers to deep networks Neural nets as geometry solvers: linear vs nonlinear boundaries Activation functions: sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, and friends How models learn: gradients, chain rule, backprop, vanishing gradients Three tasks & their final-layer activations (incl. multiclass) Multiclass classification: softmax + cross-entropy (and numerical stability) How images are represented (RGB, grayscale, quantization, flattening) MNIST tutorial: DataLoader, mini-batches, GPU, accuracy, confusion matrix Synthetic regression example (why visualization matters) Hyperparameters & the “experimentation, not philosophy” rule Why? How? Why this topic is so interesting The phrase artificial neural network comes from a big idea: biological brains are made of neurons that communicate using electrical and chemical signals. Once you accept that a brain is a physical information-processing system, a natural question appears: The motivating question If a brain is “a kind of computer”, can we simulate networks of neurons on a computer to create artificial intelligence? Of course this is a simplification—real brains are messy: many kinds of neurons, many regions, and connections that crisscross in complex ways. But for a computational model, we start with a deliberately simplified neuron, connect many of them, and see what the system can learn. Two network “wiring” patterns Feedforward: information flows layer by layer from input to output. Recurrent / feedback: connections go from a later layer back to an earlier layer (a “loop”). This tutorial focuses on feedforward networks (also called “MLPs”). A compact overview of classic and modern activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, leaky ReLU, …). Source: Wikimedia Commons. From logistic regression to a “neuron” The lecture connects a single logistic regression model to a simplified neuron: the model computes a weighted sum, adds a bias (threshold), then passes it through a squashing nonlinearity (sigmoid) and finally makes a binary decision. Single neuron (binary classification) $$a = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b \quad\text{(activation / logit)}$$ $$\hat{p} = \sigma(a) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-a}} \quad\text{(probability of class 1)}$$ $$\hat{y} = \mathbb{1}[\hat{p} \ge 0.5] \quad\text{(predict 1 if prob ≥ 0.5)}$$ Interpretation $\mathbf{w}$ controls how strongly each input feature influences the decision. $b$ shifts the decision threshold. In biology, neurons sum incoming signals through synapses. Some synapses are “strong” (large magnitude weight), others “weak” (small weight). Some are excitatory (positive weight), others inhibitory (negative weight). A neuron either “fires” or does not (an all-or-nothing spike), which resembles a binary decision. This is an analogy, not a claim that artificial neurons model biology faithfully. The useful engineering abstraction is: weighted inputs + bias + nonlinearity + learnable parameters. The logistic sigmoid $\sigma(x)$. Source: Wikimedia Commons. From one neuron to layers to deep networks One neuron can only compute one feature. The next step is to use many neurons in parallel. A whole layer can learn many different features from the same input. One hidden layer (vectorized) $$\mathbf{a}^{(1)} = \mathbf{W}^{(1)}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{(1)}$$ $$\mathbf{z}^{(1)} = \phi\!\left(\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\right) \quad\text{(apply activation element-wise)}$$ $$\mathbf{a}^{(2)} = \mathbf{W}^{(2)}\mathbf{z}^{(1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(2)}$$ Notation note: the lecture uses superscripts $(1),(2),\dots,(L)$ for layer index, and often uses $L$ for the total number of layers. Why matrices? With multiple neurons per layer, writing sums like $w_1x_1 + \dots + w_Dx_D$ becomes unreadable. Matrices let us compute all neurons’ weighted sums efficiently in one operation. A helpful perspective: “a sequence of feature transformations” A modern way to think about a deep network: each layer transforms the representation (features) into a new representation. Early layers learn simple patterns; later layers can combine them into more complex ones. This “feature hierarchy” is part of why the field is called deep learning. Classic example (as discussed) In face recognition visualizations: early layers resemble edge detectors, mid layers detect parts (eyes, nose, mouth), and later layers represent entire faces. Neural nets as geometry solvers: why linear models aren’t enough The lecture repeatedly emphasizes: machine learning is a geometry problem. A linear classifier draws a hyperplane; points on different sides get different labels. But many real problems require curved decision boundaries. Two ways to make models “more powerful” Add more input features (feature engineering). Add nonlinearity + layers (neural networks) to create curved boundaries automatically. Deep learning reduces the need for manual feature engineering—especially for unstructured data like images, audio, and text. If you remove activation functions, a deep “network” collapses into a linear map (a key lecture point): composing linear functions yields another linear function. Nonlinear activations are what make deep nets able to model more complex geometry. Activation functions: sigmoid → tanh → ReLU (and why) Sigmoid Sigmoid maps real numbers to $(0,1)$. It is natural for binary outputs interpreted as probabilities. But hidden layers want their activations to be well-behaved for learning. Tanh (hyperbolic tangent) Tanh is “sigmoid-like” but centered around $0$, producing outputs in $(-1,1)$. This better matches the idea of keeping layer inputs roughly centered (the lecture connects this to standardization). Key formulas $$\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$$ $$\tanh(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}$$ Exercise idea from the lecture: show $\tanh$ is a scaled/shifted version of sigmoid. ReLU and modern activations Sigmoid/tanh are smooth, but deep networks historically struggled with them because of vanishing gradients. ReLU is not perfectly smooth at $0$, but empirically trains deep nets much better. ReLU $$\mathrm{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)$$ The lecture mentions common variants: Leaky ReLU (small slope for $x<0$), ELU, and Softplus. In practice, many people still use ReLU as a strong default. $\tanh(x)$ plot. Source: Wikimedia Commons. ReLU “hockey stick” shape. Source: Wikimedia Commons. How models learn: gradients, chain rule, backprop, and vanishing gradients Training is still “minimize a loss with gradient descent,” but neural networks are compositions of many functions. Backpropagation is essentially the chain rule applied efficiently. Gradient descent (high level) Parameter update $$\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}$$ $\eta$ is the learning rate (a hyperparameter). Too large: divergence. Too small: painfully slow. Chain rule (the key math for backprop) If $y = f(g(x))$, then $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{dg}\cdot \frac{dg}{dx}.$$ For deeper compositions $f_1(f_2(\dots f_L(x)\dots))$ you multiply many derivatives. This multiplication is exactly what can cause gradients to shrink (vanish). Vanishing gradients (as described) For sigmoid, the derivative is at most $0.25$. Multiplying numbers ≤ $0.25$ many times makes the result tiny, so early layers receive almost no learning signal. Sigmoid derivative and the “0.25” fact $$\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)\left(1-\sigma(x)\right) \le 0.25$$ $$0.25^5 \approx 0.00098,\qquad 0.1^5 = 0.00001$$ The lecture also mentions an older workaround: layer-wise pretraining (associated with Geoffrey Hinton and students), where layers were trained one at a time. Modern practice usually avoids this by using better activations (like ReLU) and other techniques. A diagram related to the chain rule for composite functions. Source: Wikimedia Commons. PyTorch connection (important practical note) You typically do not compute derivatives by hand. PyTorch uses automatic differentiation. Your job is to build the computation graph and call loss.backward(). Three tasks & their final-layer activations A key summary from the lecture: regardless of whether the “body” of your network is a linear model, MLP, CNN, or RNN, the final layer follows the task type. Regression: identity (no activation) Binary classification: sigmoid Multiclass classification: softmax Final layer patterns (Let $\mathbf{a}$ be the final layer’s logits.) $$\textbf{Regression:}\quad \hat{y} = a$$ $$\textbf{Binary:}\quad \hat{p} = \sigma(a)$$ $$\textbf{Multiclass:}\quad \hat{\mathbf{p}} = \mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{a})$$ “Softmax is more general” (lecture note) Softmax can handle $K$ classes including $K=2$, but for binary classification sigmoid is simpler and avoids redundancy. Multiclass classification: softmax + cross-entropy (and stability) For $K$ classes, the final layer outputs a vector of logits $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^K$. We want probabilities: each is nonnegative and they sum to 1. Softmax does exactly that: Softmax $$\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{a})_k = \frac{e^{a_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{a_j}}.$$ Numerator is always positive. Denominator sums all numerators, so probabilities sum to 1. Training uses cross-entropy loss. A crucial numerical stability tip (mirroring the BCE-with-logits story): you usually don’t apply softmax “manually” before the loss. Frameworks combine these steps to avoid overflow/underflow. PyTorch rule of thumb Use nn.CrossEntropyLoss with raw logits (no softmax layer). It internally computes a stable log-softmax + negative log-likelihood. Probability vs calibration Softmax produces values that are shaped like probabilities, but a trained model can still be overconfident. Use validation data and calibration checks if the numerical confidence itself matters, not just the predicted class. Cross-entropy (one-hot target) $$\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} y_k \log(\hat{p}_k).$$ For prediction, you do not need probabilities either: the class with maximum logit is the same class with maximum softmax probability. So prediction is: Prediction $$\hat{y}=\arg\max_k a_k.$$ Softmax maps logits to probabilities. Source: Wikimedia Commons. Confusion matrix (binary example). We’ll use the same idea for multiclass (MNIST). Source: Wikimedia Commons. How images are represented in a computer (RGB, grayscale, quantization, flattening) The lecture transitions from “model” topics to “data” topics: deep learning shines on unstructured data like images, sound, and text. But how does an image become an input vector? RGB: three numbers per pixel A color image has height and width, but each pixel also has color. A common representation is RGB (Red, Green, Blue). Each pixel stores how much red, green, and blue it contains. So a color image is naturally a 3D tensor: $$A[i,j,k],\quad k\in\{R,G,B\}.$$ A dataset of $N$ images becomes a 4D tensor: $$A[n,i,j,k].$$ Quantization (0 to 255) Pixel intensities are often stored as integers in $\{0,\dots,255\}$ (8 bits per channel). That’s $256^3 \approx 16.8$ million possible RGB colors. A quick size estimate from the lecture: a raw $500\times 500$ RGB image stores $500\cdot 500\cdot 3 = 750{,}000$ bytes $\approx 732$ KB. Compression (JPEG/PNG) reduces this significantly. Hex colors (web dev connection) Hex colors like #RRGGBB are just the same 8-bit values written in base-16. RGB color cube visualization. Source: Wikimedia Commons. Grayscale images If an image has no color channels, you only store one intensity per pixel. Then an image is a 2D array (height × width). MNIST digits are grayscale, so each image is $28\times 28$. Scaling to $[0,1]$ for neural networks The lecture notes a common preprocessing step: convert uint8 pixel values in $[0,255]$ to floating point values in $[0,1]$. This keeps inputs small and numerically convenient. Flattening: the “dumb but simple” trick A fully-connected network expects a 2D array of shape $(N, D)$. The lecture’s simple solution: flatten each $28\times 28$ image into a length-$784$ vector (scan pixels left-to-right, top-to-bottom). Important practical note Flattening ignores spatial structure. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) usually perform better for vision, but flattening is a great first step to learn the training pipeline. Mini example: a $3\times 3$ grayscale image Think of the image as a matrix $I\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$. Flattening (also called vectorization) stacks pixels into a vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^{9}$. Image matrix $I$ (each entry is one pixel intensity) $I_{11}$$I_{12}$$I_{13}$ $I_{21}$$I_{22}$$I_{23}$ $I_{31}$$I_{32}$$I_{33}$ A common convention (used in the lecture) is row-major order: $$x = \mathrm{vec}(I) = [I_{11}, I_{12}, I_{13}, I_{21}, I_{22}, I_{23}, I_{31}, I_{32}, I_{33}]^\top.$$ In general, for a $H\times W$ grayscale image: $$x_{(i-1)W + j} = I_{ij},\quad 1\le i\le H,\; 1\le j\le W.$$ For MNIST: $28\times 28 \to 784$ MNIST is grayscale, so $C=1$. Each sample arrives as a tensor of shape $[B, 28, 28]$ (or sometimes $[B,1,28,28]$), and we reshape it into $[B, 784]$ before sending it into a fully-connected layer. # x: [B, 28, 28] x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) # [B, 784] (the “dumb but simple” trick) image I p1 p2 p3 p4 p5 p6 p7 p8 p9 flatten / reshape vector x = vec(I) [p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8, p9] This is not “feature engineering”—it’s only changing the shape of the data so a dense layer can consume it. MNIST tutorial: multiclass ANN with DataLoader, mini-batches, GPU Samples from the MNIST test dataset (each digit is a $28\times 28$ grayscale image). Source: Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). MNIST is a classic dataset of handwritten digits (0–9). This is a multiclass classification problem with $K=10$ classes. The training set has $60{,}000$ images and the test set has $10{,}000$ images. Why mini-batches? Large datasets may not fit in memory. So we compute loss/gradients on small batches. A batch is a random sample—its gradient is a noisy but useful estimate of the full gradient. MNIST samples. Source: Wikimedia Commons. PyTorch code: end-to-end (clean baseline) This code matches the lecture flow: load MNIST from torchvision, scale to $[0,1]$ via ToTensor(), flatten to 784 features, build a small feedforward net, train with mini-batches, evaluate with accuracy and confusion matrix. import torch import torch.nn as nn from torch.utils.data import DataLoader from torchvision import datasets, transforms # ------------------------- # 1) Data # ------------------------- transform = transforms.ToTensor() # converts uint8 [0..255] to float32 [0..1] train_ds = datasets.MNIST(root=".", train=True, transform=transform, download=True) test_ds = datasets.MNIST(root=".", train=False, transform=transform, download=True) batch_size = 128 train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True) test_loader = DataLoader(test_ds, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=False) # ------------------------- # 2) Model (flatten -> FC -> ReLU -> FC) # ------------------------- model = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 10) # logits for 10 classes ) # ------------------------- # 3) Device (GPU if available) # ------------------------- device = torch.device("cuda:0" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu") model.to(device) # ------------------------- # 4) Loss + Optimizer # ------------------------- criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss() # expects logits, applies stable log-softmax internally optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3) # ------------------------- # 5) Train / Eval helpers # ------------------------- def accuracy_from_logits(logits, y): # logits: [B, 10], y: [B] preds = torch.argmax(logits, dim=1) return (preds == y).float().mean().item() def run_epoch(loader, training: bool): total_loss = 0.0 total_correct = 0 total_seen = 0 if training: model.train() else: model.eval() for x, y in loader: x = x.to(device) # [B, 1, 28, 28] y = y.to(device) # [B] x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) # flatten -> [B, 784] if training: optimizer.zero_grad() with torch.set_grad_enabled(training): logits = model(x) # [B, 10] loss = criterion(logits, y) if training: loss.backward() optimizer.step() total_loss += loss.item() * x.size(0) total_correct += (torch.argmax(logits, dim=1) == y).sum().item() total_seen += x.size(0) avg_loss = total_loss / total_seen acc = total_correct / total_seen return avg_loss, acc # ------------------------- # 6) Training loop # ------------------------- epochs = 10 for ep in range(1, epochs + 1): train_loss, train_acc = run_epoch(train_loader, training=True) test_loss, test_acc = run_epoch(test_loader, training=False) print(f"Epoch {ep:02d} | train loss {train_loss:.4f} acc {train_acc:.4f} | " f"test loss {test_loss:.4f} acc {test_acc:.4f}") Confusion matrix and “what does the model confuse?” The lecture suggests going beyond accuracy: find which digits are confused. A confusion matrix counts how often each true label is predicted as each label. (You often expect large values on the diagonal.) import numpy as np from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix model.eval() all_preds = [] all_true = [] with torch.no_grad(): for x, y in test_loader: x = x.to(device).view(x.size(0), -1) logits = model(x) preds = torch.argmax(logits, dim=1).cpu().numpy() all_preds.append(preds) all_true.append(y.numpy()) y_pred = np.concatenate(all_preds) y_true = np.concatenate(all_true) cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred) print(cm) # rows=true labels, cols=pred labels Lecture-style interpretation idea If the matrix shows “4 is often predicted as 9”, look at example images: some handwritten 4s really do resemble 9s. Also mentioned: the dataset pipeline uses transform=ToTensor(). That’s why printing raw train_ds.data shows integers 0–255, but batches from the DataLoader are floats in 0–1. Synthetic regression example: why visualization matters (conceptually) The lecture argues that synthetic datasets are valuable because you can see where a model succeeds or fails. For a 2D input $(x_1, x_2)$ you can even visualize the target function as a 3D surface. Note about plots This page avoids generating custom plots (per your request). The code below shows the standard approach, but we do not embed a plot image unless we have a reliable reference image for that exact function. import numpy as np import torch import torch.nn as nn # Synthetic data: x in [-3, 3]^2, y = cos(2*x1) + cos(3*x2) N = 10_000 X = (np.random.rand(N, 2) * 6.0) - 3.0 y = np.cos(2 * X[:, 0]) + np.cos(3 * X[:, 1]) X_t = torch.tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32) y_t = torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32).view(-1, 1) model = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 1) # regression: no activation ) opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=3e-2) loss_fn = nn.MSELoss() for ep in range(200): opt.zero_grad() preds = model(X_t) loss = loss_fn(preds, y_t) loss.backward() opt.step() Hyperparameters: “experimentation, not philosophy” The transcript ends with an important mindset: there is no universal formula for choosing learning rates, number of layers, hidden units, activations, optimizers, etc. These are hyperparameters. You discover what works by testing and observing. Practical strategy (matches the lecture) Start with common defaults (Adam, ReLU, learning rates like $10^{-3}$). Run experiments; plot loss/accuracy curves; watch for divergence or slow learning. Use literature in your domain as a guide for reasonable ranges. Remember: rules of thumb change; results are empirical. The “don’t predict the outcome with your mind—run the program” theme is a reminder that deep learning is an experimental science. When you can test an idea quickly, testing beats guessing. Optional playground (mentioned in spirit) Interactive intuition builder: TensorFlow Playground. Try changing the number of layers/units and watch nonlinear decision boundaries appear. This optional reference consolidates the FFN concept and training path in one chapter. Source credits are retained where applicable.

description: A self-contained, practical introduction to convolution as the core operation behind convolutional neural networks (CNNs). You’ll learn the mechanics (just multiply + add), output sizing, padding modes, and why deep-l...
text: A self-contained, practical introduction to convolution as the core operation behind convolutional neural networks (CNNs). You’ll learn the mechanics (just multiply + add), output sizing, padding modes, and why deep-learning “convolution” is really cross-correlation. Visuals are served from local assets. Input ⊛ Kernel → Output Multiply + Add Valid vs Same vs Full Cross-correlation vs convolution Dot product = similarity Sliding pattern finder Qualitative intuition Hand-worked example Output size & modes Pseudocode & direct implementation Convolution equation Cross-correlation vs convolution Dot product / cosine similarity view Convolution as matrix multiplication PyTorch conv2d quickstart Local visuals and credits 1) Convolution as an image modifier Convolution takes an input image and a small filter (also called a kernel) and produces an output image. We write this conceptually as: \[ \text{output} = \text{input} \;\star\; \text{kernel} \] In math you often see a star/asterisk for convolution. In code, convolution is not written with * because * already means multiplication. Example A: blurring Using a blur kernel (like Gaussian blur) produces a softened image. Example B: edge detection Using an edge kernel produces strong responses at boundaries (edges) and low responses elsewhere. Local book diagram of blur as a convolution effect. Technical reference: OpenCV image filtering. Local book diagram of Sobel edge filtering. Technical reference: OpenCV Sobel derivatives. Why filters matter: the kernel determines what transformation happens. Change the kernel → you change the effect. CNNs learn these kernels automatically from data using gradient-based optimization. 2) Convolution mechanics: just multiply + add Convolution “slides” the kernel over the image. At each position, it performs element-wise multiplication and sums the result. That single number becomes one pixel in the output. Tiny worked example We’ll use a 4×4 input and a 2×2 kernel. (Small on purpose so you can verify by hand.) Input image \(A\) 010100 20303020 10202010 0550 Kernel \(W\) 10 02 First output (top-left): place the kernel at the top-left 2×2 patch of the image: \[ 1\cdot 0 + 0\cdot 10 + 0\cdot 20 + 2\cdot 30 = 60 \] Next output (shift right by 1): \[ 1\cdot 10 + 0\cdot 10 + 0\cdot 30 + 2\cdot 30 = 70 \] Next output (shift right again): \[ 1\cdot 10 + 0\cdot 0 + 0\cdot 30 + 2\cdot 20 = 50 \] Keep sliding until you can’t move right anymore, then move down one row and repeat. The output values stated in the transcript: \( \begin{bmatrix} 60 & 70 & 50 \\ 60 & 70 & 50 \\ 20 & 30 & 20 \end{bmatrix} \). Practice: compute the remaining outputs by hand once. If you can do that, you fully understand the mechanics. Sliding-window convolution visualization (Wikimedia Commons): 2D_Convolution_Animation.gif 3) Output size and convolution “modes” (Valid / Same / Full) If the input has height \(H\), width \(W\), and the kernel has height \(K_H\), width \(K_W\), then with no padding and stride 1, the output size is: \[ H_{\text{out}} = H - K_H + 1,\quad W_{\text{out}} = W - K_W + 1 \] This is the “valid” mode: you only place the kernel where it fully fits inside the input. Padding: making output the same size If you pad the input with zeros around the border, you allow the kernel to slide beyond the original edges. With padding \(P_H, P_W\) and stride 1: \[ H_{\text{out}} = H + 2P_H - K_H + 1,\quad W_{\text{out}} = W + 2P_W - K_W + 1 \] To get same output size (i.e., \(H_{\text{out}}=H\), \(W_{\text{out}}=W\)) with odd square kernels (like \(3\times 3\), \(5\times 5\)), choose: \[ P = \frac{K-1}{2} \] Full mode: “catch everything” If you keep padding so the kernel can slide over every partial overlap, the 1D output length becomes: \[ n_{\text{out}} = n + k - 1 \] (and similarly in 2D). This is the classic “full” convolution size. Local book diagram of padding and stride arithmetic. Technical reference: Dumoulin and Visin, A guide to convolution arithmetic for deep learning . Practical note: images “in the wild” are often rectangular, but kernels are usually square by convention (e.g., 3×3, 5×5). 4) Pseudocode and a direct implementation A straightforward 2D convolution (valid, stride 1) can be written with four loops: two for output position \((i,j)\) and two for kernel position \((i',j')\). python • naive 2D “deep learning style” convolution (cross-correlation), valid mode import numpy as np def corr2d_valid(A, W): """ Cross-correlation (deep-learning 'convolution') in 2D, valid mode, stride=1. A: (H, W) input W: (Kh, Kw) kernel returns: (H-Kh+1, W-Kw+1) """ H, W_in = A.shape Kh, Kw = W.shape H_out = H - Kh + 1 W_out = W_in - Kw + 1 out = np.zeros((H_out, W_out), dtype=float) for i in range(H_out): for j in range(W_out): s = 0.0 for ii in range(Kh): for jj in range(Kw): s += A[i + ii, j + jj] * W[ii, jj] out[i, j] = s return out A = np.array([[0,10,10,0], [20,30,30,20], [10,20,20,10], [0, 5, 5, 0]], dtype=float) W = np.array([[1,0], [0,2]], dtype=float) print(corr2d_valid(A, W)) This code matches the lecture’s “multiply + add” definition and produces the 3×3 output for the 4×4 input with a 2×2 kernel. 5) The defining equation (2D) The 2D deep-learning version (cross-correlation) at output location \((i,j)\) is: \[ (A \star W)_{i,j} = \sum_{i'=0}^{K_H-1}\sum_{j'=0}^{K_W-1} A_{i+i',\, j+j'} \, W_{i',\, j'} \] This equation is exactly what the nested loops compute. 6) “Convolution” vs cross-correlation (and why deep learning uses the latter) In classic signal processing, convolution flips the kernel (reverses its orientation). In deep learning libraries, the operation called “convolution” typically does not flip the kernel. Cross-correlation (deep learning style): slide the kernel as-is Convolution (signal processing): slide a flipped kernel If the kernel is learned automatically (as in CNN training), the flip convention doesn’t change what the model can learn: the optimizer can learn flipped patterns just as easily. Local book visualization of cross-correlation. API reference: PyTorch Conv2d. Takeaway: it’s helpful to think of CNN kernels as patterns and the operation as a sliding pattern matcher. 7) Convolution as a sliding dot product (similarity / correlation view) A dot product between vectors \(a\) and \(b\) can be written in two equivalent ways: \[ a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^d a_i b_i \] \[ a \cdot b = \|a\| \, \|b\| \cos(\theta) \] The cosine term \(\cos(\theta)\) is a similarity measure: \(\theta=0^\circ \Rightarrow \cos(\theta)=1\) (most similar) \(\theta=90^\circ \Rightarrow \cos(\theta)=0\) (orthogonal / unrelated) \(\theta=180^\circ \Rightarrow \cos(\theta)=-1\) (opposite) Geometric view of dot product (Wikimedia Commons): Dot_Product.svg Convolution/correlation is essentially the same dot-product idea, but repeated over all image locations: take a local patch of the image (same shape as kernel) compute dot product with the kernel store result in output at that location Pattern-finder interpretation: the kernel encodes a pattern. Sliding it across the image asks: “how similar is this patch to my pattern?” High response → pattern present. Cosine similarity vs Pearson correlation (conceptual link) Pearson correlation looks like cosine similarity but with mean subtraction. That’s another reason the word “correlation” is a helpful mental model for what CNN filters do. 8) Convolution as matrix multiplication (1D “Toeplitz” view) In 1D, a length-\(n\) input \(a=[a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n]\) convolved (in deep-learning style) with a length-\(k\) kernel \(w=[w_1,\dots,w_k]\) produces: \[ b_i = \sum_{i'=1}^{k} a_{i+i'-1}\, w_{i'} \quad \text{for } i=1,\dots,n-k+1 \] You can implement the same operation by building a matrix that repeats and shifts the kernel across rows (a Toeplitz-like matrix), then multiplying by the input vector. This shows convolution is a linear operation. Why we don’t do this in practice: the equivalent matrix is huge because it repeats kernel parameters many times. CNNs avoid this by storing the small kernel once and reusing it everywhere (parameter sharing). python • 1D convolution via explicit matrix multiplication (teaching only) import numpy as np def conv1d_via_matrix(a, w): a = np.asarray(a, dtype=float) w = np.asarray(w, dtype=float) n = a.size k = w.size out_len = n - k + 1 # Build "convolution matrix" M of shape (out_len, n) M = np.zeros((out_len, n), dtype=float) for i in range(out_len): M[i, i:i+k] = w # place kernel in row i, shifted right by i b = M @ a return b, M a = [1, 2, 3, 4] w = [10, 100] b, M = conv1d_via_matrix(a, w) print("M=\n", M) print("b=", b) 9) PyTorch conv2d quickstart (what CNN layers actually do) A CNN layer applies many kernels to an input. In PyTorch: input tensor shape: \((N, C_{\text{in}}, H, W)\) output tensor shape: \((N, C_{\text{out}}, H_{\text{out}}, W_{\text{out}})\) weights shape: \((C_{\text{out}}, C_{\text{in}}, K_H, K_W)\) Important: this is still “multiply + add”, just extended across channels and many filters. Local book diagram of a multi-channel CNN. Historical reference: LeCun et al., 1998. python • minimal conv2d example (demonstrates shapes, padding, valid vs same-like) import torch import torch.nn as nn # N=1 image, Cin=1 channel, H=W=4 x = torch.tensor([[[[0., 10., 10., 0.], [20., 30., 30., 20.], [10., 20., 20., 10.], [0., 5., 5., 0.]]]]) # One output channel, one input channel, kernel 2x2 conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=1, kernel_size=2, bias=False) # Manually set weights to match the earlier kernel [[1,0],[0,2]] with torch.no_grad(): conv.weight[:] = torch.tensor([[[[1., 0.], [0., 2.]]]]) y_valid = conv(x) # padding=0 by default -> "valid" print("valid out shape:", y_valid.shape) print(y_valid[0,0]) # If you want "same" output size, you typically pad (for odd kernels). # Here kernel is 2x2; "same" is less symmetric. We'll show padding=1 anyway: conv_pad = nn.Conv2d(1, 1, kernel_size=2, padding=1, bias=False) with torch.no_grad(): conv_pad.weight[:] = conv.weight y_padded = conv_pad(x) print("padded out shape:", y_padded.shape) print(y_padded[0,0]) This example uses PyTorch’s deep-learning “convolution” (cross-correlation). The values match the hand computation for valid mode. Terminology precision: classical signal-processing convolution flips the kernel before sliding it. Most deep-learning libraries, including PyTorch Conv2d, compute cross-correlation instead. Because kernels are learned, the distinction usually does not change model expressiveness, but it matters when you manually compare against a textbook convolution formula. Local visuals and source credits Gaussian blur diagram: local book asset; concept reference: OpenCV image filtering Sobel edge diagram: local book asset; concept reference: OpenCV Sobel derivatives 2D convolution animation: 2D_Convolution_Animation.gif Padding/stride arithmetic: local book asset; concept reference: Dumoulin and Visin Cross-correlation diagram: local book asset; API reference: PyTorch Conv2d Dot product geometry: Dot_Product.svg CNN diagram: local book asset; historical reference: LeCun et al., 1998 This HTML is designed to be self-sufficient: equations render via MathJax, code blocks use the shared book copy controls, and plots/animations are served from local assets.
