description: This tutorial continues convolution in the way it’s actually used inside CNNs: multi-channel inputs, multiple filters → feature maps, bias + activation, pooling / strided conv, and the two-stage CNN (conv feature extr...
text: This tutorial continues convolution in the way it’s actually used inside CNNs: multi-channel inputs, multiple filters → feature maps, bias + activation, pooling / strided conv, and the two-stage CNN (conv feature extractor → dense predictor). Input: H×W×C Weights: C_in×K×K×C_out Output: H×W×C_out Feature maps (channels) Pooling + translation invariance Strided convolution Global max pooling Color images & 3D kernels Multiple filters → feature maps Full conv formula + shapes Conv layer = conv + bias + activation Parameter savings vs dense Two-stage CNN architecture Pooling (max/avg) mechanics Why pooling works: translation invariance Conv+pool → hierarchical features Strided conv as pooling alternative Flatten vs global max pooling Putting it all together Local visuals and credits 1) Convolution with color images: add the channel dimension Real CNNs usually take color images. A color image is a 3D object: \[ X \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C_{\text{in}}} \] where \(C_{\text{in}}=3\) for RGB. To convolve a color image, you use a 3D kernel (a “small box”) that spans all input channels: \[ W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K \times C_{\text{in}}} \] Mechanically, it’s the same “multiply + add” you already know—just with an extra sum over channels: you sum over height, width, and channels. Color pattern-finder intuition: a 3D filter can match “red circles” differently from “blue circles” because it has separate weights for each channel. Local book diagram of separated RGB channels. Technical reference: OpenCV color conversions. If you convolve a 3D image with a single 3D kernel and sum across channels, the output is 2D (the channel dimension “dots out”). That’s fine for one filter—but it breaks the “stack layers” uniformity. 2) Multiple filters solve the uniformity problem A single filter finds a single feature. But images contain many features—edges, corners, textures, eyes, noses, etc. So CNNs use many filters. If you apply two different filters \(W^{(1)}\) and \(W^{(2)}\) to the same input \(X\), you get two 2D outputs: \[ B^{(1)} = X \star W^{(1)}, \quad B^{(2)} = X \star W^{(2)} \] Stack them and you get a 3D output again: \[ B = \text{stack}\left(B^{(1)}, B^{(2)}, \ldots\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C_{\text{out}}} \] Terminology shift: after the first layer, the last dimension is no longer “color”. It’s the number of channels or feature maps (one map per learned feature). Local book diagram showing stacks of CNN feature maps. Historical reference: LeCun et al., 1998. 3) Full convolution in CNN form: shapes + equation Shapes used in this lecture Input: \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C_1}\) Weights: \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{C_1 \times K \times K \times C_2}\) Output (same mode): \(Y \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C_2}\) Many frameworks store weights as \((C_2, C_1, K, K)\). The transcript’s shape is equivalent—just a different axis order. Index form (same-mode, stride 1; “deep learning style” correlation) Let \(Y_{i,j,c}\) be the output at spatial position \((i,j)\) and output channel \(c\) (a feature map). Then: \[ Y_{i,j,c} = \sum_{c'=1}^{C_1}\sum_{u=0}^{K-1}\sum_{v=0}^{K-1} X_{i+u-\Delta,\;j+v-\Delta,\;c'} \; W_{c',u,v,c} \] Here \(\Delta=\lfloor K/2 \rfloor\) corresponds to “same” padding for odd \(K\) (conceptually: zeros around the image). Concept: each output channel \(c\) corresponds to one filter (one learned feature). The output tensor is a stack of feature maps. Local book diagram of convolution arithmetic. Technical reference: Dumoulin and Visin. 4) A convolution layer = convolution + bias + activation A CNN layer mirrors a dense layer idea: \[ \text{Dense: } z = Wx + b,\quad a = \sigma(z) \] For convolution: \[ Z = X \star W + b,\quad A = \sigma(Z) \] Bias shape and broadcasting The convolution output has shape \(H \times W \times C_2\). The bias term is a vector \(b \in \mathbb{R}^{C_2}\): one scalar per feature map. In code, broadcasting adds \(b_c\) to every spatial location \((i,j)\) in that feature map. Broadcasting intuition: bias is “per-channel”, not “per-pixel”. It’s the same idea as dense layers (one bias per output unit), just expanded across the grid. python • conv layer with bias + activation (PyTorch) import torch import torch.nn as nn # Example: Cin=3 (RGB), Cout=16 feature maps, 3x3 kernels layer = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3, padding=1, bias=True), # "same" for 3x3 nn.ReLU() ) x = torch.randn(8, 3, 32, 32) # NCHW: batch=8, channels=3, H=W=32 y = layer(x) print(y.shape) # (8, 16, 32, 32) Notice PyTorch uses NCHW ordering: \((N, C, H, W)\). The “channels” here are feature maps after the first layer. 5) Why CNNs are efficient: parameter sharing vs dense explosion Parameter sharing means one small kernel is reused across the entire image. That dramatically reduces parameter count compared to flattening and using a dense layer. Worked parameter comparison (from the transcript) Input image: \(32 \times 32 \times 3\). Kernel: \(3 \times 5 \times 5 \times 64\) (64 output feature maps). Using valid convolution, output spatial size is \((32-5+1)\times(32-5+1)=28\times 28\). So output is \(28\times 28\times 64\). Convolution parameters \(3 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 64 = 4800\) Dense parameters (flattened) input: \(32\cdot 32\cdot 3 = 3072\) output: \(28\cdot 28\cdot 64 = 50176\) weights: \(3072 \times 50176 \approx 154\) million Dense would have ~32,000× more parameters in this example. This increases memory and compute and can hurt generalization, because dense must learn separate weights for the “same pattern” at every location. Local receptive fields / convolution layer concept (Wikimedia Commons): Conv_layer.png 6) A typical CNN has two stages CNNs are commonly organized as: Convolutional stage: repeated blocks that extract image features (often Conv → (Pooling or Stride)). Dense stage: a standard feed-forward network that performs classification/regression on extracted features. Local book diagram of the LeNet-5 pattern. Primary reference: LeCun et al., 1998. Mental model: the conv stage is a feature transformer designed for images. Once features are extracted, the dense stage handles non-linear prediction (classification/regression). 7) Pooling: downsampling by summarizing local neighborhoods Pooling reduces spatial size (e.g., 100×100 → 50×50 with 2×2 pooling, stride 2). Two common types: Max pooling: take the maximum value in each pooling window Average pooling: take the average in each pooling window Mechanics with the transcript’s 4×4 example (pool=2, stride=2) Input 1234 5678 16151413 1211109 MaxPool2d(2) output 68 1614 AvgPool2d(2) output 3.55.5 13.511.5 python • max pooling and average pooling (PyTorch) import torch import torch.nn as nn x = torch.tensor([[[[ 1., 2., 3., 4.], [ 5., 6., 7., 8.], [16., 15., 14., 13.], [12., 11., 10., 9.]]]]) # shape (N=1, C=1, H=4, W=4) maxpool = nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2) avgpool = nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2) print("max:\n", maxpool(x)[0,0]) print("avg:\n", avgpool(x)[0,0]) Max pooling visualization (Wikimedia Commons): Max_pooling.png 8) Why pooling helps: translation invariance Pooling supports the idea of translation invariance: we often care that a feature exists somewhere, not exactly where it is. In a small 2×2 region, a feature detector output might look like “high, low, low, low”. Max pooling returns the high value, preserving “feature found” while discarding precise location. Max pooling intuition: “if the pattern appears anywhere in this window, keep it.” This often matches what you want for recognition tasks. Pooling layers also have hyperparameters: pool size (e.g., 2×2) and stride (often 2). Overlapping pooling (stride 1) exists but is less common in typical modern setups. 9) Conv + pooling creates hierarchical feature learning CNNs often repeat the pattern: convolution → pooling → convolution → pooling. Spatial size decreases, while filters remain small (commonly 3×3, 5×5, 7×7). Why small filters start as “tiny pattern” detectors A 3×3 filter covers a tiny fraction of a 32×32 image. After downsampling to 16×16, the same 3×3 covers a larger fraction of the image; later it can cover a very large portion (e.g., on 4×4). This is one reason CNNs learn features hierarchically: early layers tend to pick up small patterns (edges/strokes), later layers pick up larger patterns (parts, then whole objects). Two linked effects: 1) spatial dimensions shrink 2) fixed-size filters “see” relatively larger areas → bigger patterns Yes, shrinking loses spatial detail (“where”). But CNNs often compensate by increasing the number of feature maps (“what”) as depth increases. 10) Strided convolution as an alternative to pooling Pooling isn’t the only downsampling option. Convolution itself can downsample using a stride: stride tells you how far the sliding window jumps each step. With stride 2, output spatial dimensions are roughly halved—similar to pooling with 2×2, stride 2. Why skipping pixels can be okay: nearby pixels are often highly correlated in natural images. Skipping every other pixel still preserves much of the structure while reducing computation. Local book diagram of strided convolution. Technical reference: Dumoulin and Visin. python • strided conv vs conv+pool (shape comparison) import torch import torch.nn as nn x = torch.randn(1, 3, 32, 32) # Option A: conv then pool conv = nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1) # keep 32x32 pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2, stride=2) # downsample to 16x16 y_a = pool(torch.relu(conv(x))) # Option B: strided conv (downsample directly) conv_s2 = nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1, stride=2) y_b = torch.relu(conv_s2(x)) print("conv+pool:", y_a.shape) # (1, 16, 16, 16) print("stride=2:", y_b.shape) # (1, 16, 16, 16) Both produce the same spatial size here; the difference is where downsampling happens and how parameters are used. 11) Flatten vs global max pooling (handling variable image sizes) The dense stage expects a 1D feature vector. A convolutional output is 3D: \[ X \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C} \] so a common step is to flatten to a vector of size \(H\cdot W\cdot C\). Why flattening fails for variable image sizes If the network outputs 2×2×100 for a 32×32 input, flatten gives 400 features. For a larger 64×64 input that becomes 4×4×100, flatten gives 1600 features. A fixed dense layer can’t accept both sizes. Global max pooling: size-independent output Global max pooling collapses the entire spatial grid: \[ \text{GMP}(X)_c = \max_{i,j} X_{i,j,c} \] producing a vector of size \(C\), regardless of \(H\) and \(W\). Interpretation: “I don’t care where the feature appears in the image—if it appears anywhere, keep the strongest evidence.” Local book diagram of global pooling. Primary reference for global average pooling: Lin, Chen, and Yan, Network in Network. python • global max pooling in PyTorch (works for any H×W) import torch import torch.nn as nn gmp = nn.AdaptiveMaxPool2d((1, 1)) # global max pooling to 1x1 x1 = torch.randn(8, 100, 2, 2) # e.g., from 32x32 after downsampling x2 = torch.randn(8, 100, 4, 4) # e.g., from 64x64 after downsampling y1 = gmp(x1).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) # shape: (8, 100) y2 = gmp(x2).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) # shape: (8, 100) print(y1.shape, y2.shape) Note: images can’t be downsampled indefinitely. If the spatial size becomes too small (e.g., 2×2), additional stride-2 operations will fail. 12) A modern CNN blueprint (as summarized in the transcript) A practical CNN often follows: Convolutional stage: repeated blocks that downsample while increasing channels Option A: Conv → Pool (repeat) Option B: Strided Conv (repeat) Keep filter sizes small (commonly 3×3, 5×5, 7×7) Increase feature maps with depth (e.g., 32 → 64 → 128 → ...) Bridge: convert 3D feature maps to 1D features Flatten (view) for fixed-size inputs or Global pooling for variable-size inputs Dense stage: standard feed-forward layers ending with task-appropriate output Regression: 1 output, identity (no activation) Binary classification: 1 output, sigmoid Multi-class (K≥2): K outputs, softmax (often combined with cross-entropy loss) python • reference CNN skeleton (conv stage → global max pool → dense) import torch.nn as nn class SimpleCNN(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes=10): super().__init__() self.features = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1, stride=2), nn.ReLU(), # stride downsample nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1, stride=2), nn.ReLU(), ) self.gmp = nn.AdaptiveMaxPool2d((1, 1)) # global max pool self.classifier = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, num_classes) ) def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) # (N, 128, H', W') x = self.gmp(x).squeeze(-1).squeeze(-1) # (N, 128) return self.classifier(x) # logits # Use with nn.CrossEntropyLoss() for multi-class classification Big picture: convolution learns feature transformers automatically during training (weights + biases), just like dense layers—only the tensor shapes and parameter sharing differ. Local visuals and source credits RGB channels diagram: local book asset; concept reference: OpenCV color conversions CNN feature-map stack: local book asset; historical reference: LeCun et al., 1998 Convolution arithmetic (padding/stride): local book asset; concept reference: Dumoulin and Visin Local receptive fields / conv layer concept: Wikimedia Commons LeNet-5 pattern: local book asset; primary reference: LeCun et al., 1998 Max pooling visualization: Wikimedia Commons Stride arithmetic: local book asset; concept reference: Dumoulin and Visin Global pooling: local book asset; primary reference: Network in Network This HTML is self-contained in structure: equations render via MathJax CDN, code blocks are readable with copy buttons, and all displayed visuals are local assets, with source attribution or primary concept references retained where applicable.

text: This tutorial turns the transcript into a practical, self-contained guide to building CNN models in PyTorch. You’ll learn nn.Conv2d basics, how PyTorch uses modules and inheritance, when you need a custom model, how to handle flattening between conv and dense layers, how dropout really works, and how to compute output sizes with convolution arithmetic. Conv2d arguments Modules & inheritance Sequential vs custom models Flatten/view Dropout (train vs eval) Output-size formulas 1) Conv2d essentials 2) Modules & inheritance 3) Sequential vs custom 4) CNN skeleton 5) Dropout (real behavior) 6) Convolution arithmetic Cheat sheet 1) nn.Conv2d essentials (what you must know before coding CNNs) In PyTorch, the standard convolution layer for images is torch.nn.Conv2d. It’s “2D” because the convolution slides over the spatial axes (height and width). The color/channel axis is handled as “channels,” not as a spatial direction. Key idea: A Conv2d layer learns a set of filters (kernels). Each filter produces one output channel (one feature map). PyTorch tensor layout (important!) PyTorch uses the NCHW layout for images: N = batch size C = channels (e.g., 3 for RGB) H = height W = width Many tutorials talk about images as H×W×C; that’s fine conceptually, but in PyTorch code you’ll usually use N×C×H×W. nn.Conv2d signature (the arguments you’ll use most) The common form is: \[ \mathrm{Conv2d}(\text{in\_channels},\ \text{out\_channels},\ \text{kernel\_size},\ \text{stride},\ \text{padding}) \] ArgumentMeaningRule of thumb in_channels Number of input channels RGB images → 3. Later layers → number of feature maps from previous conv. out_channels Number of output channels (feature maps) Often grows: 32 → 64 → 128 → … kernel_size Filter size (usually square) Usually odd: 3, 5, 7 (3 is most common in modern CNNs). stride Step size for sliding the kernel Stride 1 keeps resolution (with padding), stride 2 downsamples. padding Zeros added around image border Often chosen to preserve size (common “same-like” behavior). What does the learned weight tensor look like? Internally, the conv weights form a 4D tensor: \[ W \in \mathbb{R}^{C_\text{out} \times C_\text{in} \times K_h \times K_w} \] That is: one kernel per output channel, and each kernel spans all input channels. This matches the transcript idea: “kernel is 4D: input channels, output channels, height, width.” (PyTorch stores it as out×in×kh×kw.) python • inspect Conv2d parameters import torch import torch.nn as nn conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1) print("weight shape:", conv.weight.shape) # (out_channels, in_channels, kH, kW) print("bias shape:", conv.bias.shape) # (out_channels,) Why Conv2d and not Conv1d / Conv3d? Conv1d: sequences / time signals (e.g., audio, sensor streams). Conv2d: images (height & width are the spatial axes). Conv3d: volumes (e.g., medical CT “voxels”) or videos (height, width, time). 2D convolution animation (Wikimedia Commons): 2D_Convolution_Animation.gif 2) PyTorch “everything is a module”: inheritance and composition PyTorch neural network building blocks are modules (instances of nn.Module). A Linear layer is a module. A ReLU is a module. A Sequential container is also a module. And your entire model is a module too. Superpower: modules compose hierarchically. You can build a “module of modules,” then use it like a single module, and repeat. Inheritance (why your custom model subclasses nn.Module) To create your own model class, you inherit from nn.Module. Two key pieces: __init__: define submodules as attributes (layers you want to learn / run). forward: define the computation (how data flows through layers). python • minimal custom MLP (Linear → ReLU → Linear) import torch import torch.nn as nn class TinyMLP(nn.Module): def __init__(self, d_in: int, d_hidden: int, d_out: int): super().__init__() self.fc1 = nn.Linear(d_in, d_hidden) self.act = nn.ReLU() self.fc2 = nn.Linear(d_hidden, d_out) def forward(self, x): x = self.fc1(x) x = self.act(x) x = self.fc2(x) return x model = TinyMLP(d_in=10, d_hidden=32, d_out=3) x = torch.randn(5, 10) logits = model(x) print(logits.shape) # (5, 3) Notice the key correspondence: defining layers in __init__, applying them in forward. 3) Sequential vs Custom Models: when to use which Option A — nn.Sequential Great when your network is just a straight stack of layers (no branching, no multi-input/output). Option B — Custom nn.Module Needed when you must do operations not easily represented as a simple list of layers (reshapes, multiple paths, skip connections, multi-input/output, etc.). Why custom models matter in CNNs The classic “boundary” in CNNs is: convolution outputs an image tensor (N×C×H×W), but dense layers expect vectors (N×D). You need a reshape/flatten step in between. Modern PyTorch provides nn.Flatten(). But you should still know how to do it manually with x.view(...) or torch.flatten. python • Flatten boundary: N×C×H×W → N×(C·H·W) import torch x = torch.randn(8, 64, 7, 7) # (N, C, H, W) flat1 = x.view(x.size(0), -1) # (N, C*H*W) flat2 = torch.flatten(x, start_dim=1) print(flat1.shape, flat2.shape) # both: (8, 3136) Exercise (recommended) Recreate a tiny version of nn.Sequential: store modules, then call them in order in forward. This is a great way to lock in “modules + forward pass” thinking. 4) A CNN model skeleton (two clean ways) A practical CNN typically has: Conv stack → Flatten → Dense stack. Way 1: Custom model with two Sequential blocks + explicit view python • CNN as nn.Module (conv Sequential + view + dense Sequential) import torch import torch.nn as nn class SimpleCNN(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes: int = 10): super().__init__() self.conv = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1), # downsample nn.ReLU(), ) # We must know the flattened size here (see convolution arithmetic below). # For example: if input is (3, 32, 32), output after conv might be (64, 16, 16) # so flattened = 64*16*16 = 16384 self.fc = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(64 * 16 * 16, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, num_classes), ) def forward(self, x): x = self.conv(x) x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) # flatten x = self.fc(x) return x model = SimpleCNN(num_classes=10) dummy = torch.randn(4, 3, 32, 32) print(model(dummy).shape) # (4, 10) Way 2: Pure Sequential using nn.Flatten() This is cleaner, but you still need the correct input size for the first Linear layer. python • CNN as nn.Sequential (using nn.Flatten) import torch import torch.nn as nn model = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * 16 * 16, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10), ) dummy = torch.randn(4, 3, 32, 32) print(model(dummy).shape) # (4, 10) A practical trick: compute the flatten size automatically If you don’t want to do manual arithmetic while prototyping, you can run a dummy tensor through the conv stack inside __init__ to infer the flatten dimension once. python • infer flatten size with a dummy forward pass import torch import torch.nn as nn class AutoShapeCNN(nn.Module): def __init__(self, input_shape=(3, 32, 32), num_classes=10): super().__init__() self.conv = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, stride=2, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), ) with torch.no_grad(): dummy = torch.zeros(1, *input_shape) out = self.conv(dummy) flat_dim = out.view(1, -1).size(1) self.head = nn.Sequential( nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(flat_dim, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, num_classes), ) def forward(self, x): x = self.conv(x) x = self.head(x) return x model = AutoShapeCNN() print(model(torch.randn(2, 3, 32, 32)).shape) # (2, 10) This “dummy pass” trick is widely used during research/prototyping. You still should learn the arithmetic, but this keeps you productive. 5) Dropout regularization (the real behavior, clearly explained) Dropout does NOT permanently remove a neuron. It applies a fresh random mask each forward pass in training mode, zeroing some activations temporarily. Core math (inverted dropout) Let \(h\) be a layer activation vector/tensor. Sample a mask: \[ m_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(q),\quad q = 1-p \] Apply: \[ \tilde{h} = \frac{m \odot h}{q} \] This scaling keeps the expected magnitude consistent between train and eval. What happens to gradients? The derivative wrt activations is: \[ \frac{\partial \tilde{h}}{\partial h} = \frac{m}{q} \] So if a unit is dropped (\(m=0\)), its gradient is 0 for that sample. Next batch, the mask changes, so it can update again. Train vs eval mode (must-know) model.train() → dropout active (random masks) model.eval() → dropout disabled (identity) python • verify dropout randomness in train vs stability in eval import torch import torch.nn as nn drop = nn.Dropout(p=0.5) x = torch.ones(1, 10) drop.train() y1 = drop(x) y2 = drop(x) drop.eval() y3 = drop(x) y4 = drop(x) print("train outputs differ:", not torch.allclose(y1, y2)) print("eval outputs equal:", torch.allclose(y3, y4)) Where to place dropout in CNNs The common default is to place dropout between dense layers (the classifier head), not inside convolution blocks. For conv feature maps, people sometimes use nn.Dropout2d (drops entire channels), but you should treat it as an experiment. python • typical dropout placement in a CNN head import torch.nn as nn head = nn.Sequential( nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64*16*16, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(p=0.5), nn.Linear(256, 10), ) Local book diagram of dropout. Primary reference: Srivastava et al., 2014. 6) Convolution arithmetic (compute output sizes so your Linear layer matches) CNNs become annoying to wire up when you reach the first dense layer, because you must know the flattened size. That requires knowing the conv output size. The PyTorch formula (per spatial dimension) For height (and similarly width), PyTorch effectively uses: \[ H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor \frac{H_{\text{in}} + 2P - D\,(K-1) - 1}{S} + 1 \right\rfloor \] \(H_\text{in}\): input height \(K\): kernel size (height) \(S\): stride \(P\): padding \(D\): dilation (usually 1 unless you set it) Common case: dilation \(D=1\). Then: \[ H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor \frac{H_{\text{in}} + 2P - K}{S} + 1 \right\rfloor \] “Valid” vs “Same-like” behavior In classic terms (stride 1, dilation 1): Valid: \(P=0\) → \(H_\text{out} = H_\text{in} - K + 1\) Same-like: choose \(P\) to keep size when \(S=1\) (often \(P=\lfloor K/2\rfloor\) for odd kernels) In Keras you can write padding="same". In PyTorch you usually specify the numeric padding yourself (or in newer versions you may see padding strings in some APIs, but relying on the arithmetic is still essential). Worked example: 32×32 → (stride 2) → 16×16 Suppose: \(H_\text{in}=32\), \(K=3\), \(S=2\), \(P=1\) (a common “same-like downsample” setting). Then: \[ H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor \frac{32 + 2(1) - 3}{2} + 1 \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{31}{2} + 1 \right\rfloor = \lfloor 15.5 + 1 \rfloor = 16 \] python • helper to compute conv output size (H/W) import math def conv_out_size(n_in, k, stride=1, pad=0, dilation=1): return math.floor((n_in + 2*pad - dilation*(k-1) - 1) / stride + 1) print(conv_out_size(32, k=3, stride=2, pad=1)) # 16 Why odd kernel sizes are common With odd kernels (3,5,7…), there is a clear “center” pixel. This makes it easy to do symmetric padding (e.g., \(P=\lfloor K/2\rfloor\)) and preserve alignment. Local book diagram of stride and padding. Technical reference: Dumoulin and Visin. Shortcut if you hate arithmetic During prototyping, use the “dummy forward pass” trick shown earlier to infer flatten size. But you still want the formula in your toolbox when reading papers or debugging shape errors. Cheat sheet: what to remember TopicRemember this Tensor layout PyTorch images are usually N×C×H×W. Conv2d weights (out_channels, in_channels, kH, kW) Modules Layers/models are nn.Module; composition gives “module of modules”. Custom model Define layers in __init__, apply them in forward. Conv → Dense boundary Use x.view(x.size(0), -1) or nn.Flatten(). Dropout New random mask each forward pass in train(); disabled in eval(). Conv arithmetic \( \left\lfloor \frac{H + 2P - D(K-1) - 1}{S} + 1 \right\rfloor \) Visual sources used: local assets with Wikimedia credits retained where applicable.

description: This chapter develops Dropout from first principles: what gets masked, how often masks change, why scaling exists, how gradients behave, and why train()/eval() matters.
text: This chapter develops Dropout from first principles: what gets masked, how often masks change, why scaling exists, how gradients behave, and why train()/eval() matters. Deep-dive chapter Chapter 6 introduces dropout as part of the CNN implementation checklist. This chapter owns the detailed explanation: random masks, inverted scaling, train() vs eval(), flattening, and common mistakes. Conv2d arguments & shapes nn.Module & inheritance Sequential vs custom nn.Module Flatten/view boundary Dropout: masks, scaling, gradients train() vs eval() Dropout (updated) train() vs eval() Dropout FAQ Dropout: what it actually does (and what it does NOT do) Correct mental model: Dropout applies a new random mask every forward pass (typically every mini-batch). It does not permanently “turn off” a neuron, and it does not remove it for the whole training run. What gets dropped? In standard dropout, we drop activations (the outputs of a layer), not the parameter tensors directly. Think: “for this forward pass, some activation values become zero.” Training mode math (inverted dropout) Let a layer output be \(h\). Dropout samples a mask \(m\) where: \[ m_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(q), \quad q = 1-p \] Then it computes: \[ \tilde{h} = \frac{m \odot h}{q} \] If \(m_i = 0\): that activation is zeroed for this pass. If \(m_i = 1\): it’s kept, and scaled by \(1/q\). The scaling keeps the expected activation magnitude consistent between training and inference. Inference mode math In eval mode, dropout is disabled: \[ \tilde{h} = h \] No randomness, no masking. What happens to gradients when an activation is dropped? When an activation is dropped (\(m_i=0\)), it contributes nothing to the output, so the gradient through that activation is zero for that sample: \[ \frac{\partial \tilde{h}_i}{\partial h_i} = \frac{m_i}{q} \] If \(m_i=0\), then \(\partial \tilde{h}_i / \partial h_i = 0\). Practically: Weights feeding into that activation receive no update from that sample. But next iteration, the mask changes, so the same unit may be active and updated then. Local book diagram of dropout. Primary reference: Srivastava et al., 2014. Interactive mini-demo (mask changes every “forward pass”) This toy demo uses a vector [1..12] as “activations”. Click “Run one forward pass” multiple times in train mode and watch the mask change. Drop probability p: 0.50 Toggle train/eval train (random mask each forward pass) Run one forward pass Train mode: new random mask each click. h (input) m (mask) scaling h̃ (output) PyTorch: the exact behavior you should remember nn.Dropout(p) applies random masking only when the module is in train() mode. In eval() mode, it becomes an identity function (no change). For standard dropout, mask entries are sampled independently for activations during each forward call. Structured variants such as Dropout2d drop whole channels instead. python • verify mask randomness in train vs determinism in eval import torch import torch.nn as nn drop = nn.Dropout(p=0.5) x = torch.ones(1, 10) drop.train() y1 = drop(x) y2 = drop(x) # different mask, usually different output drop.eval() y3 = drop(x) y4 = drop(x) # same output, dropout disabled print("train different:", not torch.allclose(y1, y2)) print("eval same:", torch.allclose(y3, y4)) Where to put dropout (practical default) Most commonly: between dense layers. For conv feature maps, many projects skip it or use specialized variants. python • common pattern: Dense → ReLU → Dropout → Dense import torch.nn as nn head = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(512, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(p=0.5), nn.Linear(256, 10) # logits ) For conv nets, you may also see nn.Dropout2d / nn.Dropout3d: these drop entire channels (feature maps), not individual pixels. train() vs eval(): why dropout “turns off” for predictions PyTorch modules can have different behavior depending on whether you’re training or evaluating. Dropout is the classic example: model.train() → dropout ON (random masking), batchnorm uses batch stats model.eval() → dropout OFF (no masking), batchnorm uses running stats Standard pattern: call model.train() before the training loop, and model.eval() during validation/testing (usually with torch.no_grad()). python • training/evaluation skeleton (dropout-safe) model.train() for xb, yb in train_loader: optimizer.zero_grad() logits = model(xb) # dropout active here loss = loss_fn(logits, yb) loss.backward() optimizer.step() model.eval() correct = 0 total = 0 with torch.no_grad(): for xb, yb in val_loader: logits = model(xb) # dropout disabled here preds = logits.argmax(dim=1) correct += (preds == yb).sum().item() total += yb.size(0) print("val acc:", correct / total) Dropout FAQ (common confusions) “Does dropout stop training a random node each iteration?” It temporarily zeros a random subset of activations each forward pass. Those dropped activations have zero gradient for that sample, so their incoming weights don’t update from that sample. Next iteration, the mask changes, so they can update again. Not permanent “Is the same set of nodes masked all the time?” No—standard dropout resamples a new mask per forward pass. Some specialized variants (e.g., “locked/variational dropout” in some sequence models) reuse a mask across time steps, but that’s not the default behavior of nn.Dropout. “Does dropout remove weights?” No. The parameters are still there. Dropout modifies the activations during training. At inference, nothing is removed. “Why is there scaling by 1/(1-p)?” Without scaling, the average activation magnitude would shrink during training. Inverted dropout keeps the expected activation scale similar between train and eval. “Should I use dropout in conv layers?” Often not necessary. If you do, consider channel-wise dropout (Dropout2d) rather than pixel-wise dropout, and verify by experiment—sometimes it helps, sometimes it’s neutral. In modern CNNs, batch normalization, data augmentation, weight decay, early stopping, and larger datasets often reduce the need for heavy dropout. Dropout is still valid, but it is a regularization choice to validate, not a mandatory CNN ingredient. description: A standalone tutorial on what sequence data is, how to shape it for ML, what “forecasting” really means, and how to avoid the most common multi-step forecasting mistake: data leakage through future inputs.
text: A standalone tutorial on what sequence data is, how to shape it for ML, what “forecasting” really means, and how to avoid the most common multi-step forecasting mistake: data leakage through future inputs. Key idea Sequences are not just “lots of rows.” They have order. The value at time \(t\) is often related to values at \(t-1, t-2, \dots\). Forecasting is the discipline of exploiting that ordered dependence to predict values that have not happened yet. 1) What counts as sequence data? Time series: values indexed by time Finance: prices, returns, volume, spreads sampled every minute/day. Weather: temperature, rain, humidity, pressure, wind over time. Audio: a waveform is amplitude measured over time. Sensor streams: accelerometers, ECG, machines, IoT, clickstreams, logs. The sequence axis is the time axis: rows arrive in order and nearby rows tend to be statistically related. Example time series plot Any “value vs time” curve is a time series. Displayed as a local asset; source credit retained where applicable. Text is also sequential, but with discrete tokens A sentence is a sequence of tokens. Older ML often used bag-of-words: convert a document into a word-count vector and ignore order. That makes standard classifiers easy to use, but it destroys the sequential signal. Why bag-of-words can fail: “dog toy” and “toy dog” have the same word counts but different meaning. Time-series forecasting and language modeling are not identical, but they share one deep idea: the next output depends on ordered context. Chapter 10 uses recurrent state for ordered context; Chapter 11 replaces that with attention. 2) What makes time series different from ordinary tabular ML? Rows are not exchangeable In ordinary tabular ML, you often treat rows as independent examples and shuffle them before training. In forecasting, shuffling can destroy the question. Training on 2025 and validating on 2020 is not a forecast. The split must respect time: train on the past, validate/test on the future. The data-generating process can change Time series can have trend, seasonality, cycles, structural breaks, missing periods, outliers, and changing variance. A model trained on one regime can fail when the future regime changes. This is why backtesting over multiple forecast origins is often more trustworthy than one lucky split. A forecast is trying to separate signal from time-dependent structure The future is not just the last value repeated; it may contain trend, seasonality, shocks, and noise. trend seasonality event / shock noise / residual A useful baseline should make these ideas explicit: what repeats, what drifts, what is random, and what information is actually known at forecast time. 3) How to represent sequence data: \(N \times T \times D\) For non-sequential data you are used to \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\): samples by features. For sequences, we add a time axis: \[ X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times T \times D} \] \(N\): number of samples. Each sample is one sequence window. \(T\): number of time steps in the window. This is also called lookback, context length, or lag length. \(D\): number of features measured at each time step. Concrete examples so \(N\), \(T\), and \(D\) do not get mixed up GPS commute tracking: each trip is one sample (\(N\)); each timestamp is one step (\(T\)); latitude/longitude means \(D=2\). Single stock price: \(D=1\). If you slice the long series into windows of length \(T\), each window is one sample. 500 stocks: \(D=500\). Each time step contains a 500-dimensional market snapshot. Brain electrodes: \(D=\) number of electrodes. With 1 kHz sampling for one second, \(T=1000\). The axis order \(N \times T \times D\) is common in Python sequence modeling when `batch_first=True`. 4) Forecast origin, lookback, target, and horizon Forecasting starts from a forecast origin: the last time point you are allowed to know. You choose a lookback \(T\), then predict one or more future steps. Lookback \(T\): how many past steps the model sees. Target: the value you ask the model to predict. Horizon \(H\): how far into the future you want predictions. If steps are hours and you forecast 7 days hourly, \(H = 7 \times 24 = 168\). If steps are days and you forecast the next 5 days, \(H=5\). Forecasting vocabulary on one timeline Everything to the left of the origin is known. Everything to the right must be predicted or known in advance. forecast origin lookback window T horizon H x[t-3] x[t-2] x[t-1] x[t] t+1 t+2 t+3 Forecasting is not “predict any random held-out row.” It is “stand at an origin and predict what comes after it.” 5) Turning a long series into supervised learning windows A model such as linear regression expects input-output pairs. A raw time series is one long ordered list. Windowing converts the long list into many supervised examples. If the full series has length \(L\) and you use lookback \(T\) to predict the next value, the number of one-step training windows is: \[ \text{windows} = L - (T+1) + 1 = L - T \] Why \(T+1\)? Because each supervised example needs \(T\) input values plus one target value. Raw series Lookback \(T=3\) Target [10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 20][10, 12, 13]15 [10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 20][12, 13, 15]18 [10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 20][13, 15, 18]20 import numpy as np def make_supervised_1d(series: np.ndarray, lookback: int): """ Converts a 1D time series into supervised learning data: X[i] = series[i : i+lookback] y[i] = series[i+lookback] """ series = np.asarray(series, dtype=np.float32) L = len(series) if L <= lookback: raise ValueError("series is too short for the chosen lookback") X = [] y = [] for i in range(L - lookback): X.append(series[i : i + lookback]) y.append(series[i + lookback]) return np.stack(X), np.asarray(y) x = np.arange(10, dtype=np.float32) # [0..9] X, y = make_supervised_1d(x, lookback=3) print(X.shape, y.shape) # (7, 3) (7,) 6) A “dumb but great” baseline: linear regression as an AR model Before you reach for RNNs, use a simple baseline. For a 1D time series (\(D=1\)), treat the previous \(p\) values as features and use linear regression. \[ \hat{x}_t = w_0 + w_1 x_{t-1} + w_2 x_{t-2} + \dots + w_p x_{t-p} \] In statistics this is an autoregressive (AR) model: the series is predicted from its own past. In ML language, it is a supervised learning model built from lag features. Persistence baseline The simplest forecast is \(\hat{x}_{t+1}=x_t\): tomorrow equals today. This is surprisingly hard to beat for some noisy series and should be your first sanity check. Seasonal naive baseline If the series repeats every \(s\) steps, forecast \(\hat{x}_{t+1}=x_{t+1-s}\). For hourly daily seasonality, \(s=24\); for daily weekly seasonality, \(s=7\). 7) Exogenous variables: what is known in the future? Many forecasts use extra features besides the target’s own past. These are often called exogenous variables or covariates. Feature type Examples Can you use it for future horizons? Known in advance day of week, holidays, planned price, calendar month Yes, if it is truly known at forecast time. Observed only later future sales, future weather observations, future demand, future sensor values No, unless you separately forecast it first or use a scenario. Leakage rule: every input feature for a forecast horizon must be information you would actually have at the forecast origin. 8) The most common forecasting mistake: leaking future inputs The wrong way for multi-step forecasting: Predicting day 5 using inputs that include the true day 4 value, when day 4 is not known at forecast time. This makes the plot look nice but it is not a valid multi-step forecast. The correct recursive / rolling forecast: When you need multiple steps ahead, feed the model’s own previous predictions back as inputs. This matches reality: once you step into the future, you no longer have ground-truth observations. Recursive multi-step forecasting After the first future step, the model must consume its own predictions, not hidden true values. known history x[t-2] x[t-1] x[t] AR model xhat[t+1] xhat[t+2] slide the window: drop oldest, append prediction, repeat until horizon H This is the same autoregressive idea that later appears in language generation: predicted outputs become part of the next input context. 9) Forecasting strategies for \(H>1\) Strategy How it works Tradeoff Recursive Train one-step model; roll it forward by feeding predictions back in. Simple and uses all one-step data, but errors compound. Direct Train a separate model for each horizon step: one for \(t+1\), one for \(t+2\), etc. Avoids recursive feedback, but needs more models and less data per horizon. Multi-output Train one model to output all \(H\) future steps at once. Can learn horizon relationships, but the output layer and loss must match the forecast task. Chapter 9 focuses on the recursive version because it exposes the core forecasting issue most clearly: after the origin, real future observations are unavailable. 10) Minimal, correct forecasting code: baseline AR with recursion Train a linear model (scikit-learn style) and forecast recursively import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression def fit_ar_linear(train_series: np.ndarray, lookback: int) -> LinearRegression: X_train, y_train = make_supervised_1d(train_series, lookback) model = LinearRegression() model.fit(X_train, y_train) return model def recursive_forecast_1d(model, history: np.ndarray, lookback: int, horizon: int): """ history: last observed values, at least lookback long. Returns: horizon predictions [xhat(t+1), xhat(t+2), ...]. """ hist = list(np.asarray(history, dtype=np.float32)) if len(hist) < lookback: raise ValueError("history must contain at least lookback values") preds = [] for _ in range(horizon): x_in = np.array(hist[-lookback:], dtype=np.float32).reshape(1, -1) y_hat = float(model.predict(x_in)[0]) preds.append(y_hat) hist.append(y_hat) # key step: feed prediction back in return np.array(preds, dtype=np.float32) series = np.sin(np.linspace(0, 10*np.pi, 500)).astype(np.float32) train, test = series[:400], series[400:] lookback = 20 horizon = 30 ar = fit_ar_linear(train, lookback=lookback) history = train[-lookback:] preds = recursive_forecast_1d(ar, history, lookback=lookback, horizon=horizon) print("First 5 predictions:", preds[:5]) Important: this evaluates a real forecast. After the split point, the model does not receive true future target values as inputs. 11) Evaluation: one split is a start, backtesting is better A single chronological train/test split is better than random splitting, but it can still be lucky or unlucky. In production forecasting, you often use walk-forward backtesting: choose several forecast origins, forecast the next \(H\) steps from each origin, and aggregate the errors. MAE: average absolute error; easy to interpret in original units. RMSE: penalizes large errors more strongly. MAPE: percentage error; fragile when true values are near zero. MASE / scaled error: compares against a naive baseline, useful across series with different scales. 12) Where RNNs fit next This tutorial intentionally starts with the simplest correct approach: an autoregressive baseline. RNNs and later sequence models help when relationships are nonlinear, depend on longer context, or involve high-dimensional inputs. Chapter 10 replaces a fixed lookback vector with recurrent hidden state. It then uses translation to show the same step-by-step idea in text: tokens become embeddings, a decoder produces one output at a time, and autoregressive decoding feeds previous outputs back into the next step. The data-shape thinking (\(N \times T \times D\)) and the “no future leakage” rule remain the same no matter how sophisticated the model becomes. If the baseline evaluation is wrong, you cannot trust the advanced model evaluation either. Checklist: a correct forecasting setup Define the horizon \(H\): one-step prediction and multi-step forecasting are different tasks. Choose the lookback \(T\): enough context to model the pattern without unnecessary noise. Split by time: train on the past, validate/test on the future. Fit preprocessing on training only: scaling, imputation, feature selection, and hyperparameters must not see the future period. No leakage: future target values cannot be used as future inputs. Start with baselines: persistence, seasonal naive, and AR/linear regression before complex sequence models. Chapter transition With the forecasting contract, baselines, and leakage-safe evaluation in place, the next chapter implements the autoregressive linear baseline in PyTorch before recurrent state is introduced.

description: Goal: implement an autoregressive (AR) linear model for time-series prediction, then evaluate it in the right way for a multi-step forecast.
text: Goal: implement an autoregressive (AR) linear model for time-series prediction, then evaluate it in the right way for a multi-step forecast. 1) What this chapter is building Chapter 8 introduced the concept: turn a time series into supervised windows, train a simple baseline, and be careful not to leak future values. Here we implement that baseline in PyTorch. The model is intentionally simple: \[ \hat{x}_{t} = b + w_1x_{t-1} + w_2x_{t-2} + \dots + w_Tx_{t-T} \] That is just a linear layer from a lookback window of length \(T\) to one scalar prediction. The point is not that this model is always powerful. The point is that it is the cleanest baseline for learning the mechanics of forecasting: windowing, chronological splitting, training, and recursive evaluation. Autoregressive linear model The previous T values become the feature vector for one next-step prediction. x[t-3] x[t-2] x[t-1] x[t] input vector shape: (T,) nn.Linear T -> 1 xhat[t+1] next value This is a regular supervised model. What makes it time-series forecasting is how the supervised examples are constructed and evaluated. 2) Create a controlled time series A sine wave is useful because it is periodic, smooth, and easy to debug. We can add noise later to make the problem more realistic. Starting clean is a good engineering habit: if the simple case fails, the bug is probably in the data shaping or evaluation logic. # --- Imports --- import numpy as np import torch import torch.nn as nn import matplotlib.pyplot as plt np.random.seed(0) torch.manual_seed(0) # --- 1) Create a synthetic time series --- N = 1000 omega = 0.1 t = np.arange(N) series = np.sin(omega * t).astype(np.float32) # Optional: make the task more realistic after the clean version works. # noise_std = 0.2 # series = (series + noise_std * np.random.randn(N)).astype(np.float32) plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3)) plt.plot(series) plt.title("Synthetic time series") plt.xlabel("time index") plt.ylabel("x[t]") plt.show() 3) Build the dataset by windowing Windowing is where most forecasting bugs begin. For each target time, the model should only see values before that target. If \(T=10\), then one example looks like this: Input: \([x_t, x_{t+1}, \dots, x_{t+T-1}]\) Target: \(x_{t+T}\) The input has shape \((T,)\). The target is one scalar. Once we stack all windows, \(X\) has shape \((\text{num_windows}, T)\) and \(y\) has shape \((\text{num_windows}, 1)\). def make_windows(series: np.ndarray, lookback: int): """ X[i] = series[i : i+lookback] y[i] = series[i+lookback] Also returns target_times so we can split by the target's time index. """ series = np.asarray(series, dtype=np.float32) if len(series) <= lookback: raise ValueError("series is too short for the chosen lookback") X, y, target_times = [], [], [] for start in range(len(series) - lookback): end = start + lookback X.append(series[start:end]) y.append(series[end]) target_times.append(end) X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float32) y = np.asarray(y, dtype=np.float32).reshape(-1, 1) target_times = np.asarray(target_times) return X, y, target_times T = 10 X, y, target_times = make_windows(series, lookback=T) print("X shape:", X.shape) # (N-T, T) print("y shape:", y.shape) # (N-T, 1) print("First window:", X[0]) print("First target:", y[0, 0]) A tiny off-by-one sanity check If `series = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]` and `T = 2`, the windows should be: Input windowTarget [0, 1]2 [1, 2]3 [2, 3]4 If your code produces a different table, fix the indexing before training anything. 4) Chronological split: split by time, not randomly For time series, do not randomly shuffle examples before deciding train and validation. A forecast should train on the past and validate on the future. A subtle but important point: split according to the target time. The first validation example may use a lookback window that contains the last observed training values. That is not leakage; at the validation forecast origin, those historical values are known. Leakage begins when you use true values after the forecast origin while rolling forward. # Target times before this point are training targets. split_time = int(0.6 * N) train_mask = target_times < split_time val_mask = target_times >= split_time X_train, y_train = X[train_mask], y[train_mask] X_val, y_val = X[val_mask], y[val_mask] target_times_val = target_times[val_mask] print("train:", X_train.shape, y_train.shape) print("val:", X_val.shape, y_val.shape) # Convert to torch tensors. X_train_t = torch.tensor(X_train, dtype=torch.float32) y_train_t = torch.tensor(y_train, dtype=torch.float32) X_val_t = torch.tensor(X_val, dtype=torch.float32) y_val_t = torch.tensor(y_val, dtype=torch.float32) Where scaling belongs If you standardize the series, fit the mean and standard deviation on the training period only, then apply those same statistics to validation/test. Fitting a scaler on the full series leaks future distribution information. # Optional scaling pattern. Fit only on observed training history. train_values_for_scaler = series[:split_time] mean = train_values_for_scaler.mean() std = train_values_for_scaler.std() + 1e-8 series_scaled = (series - mean) / std # Then rebuild windows from series_scaled using the same function. 5) Define the AR model in PyTorch The AR(\(T\)) linear model is one layer: \[ \hat{x}_{t+T} = b + \sum_{i=0}^{T-1} w_i x_{t+i} \] In PyTorch, `nn.Linear(T, 1)` stores the \(T\) lag weights plus one bias. It receives a batch of windows with shape \((B,T)\) and returns \((B,1)\). model = nn.Linear(T, 1) loss_fn = nn.MSELoss() optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.05) print(model) print("weight shape:", model.weight.shape) # (1, T) print("bias shape:", model.bias.shape) # (1,) 6) Train with full-batch gradient descent Because this dataset is small, we can use all training windows each step. For larger datasets, you would use mini-batches with a `DataLoader`. The forecasting logic below is unchanged. def train_full_gd(model, Xtr, ytr, epochs=300): losses = [] for epoch in range(epochs): model.train() pred = model(Xtr) # (num_train_windows, 1) loss = loss_fn(pred, ytr) optimizer.zero_grad() loss.backward() optimizer.step() losses.append(loss.item()) return losses losses = train_full_gd(model, X_train_t, y_train_t, epochs=300) plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3)) plt.plot(losses) plt.title("Training loss (MSE)") plt.xlabel("epoch") plt.ylabel("loss") plt.show() Check the learned lag weights A linear AR model is interpretable. The learned weights show which lags are useful. For a clean sine wave, only a small number of lags are theoretically necessary, although a larger lookback can still learn a good recurrence. with torch.no_grad(): weights = model.weight.detach().cpu().numpy().ravel() bias = float(model.bias.detach().cpu()) print("bias:", bias) print("lag weights:", np.round(weights, 3)) 7) One-step validation vs real multi-step forecasting The wrong answer to the wrong question If you run `model(X_val_t)`, every validation prediction receives a window containing true historical values from the validation period. That is a valid one-step-ahead evaluation, but it is not a valid 50-step forecast from a single origin. It answers: “How good is the model if the latest real observation is always available before each prediction?” It does not answer: “What happens if I stand at the split point and forecast the next 50 unknown values?” # One-step-ahead validation. Useful, but not a multi-step forecast. model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): one_step_preds = model(X_val_t).squeeze(1).cpu().numpy() plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3)) plt.plot(y_val.squeeze(), label="target") plt.plot(one_step_preds, label="one-step predictions") plt.title("One-step validation: true windows are supplied each step") plt.legend() plt.show() The correct recursive forecast For a multi-step forecast, start from one known lookback window. Predict the next value, append that prediction to the window, drop the oldest value, and repeat. def recursive_forecast_torch(model, start_window, horizon): """ start_window: shape (T,), the last known values at the forecast origin. horizon: number of future steps to predict. """ model.eval() window = torch.tensor(start_window, dtype=torch.float32).clone() preds = [] with torch.no_grad(): for _ in range(horizon): y_hat = model(window.view(1, -1)) # (1, 1) y_scalar = y_hat.view(()) # scalar tensor preds.append(float(y_scalar)) # Drop oldest value and append the model's prediction. window = torch.cat([window[1:], y_scalar.view(1)]) return np.asarray(preds, dtype=np.float32) horizon = len(y_val) start_window = X_val[0] # known context at the first validation target recursive_preds = recursive_forecast_torch(model, start_window, horizon=horizon) plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3)) plt.plot(y_val.squeeze(), label="target") plt.plot(recursive_preds, label="recursive forecast") plt.title("Recursive validation: predictions feed future predictions") plt.legend() plt.show() Two validation modes answer different questions One-step validation is not bad; it is just not the same as a long-horizon forecast. one-step / true-window mode true x true x true x measures one-step prediction quality recursive forecast mode true x xhat xhat measures long-horizon drift and compounding error The “wrong” plot can look excellent because every step gets true context. The recursive plot is the honest simulation of standing at one origin and rolling forward. 8) Compare metrics Use the same target array for both predictions. The one-step result is usually better because it receives true validation inputs at every step. The recursive forecast is the harder and more realistic multi-step test. def mae(y_true, y_pred): return np.mean(np.abs(y_true - y_pred)) def rmse(y_true, y_pred): return np.sqrt(np.mean((y_true - y_pred) ** 2)) y_true = y_val.squeeze() print("One-step MAE:", mae(y_true, one_step_preds)) print("One-step RMSE:", rmse(y_true, one_step_preds)) print("Recursive MAE:", mae(y_true, recursive_preds)) print("Recursive RMSE:", rmse(y_true, recursive_preds)) What you should observe No-noise sine wave: both methods can look nearly perfect because the signal follows a clean recurrence. Noisy sine wave: one-step validation often still looks good, while recursive forecasting drifts as errors compound. Real business series: regime changes, promotions, holidays, missing data, and exogenous variables often matter more than model complexity. 9) Why can a linear AR model predict a sine wave so well? A sine wave has an exact 2-step linear recurrence. If \(x_t = \sin(\omega t)\), then: \[ x_{t+1} = 2\cos(\omega)\,x_t - x_{t-1} \] This means an AR(2) model can represent a clean sine wave perfectly. Using \(T=10\) gives the model more lags than it strictly needs, but the linear layer can learn weights that implement the recurrence. Noise breaks the exact recurrence, which is why recursive forecasting becomes imperfect. Sketch of the derivation Use the identity: \[ \sin(a+b) + \sin(a-b) = 2\sin(a)\cos(b) \] Let \(a = \omega t\) and \(b = \omega\). Then: \[ \sin(\omega(t+1)) + \sin(\omega(t-1)) = 2\sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega) \] Rearranging gives: \[ \sin(\omega(t+1)) = 2\cos(\omega)\sin(\omega t) - \sin(\omega(t-1)) \] 10) Extending the baseline The same shape logic extends naturally: More input features: use \(D>1\), such as demand plus price, holiday flag, and weather. Multi-output forecasting: change the output layer from `nn.Linear(T, 1)` to `nn.Linear(T, H)`. Nonlinear baseline: replace the single linear layer with a small MLP. RNN baseline: keep the sequence axis instead of flattening the lookback into one vector. # Multi-output direct forecast sketch: # input window -> next H values at once. H = 24 multi_output_model = nn.Linear(T, H) # For this model, y would need shape (num_windows, H), not (num_windows, 1). 11) Common gotchas checklist Shape mistakes: one window is shape \((T,)\), but the model expects a batch shape \((1,T)\). Random split: do not randomly mix future windows into training for forecasting evaluation. Scaling leakage: fit scalers on training history only. One-step vs multi-step confusion: one-step validation can be useful, but it is not a long-horizon forecast. Error compounding: recursive forecasts drift if early predictions are wrong. Unknown future features: do not feed true future weather, demand, sensor values, or target values unless they would be known at forecast time. Next natural step: replace the fixed linear window with recurrent hidden state. Chapter 10 shows how an RNN processes sequence inputs, then extends the same step-by-step idea to text translation and autoregressive decoding.
