description: A practical, code-oriented tutorial on why RNNs exist, what goes in and comes out at each time step, how a basic Elman unit computes hidden state, how GRU/LSTM gates improve memory, and how recurrent weight sharing ke...
text: Sequence models A practical, code-oriented tutorial on why RNNs exist, what goes in and comes out at each time step, how a basic Elman unit computes hidden state, how GRU/LSTM gates improve memory, and how recurrent weight sharing keeps sequence models compact. Big idea: An RNN processes a sequence by applying the same small neural “cell” at every time step. The cell carries a hidden state forward, so the output at time \(t\) can depend on both the current input \(x_t\) and the memory of earlier inputs \(h_{t-1}\). 1) Why not just flatten sequence data into a giant vector? Sequence data is data where order matters: a time series, an audio waveform, a sentence, a video, or a stream of sensor readings. You can flatten a sequence \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D}\) into a single vector of length \(T\cdot D\) and feed it to a regular MLP. It works mechanically, but it’s usually a bad tradeoff: Parameter explosion: dense layers connect “everything to everything”, so weights scale with \((T\cdot D)\). Ignores sequential structure: treating time steps as just “features” discards the idea of incremental processing. Hard to generalize across time: you’re not explicitly reusing patterns across positions in the sequence. RNNs exploit the structure: the same computation repeats at every time step, just like CNN filters repeat across image locations. Where RNNs show up RNNs are useful whenever the meaning of the current item depends on what came before it. Modern Transformers dominate large-scale language modeling, but the RNN mental model is still important because it explains sequence memory, hidden state, autoregressive decoding, and the historical path into attention. Problem family Why sequence memory matters Typical output shape Language modeling Words depend on earlier words and phrase context. Next-token distribution at each time step. Speech recognition Audio frames only make sense as an ordered waveform. Characters, word pieces, or phoneme labels over time. Machine translation The target sentence depends on source order, grammar, and context. A generated output sequence. Stock or demand forecasting Recent and older time steps can shape the next value. One future value, a horizon of values, or a class label. Music generation Melody, rhythm, and harmony are sequential patterns. Next note, chord, token, or audio event. Video and sensor streams Events unfold frame by frame or reading by reading. Per-step labels, anomaly scores, or a final classification. 2) The simplest RNN unit (Elman unit): equations and intuition At each time step \(t\), the RNN consumes an input vector \(x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D}\) and updates a hidden state \(h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{M}\). Then it optionally produces an output \(\hat{y}_t\). Core equations A standard “vanilla” RNN does: \[ h_t = \phi(W_{xh}x_t + W_{hh}h_{t-1} + b_h) \] \[ \hat{y}_t = \psi(W_{ho}h_t + b_o) \] Where: \(W_{xh}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times D}\): input → hidden weights \(W_{hh}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}\): hidden → hidden (recurrent) weights \(W_{ho}\in\mathbb{R}^{O\times M}\): hidden → output weights \(\phi\): hidden activation (often \(\tanh\) or ReLU); \(\psi\): output activation depends on task \(h_0\): initial hidden state (often zeros; sometimes learned) Unrolled RNN: one cell, reused weights, evolving hidden state The boxes look repeated in the diagram, but they all represent the same learned parameters. RNN cell same Wxh, Whh x1 y1 RNN cell same Wxh, Whh x2 y2 RNN cell same Wxh, Whh x3 y3 RNN cell same Wxh, Whh x4 y4 h1 h2 h3 Input changes at every step. Hidden state changes at every step. Learned weights stay shared. Unrolling shows the time loop explicitly: current input plus previous hidden state produces the next hidden state. “Single unit is used”: what that really means When people say “the same unit is used at each time step”, they mean: You do not have a different \(W_{xh}\) for each \(t\). You do not have a different \(W_{hh}\) for each \(t\). You reuse the same weights and biases at every step: that’s parameter sharing through time. The only thing that changes over time is the data (\(x_t\)) and the state (\(h_{t-1}\to h_t\)). This is exactly why RNNs can have far fewer parameters than a flattened dense design. Cost nuance: the parameter count does not grow with \(T\), but the computation still runs once per time step, and training stores intermediate states for backpropagation through time. Long sequences can still be expensive. 3) Many-to-one vs many-to-many: why you might “ignore” most outputs You can compute \(\hat{y}_t\) at every step, but whether you use them depends on the task: Many-to-one: sentiment of a sentence → use only \(\hat{y}_T\) Many-to-many: label each time step (e.g., tagging) → use all \(\hat{y}_t\) Seq2seq (translation): outputs are also a sequence → you need stepwise predictions Same recurrent cell, different output usage The RNN can emit at every step; the task decides which outputs become supervised predictions. Many-to-one h1 h2 h3 hT sentiment Many-to-many h1 h2 h3 hT one label per step Seq2seq context y1 y2 y3 target sequence Many-to-one, many-to-many, and seq2seq are not different definitions of an RNN. They are different ways of using the outputs. Compact RNN summary Feature Meaning Input type Ordered data such as text, speech, time series, video frames, event streams, or sensor readings. Core mechanism Reuse one learned cell through time while carrying hidden state forward. Memory The hidden state \(h_t\) summarizes what the model has retained up to step \(t\). Output Can be one final prediction, one prediction per time step, or a generated sequence from a decoder. Strength Handles variable-length ordered inputs with shared parameters rather than a fixed flattened vector. Main challenges Vanishing/exploding gradients, sequential training cost, and pressure to compress long context into state. Common variants LSTM, GRU, bidirectional RNN/GRU/LSTM, encoder-decoder RNNs, and attention-augmented seq2seq models. 4) Practical seq2seq example: translating “my name is dinesh” A useful way to understand RNN inputs and outputs is to walk through a tiny machine-translation problem: translate “my name is dinesh” into “mon nom est dinesh”. A classic RNN translation system uses an encoder RNN to read the source sentence and a decoder RNN to generate the target sentence. The French target is a literal teaching example; an idiomatic translation might be “je m’appelle Dinesh”, but the literal four-token target makes the step-by-step alignment easier to see. What the model sees: not raw text. Text is tokenized into IDs, IDs are looked up in an embedding table, and the RNN receives one dense vector per time step. Step A: text becomes tokens, token IDs, then embeddings Stage Example Shape / meaning Source tokens ["my", "name", "is", "dinesh", "<EOS>"] A finite sequence ending with an explicit end-of-sentence marker. Token IDs [17, 241, 9, 5021, 2] Integer vocabulary indices. The actual numbers are arbitrary. Embeddings [0.12, -0.33, 0.45, ...] for each token If embedding size is \(D=300\), each time step gives the RNN one vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{300}\). Padded batch ["my", "name", "is", "dinesh", "<EOS>", "<PAD>", ...] Padding makes examples in a batch the same length. Padding positions are masked or ignored; they are not extra meaning. import torch import torch.nn as nn src_tokens = ["my", "name", "is", "dinesh", "<EOS>", "<PAD>", "<PAD>", "<PAD>", "<PAD>", "<PAD>"] src_ids = torch.tensor([[17, 241, 9, 5021, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]]) # (batch=1, T=10) embedding = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=10_000, embedding_dim=300, padding_idx=0) x = embedding(src_ids) # (1, 10, 300) print(x.shape) # one 300-dimensional input vector per time step Step B: encoder RNN reads the English sentence The encoder consumes one embedding at a time and updates hidden state. If a 10-step tensor is used for batching, the meaningful tokens occupy the early positions and the remaining positions are padding. In production code, lengths or masks prevent padding from contributing to the loss and, depending on implementation, from changing the final state. Encoder step Input token Hidden-state interpretation 1myStarts the sentence and records a possessive cue. 2nameBuilds the phrase “my name” and the identity context. 3isAdds the grammatical relation that links phrase to value. 4dineshStores the name entity that should be copied or transliterated. 5<EOS>Marks that the source sentence is complete. 6-10<PAD>Ignored by masks/lengths; present only so the batch has a rectangular tensor shape. Step C: decoder RNN generates French one token at a time The decoder starts from the encoder’s final meaning representation. At each step it receives the previous French token and predicts a probability distribution over the French vocabulary. During training, it often receives the true previous token as input (teacher forcing). During inference, it feeds its own previous prediction back in. Decoder step Decoder input Prediction Why it happens 1<SOS>monThe start token asks the decoder to begin the translation. 2monnomThe decoder continues the French phrase “mon nom”. 3nomestThe model emits the linking verb. 4estdineshThe name entity is carried through from the encoded source context. 5dinesh<EOS>The decoder decides the target sentence is complete. 6-10<PAD>ignoredPadding positions are ignored when batching fixed-length targets. Encoder-decoder RNN for translation The encoder reads English. The decoder writes French. Hidden state is the bridge. English tokens my name is dinesh EOS enc enc enc enc context final hidden state mon nom est dinesh EOS French tokens are produced one step at a time from vocabulary probabilities. A classic seq2seq RNN compresses the source into hidden state, then decodes the target sequence token by token. Attention improves this by letting the decoder look back at specific encoder states instead of relying only on one final vector. # Decoder inference sketch: generate French tokens autoregressively. # This is conceptual pseudocode; real systems use batching, masks, beam search, # and often attention over all encoder states. prev_token = SOS_ID hidden = encoder_final_hidden generated = [] for _ in range(max_target_len): prev_emb = target_embedding(torch.tensor([[prev_token]])) # (1, 1, D) decoder_out, hidden = decoder_rnn(prev_emb, hidden) logits = output_projection(decoder_out[:, -1, :]) # (1, vocab_size) next_token = int(logits.argmax(dim=-1).item()) if next_token == EOS_ID: break generated.append(next_token) prev_token = next_token # feed the model's own prediction back in What actually learns: gradients flow through the unrolled encoder and decoder during training. The model adjusts embeddings, recurrent weights, and output-projection weights so that the right target token receives higher probability at each decoder step. 5) Pseudocode: forward pass through a sequence # Given: # X: shape (T, D) # h0: shape (M,) (often zeros) # weights: W_xh (M, D), W_hh (M, M), b_h (M,) # W_ho (O, M), b_o (O,) # Returns: # y_hats: list of length T, each element shape (O,) h = h0 y_hats = [] for t in range(T): h = tanh(W_xh @ X[t] + W_hh @ h + b_h) # hidden update y = softmax(W_ho @ h + b_o) # output (for classification) y_hats.append(y) # For many-to-one tasks, you would use y_hats[-1] and ignore the rest. 6) Cost savings: RNN vs flattened ANN Let: \(T\) = sequence length \(D\) = features per time step \(M\) = hidden size \(O\) = output size (e.g., \(O=1\) for binary classification/logit) Flattened ANN (dense “everything-to-everything”) If you flatten, input size is \(T\cdot D\). If you also keep a hidden representation for each time step (as in the transcript’s comparison), hidden size becomes \(T\cdot M\). Approx weights (ignoring biases): \[ (T D)(T M) + (T M)O \] RNN (shared weights through time) Weights are independent of \(T\): \[ W_{xh}: M D,\quad W_{hh}: M^2,\quad W_{ho}: O M \] Total: \[ MD + M^2 + OM \] This comparison is about trainable parameters. Runtime still scales with sequence length because the recurrent update is applied at every step. For many-to-one tasks, the output head may only be applied to the final hidden state; for many-to-many tasks, it is applied at each step, which changes compute but not the shared recurrent parameter count. Key win: RNN parameter count does not grow with sequence length \(T\) the way a flattened dense model does. Parameter sharing is the first RNN efficiency idea Flattened sequence models allocate weights for positions; recurrent models reuse one transition rule. Flattened ANN view position 1 position 2 position T more positions imply more position-specific weights RNN view same cell run again with new x_t and h_{t-1} parameters stay MD + M^2 + OM RNNs save parameters by reusing the same weights at each time step. Computation still grows with sequence length, but the learned recurrent matrices do not. Concrete example + Python code (and a plot) Example: \(T=100\), \(D=10\), \(M=15\), \(O=1\). import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt def ann_params_flat(T, D, M, O): # Transcript-style comparison: hidden size = T*M return (T*D) * (T*M) + (T*M) * O def rnn_params(T, D, M, O): # Shared through time return (M*D) + (M*M) + (O*M) T, D, M, O = 100, 10, 15, 1 p_ann = ann_params_flat(T, D, M, O) p_rnn = rnn_params(T, D, M, O) print("Flattened ANN params:", p_ann) print("RNN params:", p_rnn) print("ANN / RNN ratio:", p_ann / p_rnn) # Quick bar plot labels = ["Flattened ANN", "RNN (shared weights)"] values = [p_ann, p_rnn] plt.figure() plt.bar(labels, values) plt.yscale("log") # so both bars are visible plt.title("Parameter count comparison (log scale)") plt.ylabel("Number of parameters") plt.show() In this setup, you’ll see a huge ratio (thousands of times more parameters for the flattened ANN), matching the intuition from the transcript. 7) Coding it in PyTorch: manual loop (to really see weight sharing) The fastest way to “get” RNNs is to implement the loop yourself once. Below is a minimal RNN cell you can train like any other module. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class TinyElmanRNN(nn.Module): """ Vanilla RNN (Elman unit) implemented explicitly: h_t = tanh(W_xh x_t + W_hh h_{t-1} + b_h) y_t = W_ho h_t + b_o """ def __init__(self, input_size: int, hidden_size: int, output_size: int): super().__init__() self.input_size = input_size self.hidden_size = hidden_size self.output_size = output_size # These are the ONLY learned weights, reused for every t self.W_xh = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size, bias=True) self.W_hh = nn.Linear(hidden_size, hidden_size, bias=False) self.W_ho = nn.Linear(hidden_size, output_size, bias=True) def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, h0: torch.Tensor | None = None): """ x: (batch, T, D) using batch_first layout here h0: (batch, M) or None Returns: y_all: (batch, T, O) (pred at every step) h_last: (batch, M) """ B, T, D = x.shape if h0 is None: h = torch.zeros(B, self.hidden_size, device=x.device, dtype=x.dtype) else: h = h0 y_steps = [] for t in range(T): xt = x[:, t, :] # (batch, D) h = torch.tanh(self.W_xh(xt) + self.W_hh(h)) yt = self.W_ho(h) # (batch, O) y_steps.append(yt) y_all = torch.stack(y_steps, dim=1) # (batch, T, O) return y_all, h # Example usage: B, T, D = 32, 100, 10 M, O = 15, 1 model = TinyElmanRNN(D, M, O) x = torch.randn(B, T, D) y_all, h_last = model(x) # Many-to-one binary classification: use only last step logits = y_all[:, -1, :] # (B, 1) probs = torch.sigmoid(logits) # if binary classification Notice how self.W_xh and self.W_hh are created once in __init__, then used repeatedly inside the time loop. That’s the “single unit reused” idea in code. 8) Using PyTorch’s built-in nn.RNN (recommended for real projects) PyTorch provides torch.nn.RNN which handles the looping internally and exposes standardized weights (e.g., weight_ih_l0, weight_hh_l0) and batch/sequence layouts. import torch import torch.nn as nn D, M = 10, 15 # input_size, hidden_size rnn = nn.RNN( input_size=D, hidden_size=M, num_layers=1, nonlinearity="tanh", batch_first=True, # input is (batch, T, D) ) B, T = 32, 100 x = torch.randn(B, T, D) # output: (B, T, M) h_n: (num_layers, B, M) out, h_n = rnn(x) # Many-to-one classifier head head = nn.Linear(M, 1) logits = head(out[:, -1, :]) If you’re ever unsure about shapes, inputs/outputs, or the exact meaning of those weight tensors, the official docs are the source of truth. Why the next section exists: nn.RNN gives you a clean implementation of the vanilla recurrence, but it does not change the recurrence itself. There is still only one hidden vector, and every new token can overwrite it. That is enough for short dependencies and for learning the idea, but it is too blunt when the model must remember something for many steps while also reacting to new input. 9) Why vanilla RNN memory breaks: overwriting and gradient chains A vanilla RNN has only one state vector \(h_t\). Every step computes a new state from the current input and the previous state: \[ h_t = \tanh(W_{xh}x_t + W_{hh}h_{t-1} + b_h) \] That compact formula is elegant, but it gives the model no explicit mechanism for deciding how much old information to keep and how much new information to write. The new candidate state can overwrite the old state too aggressively. During backpropagation through time, gradients also repeatedly multiply through recurrent transformations. Those products can shrink toward zero (vanishing gradients) or grow too large (exploding gradients). The missing idea: a good sequence model needs a learnable way to say “keep this memory”, “forget this part”, “write this new information”, and sometimes “hide this internal memory from the output”. Why vanilla recurrence runs out of control One hidden vector must both store old facts and absorb every new token. h1 h2 ... hT old information must survive every rewrite training signal long products can vanish Gates are introduced because vanilla recurrence has no explicit keep/write control and because long recurrent chains are hard to train. 10) Gates: learnable valves for memory The next improvement is not “make the hidden state bigger” as the first move. A larger state can store more numbers, but it still gives the model no explicit instruction for which numbers should be preserved, overwritten, or exposed. GRUs and LSTMs solve that problem by adding gates. A gate is usually a sigmoid output: \[ \sigma(a) \in (0,1) \] Because a gate is between 0 and 1, it behaves like a soft valve: A value near 0 means “block this signal”. A value near 1 means “let this signal pass”. Intermediate values blend old and new information. The progression is: Model Problem it fixes Remaining pressure that leads to the next idea Vanilla RNN Introduces hidden state and weight sharing through time. The hidden state is overwritten by a single update rule, and long gradients are fragile. GRU Adds reset/update gates so the model can keep old state or write new state selectively. There is still one vector doing two jobs: long-term memory and exposed hidden representation. LSTM Separates protected cell memory \(c_t\) from exposed hidden state \(h_t\). The computation is still sequential, and seq2seq still pressures memory into recurrent states. Attention Lets the decoder look up relevant states directly instead of relying only on what survived in memory. The Transformer generalizes lookup so all tokens can read context directly and train in parallel. How recurrent memory becomes more controllable Vanilla RNN overwrites one hidden state. GRU adds update/reset gates. LSTM separates long-term cell memory from exposed hidden state. Vanilla RNN one hidden state h_t = tanh(...) simple, but old memory is easy to overwrite GRU hidden state + gates reset update learns how much to keep and how much to rewrite LSTM cell state + hidden state forget write output separate long-term cell path helps memory persist GRU and LSTM do not change the basic sequence loop. They change the cell used inside the loop so memory is easier to preserve. Historical note: LSTM was introduced before GRU. This chapter teaches GRU first because it is the simpler gated cell to understand, then LSTM as the more explicit long-term-memory design. 11) GRU: the simpler gated memory cell A Gated Recurrent Unit is the smallest useful step beyond the vanilla RNN. It keeps one state, \(h_t\), like a vanilla RNN, but adds two gates: Reset gate \(r_t\): controls how much of the previous state is used when computing the new candidate. Update gate \(z_t\): controls how much old state is kept versus how much candidate state is written. One common convention, matching PyTorch’s documentation, is: \[ r_t = \sigma(W_{ir}x_t + b_{ir} + W_{hr}h_{t-1} + b_{hr}) \] \[ z_t = \sigma(W_{iz}x_t + b_{iz} + W_{hz}h_{t-1} + b_{hz}) \] \[ n_t = \tanh(W_{in}x_t + b_{in} + r_t \odot (W_{hn}h_{t-1} + b_{hn})) \] \[ h_t = (1 - z_t) \odot n_t + z_t \odot h_{t-1} \] With this convention, if \(z_t\) is close to 1, the GRU mostly keeps the old state. If \(z_t\) is close to 0, it mostly writes the candidate \(n_t\). That “keep vs update” interpolation is the key mental model. GRU mental model: “I have one memory vector. At each step I learn whether to keep it, partially reset it, or overwrite parts of it with the new candidate.” This directly addresses the first failure mode of a vanilla RNN: accidental overwrite. If the model sees an important token early in a sequence, the update gate can keep that memory alive while less important later tokens only adjust part of the state. The reset gate gives the model a second useful behavior: when the current input starts a new local pattern, it can temporarily ignore older state while computing the candidate update. GRU: one memory vector with controlled overwrite The reset gate controls candidate construction; the update gate blends old memory with the candidate. old state h_{t-1} input x_t reset gate r_t update gate z_t candidate memory n_t new state h_t h_t = (1-z_t) * n_t + z_t * h_{t-1} A GRU still has one memory vector, but the update gate makes the final state an explicit blend of old memory and candidate memory. import torch import torch.nn as nn B, T, D = 32, 100, 10 # batch, sequence length, input features H = 64 # hidden size gru = nn.GRU( input_size=D, hidden_size=H, num_layers=1, batch_first=True, ) x = torch.randn(B, T, D) out, h_n = gru(x) print(out.shape) # (B, T, H): hidden state at every time step print(h_n.shape) # (1, B, H): final hidden state for the last layer # Many-to-one classifier: use the final time-step representation head = nn.Linear(H, 1) logits = head(out[:, -1, :]) Why move from GRU to LSTM? A GRU is compact and often very strong, but its single state vector still has to be both the long-term memory and the visible representation passed onward. If you want a more explicit design where long-term memory can be preserved while only part of it is exposed at the current step, you need a separate memory path. That is the reason for the LSTM cell state. 12) LSTM: separate long-term memory from exposed hidden state A Long Short-Term Memory cell takes the gating idea further by adding a separate cell state, \(c_t\), alongside the hidden state, \(h_t\). The cell state is the long-term memory path. The hidden state is the exposed representation used for outputs and for the next recurrent computation. LSTMs use three main gates plus a candidate update: Forget gate \(f_t\): how much old cell memory \(c_{t-1}\) to keep. Input/write gate \(i_t\): how much new candidate information to write. Candidate \(g_t\): proposed new content for the cell memory. Output gate \(o_t\): how much cell memory to expose as hidden state \(h_t\). \[ f_t = \sigma(W_{if}x_t + b_{if} + W_{hf}h_{t-1} + b_{hf}) \] \[ i_t = \sigma(W_{ii}x_t + b_{ii} + W_{hi}h_{t-1} + b_{hi}) \] \[ g_t = \tanh(W_{ig}x_t + b_{ig} + W_{hg}h_{t-1} + b_{hg}) \] \[ o_t = \sigma(W_{io}x_t + b_{io} + W_{ho}h_{t-1} + b_{ho}) \] \[ c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t \] \[ h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) \] LSTM mental model: “I keep a protected long-term notebook \(c_t\), decide what to erase, decide what to write, and decide how much of the notebook to show as \(h_t\).” LSTM: protected cell memory plus exposed hidden state The cell state carries long-term memory; gates decide what is erased, written, and revealed. c_{t-1} c_t forget f_t write i_t g_t output o_t x_t, h_{t-1} h_t c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * g_t, h_t = o_t * tanh(c_t) LSTM explicitly separates the protected cell-memory update from the exposed hidden-state output. import torch import torch.nn as nn B, T, D = 32, 100, 10 H = 64 lstm = nn.LSTM( input_size=D, hidden_size=H, num_layers=1, batch_first=True, ) x = torch.randn(B, T, D) out, (h_n, c_n) = lstm(x) print(out.shape) # (B, T, H): hidden state at every time step print(h_n.shape) # (1, B, H): final hidden state print(c_n.shape) # (1, B, H): final cell state head = nn.Linear(H, 1) logits = head(out[:, -1, :]) Compared with a GRU, the LSTM is more explicit: one gate forgets old cell memory, one gate writes new cell memory, and one gate controls what part of the internal memory becomes visible as \(h_t\). That makes the design easier to reason about for long dependencies, but it also adds parameters and computation. In practice, GRU is often a good first gated baseline; LSTM is the stronger choice when you want the separate cell-memory path and can afford the extra complexity. Why LSTM still does not finish the story: LSTMs make recurrence better, but they are still recurrent. Step \(t\) still waits for step \(t-1\), and an encoder-decoder LSTM still tends to compress source information into recurrent states. The next idea is not another gate; it is a different memory interface: direct lookup over earlier token states. 13) GRU vs LSTM vs vanilla RNN: when to use which The choice is therefore not a popularity contest. It follows the problem you are trying to solve. Use the simplest recurrent cell that carries enough memory for the task, then move to the next mechanism only when the limitation becomes the bottleneck. Cell State carried through time Memory control Practical use Vanilla RNN One hidden state \(h_t\) No explicit gates Best for teaching and very short dependencies; rarely the strongest production choice. GRU One hidden state \(h_t\) Reset and update gates Simpler than LSTM, fewer parameters, often a strong baseline for sequence classification/forecasting. LSTM Hidden state \(h_t\) plus cell state \(c_t\) Forget, input/write, candidate, output gates More explicit memory control; useful when long dependencies matter and recurrence is still appropriate. Attention/Transformer Token representations plus attention over context Content-based lookup instead of recurrent compression Dominant for LLMs because training parallelizes and each token can directly access relevant context. Bidirectional recurrent models After gates, another natural question is direction: if the entire input sentence is already known, why should the model only read left-to-right? A bidirectional RNN/GRU/LSTM runs one recurrent model left-to-right and another right-to-left, then combines their representations. This is useful when the full input sequence is known, such as classification, tagging, or embedding a sentence. It is not valid for pure left-to-right generation, because a generator cannot use future tokens that have not been produced yet. import torch import torch.nn as nn B, T, D = 32, 100, 10 H = 64 encoder = nn.LSTM( input_size=D, hidden_size=H, batch_first=True, bidirectional=True, ) x = torch.randn(B, T, D) out, (h_n, c_n) = encoder(x) print(out.shape) # (B, T, 2*H): forward and backward states concatenated 14) Why attention still mattered after GRU/LSTM At this point the story has fixed three problems: weight sharing made sequence models compact, gates made memory controllable, and bidirectionality let encoders use both left and right context when the full input is known. But none of these changes remove the deepest recurrent limitation: Sequential compute: step \(t\) depends on \(t-1\), so training cannot parallelize across time as easily as Transformers. Compression pressure: encoder-decoder recurrence still tends to squeeze a whole source sequence through hidden states. Long-context access: a decoder may need a specific old token directly, not just whatever survived in state. Attention keeps the useful idea of sequence-conditioned output, but changes the memory interface. Instead of asking one hidden state to carry everything, the decoder can look back at all encoder states. The Transformer then takes the next step: it uses self-attention so tokens can read other tokens directly. Bridge to Transformers: GRU/LSTM make recurrent memory more controllable. Attention changes the shape of memory itself from “carry a state forward” to “look up the relevant token states when needed.” From carrying memory to looking up memory Gates improve what survives in state; attention changes the interface so old states remain directly addressable. Recurrent memory h1 h2 hT decoder gets summary Attention lookup h1 h2 h3 h4 decoder query high weight can select the specific useful state Attention does not replace the idea of sequence-conditioned output; it replaces the memory interface from “carry everything forward” to “look up what is needed.” 15) Quick mental model recap RNN = MLP cell + memory. The “memory” is the hidden state \(h_t\). One cell reused at every time step. Same weights, new data + updated state. GRU = RNN + keep/reset gates. It has one hidden state but learns how much old state to preserve. LSTM = RNN + protected cell state. It separates long-term cell memory \(c_t\) from exposed hidden state \(h_t\). Outputs at every step are optional. Many tasks use only the last output; translation uses stepwise decoder outputs. Cost savings come from sharing. Parameter count doesn’t blow up with \(T\). Padding is not meaning. Padding makes rectangular tensors; masks/lengths stop it from affecting learning. Encoder-decoder RNNs are historical but important. They explain the vocabulary of hidden state, teacher forcing, autoregressive decoding, and attention. Next step: the Transformer chapter keeps tokens, embeddings, decoder outputs, and autoregressive generation. It first fixes the RNN encoder-decoder bottleneck with cross-attention, then generalizes the idea into self-attention and GPT-style causal generation.

headings: 1) Start from the RNN problem: one vector is too small a bridge
2) Cross-attention: the decoder asks the source sentence a question
3) Self-attention: make every token both reader and memory
4) Causal self-attention: the GPT training and generation mental model
5) The intuition: a soft, content-based dictionary lookup
6) Scaled dot-product attention
7) Multi-head attention

text: Where this fits Chapter 10 gave you encoder-decoder RNNs: the encoder reads a sequence, the decoder generates a sequence, and hidden state carries information forward. This chapter keeps that mental model but removes the fragile bottleneck. First the decoder learns to look back at encoder states using cross-attention. Then tokens learn to look at other tokens in the same sequence using self-attention. Finally, causal self-attention gives us GPT-style next-token generation. Read this chapter as one continuous design path. We are not introducing attention as a separate trick. We are answering the question left open by GRU/LSTM: if a decoder needs a specific old token, why force that information to survive only through recurrent memory? Cross-attention lets a decoder look up source states directly. Self-attention then applies the same lookup idea inside a single sequence. Causal self-attention finally makes that lookup safe for next-token generation. 1) Start from the RNN problem: one vector is too small a bridge In the RNN translation chapter, the encoder read my name is dinesh and passed a final hidden state to the decoder. That works as a first mental model, but it has a bottleneck: the decoder must recover every useful source detail from one vector. For a short sentence this is manageable. For a long paragraph, one compressed state is a weak memory interface. LSTMs reduce the damage because their cell state can preserve information better than a vanilla RNN or a GRU. But even an LSTM encoder-decoder still asks the decoder to recover source details through recurrent state. The next idea is to keep every encoder state available and let the decoder choose which ones matter at each output step. RNN seq2seq bottleneck Encoder reads source tokens one by one. Final hidden state summarizes the whole source. Decoder depends heavily on that single summary. Long-range details can fade through time. Attention idea Keep the encoder state at every source position. At each decoder step, ask: “which source tokens matter now?” Take a weighted average of the relevant source states. The decoder gets a fresh context vector at every output step. From RNN bottleneck to attention Attention does not force the decoder to depend on one final encoder vector. RNN encoder-decoder my name ... one final hidden vector decoder Attention bridge h1 h2 h3 h4 decoder decoder query looks back at all encoder states The key step from RNNs to attention is simple: keep all encoder states, then let the decoder choose which ones to use. 2) Cross-attention: the decoder asks the source sentence a question Cross-attention is the easiest form to understand after RNN translation. The decoder is currently trying to produce a target token. It builds a query: “what source information do I need right now?” The encoder states provide keys: “what information can I match against?” and values: “what information should I return if matched?” \[ Q = H_{\text{decoder}} W_Q,\quad K = H_{\text{encoder}} W_K,\quad V = H_{\text{encoder}} W_V \] \[ \text{CrossAttention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V \] ObjectComes fromMeaning in translation Query \(Q\) Decoder hidden state The output side asking what source context it needs for this target step. Keys \(K\) Encoder states Search handles for each source token/state. Values \(V\) Encoder states The information blended into the decoder context vector. For the example my name is dinesh → mon nom est dinesh, when the decoder is about to produce dinesh, its query should strongly match the encoder state for the source name token. The attention weights are learned, soft alignments; they are not hand-coded word links. What cross-attention fixes The decoder no longer depends only on the final encoder hidden state. Each output step gets a fresh context vector computed from all source positions. This is the direct answer to the seq2seq bottleneck. Cross-attention still assumes two sides: a source memory and a decoder query. That is perfect for translation, but it raises the next question: if attention is just content-based lookup, do we need a recurrent encoder at all? Could each token in a sentence look directly at the other tokens and build its representation in parallel? 3) Self-attention: make every token both reader and memory Cross-attention has two sides: decoder queries, encoder keys/values. Self-attention removes that separation. The same sequence supplies queries, keys, and values: \[ Q = XW_Q,\quad K = XW_K,\quad V = XW_V \] Now each token can ask every token in the same sequence for context. In an encoder, this is usually bidirectional: every token can look left and right. In a decoder-only language model, this must be causal: each position can look only at itself and earlier positions. This is the move from “decoder looks at encoder memory” to “tokens are the memory.” Self-attention removes the recurrent scan inside the encoder because all token-to-token relationships can be scored at once. That is why Transformers train so much more efficiently than RNNs on modern hardware. The price is that attention by itself has no sense of order and, for generation, no built-in protection against peeking at future tokens. Those two pressures lead to positional encoding and causal masking. Attention patterns: cross, self, causal self The same Q/K/V operation changes behavior depending on where Q, K, V come from and which positions are masked. Cross-attention decoder queries source memory decoder query: “what do I need?” src 1 src 2 src 3 Self-attention tokens read the same sequence tok 1 tok 2 tok 3 no mask: each token may use all tokens Causal self-attention future positions are hidden lower triangle = visible context Cross-attention reads a separate memory. Self-attention reads the same sequence. Causal self-attention blocks the future. 4) Causal self-attention: the GPT training and generation mental model If self-attention lets every token look at every other token, a language generator needs one more rule: the future must be invisible. GPT is a decoder-only Transformer: a stack of masked self-attention blocks plus feed-forward networks. It is trained to predict the next token from the previous tokens. The important correction is that position \(t\) can attend to positions \(\le t\), and its hidden state is used to predict token \(t+1\). It does not peek at future target tokens. Prefix available at a positionTraining target myname my nameis my name isDinesh my name is Dinesh<EOS> or next punctuation/token \[ p(x_{t+1}\mid x_1,\dots,x_t) = \text{softmax}(W_{\text{vocab}} h_t) \] During training, the full sequence is processed in parallel with a causal mask. During inference, generation is autoregressive: predict one token, append it, then predict the next token from the extended prefix. PhaseWhat the model receivesWhat it predictsWhy it matters Training A full token sequence, processed in parallel under a causal mask. The next token for every visible prefix position. Efficient learning: one forward pass creates many next-token training examples. Inference step 1 [my, name, is] A distribution where Dinesh may be the selected token. The model emits one token, not a whole final sentence in one atomic action. Inference step 2 [my, name, is, Dinesh] The next distribution, perhaps selecting .. The generated token becomes part of the next input prefix. Stopping [my, name, is, Dinesh, .] <EOS>, another token, or a stop caused by length limits. Generation repeats until a stop condition is met. KV caching The new token plus cached keys/values from earlier positions. The next-token distribution without recomputing all old attention states. Same conceptual loop, much lower decode cost in real systems. GPT generation loop Training predicts every next token under a mask. Inference appends one sampled token at a time. input tokens my name is decoder-only Transformer masked self-attention logits at last position next-token distribution Dinesh, ., ... sample / choose token, append to prefix, repeat until stop token or length limit The output token becomes part of the next input prefix. KV caching makes this efficient by reusing previous keys and values. # Conceptual GPT inference loop. # Real systems batch requests, keep per-layer KV caches, and use sampling controls. tokens = tokenize("my name is") while len(tokens) < max_len: logits = gpt(tokens) # simple mental model: full prefix next_logits = logits[-1] # distribution for the next token next_token = sample(next_logits, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95) tokens.append(next_token) # feed output back as input if next_token == EOS_ID: break Training vs inference Training can process all positions at once because the causal mask prevents future leakage. Inference must generate one new token at a time because the next input token does not exist until the model has produced it. Now the architectural flow is complete enough to name the math. Cross-attention, self-attention, and causal self-attention are not three unrelated mechanisms. They are the same query-key-value operation with different sources for \(Q,K,V\) and different masks. The next section writes that common operation once. 5) The intuition: a soft, content-based dictionary lookup Think of attention as a dictionary lookup that is differentiable. For each token you want to update, you compute a query vector q: "what kind of context do I need?" For every token in the sequence (including itself) you have a key k ("what kind of context do I provide?") and a value v ("what would I contribute if attended to?"). You score each (q, k) pair, turn the scores into a probability distribution with softmax, and return the weighted average of values. That's it. The whole Transformer is this operation, stacked, with a small feed‑forward network in between, and residual connections + LayerNorm. 6) Scaled dot-product attention Stack the queries, keys and values into matrices $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d_k}$, $K \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d_k}$, $V \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d_v}$ where $n$ is the sequence length. Then: $\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\dfrac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V$ Scaled dot-product attention as a soft lookup Queries ask questions, keys are compared against those questions, values are blended by the resulting weights. Q queries K scores QK^T scale + mask divide by sqrt(d_k) softmax weights weighted values causal masks set future scores to -infinity before softmax Scaled dot-product attention is a soft lookup: compare queries to keys, mask if needed, normalize into weights, then blend values. The $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling keeps the dot products from growing too large with dimension, which would push softmax into a near‑one‑hot regime and kill the gradients. Implemented in PyTorch: import torch, torch.nn.functional as F def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=None): d_k = Q.size(-1) scores = (Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)) / d_k**0.5 # (..., n, n) if mask is not None: scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float("-inf")) weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) # (..., n, n) return weights @ V # (..., n, d_v) Causal (decoder) masking For language modeling, position $i$ may only attend to positions $\le i$. The mask is the lower triangular matrix of ones; everything above the diagonal is set to $-\infty$ before softmax. n = Q.size(-2) causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(n, n, device=Q.device)) out = scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=causal) One attention operation gives one way to judge relevance. That is already more flexible than recurrent state, but language has many relationships at once: subject-verb agreement, reference resolution, local syntax, topic, and formatting. This leads directly to multi-head attention. 7) Multi-head attention One attention head learns one notion of relevance. Real language has many in parallel — syntactic agreement, coreference, topic, etc. Multi‑head attention runs $h$ attention operations in parallel on linear projections of $Q, K, V$ into smaller subspaces, then concatenates and projects back: $\mathrm{MHA}(X) = \big[\mathrm{head}_1; \dots; \mathrm{head}_h\big] W^{O}, \quad \mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Attention}(XW_i^{Q}, XW_i^{K}, XW_i^{V})$ Multi-head attention: several relevance functions in parallel Each head sees a projected subspace, attends with its own pattern, and the model learns how to recombine them. token states X head 1: syntax head 2: reference head 3: topic concat heads project W^O The labels are mental models: heads are not hand-assigned, but specialization often emerges. Multi-head attention gives the model several parallel relevance functions before merging them back into one token representation. import torch, torch.nn as nn class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module): def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads): super().__init__() assert d_model % n_heads == 0 self.h, self.d_k = n_heads, d_model // n_heads self.W_q = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False) self.W_k = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False) self.W_v = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False) self.W_o = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False) def forward(self, x, causal=True): B, N, _ = x.shape def split(t): return t.view(B, N, self.h, self.d_k).transpose(1, 2) Q, K, V = split(self.W_q(x)), split(self.W_k(x)), split(self.W_v(x)) out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, is_causal=causal) out = out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, N, self.h * self.d_k) return self.W_o(out) Use the built‑in Since PyTorch 2.0, F.scaled_dot_product_attention dispatches to fused kernels (FlashAttention‑2, memory‑efficient attention) where available. Hand‑rolling the einsum version is good for understanding, not for production. Masking nuance The compact class above demonstrates decoder-only causal attention. Real training code also handles padding masks, packed sequences, and sometimes non-causal attention; pass those masks explicitly instead of assuming is_causal=True everywhere. Multi-head attention can learn several kinds of relationships, but the operation still treats the input as a set unless we give it position. If the tokens my name is are shuffled, self-attention alone has no built-in reason to know the order changed. That is the next missing piece. 8) Position information: sinusoidal vs RoPE Self‑attention is permutation‑equivariant — shuffle the input tokens and you get the same shuffled output. Language is not permutation‑invariant, so we add positional information. Sinusoidal (Vaswani et al., original) Add a fixed sinusoidal vector to each token embedding before the first layer: $\mathrm{PE}(p, 2i) = \sin\!\bigl(p / 10000^{2i/d}\bigr),\quad \mathrm{PE}(p, 2i+1) = \cos\!\bigl(p / 10000^{2i/d}\bigr)$ Pros: simple. Cons: weak length extrapolation; baked into embeddings. Rotary Position Embedding — RoPE (used by LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma) RoPE rotates pairs of dimensions of $Q$ and $K$ by an angle proportional to the position. Because it acts on $Q$ and $K$ multiplicatively rather than additively on the embedding, the dot product $Q_m^{\top} K_n$ becomes a function of the relative position $m - n$: $\langle\mathrm{RoPE}(q, m),\ \mathrm{RoPE}(k, n)\rangle = f(q, k, m - n)$ This often improves long‑context behavior and is why many modern open‑weights LLMs use it. Variants like YaRN and NTK‑aware scaling stretch RoPE's effective range to extend a 4k‑trained model to 32k+ tokens at inference. Once tokens can read each other and the model knows where those tokens sit, the rest of the Transformer block is engineering around stable deep learning: residual connections preserve signal, LayerNorm controls scale, and the feed-forward network transforms each token representation after attention has mixed context into it. 9) The full Transformer block One block (decoder‑only flavor) is: class Block(nn.Module): def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, d_ff): super().__init__() self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model) self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, n_heads) self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model) self.ff = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model), ) def forward(self, x): x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x)) # pre‑norm residual x = x + self.ff(self.ln2(x)) return x Stack $L$ blocks, prepend a token‑embedding + positional encoding, append a final LayerNorm and an unembedding (often tied to the input embedding), and you have a GPT‑style language model. One modern decoder block Pre-norm stabilizes deep stacks; residual paths preserve the token stream while attention and MLP update it. input x LayerNorm masked self-attention + LayerNorm feed-forward MLP + output Each block keeps token shape n x d_model, so many blocks can be stacked. A modern decoder block is pre-norm plus residual attention, followed by pre-norm plus residual feed-forward transformation. The same block can be arranged into three families depending on what information is allowed to flow. If the whole input is known, use bidirectional encoder attention. If the model must generate left-to-right, use causal decoder attention. If the task has a separate source and target sequence, combine a bidirectional encoder, a causal decoder, and cross-attention. 10) Encoder, decoder, encoder-decoder VariantAttention patternExamplesUsed for Encoder‑onlyBidirectional (no mask) BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, modern embedding models Classification, embeddings, retrieval Decoder‑onlyCausal mask GPT‑x, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, Claude, DeepSeek Generation, chat, code, agents Encoder‑decoderBidirectional encoder + causal decoder + cross‑attention T5, FLAN‑T5, BART, original NMT Transformer Translation, summarization, seq‑to‑seq Transformer families are attention-permission patterns The core block stays recognizable; masking and cross-attention determine what information can flow. Encoder-only bidirectional understanding Decoder-only left-to-right generation Encoder-decoder encoder decoder cross-attention The main Transformer families differ by masking and where information is allowed to flow, not by a completely different core operation. 11) Inference: KV cache At training time you process the whole sequence in parallel. At generation time you produce one token at a time. Naively you would recompute all of $K$ and $V$ for every prefix — quadratic per token. Instead you cache the per‑layer $K$ and $V$ tensors: For token $t$, compute only the new $q_t, k_t, v_t$. Append $k_t, v_t$ to the cache. Attention is now $q_t$ against the cached $K, V$ — linear in $t$. KV cache: keep old keys and values instead of recomputing them Prefill builds the cache for the prompt; each decode step appends only the new token's key and value. prompt prefill all prompt tokens per-layer cache K,V K,V K,V decode step new q,k,v next token append The next step queries all cached K,V, but only computes projections for the new token. KV caching preserves the same autoregressive loop while avoiding recomputation of old keys and values at every decode step. During decode, the KV cache is a major reason LLM inference often becomes memory-bandwidth-bound: every new token must read the cached keys and values. Prefill over a long prompt can still be compute-heavy. The cache is also why context length costs RAM (each extra token adds roughly 2 · n_layers · n_kv_heads · d_head · dtype_bytes per request; with MQA/GQA, n_kv_heads can be smaller than the number of query heads). # Cached decode sketch. # Prefill computes K/V for the prompt once. Each later step only computes # the new token's q/k/v and attends q_new against cached K/V. tokens = tokenize("my name is") logits, cache = gpt_prefill(tokens) # cache stores per-layer K/V for the prompt next_token = sample(logits[-1]) while next_token != EOS_ID: tokens.append(next_token) logits, cache = gpt_decode_step([next_token], cache=cache) next_token = sample(logits[-1]) KV caching fixes wasted recomputation during generation, but it does not make attention free. Long context still means more cached keys and values to read, and full attention over long prompts still has heavy memory traffic. That pressure is why modern LLM systems use optimized attention kernels and smaller key/value layouts. 12) Efficiency: FlashAttention, MQA, GQA, sliding window FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022; v2 2023; v3 2024) computes the same softmax attention but tiles the work to keep $QK^{\top}$ in on‑chip SRAM and never materializes the full $n \times n$ matrix in HBM. Result: ~2–4× speedup and much less memory. Multi‑Query Attention (MQA) shares one $K$/$V$ projection across all heads — shrinks the KV cache by $h\times$. Used in PaLM. Grouped‑Query Attention (GQA) is the compromise: one $K$/$V$ per group of $g$ query heads. Used in LLaMA‑2/3, Mistral, Qwen2, Gemma 2 — a common modern choice for decoder-only LLMs. Sliding‑window attention (Mistral, Gemma) restricts each token to attend only to the last $W$ tokens, lowering the attention cost from $O(n^2)$ to $O(nW)$. Mixture of Experts (MoE) (Mixtral, DeepSeek‑V3) replaces the feed‑forward block with a router that picks $k$ of $E$ experts per token — more parameters, similar FLOPs. 13) Pulling it all together Embed tokens; add positional info (sinusoidal, learned, or RoPE). Stack $L$ Transformer blocks (pre‑norm + residual + GQA + SwiGLU/GELU FFN). Final LayerNorm + tied unembedding → logits over the vocabulary. For generation: KV cache + sampling (greedy / temperature / top‑p / top‑k). What to read next Chapter 12 — LLM fine‑tuning — picks up exactly here, taking a pretrained decoder‑only Transformer and adapting it with PEFT (LoRA / QLoRA), then Chapter 13 covers preference alignment beyond DPO.
